paragraphs.text:
A homily of our father among the saints, Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, on the Annunciation of the most holy Theotokos. Bless, Father.

1. Good tidings, brethren, good tidings, and again I say, good tidings! I say it three times, but not because these tidings are higher than all other good tidings, more divine and more elegant, surpassing them beyond all comparison. Nor is it because they make me, their messenger, beautiful, and make my feet beautiful. (For they are better than all good things, kinder than all kind things, more wondrous than all wonders, more compassionate than all compassionate things, and more fearful and awesome than all fearful and awesome things.) It is because, spoken three times, they also point to the supreme and divine numbering of the blessed and sovereign Trinity. For whatever is threefold in sacred and divine doctrines, in God-wise preaching and in venerable announcements, is meant as honour to the blessed Trinity: to the Father, I mean, and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. This Trinity is a Trinity and is beheld as a Unity; it is a Unity and is found to be a Trinity. It is a Trinity in its three hypostases, and a Unity in its one and only Godhead, that is, in its essence and nature. 2. For the superessential Trinity, the source of life, is proclaimed to have one essence, since it is gathered up into one sole Godhead. Therefore its consubstantiality, its kinship and oneness of kind, remains unbroken, firm and undispersed, and indeed it is not multiplied. The holy Trinity rules and governs all things that exist, and is sovereign over all created things as a king and as God. It is numbered in its own hypostases, for it is, and is believed to be, a Trinity. But in essence and nature, and likewise in Godhead, it is beyond all numbering. For it is not counted as three according to essence, since its threefold numbering belongs to its personal hypostases. For this reason it is shown to be divided in the hypostases, yet remains undivided in essence; it is proclaimed distinct in the persons, for each of them appears in its own individuality, and yet is

undivided in nature. Hence it possesses a division and a union that are truly paradoxical and astounding. Because of the one, which is the nature, it is not confounded [?] and driven into one sole hypostasis. Nor, because of the three, which are the enhypostatic persons, is it cut apart into alien kinds and utterly severed. Rather it is unbroken and undivided, and [beyond?] all division and conjunction [?]

3. This is what is wondrous and most awesome about it. It is one and the same in nature, one God and one Godhead, and yet it is found to be three in persons. It does not cut the nature or the Godhead apart, but extends its own hypostases and persons into a numbering without confusion. For just as the Father is God, so the Son is God, and so the Holy Spirit is God. Insofar as each is called God, this presents the one essence of the three persons. But insofar as they are Father and Son and all-holy Spirit, they truly are three and are believed to be three. (For these are precisely the names of the three persons, the three true hypostases, by which this blessed Trinity is distinguished within itself without division of nature.) So they are loudly proclaimed and glorified by all the faithful and by the heavenly and invisible powers: hymned in three sanctifications, yet coming together into one natural lordship. 'Holy, holy, holy, Lord Sabaoth!' cry the six-winged Seraphim, who know the words of theology better than we do, since they draw nearer to God than we, share in his pure radiance, and are illumined by his undimmed rays. By them the thrice-holy Trinity is hallowed three times and honoured with three sanctifications and doxologies, and is gathered without confusion into one lordship, the phrase 'Lord Sabaoth.' For the 'Holy, holy, holy,' sung three times by the Seraphim themselves, shows the numbering of the three persons of the blessed Trinity that is being hymned. In the same way, 'Lord Sabaoth,' said only once, shows their one and only lordship. In that lordship the three are also one God without confusion and are glorified, and the one Godhead in

Trinity is honoured. Why did the Seraph not fall silent after saying 'Holy' once, or stop after crying it twice, but take it up three times? Because the Trinity does not have one sole hypostasis (away with the abomination of the Sabellian impiety!), nor does it have only two persons (away with the godless loathsomeness of the Macedonians!). Rather it cries and shouts 'Holy' three times, as I said, offering it with lips that never cease and announcing it with mouths that are never silent. For the hypostases of the blessed Trinity, sovereign above all, are defined as three, and its persons, akin and of one kind, are three. In equal honour they possess one Godhead, in equal power one lordship, and one unbreakable rule and kingdom over all things.

4. So we too, the least, who are its worshippers and servants, wishing to proclaim good tidings to you without restraint, speak good tidings three times. We say 'Good tidings, good tidings,' and cry 'Good tidings' again, and so bring in the honour of the blessed Trinity. We do this even though our discourse is not about the Trinity but about the economy. It concerns the One of the same all-venerable Trinity and announces to us only the coming of the Word. For it is good, and most dear to all the faithful, to announce both of these in both settings while keeping the declaration of each unconfused. That is, words about the Trinity may be proclaimed in hymns of the economy, and words of the economy may be offered in proclamations about the Trinity, that is, in theology. (For one of the Trinity, the Word, is known to have undergone the human economy and to have saved the whole lump of our humanity.) Yet this must be done with distinct ideas proper to each, and indeed with distinct terms. Otherwise God the Word's condescension to us lowly ones might lead to a mixing and confusion between proclamations about theology and the Trinity on the one hand, and the different terms of the economy on the other.

5. So let them be driven from this sacred festival of ours: the Sabelliuses, Marcelluses, Ariuses, Eunomiuses, Eudoxiuses, Asteriuses, and all who are like them and share their godless religion. They mix the words of theology

with the doctrines of the economy. They are themselves mixed up and confused, and cannot find the truth. Let the Peters and the Severuses go too, and the whole many-headed [?] and many-tongued heresy of the Acephali. Out of their most impious and foul hostility toward us, the faithful and godly-minded, they wove the cross into the Thrice-Holy hymn, and so confused the words of the Trinity, which admits no confusion. For they too say 'Holy, holy, holy' three times, and then impiously attach the cross to the three sanctifications. If the Trisagion is a hymn proper to the Trinity, how can those who are truly ignorant of divine wisdom ignorantly fit a cross to it? For the cross is not proclaimed of the Trinity. It belongs to the incarnate Son, the One of the Trinity, and proclaims his loving incarnation; his are the cross and the crucifixion, proclaiming his saving [?]

6. For these wretches do not mention the incarnation of the Word. They do not name the union of heterogeneous essences, of Godhead, I mean, and manhood. They do not proclaim his birth from the divine Virgin, who is properly Theotokos. All of this ought to come before the cross, yet they lawlessly bring in the cross, wishing to mix the foul doctrine of a suffering Godhead into the sacred doctrines. For they have caught the whole confusion of the foul and deranged Eutyches and drunk the whole of his muddled cup, and so they confound everything. They mingle the economic with the theological and crush the theological into the economic, joining both natures into

(Codex: πεποκότες.)

one. They cast the two forms, of Godhead and of manhood, out of their own doctrines and want Christ to have one form, one essence and one nature. As a result the words of theology do not remain pure and intact, and the doctrines of the economy are not free from their Eutychian, or rather ill-starred, change and confusion. But let them plunge headlong into the depth of impiety and be swept away [?], and let the [waves?] of impiety engulf them.

7. But we are nurslings of true piety and opponents of their headless babble. Let us hold faithfully to the doctrines of our fathers and become sleepless guardians of the apostolic traditions. We understand the words that concern the Trinity and know the words of the economy, so let us not confuse these with those or mingle those with these. Let us fit to each what is proper to it, and set apart for each its own place, manner and time. In this way we shall be beyond the reach of stumbling blocks, have no share in the error of heretics, and be free of the madness of the heterodox. We shall stand firm on the inspired faith, whirled about by none of the evil spirits and not carried off into evil thoughts. Our opponents have pitiably fallen into such thoughts. They rejected standing firm and abandoned the safe keeping of the piety of our fathers, and so they have perished and are tossed about by the waves of heretical impiety.

8. We, then, have happily escaped the abyss of their impiety and planted our feet securely on the unshaken rock of the faith. Let us go up onto a high mountain and stand on the heights of doctrine, as the commands of the gospel and the prophets direct. Let us lift up our voice as far as our strength allows, or rather as far as God grants, and cry 'Good tidings, good tidings,' and again say 'Good tidings.' In this way we honour the majesty of the Trinity and sing of the condescension toward us of God the Word, One of the Trinity. For these, brethren, are our good tidings, which we have come forth to announce to you, most faithful ones, and which we wish to proclaim.

We urge you, beloved, to cleanse yourselves fittingly and to receive these good tidings of ours. For these sacred good tidings of ours do not loathe or turn away from someone who has cleansed himself as he ought. Instead they make a saving dwelling with him. They fill him with light and illumination and make him a divine sanctuary of God, so that though he is a man by nature, he is rich in the manifestation of God.

(Codex: ἀφορίζομεν. Codex: ποιῆται.)

All of you, gather! All of you, assemble! All make haste, all run together, all hurry along, all race ahead of one another! Put on the wings of a dove so that you may fly and come happily to rest upon Christ. Or take the feet of a swift-running gazelle, so that you may hear heavenly good tidings, may trust an angel who speaks good tidings, and may listen with God-loving ears as he announces God's coming to men. Then we too, seeing you gather so swiftly and assemble so eagerly to hear our lofty good tidings, may rejoice and exult together and cry: 'Good tidings, good tidings, good tidings!' By proclaiming the good tidings three times we confirm that they can be trusted.

9. For where truth goes forth, falsehood never rules, and unbelief will find no room for its most wicked entry. Nothing is more harmful to divine words than unbelief. This is how the Jews have fallen, how the Samaritans have gone astray, and why the Greeks live in darkness. This is how the heretics have been cast down. They did not believe God's good tidings and would not yield to them, but remained opposed and hostile. They have become dead in soul and body, have no share in eternal life, and have proved to have no part in the true light. For falsehood never lays hold of the truth as long as it is falsehood and is known as such. Darkness is never illumined as long as it is darkness, sunk in gloom and wholly without the shining of light. That is why our luminous good tidings are loudly proclaimed to you who receive the light. They do not wish to be deposited in the ears of unbelievers, and they do not like to dwell in dark hearts.

10. So you, as children of light and offspring nourished by light, hear our luminous and enlightening good tidings. For you have been enlightened by their power. Their God-wise mystery has shone upon your luminous souls, and you have received it in pure hearts. You have become children of God, because you received the Son of God faithfully and gladly and acknowledged him alone as your Saviour. 'For as many as received him,' it says, 'to them he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.' So you, as God's most radiant children, hear God's most radiant good tidings. Through them you have become children of God by grace and gained a heavenly nobility, having cast off your earthy lowness of birth. You have taken on a divine birth and laid aside your merely human origin. So hear the sacred good tidings, you who have been counted worthy of the divine initiation into their most perfect faith.

What, then, are our good tidings? What do they accomplish? Listen faithfully as we tell you. For we shall speak in a most fitting way, as he himself grants us, he who now brings you good tidings through us.

11. In the beginning God created out of nothing all things that come after him and were brought into being by him: things visible and invisible, perceived by the senses and grasped by the mind, heavenly and earthly. Then he creates man too after his own image, forming him of a rational soul and a body. He made him an image and likeness of his own goodness, granted him a life of free will, and made him the inhabitant of a divine paradise. Having fashioned him good, he laid down for him a divine and saving commandment, so that the greatness of the image would not make him proud, and his likeness to God would not lead him foolishly to imagine that he had God's nature. He had received so many gifts from God who fashioned him. (For God had appointed him king of the things on earth, while plainly he himself was ruled and governed by God his Creator, like all created things.) Yet he could not bear the greatness of these gifts. He strives to seize identity with God, and man, a creature, desired to be God. Through the serpent's deceit he wickedly set his fancy on the divine, lofty and supreme things, and so he is brought down to death and corruption. He who wished to seize the dignity of the divine nature falls a most terrible fall. And this was entirely just: that he who wished to exalt himself beyond his worth should be humbled to the utmost. For 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled,' since he wickedly tries to seize what God has not given him. 'For no one takes the honour upon himself,' as the great Apostle said, 'but he who is called by God,' who gives it.

12. So this man was held fast by death and wasted away in corruption. He who had come forth from the earth and had dared to seize God's honour was dragged down again into the earth. Today he is born by a fleshly birth, and tomorrow he is put to death by a fleshly death. Today he is seen among the living, and tomorrow he is numbered among the dead. This was the penalty borne by man, who had wished to wrong God. He suffered it by his own will and choice, because he misused his free will. With that free will he had been honoured by his Creator, because of his most comely likeness to him and the splendour of the image. 'For God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living.'

[?]: and in the Cres. codex, fol. 1, line 12: 'End of his theology and of the [?]' … 'did not make death, nor does he take pleasure in destruction.'

How pitiable and wretched he truly was, he who had once been most blessed! Once he appeared as the owner of paradise and had been placed there as its first inhabitant. Once his life was free of toil and labour. He lived naked and without a tunic and did not fear the changes of the weather. He knew nothing of freezing frost or the blaze of scorching heat. He went about naked and was not ashamed. He suffered no assaults of the passions and felt no pain of disease. He was free from slavery to other men and liberated from barbarian tyranny. He heard no harassment from tax-collectors and saw no visits from creditors. He did not dread being mauled by wild beasts. He enjoyed the height of prosperity. He was fed by the fruits of paradise and enjoyed all good things in abundance. He received God's radiance. Though himself a creature, he reigned over the creatures of the earth. He bore the title of God's image and was wondrously brightened by his likeness to God. By transgressing God's saving commandment he sinned against God himself, and so he is robbed of all these things. He is left naked and stripped of his former splendour. He is immediately banished from paradise and returns again to the earth, having become corruptible through sin. Through the greatness of his folly he becomes like the beasts, having put off the former honour with which God his Creator had adorned him. And so he is enslaved to corruption, death and the passions, because he had thought to gain Godhead by usurpation.

13. But he who had created him and brought him forth when he did not yet exist saw him in this state and pitied him. In his pity he had mercy, and in his mercy he is moved with compassion. Moved with compassion as the lover of mankind (for good and loving toward mankind is what he is), he rises up in divine compassion to save man and call him back. He fulfils an ancient and loving counsel, which in his love he had resolved from the beginning. For as the Fashioner he could not bear to watch his creature being corrupted and perishing into earth and corruption.

14. And what is the counsel that God resolved for the salvation and redemption of men? Let the wondrous Isaiah come forward and cry it aloud, he who foretold the seedless conception of God and described his virgin birth in advance. At the fulfilment of the divine will he sang a song of thanksgiving to God and cried: 'O Lord my God, I will glorify you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things [?]'

'… foundations. The city of the ungodly shall never be built. Therefore the poor people will bless you, and the cities of wronged men will bless you. For you have become a help to every lowly city, and a shelter to those disheartened by want. You will deliver them from wicked men.' These, brethren, are our divine good tidings. We announce them to you today, not as things that are going to happen later, but as things already divinely accomplished. They have saved man from condemnation, led him back to his former brightness and blessedness, and made him a friend of God as before.

15. How does God work out our salvation? How is our recall accomplished? Listen with understanding and with all wisdom, for these things are wise, more than wise, and beyond all human wisdom. Take up a divine understanding, one worthy of a divine announcement. He who fashioned man in the beginning and made him after his own image decides to save man and redeem his own image in only one way: by becoming man by nature and making his own image his own garment. From this the unmixable is mixed, and the unblended is blended without being blended. From this the uncompounded is compounded and the unbound is bound tight. From this divine things become human, so that human things may become more divine. From this the Word of God, remaining God and the Word of God, takes on bodily thickness. From this the Uncreated, begotten of the uncreated God, is created while remaining uncreated. From this the Most High is proclaimed lowly, the invisible is seen as visible, and the intangible accepts touch. The bodiless comes forth embodied, the fleshless is recorded as flesh, and the impassible is proclaimed passible. He whose nature is immortal is declared mortal by nature, so that he might lead passible and mortal humanity to an immortality radiant and

…freedom from passion, and might first reconcile to God and the Father the nature that was hostile to God and at war with him. 16. And how is this fulfilled and done, and how does it come about as a deed that cannot fail [?]? For it is fearful and astonishing, and quite beyond belief to the ears of people who think about the most divine things with human reasoning. But where God is proclaimed, the poverty of human reasoning falls idle. For all things are very easy for God, possible and within reach, whatever he may wish to do. This is the clearest and most distinctive mark of the divine and supreme power, and no created nature has any share in it at all. That is why the things that are beyond human nature and surpass every created power are so wonderful and astonishing. And how does God accomplish this and bring it to its glorious end? The divine Luke teaches us clearly, he who wrote our Gospel, the holiest of all holy things. He does so that no one may disbelieve the greatness of the matter, and that no one may falsely charge God with weakness, when he is himself weak and powerless and unfit for any divine work. As you have just heard him proclaim: “In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a city of Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.” You hear that God sent him, and you still want to disbelieve it? Do not disbelieve God’s decree. Rather, believe with all reverence that God is fully able to accomplish whatever he wishes to do. And by whom else would an angel be sent, if not by God alone, who made him, brought him into being from nothing, and fashioned the whole angelic nature? If, then, God is known to be the sender, and an angel is proclaimed as the one sent, how can what is said not be true? Let everyone marvel at these things, but let no one disbelieve the message, knowing that God’s strength is all-mighty and truly omnipotent. 17. And what does the most blessed angel, sent to the…

…he knew that the world would be lit up with the knowledge of God; he knew that the fog of error would be cleared away; he knew that the sting of death would be blunted; he knew that the power of corruption would itself be destroyed; he knew that the victory of Hades would be pulled down; he knew that perishing man would be saved, man who had long been enslaved to these things, ever since he was driven out of the paradise of delight and banished from the blessed life he had led there. That is why he makes joy the opening of his good news; that is why he speaks joy before all his other words; that is why joy led the way for these good tidings, since they would become joy for all who believe. For the divine messages of joy had to begin with words and sayings that bring joy. That is why the angel cries out joy before anything else: he knew the outcome of his good news, and that his message, once fulfilled, would prove to be joy for the whole world. 18. For what joy and what fervor does the message given to the blessed Virgin, the mother of joy, not surpass? Hail, you who give birth to heavenly joy! Hail, you who bring supreme joy to birth! Hail, mother city of saving joy! Hail, cause of undying joy! Hail, mystical dwelling of unspeakable joy! Hail, admirable field of ineffable joy! Hail, all-blessed spring of unfailing joy! Hail, God-bearing treasure of eternal joy! Hail, flourishing plant of life-giving joy! Hail, unwedded Mother of God! Hail, Virgin left inviolate after childbirth! Hail, most wondrous sight of all wonders! Who will be able to describe your splendor? Who would dare to speak of your wonder? Who will be bold enough to proclaim your greatness? You have adorned the nature of humankind; you have surpassed the ranks of the angels; you have outshone the radiance of the archangels; you have shown the high seats of the Thrones to be second to you; you have made the height of the Dominions seem small; you have gone ahead of the leadership of the Principalities; you have unnerved the strength of the Authorities; you have come forth as a power mightier than the Powers; with earthly eyes you have surpassed the many-eyed Cherubim; with the God-moved wings of the soul you have gone beyond the six-winged Seraphim. You have excelled all creation, since you shine with a purity greater than all creation, and have received the Creator of all creation, carrying him in your womb and giving birth to him, and you alone of all creation have become the Mother of God.

19. That is why I address you: “Hail, full of grace,” since you have been graced more than all creation. And I recognize and know the cause of such joy and grace in you, and so I go on to cry aloud: “The Lord is with you.” As Creator, he is Lord of all creation; but he is with you as one carried in your womb and borne in a gestation beyond words. “The Lord is with you”: he was begotten eternally from the Father and is always beheld with the Father, but now he is with you in the conception, and from you he has taken an awe-inspiring incarnation. “The Lord is with you”: he has a first, eternal birth, and from you he receives a second birth. “The Lord is with you”: together with the Father he is Lord of all creation, yet from you he puts on the form of a servant and frees humankind from slavery. For the Lord becomes a servant for this reason, that by grace he may make the servant a lord. “The Lord is with you”: he who was formerly outside all creation is now seen with you as one of created nature, and through you he has become numbered among created things. For in you the Uncreated is created, and from you the Creator comes forth as a creature. I see the Uncreated become a creature in you, and I behold the Fleshless made flesh. 20. Up above, O Virgin, when he sent me to you, he was without flesh and without body; but here I see him become flesh and body. Up above he was uncreated, raised far above all creation; but here I find him a creature and a thing made, having become this in you, the Virgin, without change. Up above I saw God bare of humanity (for where could humanity be seen in heaven? Let the Origens stop their babbling; let the Didymuses stop their raving; let the Evagriuses stop their angry ranting, telling empty myths, dreaming up a pre-existence of souls, and making common cause with the abominable pagans); but here I see him become man without alteration, a wonder within a wonder: he is God without alteration and man beyond explanation. He is twofold in nature but not twofold in hypostasis, having one and the same person. He is known in two natures, yet he is neither divided because the natures are two, nor, because his hypostasis is the same, single and unpaired, does he produce a confusion of the natures from which he is. Nor does he increase the number of the Trinity above, the source of all things, and one…

…of men, shown to men [?]. I find the same one to be both God and man, and I marvel at the greatness of the wonder. 21. “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” What could be higher than this joy, O Virgin Mother? What grace could be greater than this, which you alone have received from God as your inheritance? What could be more gracious or more radiant? Everything walks behind your wonder; everything lies beneath your grace; every excellent thing takes second place and receives a smaller share of splendor. “God is with you”: who would dare to compete? God is from you: who will not at once admit defeat, and rather rejoice with you and yield you the first and highest place? That is why I speak the greatest things to you, seeing your privileges above all created things: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” For from you joy has been granted not only to human beings; it is also given to the powers above. 22. Truly “blessed are you among women,” because you have changed Eve’s curse into blessing; because through you Adam, who was at first accursed, has been made blessed. Truly “blessed are you among women,” because through you the Father’s blessing has dawned upon humankind and set them free from the ancient curse. Truly “blessed are you among women,” because through you your forefathers are saved; for you will bear the Saviour who works divine salvation for them. Truly “blessed are you among women,” because without seed you have brought forth the fruit that grants blessing to the whole earth and redeems it from the curse that bore thorns. Truly “blessed are you among women,” because, though a woman by nature, you will become the Mother of God in fact. For if the one to be born of you is truly God made flesh, you would most justly be called Mother of God, since truly God…

23. But the blessed and God-filled Virgin, seeing the divine angel come to her in this way [?] and address her with such words, was troubled in her holy soul; and the words with her rea- [Notes: other manuscripts read θελήσειε. Ibid.: μετέβαλες.]

-soning she sifted, pondering within herself and searching out the meaning of the angel’s words; for she was astonished and wondered at what kind of greeting the angel had given. “But she,” it says, “seeing him, was troubled at his word, and considered what sort of greeting this might be.” For she was, indeed she was, full of human understanding, and accepted nothing that was said without testing it. She was afraid and trembled, knowing how Eve had been deceived, lest the crafty serpent should deceive her too, a second time, as he had deceived Eve. That is why she examined everything with understanding, lest a greeting with the serpent’s fate should cast her out of the divine splendor. 24. But the heavenly angel who had been sent to her, seeing her in such distress, frees her from all fear and dread, drives out all disturbance and agitation completely, and says to her most cheerfully, graciously and sweetly: “Do not be afraid, Mary.” I am not like the one who deceived your mother; I am not like the one who long ago tripped man up; I am not like the one who once exiled your forefathers from the paradise of delight; I am not like the one who cast man out of a blessed life and bound him to a life of pain; I am not like the one who out of envy gave birth to death and made all human beings mortal; I am not like the one who made all human beings, who came from the earth and were shaped by the hand of God, transgressors of the divine commandment, and returned them to the earth again; I am not like the one who made Adam, once called the friend of God, into God’s enemy. I am an angel of God almighty; I lead one of the angelic hosts, and among the angels of God I am called Gabriel. I have been sent by God the Father almighty to tell you, the spotless and blameless Virgin, of the descent upon you, the Virgin, of his only-begotten Son, who brought all things into existence and called them from nothing into being; of the much-hymned conception in you; of the all-surpassing incarnation from you; of the most wondrous pregnancy in you; and of the incomprehensible birth from you. Through these all the enemy’s schemes are undone; through these all the enemy’s devices, together with…

…[?] is saved and rises up from the corruption of death; through these the night of error is dispelled; through these man, who had become an exile from paradise, dwells in paradise once more; through these the one who was stripped of God’s friendship by the dragon’s counsel becomes God’s friend again [?]. And that is why I cry to you, O blessed Virgin, who are to become the mother of God, the Saviour of all: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.” For you have been found worthy to receive such great things; for heavenly joy will be born from you for the world, and the divine blessing, which blunts the ancient curse, will come through you to humankind…

25. I too, O Mother of God, praise your caution, and I fully approve of your good sense, because you fear the snares of the crafty one; because you fear the tricks of the beast who hates humankind; because you dread the hidden arrows of the devil; because you are afraid of the serpent’s varied and truly deadly hissings, lest you too should come to be called another Eve like her. “Do not be afraid, Mary; for you have found grace with God”: the grace that is immortal. You have found grace with God, grace surpassingly bright; you have found grace with God, grace long prayed for; you have found grace with God, grace full of light; you have found grace with God, grace that saves; you have found grace with God, grace that cannot be shaken; you have found grace with God, grace that cannot be moved; you have found grace with God, grace that cannot be conquered; you have found grace with God, grace that is eternal.
…could be said more sublimely: we could not rightly say that there is anything higher.

Many saints have lived before you, but none has been graced as you have; none has been blessed as you have; none has been sanctified as you have; none has been magnified as you have; none has been purified in advance as you have; none has been bathed in radiance as you have; none has been enlightened as you have; none has been exalted as you have. For no one has drawn near to God as you have; no one has been enriched with God’s gifts as you have; no one has received God’s grace as you have. You surpass everything that is held excellent among human beings; you surpass all the gifts God has given to all. For more than all others you are rich in God’s indwelling. No one has been able to contain God as you have; no one has had the strength to receive God’s presence as you have; no one has been found worthy to be enlightened by God as you have [?]. And therefore you have not only received God, the Creator and Master of all, but you have him from you, wondrously made flesh, carried in your womb, and after this born; redeeming all human beings from the condemnation inherited from their fathers, and granting them a salvation that will never cease. 26. That is why I have cried out to you, and I will say it again aloud: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.” Do not be troubled

when you hear my words; do not be afraid as you learn of my message to you. I do not bring humankind a deadly deception; I have not come to procure for my fellow servants the envy that gives birth to death. Drive all disturbance from your heart; banish all doubt from your mind; chase all fear from your soul. I have not come to you as one to be feared, even though to all others I appear most fearsome; I have not made use of the dignity of my rank. For I know with whom I am speaking now that I am here; I know to whom God has sent me; I know whom I have been appointed to serve. On the contrary, I am astonished as I look at you, and I am filled with fear and awe; on the contrary, I marvel at your greatness, and I am filled with trembling and dread; I stand in awe of your grace; I am amazed at your splendor. I am God’s servant and minister; but you will be the Mother of God, my Master and Creator, and not only that, but also the one who bears him and the indescribable nurse who feeds him with the streams of virgin breasts, him who “gives food in due season to all flesh.” I am a worshipper of God and a minister of his messages; but you have God himself within your womb, living in you in the flesh, and coming forth from you like a bridegroom, dispensing joy to all and bestowing divine radiance. For in you, O Virgin, as in a most pure and shining heaven, God “has set his tabernacle,” and “from you, like a bridegroom from his chamber, he will go forth,” and imitating “the course of a giant,” he will run in this life a road that will bring salvation to all who are in this life, stretching “from the heights of the heavens to their ends,” and filling all things with divine “heat,” and with it the brightness of life-giving light. 27. Therefore I cry to you once more the blessed greeting of joy: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” I have come bringing joy, not a fear ruinous to humankind; I am a minister of joy, not known as a servant of grief; I have been sent as a messenger of joy, not known as a herald of sorrow. Why do you fear one who, on the contrary, fears you? Why do you dread one who dreads your dignity? Why are you afraid of one who stands in awe of your grace? Why are you wary of one who reveres your splendor? I am a servant and the least worshipper of your Child and offspring. He made me when I did not exist; he sent me to you from the heavenly regions, to announce to you his joyful coming; I cry out to you his uncircumscribed conception; I proclaim to you his inexplicable incarnation; I declare to you his birth, which is the mother of all joy. 28. And that is why I say to you, all-praised Virgin,

…God. “You have found grace” that no woman at all has found; you have found grace that no one has beheld; you have found grace that no one has received. What kind of grace? Listen: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there will be no end.” I have been sent from heaven to proclaim these things to you. The one who is to be born of you sent me to bring you this good news clearly; the Word of the Father commanded me to make these things known to you in words and sayings; the only-begotten Son of God decreed that I should tell you these things. Up above he gave me the message, and here I see him altogether [?]; in heaven he entrusted to me what was to be said, and in you, the Virgin, I see him dwelling. He who has come to you, the Virgin, was eternal; he who is now conceived by you in time was timeless; he who will be born of you in the flesh was without flesh; he who submits to being contained in you was uncontainable. 29. “Behold, you will conceive in your womb.” And do not think, O Virgin, of the way other women conceive. Behold, you will conceive in your womb a conception without seed, a conception beyond words, a conception unspeakable, a divine conception, which no union with a man has cultivated, no coupling with a male has brought about, and which no human being is able to describe. For how will those born according to nature be able to tell of it? Since, then, your conception is beyond nature, do not examine it by natural reasoning. “And you will bear a son,” not only temporal and mortal, but also eternal and more primordial than all temporal things. “And you will bear a son,” not only seen in the flesh, but also bodiless. “And you will bear a son,” not only appearing from the Virgin, but also known as the Son of God. “And you will bear a son,” not only recognized as man, but also shining forth as true God [?]. “And you will bear a son,” not in need of salvation from another, but granting salvation to all human beings. [Notes: Nic., p. 215: τὸ σύνολον. Nic.: ἐδέξατο.]

“And” for this reason “you will call his name Jesus,” a name which means Saviour. For it was fitting, O Virgin, that the Saviour of all, when he was born, should receive the very name of Saviour, so that the power of the one born might be shown by the name itself, and the saving birth of your Child might be made known to all humankind. 30. “He will be great,” since he is called “Angel of great counsel,” praised as “mighty God,” celebrated as the Father’s “wonderful Counselor,” revealed as “Prince of peace,” having authority as Maker over all creation, and making peace between heaven and earth. For he carries the achievements of his own rule on his own shoulder and arm; he accomplishes what he does not by another’s power but by his own, pouring forth for all a settled state of peace [?]. But he is also “Father of the age to come”: he alone was begotten of God, the only Begetter; he is Father of the age to come, and is glorified with the Father himself before all ages. Isaiah prophesied of him long before, saying: “A child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us”: your child, O Virgin, whose birth I now announce to you, “whose rule is upon his shoulder; and his name is called Angel of great counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, mighty God, Ruler, Prince of peace, Father of the age to come.” “He will be great”: not as though he were not great and would become so later, but as one who is always great, and will be so hereafter as well. For since he is known as the Son by nature of the great God and Father, he too is declared great, and will be proclaimed God by nature. Being of one nature with God who begot him, he will certainly also have identity of essence [?] with him. For God would never beget a Son unequal to himself and unlike him, but surely one of the same nature, wholly like him, and identical in every natural property. 31. “He will be great, and will be called Son of the Most High.” For he is always great, and he is named Son of the Most High God, since he is proclaimed to be from the great God himself and his only-begotten Son. But “he will be,” I say, and “will be called,” not as though he were not these things already; do not suspect that. [?] these things [refer to] his much-wondered birth and his becoming man in the flesh from you. For “will be” and “will be called” are expressions of time, and are said of him as one who became man like you human beings, since he truly became like you… [Note: the manuscript reads δηλοῦται.]

…having heard of a divine conception, and learning [?] of a wondrous pregnancy, and receiving the good news of a paradoxical birth, she marveled at what was said. She knew the nature of women; she considered how they naturally conceive and wisely weighed how they give birth, and that these things never happen without union with a man. She saw that she herself was untouched, without any taste of such intimacy even in thought. So she says to Gabriel the archangel, who was announcing to her these mighty things, the great deeds of God, and proclaiming the good tidings of joy: “And how will this be for me, since I do not know a man? [?] How shall I believe your words, which go beyond human nature? I have seen [?] very many women, and I have seen none give birth without union with a male. How then will these things happen in me, who have not run the courses of nature? How do I become the mother of a male son, I who know nothing at all of union with a male? Perhaps, O angel, you suppose that because I am betrothed to a husband according to the law of Moses, I have also known a human marriage bed, from which conceptions, pregnancies and births spring? Not yet have I come together in marriage with my betrothed and guardian. How then do you announce to me conception and birth, and even the nursing of a child that is surely to be born?

33. Or rather, do you not know, O minister of good tidings beyond nature, that Mary was not brought up among men, nor did she keep company with boys [?]? Know the splendor of my virginity, and you will not speak to me of a conception without a husband. Know the greatness of my chastity, and you will not tell me of a pregnancy without marriage. Know the blamelessness of my modesty, and you would not speak to me of an unnatural birth. Know my untouched purity, and you will not cry out to me of an incredible nursing. Or rather, have you not learned that from the very moment of my birth I was brought up in the Holy of Holies, where no man is found, where no man enters, where no male is ever seen passing by? Know the reverence of my conduct, and do not speak to me of fleshly thoughts. Know the all-pure character of my way of life, and do not [?] to me the customs of mothers

…celibacy and union are not the same; [?] all-holy [?] and the bed of female and male are not the same. For even if “marriage is honorable” and the bed according to the law of Moses is “undefiled,” the grace of virginity still far surpasses these. [?] the difference between these and that, and they admit no comparison with one another at all. How then do you set aside the marks of virginity and announce to me the [?] of marriage and [?]? For this reason I fear your [?]; for this reason I dread your address; for this reason I do not accept your greeting without prudent investigation, without wise scrutiny, without true examination, lest [?] I too be deceived in my mind, and walk in the footsteps of my mother Eve, and become for wretched mankind the matchmaker of greater evils and worse calamities. [?] “But again the war is upon us against a second [?], against an incorrupt woman [?] … to partake [?] of the surpassing [?]…”

Therefore I answer you again according to nature: “And how will this be for me, since I do not know a man?” And how shall I bear a male child, as you said? It is an incredible announcement, [lacking] [?] any logical sequence; the word is foreign and alien to common custom. Therefore I would never accept it unless you give a reason that accords with the outcome of what you say; for without an account given, nothing of the kind would ever come about. Give, then, an account of your announcement, and then I will believe your words. Eve’s fall makes me more prudent and more sensible: that deceitful hissing of the serpent, the author of evil, brought her down into it, for she was guileless and simple and had no part in searching reasoning. I would never become a second Eve by believing unaccustomed words.”

34. When the archangel heard these things spoken to him by that virginal and blameless mouth, he again answers her gently. For difficulties raised according to nature he provides a solution beyond nature, and frees the all-pure one from her searching reasonings. “I know, O Virgin, and I am persuaded, that you have not seen a man’s bed. I see the spotlessness of your virginity; I behold the godliness of your mind; I see the untouched state of your chastity; I perceive your unmixed purity. I know that you were brought up and grew in the Holy of Holies, and that from there you have holiness in both body and soul. I know that Joseph has been allotted only the name, empty of the harvest; for he has not come forward as the farmer of your offspring, but as the faithful and God-loving servant of the birth. Why do you now speak to me of the exceptional [?]? I will speak to you of things higher than these. You speak to me of natural and human things, but I cry out to you things lofty and most divine. Had you known the power of my words, you would not bring before me the customs of women; you would not offer me lowly words; you would not cry out to me the laws of nature, apart from which females never give birth. I too know human custom, even though I am not human by nature. I too know that the union of man and woman normally begets the human being who is born. I am not ignorant of these things in knowledge, though I have no experience of them in practice. For the incorporeal nature is one thing, and the nature of bodies is quite another; and the law and way of life of the

incorporeal is one thing, and the custom of bodies another. Leave aside, I beg you, the things that creep upon the ground and are earthly, and look at the things on high and heavenly; leave aside the paltry and the least, and see the wondrous and the greatest. I do not announce to you today a natural birth, one that proceeds from the will of man and of flesh; I tell you of a birth beyond nature and custom.

35. I know, O Virgin, that a virgin has never given birth; but you will give birth, seen to be a virgin and remaining one. I know that a woman has never given birth without union with a man; but you will indeed bear a child, for God decrees the birth. Human nature did not make itself, so that it should also set its own laws. God, who fashioned it and set the fitting laws, is also able, whenever he wishes, to change the laws of nature which he himself laid down when he brought it into being. It is God who wills it, and who could oppose God’s ordinances? All women who become mothers first come together with men; but you, kept a virgin and remaining one, will become a mother by the divine will. God will make new in you another kind of conception; God will show in you another kind of birth. For nothing whatever that he may wish to do is impossible for him; his will at once becomes deed, and no creature resists him, since he himself is their all-powerful maker. How then could God, who can do all things, not be able to make you too, O Virgin, a mother, except by the laws and boundaries and customs which he himself laid down before, as though he too were subject to them and a slave to the laws he decreed that humans should serve? That is not a good saying; that is not a pious answer; that is not a God-loving statement, which makes God a slave of his own laws and has God willingly serve the customs of slaves. I rejoice to see your sobriety; I rejoice to perceive your caution; I rejoice to see your prudence, even though you answer my addresses with objections. For I do not judge your words to be words of unbelief, nor do I take your utterances as contradiction, but as wise and intelligent investigation, an inquiring mind and prudence.

[?] 1:15.

…of God, and God, O Virgin, you will bear—not bare of humanity, as he was born [?] of the Father, but [?] become flesh and man, without change and confusion, without alteration and diminution, without bodily change. For God, who is also the all-powerful creator of these things, is by nature untouched by them; for he set [?] the boundaries for you, not for himself

You will bear, then, as I said before, the eternal Son of God, who is also the Word of the One who begot him; and not without flesh, but interwoven with flesh and blood, having a rational and invisible soul, and all that the visible human being is by nature. He will come down upon you, the undefiled one, “like rain upon a fleece”; he will take flesh from your virginal blood, and himself create a soul as he wills, and unite and join these to himself according to hypostasis into the undivided hypostasis of one Son. So he will be born of you in a way beyond all expectation, keeping you a virgin as you give birth, and making you, who know no man, the Mother of God. And you will give birth when you have completed the time of pregnancy. For the Lover of humankind wills, he wills to make himself like human beings in this respect too, so that he may become man in all things, neither departing from being God nor sharing in human sin. So do not go on saying to me with human thoughts, “And how will this be for me, since I do not know a man?”

37. To him the all-holy Virgin, with fearless courage, answers once more with untrembling lips: “Listen, O angel of my paradoxical conception and of my virginal childbearing and birth: how can I not marvel at your [?], how can I not be astonished at your words? For you tell me of things most high, which until now have never happened among human beings. I know that God accomplishes all that he proposes to do. But what you announce to me in your words has never happened until this day. Often indeed women who were barren, like dry rocks, have given birth when God afterwards decreed it. But a virgin with uncorrupted chastity, pure of union with a man, has never until this day given birth. I know that Sarah spent many years barren, but later bore Isaac, when she was seen to be advancing into old age and bore white hair as witness to her years; for God had ordained it, and it was impossible that it should not happen. I know that Rebekah was barren and afterwards brought forth twin offspring, the brothers Jacob and Esau, who came forth after many years from one father and a mother plainly barren. I know Hannah, who undid her childlessness: she wept over her barrenness and lamented the deadness of her womb,

and for this abstained from food and drink, since she could not bear the pain of her barrenness. Yet she too, beseeching the God of all with tears, gave birth to Samuel and set aside the statutes of barrenness, for God heard her cries and, being mighty, fulfilled her request. Along with these I will also count the woman who brought me forth after barrenness and bore me, Mary, in answer to her supplication; for she too bore the name of Hannah, and with the name, the barrenness. But she too entreated the God who is over all and brought him many petitions, and received the gift of becoming a mother: she gave birth at God’s ordaining, setting aside the statutes of sterility. And I can count many barren women who became mothers by divine command. But a virgin who in the whole of life has given birth I have never heard of until this day—which you yourself [?], as you say,

38. So I do not disbelieve God’s command, for he shows himself the worker of all that he wishes to work. But I marvel at the power of what is said, and I am astonished at how paradoxical and strange it is, and unaccustomed to human ears; and I rightly ask how this will happen, or in what manner it will be fulfilled. That is why I did not give you the answer, ‘This will not be for me, since I do not know a man,’ as you said [?], but asked you, ‘How will this be for me, since I do not know a man?’ For it has never happened, nor is any virgin seen to have given birth. Therefore I sought to learn the manner in which I, a virgin, shall become a mother and bear a child without receiving the seed of child and offspring. And for this reason I ask you again and say most soberly: ‘And how will this be for me, since I do not know a man?’ For I am not uttering words of unbelief; I am seeking a precise demonstration. Tell me the manner of the conception, and explain the cause of the birth, and you will find me not disbelieving your words but obedient to what you say. For it is impossible that what God has resolved should not come to pass [?].”

39. When the herald of good tidings, the [?] angel, heard these words from her who was truly to become Mother of God, he marveled at her answer and her understanding, and replied: “Most excellently and most wisely, O Virgin Mother of God, have you set out how of old women

who had at first been barren later became mothers of children, and in a sense healed their own nature and bore children beyond nature, because God had compassion and the Master, Creator and Fashioner of nature took pity. For where God gives his assent, the boundaries of nature fall idle. So, just as those women, at God’s ordaining, overcame the weaknesses of their own nature, and, freed from the great weaknesses of nature, brought forth the fruit of the womb, so you too, who sprang from barren Anna and overcame the nature of her who bore you, being a pure virgin and remaining a virgin afterward, will in a way beyond expectation bear a son without seed and without plowing, at the command of the very one who is born. For he is also Lord of nature, being its Creator and ruler. He is God incomprehensible, even though as man he will be born of you, the Virgin. For it was fitting for him, and due, as he became man out of love for humankind for the redemption of all people, to display a birth from a virgin alone, making his glorious and saving incarnation from you without marital pleasure and union.

40. But if the fact that no pure and undefiled virgin has given birth until this day, nor has anyone ever been proclaimed the mother of a child without seed, makes your mind doubtful, and you seek to learn when a virgin has given birth, then I in turn ask and inquire of you: when, then, did God become man? Or when did God consent to be made flesh? Or when did God become a human being? Or when was God conceived without seed? Or when did God endure being carried in the womb? Or when did God display a fleshly birth from a woman? Or when did God suck at a woman’s breasts? Or when did God utter an infant’s cry? Or when did God grow in stature? Or when did God live as one of us among human beings? Or when did God die for human beings? Or when was God nailed to a cross? Or when was God’s side pierced by a lance? Or when did God undergo a three-day burial? Or when has God been seen suffering all these things, so that he might [free] [?] humanity from all its sufferings,

destroy the assault of death and corruption, and raise up incorruptible and immortal his own image, the human being? If, then, O Virgin, these things have never happened, but were kept for the present time and foreordained to be fulfilled through you, how could another virgin have given birth before you—which is what you sought to learn from me as assurance and proof of your virginal childbearing? No virgin has ever given birth, O Virgin, none has; nor will any other virgin after you, O Virgin, ever give birth; nor has any virgin, O Virgin, become Mother of God; nor after you does any other virgin, O Virgin, become the one and only Mother of God. For you alone among women will give birth as a virgin, and you alone among women will be called Mother of God. For “once, at the consummation of the ages,” the only-begotten Son of God the Father will become man and will display the wondrous [birth] from you alone

41. And that this promise of God was to be fulfilled through you alone, I will assure you with prophetic words. The wonderful Isaiah, foreseeing the incarnation of the Word and God from you—a divine and seedless conception, a painless pregnancy, an ineffable birth and an unspeakable nursing—cried out clearly beforehand: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.” Do you see, pure and undefiled Virgin, how he foretold beyond dispute that it is a virgin who is to bear Emmanuel? That virgin is you alone, and no other will be seen before you or after you. For the God-inspired prophet does not say, “Behold, the virgins shall conceive and bear sons, and they shall call their names Emmanuel,” so that I could present you with another virgin giving birth. For Emmanuel is one, whom you, O Virgin, will bear in the flesh; there is no other Emmanuel who either came before or will come after, so that another virgin might bear a child beyond expectation. You alone, O Virgin, are his divine mother, and no other before you has been called Mother of God, nor will any come after you.

42. Therefore I cried out to you most excellently and most fittingly: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” For Emmanuel, as it is said in the Hebrew tongue, when rendered into Greek is taken to mean “God with us.” And when has God been with human beings and numbered among you humans, Mother of God,

(Note: the manuscript reads γεννήτρεια.)

if not now, in the last times of the age, when he also “took hold of the seed of Abraham” and assumed flesh from you? For the name Emmanuel, when interpreted, carries a twofold meaning: of human and of divine nature, from which he is composed and in which he is known. Being perfect God before the ages, he became perfect man in you, taking human nature from you and uniting it to himself according to hypostasis, keeping unchanged the natural quality of each nature and their natural and essential distinguishing marks. For God the Word remained God the Word, even though he naturally clothed himself in the nature of flesh. And the flesh, rationally ensouled, which he took from your spotless blood and ensouled with a spirit of rational life, remained flesh rationally ensouled, even though it was known as the flesh of God the Word alone, united to him according to hypostasis and running together into the undivided concurrence of one person and one hypostasis, yet without changing the things united or reducing them to an identity of essence. So, even though Christ preserved the difference of both natures and essences, one Son and Christ will appear from you to the world, showing no distinction of sons or of christs. For he who is true God will also be born true man, displaying nothing false in whatever he may be called and said to be. For this reason he will be called Emmanuel, as being truly both: the same uncircumscribed God, and the same truly man—the one by his eternal birth from the Father, the other by his temporal and embodied conception from you, his Mother. For thus he was pleased to save human nature: the inexhaustible one lowered himself to such an emptying in order that the humanity which had fallen [?] to the earth of corruption he might raise again from the earth and make a sharer in the heavenly inheritance, in place of the delight it once enjoyed in paradise.

43. And how this will come about, O Virgin who receives God, I will tell and declare in words, since I have come to say this to you as well: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one to be born will be called Son of God.” You have a clear demonstration; you have a true declaration. The Holy Spirit comes down upon you, the undefiled one, to make you purer and to give you a fruit-bearing power. “And the all-powerful power of God will overshadow you,” that is, the Word and consubstantial Son of God. For he is the hand and arm and power [?] of God the Father himself

…power, and through him the Father, as through a Son, has made all things, and "in him all things hold together." He will work from you an incarnation beyond explaining, display from you a conception from unploughed ground, and accomplish from you a birth beyond understanding. 41. "Therefore the holy one to be born will be called Son of God." If, then, the one to be born of you, the Virgin Theotokos, will be called Son of God, how will she who gives birth to him not be shown to be a virgin? For this will be a clear proof and an unshakable token of his Godhead, which rules over all things: that you, a spotless virgin, give birth in an ineffable birth, and remain a virgin after an incorrupt childbirth. For if the one born of you, the virgin, is God, as indeed he is God and is proclaimed to be, what would he not accomplish if he willed it? For he is God, even if also as…

"For this reason I myself, Gabriel, have been sent to you, the Virgin, so that even by my very name I may show that the one born of you, the immaculate Virgin, is God and man. For the name Gabriel, when interpreted, means God and man. There were many angels in heaven, yet he did not choose to send any of them; he sent me, who am one of them and am named Gabriel, so that by my word and by my name I might show you clearly that the one to be born of you is God and man, and 'upholds all things by the word of his power'; that he is holy and will sanctify the birth of all human beings; and that he will be called Son of the Most High and will by grace make those who believe in him sons of the Most High. So then, O Virgin, believe my words, for they will certainly be fulfilled in deed. I speak the truth to you, as a herald and messenger of truth. And for your fuller assurance and confidence in the fulfilment of my words, I also give you an indisputable sign, so that you may remain unshaken in faith: 'For behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren. For nothing

will be impossible with God.' And this will be the strongest proof for you that all my words, the good tidings brought to you whom all revere, will receive a true and saving fulfilment for the life and redemption of all human beings. For it belongs to the same power of God both that a barren woman who does not bear should give birth, and that a virgin who has known no bridegroom should give birth. Rejoice, then, O Virgin full of grace and filled with God, for what God, the Master of all, has graciously granted you, and because you will bear the Son of God, who will become the joy of the whole human race." 45. [?] Then the Virgin Mother of God, believing, and taking courage that what had been spoken to her by the Lord would certainly be fulfilled, answers meekly and humbly, and virginally as well — for the all-pure one was to give birth to Christ, "meek and lowly in heart," and she had to be rich in his own lowliness and meekness: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word." 46. So Gabriel the archangel, having heard this from the Virgin Theotokos, went back up to heaven, from where he had been sent to her. And she carried in her womb God who had sent him: the one glorified above with the Father, and here below, from her, enduring to be carried in the womb in the flesh. For at once the Word and God came to her, and through the angel's voice entered her divine womb and was made flesh; without change he became embodied, taking from her flesh from unploughed ground and truly uniting it to himself — flesh animated with a rational soul, but not having subsisted before its ineffable union with him. For at once it was flesh, at once it was the flesh of God the Word, at once it was flesh animated with a rational soul; for it had its hypostasis in him, and not its existence before him.

Nor did the flesh of some other human being like us ever come into being and then come together with God the Word and be united with him; rather, in him it received at once both to be flesh animated with a rational soul and to be the flesh of God the Word, animated with a rational soul, taken from the virginal and immaculate blood of the immaculate Virgin. For those who most impiously wish to divide the one Son and Christ into two sons and two christs have no

evidence or pretext for saying that it ever subsisted by itself and had its own person, and only then came together with the Word and God into natural union. For things that are two parts and are viewed as separate from one another never admit of natural union, or union according to hypostasis. And where natural union does not come first, neither does composition according to hypostasis come about; nor is one and the same hypostasis shown, nor one and the same person proclaimed, at once undivided and unparted and rejecting every severance.

47. And just as the undivided and unparted incarnation of the Word turns aside such madmen and removes them entirely from the nurslings of true religion (these are the Nestoriuses, the Pauls, the Theodores, and their companions in God-fighting madness), so too it sends out of the assembly of the pious those who wish to confuse the natures and are eager to make one nature out of both natures. For, contrary to their madness, the Word did not become flesh by changing his own nature into flesh; nor did he alter the flesh endowed with mind and soul, which he assumed from this Virgin Theotokos, into his own divine nature and transform it into the divine essence. Rather, he remained unchanged, above every kind of change and free of all confusion, both made flesh in flesh consubstantial with us and truly become man for our sake. And the flesh likewise remained unaltered, beyond all change and confusion. It came together with the Word into a single existence and was united to him according to an indivisible hypostasis; it keeps unchanged its consubstantiality with us and preserves, as far as nature, essence and existence are concerned, an exact likeness to us. Yet it undergoes no division from the Word and suffers no severance or separation, but is called the Word's own and his alone, and concurs with him into one hypostasis. Because of its hypostatic union with him, it is shown to stand and remain within the proper bounds of its nature: displaying a natural difference from him, but knowing no personal difference from him. Together with him it makes up one sole hypostasis, and that a unified and composite one (for it is not simple and incomposite), but it does not run together into one composite nature; for that is the beginning of confusion and the foundation of a mutable…

Just as, then, the incarnate Word shakes off those who divide and sever, so too he casts out of the sacred precincts those who confuse the two natures and speak of their mixture and alteration. These are the Severuses, the Eutycheses, the Dioscoruses, the Apollinarises

and the Polemons, and before them the Simons, the Valentinuses, the Marcions, the Basilideses, the Maneses and the Menanders, and the whole many-headed heresy of the Acephali, now wickedly sprouting up, which wages a single common war against true religion but carries on countless wars against itself that never cease. These truly holy and all-holy good tidings, then, worthy of the godly ears of us who are pious, gladly welcome us, but drive those foul madmen out of this festival of their good tidings, since they understand them and speak of them impiously. 48. And I, the least, who have come forward today as their herald, cry aloud to you alone, children of true religion and faith, who receive piously what is said, and I proclaim and declare distinctly: "Good tidings, good tidings, good tidings!" Good tidings of our Saviour; good tidings of God made flesh for us; good tidings of God's coming to us; good tidings of God's becoming man from us; good tidings of God's seedless conception; good tidings of God's being carried in a virgin's womb; good tidings of God's coming together with flesh without change; good tidings by which we, the castaways, are exalted and deified and become gods by grace. No longer dreading corruption; no longer fearing passions; no longer trembling at death; no longer shuddering at the foul devil; no longer on guard against his unseen assaults; no longer afraid of his open tyrannies; but all appearing divine, all found godlike, all enrolled in the choir above, all

seen as citizens of the Jerusalem above. For where we have our citizenship, there we shall also receive our inheritance and dwell in the ineffable mansions. 49. Bringing the good tidings of all these things, brothers, we have come to you, our dearest, today. For the good tidings now brought to you are the beginning, root, base and foundation of them all. From them, as you have learned, flows all our abundance of good things, gushing up as from a spring, watering the whole world at once, gladdening and nourishing it, raising it to the heavenly courts, and making it a partaker of the most divine mansions there and of the blessed gifts. And for this reason I cry out again and again, joyfully and loudly: "Good tidings, good tidings, good tidings!" — to these I call and urge you, and these I wish you to celebrate today. For from here our salvation proceeds; from here our freedom is kindled like a beacon; from here our adoption as sons of God is brought to birth; from here our recall is born; from here the Word and God, having come to save us, makes the beginning of our salvation. This he makes the prelude of his compassion toward us; this he displayed as the beginning of our deification. Nothing is more welcome to human beings than this, nothing more precious to those of earth, nothing more gracious to mortals. Hence the second Adam, taking the virgin earth and forming himself in human shape, lays down a second beginning for humanity, renewing the oldness of the first and showing us a second beginning that does not grow old — one that shares kinship and stock with the first, yet does not share its manner of life, nor is it merely equal in worth and sacred glory. The first was condemned through the first Adam; the second has been freed from blame through the second Adam. The first, through the first Adam, was bereft of divine radiance; the second, through the second Adam, has been refashioned with heavenly radiance. The first, through the first Adam, who was of the earth, earthy and earthly-minded, bore the yoke of slavery; the second, through the second Adam, the consubstantial Son of God, receives the dignity of adoption and has been enriched with the right to cry out and call, "Abba, Father." 50. Are our good tidings small, then, brothers? Is the proclamation of our good tidings cheap? Is the shining forth of our good tidings lowly and contemptible? Or does it not surpass all

brightness, rise above all radiance, and outshine all elegance? And for this reason I cry to you, my partners and like-minded friends, and as I cry "Good tidings, good tidings, good tidings!" I am never sated. Though my speech wants to run on still and longs to run its course well, I hold it back. For I see that my hearers are weary, even though they are not sated with hearing our sacred good tidings. You have a willing spirit, but the flesh is weak; you are weighed down with a surfeit of words and cannot labour any longer. And I know that a surfeit of words is hostile to the ears, even if the words are divine and most exalted — especially to ears quickly sated in listening to speeches. So let us celebrate in a holy and exalted manner the exalted and holy feast of our exalted and holy good tidings, and honour it worthily and fittingly, so that through it we may attain the heavenly goods without any contest. Of these it has shown itself to be root, spring and mother, in Christ Jesus our Lord himself, with whom to the Father and the Holy Spirit be glory, honour, might and majesty, to the ages of ages. Amen.

A sermon of Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem, on the Exaltation of the precious Cross and on the holy Resurrection. A festival of the Cross — and who would not leap for joy? A proclamation of the Resurrection — and who would not laugh? For the Cross, fixed in the place of the Skull, and having the Master of creation nailed to it, tore up "the bond written against us"

and freed us from the bonds of sin — the bond that our forefather Adam signed when he transgressed God's commandments — and made us leap with gladness like calves let loose from their bonds. "For where sin abounded, the grace of God abounded all the more." And the Resurrection banished the corruption of death, drove away the gloom of Hades, raised the dead from their tombs, and, to speak with the prophet, wiped away every tear from every face; and it has bestowed on every human being the grace that truly has no successor. For the gift of the resurrection is not partial, nor was its achievement shown to only a few. For he who made his burial in it in human flesh — or rather, his resurrection — was God of the whole creation. He does not know how to grant partial graces, nor does any favouritism hold sway with him. Known as the true God of all, he extends the gift of salvation to all people, sparing his own image and renewing it most perfectly, since every human being on earth has been fashioned in the image of God. The commemoration of the Cross has come — and who among human beings will not [?crucify] himself? For the Cross knows this one as its most genuine worshipper: the one who has crucified himself to the world and shows it by his deeds; he is found to be a genuine friend of the Cross. The dedication-feast of the Resurrection — and what believer will not be renewed, thrusting away all the deadness of the passions and putting on incorruption of soul? For one death is defined as that of the soul, and another is known as that of the body that surrounds it. The former death is conceived by sin, as James the Brother of God, founder and leader of this see, wrote. The latter is naturally begotten by the dissolution of the elements of which the body essentially consists — and indeed also by the departure of the immortal soul, even if this does not seem so to the sons of physicians, who profess to heal only bodies; for this very thing was given by the Creator as a clear penalty to man when he disobeyed the divine commandment. The Cross is lifted on high — and who will not be mystically lifted up from the earth? For where the Redeemer is raised up, there the redeemed also goes and leaps, longing always to be with the one who saved him and to reap from him help that does not perish. Today the Resurrection goes forth and brightens all things with its procession; tomorrow the Cross is displayed and bestows its gifts on its worshippers. Today the Resurrection is spread out, and tomorrow the Cross soars above: the one exposing corruption to shame, the other the battle lines of the demons; the one proclaiming through itself that death has truly been put to death, the other announcing to all that all the evildoing of demons has been abolished and all their foul and soul-destroying activity has been deadened. O the wonder! What am I to say? I am at a loss before the

mystery. For of old the Cross went before the Resurrection, but now the Cross has the Resurrection as its leader and forerunner. O wondrous exchange! For here too I see the Saviour's saying plainly fulfilled in them: "For behold, the last have become first, and conversely the first have turned out last." Who, then, will be able to tell the cause of these exchanges and alterations? For it is not that they were running a race, and one leapt ahead while the other, being slow, fell behind. Why, then, does the divine Cross not dawn and flash forth first, as before, and the light-bearing Resurrection shine after it on the third day? What our fathers knew when they made this exchange we cannot say with certainty. But we suppose and conjecture that those who come from the ends of the earth to venerate these life-bearing things are the cause of one being placed after and the other going before. For in this way, having first celebrated the joyful and bright feast of the Resurrection, and immediately afterwards beholding the blessed exaltation of the Cross, they may have its all-powerful companionship as good and saving provision for the road: running with them on their journeys, sailing with them on the sea, awarding salvation everywhere, guarding them from every adversity, and showing you by the facts themselves that the all-mighty power of the Cross has embraced all the ends of the world, that it fills all things and is present everywhere without effort, rescuing the faithful from hardships, kindling salvation for them in their piety, and bringing to nothing the plans of all their enemies. Perhaps there is also some other, hidden reason, which the teachers of this church in former times knew and understood, and which we, the least, are not ashamed to confess that we do not at present clearly know. May God grant knowledge of this too, as we firmly believe he will, solely for the benefit of you, most faithful ones. What, then, is more exalted for us than these blessed feasts? What among all things that exist is holier for us than these sacred festivals? Or how shall we rejoice and leap as we celebrate their feasts? The shining forth of the Resurrection, and the torch-bearing veneration of the Cross: these are the trophies of all our salvation. These redeemed us from death and the passions and from the most wicked ravaging of the demons, and led us back to our Master, dispelling all that is downcast and gloomy and spreading over us the radiance of things that bring joy. Does not the life-bearing Resurrection grant us entrance to immortal life? Does not the Cross, as it is lifted up, engender for us redemption from [?sufferings]? For truly these have once more made us sharers in kinship with God, for whose sake he was both born and dawned upon all of us on earth…

Knowing, therefore, their mystical power, and how greatly they have benefited us, and what blessings they have procured for us, let us celebrate them well and piously, in the way they wish to be honoured: "not in debauchery and licentiousness, not in strife and jealousy," not in robbery and injustice — and I pass over the rest of the list in silence.
