For I dare to say, my most genuine brothers, joint heirs of our same faith and enriched together with the same spiritual parentage, that anyone who wishes to celebrate them in that way they not only refuse to look upon or admit, but even turn away from and abhor, as one who behaves unfittingly toward them and does what is utterly hateful to them. Therefore I exhort and urge you to hate and shun what our venerable feasts hate, and to love and practise what we know pleases them. And they know as pleasing and delightful whatever leads the one who does it back to salvation and guides him to eternal life. Has not Christ, shining forth upon humankind, flashed upon us life that does not end and light that does not set? Let us, then, change our own way of life too, and, stripping off our former conduct as harmful and ruinous, let us run well in newness of life. Does not the Resurrection grant us the inheritance of life? Has not the Cross crucified our old self? If, then, we revere the Resurrection and celebrate its feast, let us also love a newer life, through which we shall be not friends in word only, but its most intimate initiates. And if we also embrace the Cross, why do we not crucify the passions together with our members, so that we too may cry out with Paul, "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me"? If, then, Christ promises to live in those who have crucified themselves to the world and "put to death their earthly members," as Paul cries out and testifies, why do we not also do such things and put to death every earthly member — passion, evil desires and the rest of that list — so that Christ may live in us too and grant us ageless life? Let us therefore pursue peace with all, and with it acquire holiness; for without these "no one will ever see the Lord," as Paul has again testified to us. And for this reason Christ is proclaimed as peace — "For he himself," it says, "is our peace" — and has been called "sanctification." He is peace because he brought peaceful concord, uniting heavenly things with those on earth and making both one Church. He is sanctification and redemption (for this too is proclaimed in addition to the former) because he became the redeemer of us captives, and not only redeemed us from demons and passions, but also implanted in us a holiness filled with God.

What you have heard from my voice, let us pursue with all zeal and resolve; let us acquire it and seize it, and through it be joined to Christ in that fair and blessed union. For whoever comes to him in this way he will never cast out of his goodness and blessedness—far from it! Let us hasten, then, to gain this harmony with him, than which nothing is more precious; let us run to purchase Christ living in us, than which nothing is mightier; so that, having gained this wealth, we may enjoy the kingdom of heaven and find eternal life in Christ himself, our God and Savior, with whom be glory to the Father, together with the Holy Spirit, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

A homily of Sophronius, most holy among monks and afterwards patriarch of Jerusalem, delivered on the veneration of the precious and [?] cross in the middle week of holy Lent; and that through sincere fasting it is possible for those cleansed in mind to approach the divine mysteries without condemnation and to partake of them.

Physicians, all of them, often recognize the first approaches of the diseases coming upon us and deliberately mix certain remedies to turn aside the illnesses about to invade the body through its lack of appetite [?], so that the illness may not spread and cause the sufferer unbearable pain. Often, too, from their long experience they are able to drive off with ease even ailments that have lingered long in the body, especially if the patient has given himself into the physician's hands and obediently follows his directions. Our good God has acted in the same way. As a painless remedy he sets before us this holy and most excellent fast, not limited to particular times and seasons but kept continually, so that it bridles the appetites of the flesh and checks the spreading that comes upon the body from soft living. Otherwise the body, waging war through its own love of pleasure, might plunge the spirit under water and bring about no small fall. For truly, as the great herald Paul says, they are drawn up in battle against each other: "For the flesh," he says, "desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are opposed to one another."

[Note: Gretser wrongly reads "All the physicians often"; Latin: "Physicians, mostly all" [?].]

For this reason, beloved, the God of all has set the forty-day fast plainly before us all, for more contests and for the routing of the spirits of the air, so that, having cleansed ourselves completely, we may arrive through pure living at the sovereign day of the life-bearing resurrection on the third day. Then, being pure, we may be seen by our pure God, and rise with him, and be glorified with him, and be welcomed by him as friends. For a traveler too, when he has to press on day after day toward some place, if he only catches sight of his resting place, makes his journey with greater eagerness. Even if he is worn out by the length of a very hard road, he is greatly sustained by the hope of refreshment. And we too are travelers, running through our short life and making our passage. Those who have lived well arrive at the kingdom above, where our citizenship is. But those who have lived impiously will, I think, appear buried there in some lowest pit of their own passions, by which they were enslaved and held fast while they lived. "And how," they say, "can anyone run up to the things above while still remaining in this life?" How? I tell you: by taking wing through the purifying mind, rejoicing with the powers above, and celebrating the overthrow of the all-destroying enemy. Then, cleansed on both sides, in soul and in body, through gentle fasting and through touching the life-giving and immaculate wood, we may leap for joy, as we said, together with the heavenly powers, whose fellow citizens we shall become when the Judge comes from heaven. "And how," someone says, "could this happen?" When, through the illumination of our ruling faculty and the repelling and resisting of the hostile spirits, we are found worthy to touch the life-giving and immaculate cross purely, with pure lips. For our good God, through the tradition of the holy Fathers, has shown us this way—the way, I mean, of beneficial fasting—so that, having found a little relief from our wretchedness, being cleansed of our filth, and having checked the assaults of the passions, we may receive complete forgiveness, through touching the life-giving wood, from him who was fixed upon it. So it may be seen henceforth how each in its own way assists the other and leads us by the hand toward the day of the resurrection: the fast brings lightness to the body, and the most pure veneration of the divine cross draws our mind away from the confusion of the most shameful deeds and leads it up toward the kingdom above. The Mediator between God and men has brought this about. He wrought our salvation in the midst of the earth when he was nailed to the cross for our salvation, and at the midpoint of this divine fast he has shown us good hopes of the resurrection.

O fasting, God-given tool, which like an axe cuts down the passionate appetites that have sprung up in us! When Adam lost it, he was shown to be banished from life in paradise; when Moses kept it, he became one who saw God. O fasting, mightier than fire, which reduced the Chaldean fire to ashes and kept the three youths unharmed! O fasting, which grieved the prophet Jonah and preserved the city of the Ninevites! If anyone should wish to trace out the paths of fasting, perhaps he could grasp the boundless judgments of God. But so that we may not praise fasting alone and its life-giving gifts, come, let us set in the midst the life-giving wood of the precious cross. It has been set before us in the midst of the fast, and it was fixed in the midst of the earth for our salvation. What shall we say, and how shall we sing its praise with mouth and heart? Let us cry out and say to it: Hail, precious cross, on which the Son and Word of God stretched out his hands, embraced us, and brought us to the heavenly Father! Hail, cross, through which our senses are cleansed of every stain as we embrace you with all our heart! Hail, cross, who truly brought unspeakable joy to the fathers [?] through him who was nailed upon you! Hail, cross, terror of the flaming sword, which turned its back through you to the grateful thief! Hail, cross, whom we, the faithful people, the holy nation, now hold and bring as our plea for mercy to Christ our God, who was fixed upon you! Therefore we greatly boast in you, for upon you our Master stretched out his immaculate hands, and upon you was poured out the divinely flowing blood of the Son and Word of the invisible Father. Those who piously partake of it today make propitiation to our life-giving God for the wrongs they have already committed, and we readily obtain release from them through his supreme condescension toward us and through the remembrance of his life-giving passion. Hail, cross, victory-bringing weapon of the great King! At his second and dread coming you will travel with the heavenly powers and the assemblies of all the righteous. They will shine with you like luminaries, announcing and preparing the way for the coming of the King of all creation. The working of his grace and inconceivable beauty, the glory stored up in you, which you received from Jesus who was nailed upon you, will then flash forth more plainly together with the righteous, to the shame of the Jews but to the boast of those who have beheld

your own divine workings while still in this thick and most heavy flesh. But, O precious cross, most secure guardian of Christians, most powerful destroyer of every hostile assault, illumine us with the radiance stored up in you; enlighten the eye of our heart, so that we too may choose to suffer something like what the Son and Word of the invisible Father suffered upon you—that we, for his sake, as he for ours, may lay down our lives even to death. For if we are willing to choose to suffer this, and to prefer this good and kindly [?] path, we shall be able easily to be conformed to his sufferings. Grant that, through the power of your workings, we may reach it [?] without condemnation and become worthy beholders and worshipers of the invincible authority of him who through you put death to death. Grant us also to behold with cheerful gladness the bright and light-bearing day of Pascha, as a pledge of the clearer and truer Pascha and for the enjoyment of those eternal goods. May we all share in them by the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father, together with his Holy Spirit, now and always, to the ages of ages. Amen.

1. Give us a voice, O voice of the Word; give us radiance, O lamp of the light; give us, O Forerunner of the Word, the course of our speech, so that, praising you worthily with your own gifts, we may delight in you today. For we are eager to sing your praises as a debt both inherited from our fathers and owed by ourselves more than by all others, O [?].

Since we have been enriched with your gifts more than all others, and cannot do this from our own resources, we run once more to you, the generous giver, and ask you to supply us with your praises. Otherwise, honoring you only with words of our own, we might seem to insult you by the meanness and unworthiness of our words rather than to praise and thank you. So it would seem to those who do not know our poverty of speech, but demand that the speech match the greatness and worth of the one honored. They grant no pardon to the speaker's intention, which cannot bear the flame of its longing if it is forced to lay hold of what is beyond it. For that those who would crown you with praises fall far, very far, short of your worth, no one would fail to proclaim with his whole mouth, unless he were mad and had lost his natural good sense. What, then, should one like me do? Every hour I am watered by your countless gifts, like a tree whose lot was to be planted by the waters, with the outpouring of your active stream flowing past it ceaselessly. Should such a one keep silent and cry out no thanksgiving at all, because he cannot do so worthily? Or should he cry out as far as he is able, and so show the irrepressible disposition within him, even if his cry, being small, cannot reveal its greatness? The latter is judged worthy of acceptance and is counted among the grateful, like that foreigner of another race among the ten lepers cleansed by the Savior. But the former joins the band of the ungrateful, because he does not praise his benefactor as far as he can, like those who received cleansing from their disease but gave no glory to Christ, who gave them that cleansing. 2. We must not keep silent, then, but must speak your praise with longing, even if we fall far behind your greatness, so that we may not reap the blame of those nine but may lay hold of the praiseworthy company of the one judged grateful. Cry out, then, O Baptist, now also in us, as once in the wilderness. For we too are a wilderness, bereft of word and voice and of the radiance that makes them sprout, from which and through which the wreath of praise is woven for you. Cry out now in us more loudly. For we shall cry out if you cry out, and we shall be silent if you are silent, even if we have chosen to cry out loudly. Our cry will count for nothing unless it takes its strength from your more divine cry; and nowhere on earth will our voice be heard unless we receive its resonance from your great voice. Therefore more and more we summon you to our aid and beg you to loosen our tongue, enslaved to speechlessness, as you once loosed your father Zacharias's tongue when you were born to him. We implore you to give us a voice to proclaim your praise, as at your birth you gave him a voice to announce your name publicly. For if his tongue was fettered until your coming forth loosed it, and the giving of your name set it moving, how could we move our tongue to praise you

unless you move it, turn it, and direct it toward your racecourse? 3. But my speech, having come to the starting line and standing amazed at the multitude of your wonders, is gripped by a greater perplexity: where should it begin its account of you? Should it tell first of the conception, which Gabriel announced beforehand as a prelude of joy for the world? Or of the pregnancy, which the barren old woman hid as something beyond nature? Or of the leaping in the womb, which first proclaimed to all that God was in the womb? Or of the delivery from a barren woman, which [the Virgin] longed to witness [?]? For she even made a three-day journey and stayed three months, so that, having seen your wondrous birth, she might believe firmly and steadfastly that she would be the virgin mother of the One of the Trinity whom she had conceived. Or of the nursing, when a breast dried up by deep old age wondrously poured forth milk for you? Or of the life in the wilderness, which the world could not contain? Or of your manifestation to Israel from the wilderness, last and first, through which you revealed Christ to them and proclaimed the kingdom of heaven? Or of the Jordan, in which you cleansed the people, and through which Christ cleansed you when he took you and made you the minister of his own baptism? Of the laws you kindly laid down for those who obeyed? Of the threat you weightily held over the disobedient? Of the boldness with which you struck rulers and kings with awe, which King Herod rightly dreaded, and whose fear he cast off through passion for a woman? Of the noble beheading and the removal of your precious head, by which you made yourself the Savior's forerunner twice over? For you not only went before him and ran ahead of him on earth; you also became his Forerunner in Hades to those who were waiting and watching there, just as on earth you had proclaimed beforehand his saving forgiveness. 4. But which of your deeds shall we take up first? Which shall we leave for second? Each has its share of excellence and rightly contends to be placed at the opening and to receive, in itself, the conclusion of this whole discourse of praise. None allows the tongue to pass on to any other story, lest it be left unfinished and incomplete. It seems best to us, then, to keep the order of time ourselves, so that what came first in time may now come first in our words. In this way the speech may take its fitting order, giving each event a suitable and brief account, and avoid the confusion of jumbling the times. In this we would be praising Laban the crafty, because he would not allow the younger of his daughters to be betrothed before the elder, even though the younger was the one desired and preferred by the man who married her, not only for her bodily but also for her spiritual beauty. Let our speech, then, return to its beginning and to the conception of the one we admire, as the prelude of his passage into being, and let it set out its praise of everything in order, one after another, as the very one we praise may consent to supply us with the words.

Perhaps, though, it would not be unprofitable to take the speech back even further than this. For in this way it would show that, even before this conception in the womb, he was destined to become someone great and would appear in expectation of greater goods, since our fall in Adam is not unknown. Through that fall we fared altogether wretchedly and ended in earth and corruption, since all of us, once and for all, were subject to the sentence "You are earth, and to earth you shall return"; for this was the condemnation our nature received for our disobedience. Nor was this the only misery shown in human life: godlessness was mixed in with it. For we abandoned the Creator and Master of the universe and worshiped created things, our fellow servants, and called the works of our own hands gods. Therefore we were enslaved to dishonorable passions, since we offered to dishonorable idols and demons the honor due to the only honorable God. This was the sickness of our nature. It could not have been greater, and it needed the greatest healing. And the healing was this: that the Creator should be made like us creatures, and God become man like us by uniting himself with human flesh, and take up in himself all our natural and blameless passions; and so display this complete separation [?], and thus manifestly save man, who had willingly been mastered by these things and was still mastered by them, and bring him back to the first blessedness with which he had joined him when he created him in the beginning. 5. God first promised Abraham that he would accomplish this, and granted that in his seed all the tribes of the earth would be blessed through the incarnation, from his line, of God's only-begotten Son and Word. After Abraham he swore this to David, and covenanted to set the King of glory, the fruit of his body, upon his most royal throne, when the present age should reach its end and the time he had appointed for the written law should come to its fulfillment. Not only Abraham and David, who were deemed worthy to receive such promises, but also many prophets and kings after them longed to see and behold it, as Christ himself, the desire of all the saints, declared in the Gospels to the blessed company of his own disciples. So the last times of the present age had arrived. The promise was receiving its fulfillment, each in its turn, and the law was receiving the fulfillment through Christ that it had awaited. All the prophets and righteous in Jerusalem who were awaiting the redemption of Israel, and who learned through the Spirit that it was at hand, longed to see its coming, not only with the eyes of the soul but also with those of the body, before they departed from this present life. And they not only longed for it but also prayed and offered petitions to God, and they obtained what they asked, for they were worthy. Such was Simeon, who as a priest received Christ in his arms and confessed him Master of all

creation. Such was Anna, who passed that long widowhood of hers in modesty and served God in the temple night and day; then, standing by in the prophetic Spirit, she revealed Christ as present to those who were there. Such was Joseph of Arimathea, the daring burier of the Life of all, who is proclaimed a "respected councilor" all the more for this: he rejected as shameful and unseemly the counsel of the Jews against the Savior. "For this man," it says, "had not consented to their counsel and purpose." But he alone counseled this deed as splendid and seemly, and he carried it out seemly and splendidly. Such too was Zacharias known to be, both an elder and a priest. Because his age was past its prime, and because death, which attends old age, comes without warning, he offered earnest and frequent petitions to God that he might not be deprived of the sight awaited by all, nor see the death he expected, already at the door, before he had seen that sight. The old man offered this petition constantly, praying on the one hand that the light of salvation might quickly shine on all, and asking on the other that he himself might see the dawning of this light. He interceded without ceasing that he might not be snatched away without sharing in that sight at the very time when it was flowering, and especially when he offered God the services prescribed by the law. He prayed that these might soon be exchanged for something more spiritual and perfect, and that the priestly divisions which bore the same yoke might be freed from its burden. Then, at the time of his division's service, [it fell to him] [?] to make the entry with incense into the Holy of Holies, where the high priest alone went in, once a year, bringing blood in his hands. By this figure he clearly showed the one and only offering of Christ the Savior that was to come, which he, as high priest and lamb, brought to God the Father, offering himself for us as a sacrifice on behalf of mankind. 6. So Zacharias came there, for he was worthy of such a service. He stood at the altar, and the Father had heard his persistent prayer concerning the coming of the Word. On the right side of the altar at which he was offering the fragrance of incense, he saw a heavenly angel standing, bringing him a favorable and heavenly message. This was Gabriel, the minister of these tidings, who by his very name, even before he spoke, made known his message; for he had come to announce the first beginnings of the divine incarnation of God the Word, for which the old man had earnestly prayed. The divine angel saw him shaken at the vision, his trembling increased by fear—"For Zacharias was troubled," it says, "when he saw him, and fear fell upon him"; for he pictured in himself the shaking of the law and foreshadowed its transfer to the gospel way of life. So the angel first removes the turmoil of his fear, and only then begins the good tidings. For what he said was not meant to cause fear, but to bring fearlessness and delight. What does he say? "Do not be afraid, Zacharias, for your prayer has been heard." As if crying out: Why are you afraid, old man? Why

[?] receiving an answer about the things you ask. Why are you afraid when you are being set free from [?] distress? Why are you troubled at seeing the shadow pass away? Why are you dismayed at seeing the things that are shaken removed? The things I am revealing are indeed awesome, but they are not meant to make those who hear them afraid. I have great mysteries to tell you, but as you listen closely to them you should not be gripped by [?] and fear. Rather, rejoice with me and be glad, for these things bring gladness and joy. The restoration of humankind is at hand; the raising up of the fallen has come; the end of the shadow [?] has arrived; the time of grace has dawned. Before long you will see with your own eyes the sum of all this: God the Word taking flesh from a Virgin, becoming man like us men, and the whole human race [being saved?]. And you will not only witness the things you longed to see, but you will also become a blessed servant of them. So that you may believe what I say, I lead you to faith by a strange wonder, telling you of things you no longer believed you would see. What are they? "Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John. He will be a joy and a delight to you, and many will rejoice at his birth. For he will be great before the Lord; he shall drink no wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb. He will turn many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God. He will go before him in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers to their children, and the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, to make ready for the Lord a people prepared."

7. Do you see what glories of John are attested by angelic voices even before his conception in the womb? Samuel too was born of a barren woman, but not of an old woman, nor of an aged and elderly father. Isaac too was born of parents who were old and past the time and the strength for bearing children, but he was not filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother's womb. Nor was any of them adorned with all the other graces that adorned John even before his birth. Samuel was a prophet, and was rightly called a seer, for he saw things to come as if they were present; and he drank neither wine nor strong drink. But he did not live in the desert, nor did he live on food unknown to other men. Nor did his birth bring joy to many, as did the birth of John, the greatest [?], who ran ahead of the joy of the whole world, being born before it as its forerunner. Joseph the most wise was also the fruit of a barren woman, and so, before him, was blessed Jacob, who fathered him by the barren Rachel. Joseph was certainly chaste, for he set up an admirable trophy of chastity against [?]. But he did not become a general of virginity as John did. How great the difference is between virginity and chastity is proclaimed by the very ranks of these virtues, and by that place better than sons and daughters which is given there only to those who in soul and

body have honored virginity in Christ, and who have become imitators of the immaculate Virgin who bore him. The Saviour himself made this plain to all when he said that not everyone can receive it (the gift of virginity, I mean), but only those whom Jesus has prepared as worthy, according to divine foreknowledge. Jacob too was loved by God while he was still living in his mother's womb, for a divine voice said to her who carried him, "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." Yet he was not filled with the Holy Spirit while he was carried in the womb. He was able to wrestle with God all night long, for the night of ignorance of God was then spread over everyone. But he could not run before God and baptize God, which John alone among men dared to do. For by then the dawn of the knowledge of God had risen, and the brightness of the true day was already shining. And after the wrestling, the one whom no one could throw limped on his thigh, because of those who would be born of him from his thigh, and could no longer run swiftly at all. By this riddle he plainly foreshadowed their slowness and sluggishness toward the divine grace that was coming to dwell in the world, and the utterly ruinous lameness that would show itself in them as a result. John suffered nothing of this lameness, although he was descended from Jacob as they were. Instead he became a swift runner toward grace and a Forerunner who outran Jewish unbelief, leaving far behind the things of night

[?] for comparison. For he too was born of a barren woman, appeared as the fruit of prayer to God, and never cut his hair: "No razor," it says, "came upon his head" [?]. He was also adorned with certain other divine gifts. But Delilah, that little harlot, has again overpowered him mightily even now, and will not let him follow us to John. All these men were indeed great before the Lord, but they are not seen to have turned many of the sons of Israel to the Lord their God. They did not go before Christ God in the power and spirit of Elijah. They are not shown to have turned the hearts of fathers to their children, that is, the hearts of those raised under the law to those born under grace. They did not lead the Jews out of disobedience into the wisdom of the just, those justified in Christ. They did not prepare a people made ready for the Lord who shone forth on earth. Nor did they possess anything greater than these. For what is greater than to see the Lord in the flesh and to baptize him in the waters? They did have their birth from barren mothers, and they flourished with certain other advantages, great if compared with the virtues of others, but very small if they dared to be measured against the gifts of John. Faced with these, because of their unsurpassable greatness, Zacharias, who was then about to be shown as the father of John, was struck in his mind as if before something impossible, and received the sting of unbelief. Wounded by it, he said to the blessed angel those words of [?]

[?] sought his downfall, saying, "How shall I know this?" He knew that the devil is a liar from the beginning and does not know how to speak the truth, and that, having lied the first time and been fully believed in his lie, he would have no trouble lying a second time, so as to carry off captive by greater deceptions the one he had caught with his first assaults. But Zacharias, the father of the great John, was no such simpleton—far from it! Nor did this sweetest fruit, John, spring from so foolish a root. Perhaps that is also why he was fed on honey: because he is sweet, most sweet, to all who love the exceptional life, and through a divine delight he calls and urges them to imitate him [?]. Rather, as we said, I think the old man underwent an ecstasy like Isaac of old, so that he might foreshow the silence of the law and the unbelief of those under the law, and foretell the thunder of the Gospel resounding through all the ends of the earth, and the faith of the nations under grace.

10. So the great priest disbelieves in a mystical sense, and in a still more mystical sense he is deprived of the use of speech, because of the senselessness of Jewish unbelief. And from him John comes forth as Forerunner of the Word, bearing in himself the virtue of his father, since a tree is known by its fruit, and a rotten tree cannot bear good fruit, according to that divine and God-given saying. For if anyone refuses to understand the old man's unbelief in this way, Zacharias will turn out to be far inferior in virtue to Elizabeth. She had heard nothing of these things, since the old man was speechless toward her; yet she [?] on seeing the blessed Virgin coming to her, and on hearing the Virgin's greeting she at once proclaimed her Theotokos, crying with a loud voice: "Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, when the sound of your greeting came to my ears, the babe leapt for joy in my womb." And she rightly called her blessed, saying, "Blessed is she who believed that there would be a fulfillment of what was spoken to her from the Lord." For she not only recognized by the Spirit that Mary was with child, but was also rich in knowledge of what God had spoken to her through the angel's voice. That Zacharias should be inferior to her would be utterly incredible and implausible. For Zacharias's perfection before God is shown not only by the angel being sent to him, the angel who graced such events on earth with his announcement; and not only by his becoming the father of John the Baptist, and by his being honored with kinship to Christ—"For behold," says the very angel who brought the good news to the holy Virgin, "Elizabeth your kinswoman"—but also by what he sang prophetically after John's birth, when he foretold the things concerning Christ, crying out: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and brought redemption to his people, and has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old"; and by the other things about him that he added to these, which he [was granted?] to see even before his death [?].

11. It is shown likewise by what he prophesied about his own child toward the end of the song, saying: "And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways, to give knowledge of salvation to his people in the forgiveness of our sins, through the tender mercy of our God." He did not speak these words from his own heart, but because he had been filled with the Holy Spirit. For this is what is written about him in the Gospels: "And Zacharias his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying"—saying what? Clearly, the words we quoted above. It is obvious that this Zacharias would not have been so plainly filled with the Holy Spirit unless he had been faithful to the Spirit and worthy of its longed-for fullness, and that he would not have been called the father of John unless he had been equal to that dignity as well. Let all these things, then, stand before John's conception, showing that even before his conception he was greater than all those born of women—just as Christ, the Truth, truly bore this witness to him—so that no one might suppose him inferior to any man on the ground that he was not born of great parents. The Gospel text, taking care of this, I think, used the passage set out about him beforehand to forestall the suspicion of those who would come to suspect it, saying plainly: "And they were both righteous before God, walking blameless in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord." What then? That the Gospel's verdict should choose Zacharias and Elizabeth as John's parents, and testify that they had reached the very citadel of virtue, is to behold what is most excellent among men. For that impartial verdict not only granted them righteousness but added "before God." For they strove to appear righteous to God alone by the laws of the Gospel, foreseeing them with prophetic eye as though already laid down. They tried to live by the rule of hiding the right hand from the left, anticipating in work and deed the command of that legislation. And the verdict plainly adds the blameless fulfillment of all the Mosaic commandments and ordinances together, to show that those who kept this lawful life excelled in both respects: they were crowned with the glories of the old legislation and made radiant by the heights of the Gospel way of life.

12. For it was necessary and fitting that John's parents should be seen to be such people, since the one born of them was to be shown to us as the mediator of both Testaments, truly holding within himself what is excellent in both. For it is agreed that he was marked out as the end of the Older—he completed the number of the prophetic choir, since all the prophets prophesied until John the Baptist—and as the beginning and prelude of the Newer. For of all the apostles he [?], since he was sent with the dignity of the holy angels to go before Christ and run ahead of him. He was commanded to go before him as God's messenger. "And from the days

of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force." For it took its beginning from him, suffers violence through the Gospel way of life, and is willingly seized by all. So then, from a father who was priest and prophet and in every way illustrious and godly-minded, in the womb of a holy mother who was a prophetess, this John, who surpasses all the prophets, is conceived. He alone prophesied in the womb, since he [recognized?] the Master present in the virginal womb. He alone, while in the womb, became pregnant with the Holy Spirit, both carrying and carried: carried by a barren mother, and carrying the grace of the Spirit. He was in prophetic labor before he himself was labored for, and before he was born he gave birth to the gift of the Spirit—if indeed, according to the divine Isaiah, those who serve the Spirit as prophets conceive in the womb and travail and then give birth, proclaiming his hidden counsel openly. But John did these things later, after his own wondrous conception: for he was conceived in a barren womb, and was begotten by an aged father in an aged mother. Until then he keeps still—by force, but still obeying his mother's command. For he did not want to carry the grace of the Spirit idle, the grace with which, according to the angel's word, he was filled while still in the womb. Then that five-month period passed, which signifies for us the law of the senses, through the corresponding and congenial number five of the bodily and swifter senses. During those months the mother hid herself, as one become a mother, and hid along with herself this prophet who could not keep silent.

13. Then the sixth month came, and the Virgin came too, carrying in her womb the Uncreated One being formed. For in the sixth month she conceives the one who in six days made the six-day world, who on the sixth day created man, and who through the cross created him anew when he had fallen into ruin. John could no longer bear to keep still; with the Word present, the voice would not consent to stay quiet. He became a herald before his time, his proclamation in no way hindered by the bonds of his tongue. By his leaping he cried out that the one who redeems us men from our bonds was present. He rejoiced, crying out in the Spirit, at the one who grants us to leap as if freed from our bonds, who has come to wipe away every tear from every face and to give lasting joy to the whole race. He stretched out his finger and pointed out the Lamb of God, slain for us in place of the goats offered for sin, who takes away completely the sin of the world. He stretched out both hands and proclaimed in advance the trophy of the cross, which the one present in the Virgin's womb had come to set up against the demons. He stood upright, and by his posture he mystically sang of the resurrection of all from Hades. He showed that the one then hidden in a womb without seed would be hidden in a tomb. And perhaps he would have fought with his mother, because when he longed to cry out such things she hindered him with natural

bonds and held him captive against his will, had she not quickly lent him her voice and allowed him to say plainly to the blessed Virgin through her: "Blessed is the fruit of your womb. And why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" For perhaps this is John's own proclamation, even if it was proclaimed by Elizabeth's mouth. For he cried out to Christ the Saviour with a kindred voice and in the same words when Christ came to him again at the Jordan, while he was baptizing the crowd, to be baptized by him. Then too, as he saw him approaching, he cried out: "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" Do you recognize the kinship of the voices? Recognize, then, that it was he who uttered both: the one through himself, the other through his mother's mouth.

14. I imagine that he who was so eager to proclaim Christ silently appealed to the one who had sent him, against her who carried him and hindered his course: "Master, you sent me to proclaim your ineffable coming on earth, and my mother holds me in fetters. You command me to cry out, and she has bound my tongue. You sent me to run ahead, and she has shut off my course. You are the Master of nature: command, and nature will do what is commanded. Only give the order, and my mother cannot hinder me; only say the word, and what you say will happen at once. For your power runs together with your will, and all things serve your almighty decree. But if you do not command me to do this, do not condemn me for slackness in running, since it was you who decreed the hindrance to my running. For you yourself set the bounds of nature, which those who serve nature [?] cannot overstep." But despite John's eagerness to preach, the Master ordered nothing contrary to the nature well decreed for him from the beginning, whose laws he himself, having become man like us for our sake, deigned to serve along with us. Perhaps here too he answered him with the words he spoke later, when he came to be baptized: "Let it be so now, for it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." Hearing this, as is likely, John kept still and dared speak no more, although he was very eager to come out of the womb that held him before the time appointed for all who are conceived, and to begin the proclamation given him by God. And so, while for three more months he saw the Creator dwelling with him and submitting to the same laws of nature, the time of his birth arrived. For the Virgin who carried the Lord stayed with Elizabeth for those three months, so that the one coming forth from her, sent to the world as a true herald, might be fully initiated into the mysteries of the supreme Trinity in his mother's womb, as in the cloud of Moses. And he is born by the ordinance of God, who lay hidden in the virginal womb.

15. Once born, he at once ended his mother's reproach, which she had borne on the charge of childlessness. But he did not loosen the bridle on his father's tongue, which his father had received for stumbling into unbelief. And to all who saw him the child was

[?] beyond dispute. His mother, her soul illumined by the Spirit, wanted him to be called John. The name is spoken in Hebrew, but rendered into Greek it means grace and presence of God. But the kinsfolk, friends and nurslings of the synagogue, hearing the prophetic name and supposing that the grace of God the Father was present to the world, rejected it, shunned it together with its meaning, and indeed tried and wanted to change it, and said rather boldly to the mother: "There is no one among your kindred who is called by this name." For those who made up the Jewish kinship were [?]. But he, asking for a tablet by a sign, since he could not speak, inscribed: "John is the child's name." And he not only wrote this on the wax; while he was writing the letters, he also cried out the words, showing by the movement of his hand that the movement of his tongue was running alongside it, and showing by the running pen that his speech was running with it. The blessed evangelist, wishing to indicate this, said more expressively: "And asking for a tablet, he wrote, saying, 'John shall be his name.'" For he wrote and spoke at the same time, and let them see tongue and hand at work simultaneously. He did not write without speaking, or speak without writing; he spoke and wrote equally. His hand ran below, and his speech flowed above; neither claimed victory over the other, but both, as friends, greeted the turning-post of the course together. It was as if both had run out from the starting gates and both received crowns of victory at the finish, neither willing to admit defeat. At this everyone marveled, for what happened was truly worthy of wonder. And if those who marveled at it then marveled only at the bodily event, since it appeared to them only in bodily form, yet for those initiated by the Spirit the things of the Spirit will not stop at what is seen. The text shows that it holds something hidden; let us search it out by the Spirit and trace it spiritually. And when we have hunted it out—clearly with the help of the lamp that sends its radiance down to us—let us set it before you, the children of the Spirit, as spiritual food.

16. We said that the name John means grace of God, since he was sent as the forerunner of that grace, as its good herald. And the grace of God is believed to be the Word of God, who for our sake, weighed down as we were with the shames of sin, was manifested in the flesh like us. He redeemed us from those shames and filled us with his own glory and grace. In this way, as God of all, as propitiator and ruler, he shone upon all alike—Jews, Greeks, barbarians, the unlearned, the wise, the unwise, slaves, masters—and set before all, equally, the radiance of his love for mankind. This is so even though he was born according to the flesh from the Jews, because of the promise and covenant made to Abraham the patriarch, who had his birth from the nations but became father of the Jewish race. "For," says the most wise Paul, "is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not the God of the Gentiles also?" For God is truly the God of the Gentiles as well.

since God is one and only, “who will justify the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith.” He was showing, then, that divine grace would appear equally and alike to both of these. Again Zechariah, moved by the prophetic Spirit, brought forward the wondrous name of John both by word and by letter. By making the two utterances match each other, he showed that one grace of adoption will be given to all who turn to it, whether from the law or from the nations, and who [?] and receive it with true faith and purity of soul. “For as many as received him,” it says, “to them he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.” For it is plain that the Jews were signified by the letter on the tablet, since they serve the letter of the law, while the nations were signified by the Word and Spirit of the mouth, since they share more fully in the Word and have come over to the Spirit of the law. For the law itself was known to be twofold: one part fleshly and in the letter, the other rational and in the spirit. Interpreted for us in this way, this is the reason [?] for this Gospel mystery of John's double, and at the same time mystical, naming. We could not have found it out from them by ourselves. John himself pointed it out, the unquenchable lamp who flashes forth and lights up hidden things. So now we marvel more than they did, for they of old marveled only at what they saw. In this way John comes forth into life, running ahead with leaps before the Sun of righteousness, like a morning star in its radiance. He is most brilliant and astonishes everyone by the greatness of his own brightness. That brightness was granted him by the great, conspicuous and inseparable advance of the Sun, which rose immediately after him with surpassing radiance and the utmost light and brilliance. 17. This child was born and called John, and by his own name he made known the power of the One who would be born after him from the Virgin. He loosens the tongue of the one who begot and named him, and of the law, a tongue that until then had been enslaved to the bonds of slow speech. And the voice gives a voice to the heavy-voiced law and father, so that they might loudly proclaim the Word who would appear after him, the Word who also drives away the heaviness of voice that belonged to Moses the lawgiver. For when the voice was born before the Word, how could the one who had begotten it be held fast by voicelessness? Or how could his tongue be pressed in the bonds of wordlessness, when the Word was on the very point of coming forth and being born? For it is plain that after John, the voice, Jesus, who is the Word, freed the tongue of the law from the bonds of slow speech. Its hidden things, and those of the prophetic promise, had been sealed. He gave it a great and well-measured voice, driving away its former apparent voicelessness, and by the manifestation of his own brilliance he removed the voicelessness that had invisibly oppressed it before. This is why both things were mystically fulfilled in Zechariah, who was at that time priest and prophet, since he clearly represented both. By his priesthood he represented the law, and by his old age the antiquity of the law; by his

gift of prophecy he represented the assembly of the prophetic age. “For his mouth was opened at once,” it says, “and his tongue, and he spoke, blessing God.” And truly, when Christ, who is the Word and Wisdom of the Father, appeared on earth to those on earth, the seal of the prophetic mouth was unsealed and the bond of the legal tongue was loosed. Both alike, the law and the prophets, openly speak the mystery of Christ and bless him as God before the ages, striving together and [?] with the proclamation of the Gospel. Because of this, the gathering of those who were present then and of the neighbors who lived there were seized with great fear and talked anxiously about him. They kept asking themselves what John would be, and who, because at his birth such wondrous things had [?] as we have not known to happen to anyone else. 18. But I will answer their question: no one else like him had been born of a woman up to his time, and so such wondrous and unexpected things happened as well. Since he has been declared greater than those born of women, he was for this very reason found worthy of such great glory, so that by it he might glorify Christ, who would be born after him for our sake. Christ not only clothed his own Forerunner with this glory that came through wonders. He was also invisibly present with him as God, and made him appear great and glorious before all. For the narrative of the Gospel says this about these things: “And fear came upon all who lived around them, and all these things were talked about through all the hill country of Judea. And all who heard them laid them up in their hearts, saying, ‘What then will this child be?’ And the hand of the Lord was with him.” For the hand of the Lord, the only-begotten Word of God, was in no way prevented from being with him by his divinity and magnifying him as his first and greatest herald. He himself has been called the right hand and the hand and the arm of God, since the Father does through him all things that come to be, even though he had been conceived in the flesh in a virgin womb and lay there royally as in a bridal chamber. So John, at his birth, was shown to surpass all who are born of women. He brought forth very great fear, not only in those who lived with him, who were of one mind and longed for Christ's divine appearing among us, but also in those who lived around them. These remained outside grace because they dwelt in the written letter of the law, from which they can hardly be torn away. For I think these people “live around” us, because they accept the law only in part and keep in line with the letter alone. For this reason we have put them out of the house, and they have been removed from the grace of the law as it is spiritually understood. So the wretched people were cast out, through their own ill will, from the life hidden in the law. But its herald and Forerunner, born with such power, is nursed, and after he is weaned he goes out into the desert. He renounces entirely all life among men, as unworthy of his conduct and way of life, which were above the human. For how could one who had nothing groveling or

human about him have lived with men in cities or villages? He had no house, no food, no shelter, no friendship, no dealings, no [?] for kin, no union with a woman, nothing else of what goes on in villages and cities. He goes out, but not in emulation of Moses, excellent as Moses was, though he is taught divine things more than Moses, returns as a lawgiver, redeems a wandering people, and leads well toward piety a people cruelly oppressed by spiritual Egyptians. Nor does he imitate Elijah of old, who worked great wonders on earth, though he is called a new Elijah and goes forth in the spirit and power of Elijah. He too returns to chasten Herod, the new Ahab, is persecuted by Herodias, another Jezebel, and is killed in that persecution. Yet he set neither of these men before himself as the goal of his own life, for the godly and the self-controlled usually compete not with those inferior in virtue but with their betters. Nature did not allow anyone greater than John to be seen among men. I mean among males, because of the all-holy Virgin and venerable Mother of God, who is above all human beings, female and male. Nor did Christ allow anyone greater to be imagined. So it is clear that he imitated no human beings but the heavenly angels when he went out into the desert, since he had also been counted worthy of their name. 19. It was right that he, the only embodied angel ever to appear on earth, should enter into this good and God-loving rivalry with them. He shared in their heavenly dignity, and he would offer Christ a service equal to theirs when Christ was baptized in the streams of the Jordan, as well as all the other ministry that he carried out like an angel throughout his earthly life. With such longing, then, John left his father's hearth and dwelt in the desert as in some lofty and heavenly place. In this riddle he let all see that the grace of God, Christ, would leave the synagogue of his fathers, which had begotten him according to the flesh, and would dwell in the desert Church of the nations. He would do this not for a time but forever, until he appears again a second time from heaven with great glory and power and is revealed to the true Israel. “And the child grew and became strong in spirit, and he was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel.” Those endowed with the wisdom of the Fathers know this. When Christ said to the Jews [?], “Behold, your house is left to you desolate,” he made the desert Church of the nations his own house. He counts those who are called as his own body and is set over them as their head. “For we are the body of Christ, and members in part,” and we have him as head, as the chosen vessel says in his teaching. He grows, making our growth his own, the growth of the members and the body. And he who strengthens our spiritual strength grows strong in spirit, counting this strength as his own because he counts us as his own. And when it says that he was in the deserts, it shows [?] well.

For it says this more emphatically to show that Christ is not, and does not come to be, in one nation only, as formerly in Israel alone, but in all the nations and in the Churches formed from them. This is why in many places in Scripture they are named in the plural and signified figuratively: sometimes as high mountains, sometimes as hills, sometimes as springs, at other times as islands of the nations, and elsewhere as ships of Carthage. You, then, O blessed Baptist, took to the deserts in this way and for these reasons, as far as I have been able to understand and express it. (I will call you Christ's baptizer, even though the Word has not yet shown you doing this.) In a more mystical way you were announcing to the deserts the saving coming of divine grace that would soon reach them. 20. I intend to follow you with my discourse, but I am held back and firmly prevented. One reason is human weakness. I am not ashamed to tell you the truth, since you knew it even before I spoke. The other reason is that the time of the holy liturgy has come, as you see. It compels all of us to keep to it and does not allow us to go with you to your beloved desert. To neglect it even briefly would be neither acceptable to you, nor possible for me, nor fitting for your festival. So I ask your pardon and beg you to remain with us in spirit, even if in body you go off to the desert, and to grant your help without ceasing to those of us who unceasingly take this festival in hand [?]. No place prevents you from helping once you have consented, since you are present in heaven in spirit and easily watch over us all. Grant that we may celebrate this venerable festival of yours with fitting delight, in a way that is dear to you, the Forerunner of grace, and suited to your way of life, which was so pleasing to God. Guide and protect the rest of this present life in the way the law of the Spirit commands, for you have been set before us as its type in Christ. Then, made doers of that law by your inspiration, may we be called by Christ, the giver of this life, when we depart from life here, into one of the cities subject to you, which [?] promised to give to you and to the divine men who came after you. For I will not dare to say, as you did, [?] as one who has briefly obeyed your holy laws here as well [?]. So may we too come to be in those cities, joined [?] to you as our shield-bearer and guardian, lawgiver and teacher of the [?] way of life, and to your fellow servants who finished their course here, and to the true [?]. And may we become sharers in the eternal life laid up for you, in Jesus our Lord, through whom be glory, honor and might to God the Father with the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages.

Of our father among the saints Sophronius, archbishop of Jerusalem, on the holy Peter and Paul, the blessed apostles, on the fourth day of the Nativity. 1. Again an indissoluble pair has shone upon us. Again an inseparable yoke has blossomed for us. Again an undivided couple [?] has flowed forth for us. The apostolic [?] have run together into one feast and festival. They brighten us with a double radiance, appearing in the one brilliance of the sun's light. For today we have Peter, the chief of the apostles, and Paul, who is Peter's equal in grace and like him in the dignity of apostleship. Paul was not one of that holy twelve of the [?] apostles, whose election and calling no mere man devised. No prophet did so, no patriarch, no righteous man, and no heavenly and bodiless angel. All of these are servants, and fellow servants with us human beings, even if they greatly surpass us in virtues and in spiritual dignities and graces. It was Christ himself who did it, the Master of all, at once God and Lord. He is twofold in nature and single in hypostasis. He is composed of divine and human nature and is clearly known in divine and human essence. Yet he is in no way divided into them and admits no division whatever, because of the unchangeable and indivisible union. He did not confuse the natures from which he is, though he united them to each other according to hypostasis. Nor did he separate from each other the natures in which he is, though in them he is perfectly known as God and man, one and the same, contemplated in himself. He knows hearts and reins and sees the counsels of the invisible soul, which each man plans secretly in his heart, even if he seems, like a thief, to escape the notice of those who share his nature. 2. So, caring for our salvation, for whose sake he came down to us from heaven, he chose fishermen and distributed to them the grace of apostleship. This grace was counted out according to their number, yet it neither divided their dignity nor confused their order. Instead, within the unity of apostolic dignity and grace, it preserved the difference of order. For the Wisdom and Power of God, the Word, who knows best of all that can be known, judged it good that the dignity of apostleship be kept one and that the difference of order be recognized without confusion. So order would not turn into disorder,

for disorder is hateful to God; nor would the grace of the dignity be cut up into unequal graces, for the gifts are irrevocable, and the boundary that he sets will in no way be passed, as the psalm says. He governs all things by balance and weight and gives his gifts to each by a counsel that shows no partiality. He made a first election of twelve apostles and a second of seventy-two disciples. Then, after his ascent into heaven from earthly affairs, which took place because of the flesh he took from us (for before he was without flesh and without body, as [?]), he reveals a third election as well. In this way he [?] well the number of the apostles without [?] the apostleship. For God, the potter of us all, has authority over the clay and over what he forms, to make vessels and bring them forth as he wishes, and no one opposes his counsels. When he plainly chose Paul, he spoke to Ananias, Paul's baptizer and teacher. Ananias enlightened him when he had been blinded [?], baptized him once enlightened, and once baptized taught him the divinely inspired teaching. Christ said: “Go” to give him divine instruction and also to restore his sight, “for this man is a chosen vessel of mine, to carry my name before nations and kings and the sons of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.” Paul himself, that wonderful man, showed how he was appointed to his own dignity when he wrote that “he who worked in Peter for the circumcision worked also in me for the nations.” 3. The Savior's appointment by election, then, joined the godly Paul to Peter, the first of the apostles and heralds, and gave one dignity to both, even though it put forward the one as apostle to those of the circumcision and allotted the other to the flocks of the gentiles. To those who turn through him to him as Christ he gave one grace and God-given dignity, I mean the adoption as children of God the Begetter. And he graciously bestowed one name on both, so that they are called Christians after Christ himself. So it is fitting that we too, their disciples and followers, who keep their faith and embrace their teaching, have joined to each other those whom the grace of the Spirit joined. We hold a common festival for them, since they received a common and equally glorious appointment. And we keep one feast to Christ, since one spiritual brightness flashes upon us through them both. Those who begot us in Christ decreed that it is not without danger to separate from each other those whom Christ himself fitted together and adorned with one grace. That is why they appointed one festival for them, so that they would not seem to fight against Christ's decree. We, the least of all, hasten to follow them in everything, and we come together in a common gathering and assemble [?]. In this way we honor most clearly their

union. For where Peter the chief is proclaimed, Paul too is named at once, and wherever Paul, the man of God, appears, Peter too is shown in his company. 4. So these wise and divine men form an ineffable companionship with each other. They [?] wish to be separated. They turn away from partition, avoid divisions, flee from cuts and have no love for separations, since these are offspring of hatred and bulwarks of enmity. Through this they wish to teach us the benefit of spiritual love and the usefulness of friendship according to Christ. For what is not done according to Christ our God can bring no benefit to those who do it. This is why both of them, teaching us the benefit of love and imprinting its working in themselves, also keep a common festival. One of them knew that the bond of love toward one another cannot fail. He defined love as greater than all the gifts, since it does not know how to work evil against a neighbor: “For love,” he says, “works no evil to the neighbor.” He commands those who have put on love to bear with one another. More than this, he orders them not to seek their own things but to care for their neighbor out of love. Love makes those who share in it one body and one Spirit. It places them in one hope of their calling and shows them to be sharers in eternal life. The other [?] says: “Having purified your souls by obedience to the truth for unfeigned brotherly love, love one another earnestly from the heart. And as servants of God, honor all; love the brotherhood.” He knew that love makes us brothers to one another. For this reason he also commands us above all to keep our love for one another earnest, because he declared plainly that love covers a multitude of sins. 5. But we strive to do the opposite of what they teach. Not only do we not wish to love one another; we would even like to hate our neighbors as enemies. It seems we do not know that enmity and hatred are offspring of the evil spirit. So we wrong our neighbors, afflict them, shoot countless slanders at them and work every kind of evil against them, once we have been left bereft of love, which, according to the all-wise Paul, works no evil to the neighbor. For truly the work of love [?]

…we have been [?] with the anointing of faith. Let us stop doing harm to one another, and let us share with them the heavenly rewards of love. Then we will be called their true disciples, and be their children and be known as their sons, because we hold fast to their love, honour their commands exactly, and corrupt nothing at all of their sacred teachings.

6. But why do these wise and supremely great men act as they do now? They come forward for us to see plainly after the most excellent Stephen, and of their own will they choose the fourth place. Yet by the dignity of their leading apostleship and appointment they take precedence not only over Stephen, the illustrious protomartyr, but over all God-loving men together, and they surpass them in greatness. For it is well known that the brilliance and radiance of a martyr fall far short of the splendour and standing of an apostle. They gave Stephen his festival on the third day after Christ's saving birth and kept the fourth for themselves, because they remembered the Master's commands and wished to fulfil them here too. To those who wish to take first place and who seek the greater dignities, he ordained that they take the last place, and he said to them plainly something like this: "Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be last of all"; and, "Whoever wishes to be first among you, let him be your slave"; and again, "Let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." Moreover, those who were called last to work in the vineyard were the first to receive their wages. Because they know this clearly, they take the second place and give the first place to the divine Stephen. In this way they most justly become first, and by their own example they teach us the best road to exaltation. I mean lowliness and humility, the road that Christ was the first to cut by practising it. By their deeds they are saying, "Learn from us, for we are meek and humble of heart," in keeping with the command of Christ, our Master and Teacher. For this reason one of them told us to regard one another as better than ourselves, and the other wants us to clothe ourselves with humility toward one another: "For God," he says, "opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble." That is why he adds to this teaching: "Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation." Most beloved brothers, since we are called their hearers and disciples, let us join imitation to learning and deeds to hearing the word, and let us take from them love for one another. Then, eager to imitate them in word and deed, bearing their likeness, and celebrating their feast in a way that is like them, we may gladden our souls and spirits and brighten with our senses

their most radiant festival. When they see this they rejoice and exult all the more, and with joy and delight they offer prayers to God on our behalf, interceding for a peaceful life for us and asking for the kingdom of heaven for us. May all of us order ourselves as we ought, make ourselves radiant with divine repentance, and bind ourselves tightly with the bond of love. Then may we reap the joys and radiance of that kingdom and receive the ageless and unending life, in Christ Jesus our Lord, with whom be glory, honour, might, majesty and praise to God the Father and the all-holy Spirit, always, now and ever, and to the ages of ages. Amen.

From the encomium of Sophronius, most holy archbishop of Jerusalem, on Saint John the Theologian and Evangelist, which begins, "John"

ON CONFESSIONS, FROM SAINT SOPHRONIUS OF JERUSALEM.

There are many kinds of confession. One person confesses of his own will, another because of temptation or illness. Some people avoid those who are [?] and versed in Scripture, and run instead to the unlearned. But a sick man treated by a proven physician benefits in one way, and a sick man treated by someone with no experience of medicine in quite another. Confession also takes different forms for rulers, for soldiers, for the rich, for the poor and needy, for the old and for the young. It takes different forms for the clergy, for monks, for those in a coenobium, for hesychasts and for anchorites. The one who receives penitents must know all of these exactly. A proven physician knows and understands, for every pain, ache and suffering, the right herbs, purgatives, drying powders and remedies for healing wounds. In the same way, those who receive confessions must know what a disease of the soul is, what a sickness of the mind, what a disturbance of the heart and what a bodily passion. They must know what fornication of the mind is, what adultery of the soul, what the breezes of the understanding and the fannings of the conscience are. They must know what sin is, what injustice, what greed, what falsehood and what perjury. Someone who argues doctrine with heretics without knowing what essence and nature are, what hypostasis and individual person are, or what difference, quality and property are, harms himself and does not benefit others. The same is true of those who receive confessions. They have not treated their own passions. They have not used the herbs, purgatives and ointments of Scripture to purge the bile of sin, the phlegm of injustice and the stench of greed from their own souls and bodies. They have not healed their own weakness, and

they have not had mercy on themselves. How can they have mercy on others and help them? They do not know the divine canons and falsify them out of vainglory and the desire to please people. In this way they have put those who confess to them to death spiritually, teaching one thing in place of another, and they have sent sinners away still loaded with the burden of death. On the day of judgement the impartial Judge will require the blood of those who confessed from such teachers.

If anyone bathes after receiving the Body and Blood of the Lord, let him be accursed.

If someone is fasting in order to receive communion and water accidentally gets into his mouth while he is washing or bathing, he shall not stay away from communion, so that Satan may not find a pretext for keeping him from it.

Whoever undoes the arrangements made by his parents, whether they are living or dead, let him be anathema.

Whoever pulls his parents' hair, strikes them in the face or simply despises them, whether during their life or at their death, let him be accursed.

If anyone does not allow the poor to gather the ears of grain that fall, let him be accursed.

If anyone gives soothsayers a ransom-offering and receives a written charm, or chants incantations, let him be accursed.

If anyone does not give the firstfruits of the threshing floor and the winepress to the Church and to the poor, let him be accursed.

If anyone slanders a brother, he is condemned along with the devil.

If a monk gets drunk, he has committed fornication. If he vomits from gluttony, he has committed fornication. If a monk laughs in public, he has committed fornication. If he answers back to his abbot, he has committed fornication.

If any monk takes off his belt in his bed and sleeps like that, let him do 150 prostrations.

Whoever prays with an excommunicated person, let him also be excommunicated. Whoever prays with a heretic, in church or in a house, let him also be excommunicated. Whoever prays with a deposed cleric, let him also be deposed. Whoever shares communion with excommunicated people, let him also be excommunicated.

A bishop, presbyter or deacon who takes on worldly business is deposed.

A cleric does not stand surety for anyone; if he does, he is deposed.

A priest who strikes a believer or an unbeliever is deposed.

Whoever becomes a priest by means of money shall be deposed together with the one who ordained him, as happened with Simon.

A priest who demands interest is deposed if he does not stop.

A priest who plays dice and gets drunk, let him be deposed if he does not stop.

If anyone puts away his own wife and marries another, let him be excommunicated.

A cleric who eats in a tavern without the necessity of travel is to be excommunicated.

Whoever mocks a lame, blind or deaf person, or someone otherwise maimed in body, is excommunicated, because he is finding fault with the one who formed that person.

A bishop who does not teach piety is excommunicated, and he is deposed if he goes on failing to teach.

A bishop who does not provide for a cleric in need is excommunicated.

Whoever rapes an unbetrothed virgin and defiles her is excommunicated. He shall not be allowed to marry another woman, but must keep the one he chose, even if she is poor.

A cleric who tastes meat sacrificed to idols, strangled, killed by wild beasts or dead of itself is deposed; a layman who does so is excommunicated.

A man who is lame or blind in one eye may become a bishop if he is worthy, but a blind or deaf man shall not.

(1) The sense requires: "not knowing the divine canons, falsifying them out of vainglory and the desire to please people."

…they decided that people who are unsure whether or not they were baptized should be baptized, so that their doubt does not deprive them of the divine cleansing.

An altar set up in a field or in a vineyard with no relic of martyrs placed in it, let it be overturned. Altars set up because of dreams and revelations are also to be overturned. The devil is darkness but pretends to be light, and he lures people's souls under a show of piety.

If anyone is found tonsuring someone without the abbot present who is to receive that person into obedience, let him be deposed, and let the one who was tonsured be handed over to obedience and to a monastery.

If a cleric commits fornication, he is removed from the rank of the priesthood. He is not barred from divine communion, but receives communion with the laity.

The divine mysteries must not be given to those who take interest, and one must not eat with them while they persist in this transgression.

Whether a man who has had a nocturnal emission ought to receive communion: if it came from desire for a woman, he ought not. But if it came from Satan tempting him, let him partake of the divine mysteries, because otherwise the tempter will never stop attacking him at the very time when he is due to receive communion.

If it is not possible to go to church, O bishop, you shall hold the assemblies at home, so that the pious do not enter a church of the impious. It is not the place that sanctifies the person, but the person who sanctifies the place. You must avoid that church because they have profaned it. Just as holy priests sanctify, so the defiled pollute. If it is not possible to gather either in a house or in a church, let each person sing psalms, read and pray by himself, or two or three together. "For where two or three are gathered in my name," says the Lord, "there am I among them."

If a priest drinks wine and vomits, let him not receive communion for 40 days. The same applies to a monk.

If any bishop, presbyter or deacon falls into sin with a woman, let him be deposed.

If anyone commits this sin with another person and one of the two dies, let the one who is still alive do the penance enjoined on him by his spiritual father, and spend a year praying for the one who has died.

Those who give money to escape torture are not to be blamed. They chose to lose money rather than their souls, and "a man's ransom is his own wealth." Nor are those who saved themselves by flight to be blamed, even if others were seized in their place, for the others could have fled too.

If any presbyter or deacon, as though he had condemned his own bishop on some charge, withdraws from communion with him before the synod has judged the matter and does not commemorate his name, let him be deposed. If any bishop dares to do the same against his own metropolitan, let him be deposed. Likewise, if any bishop or metropolitan dares to do these things against the patriarch, let them be removed from the priesthood. But if some separate themselves from someone, not on the pretext of a charge but because of a heresy condemned by a synod or by holy [?]

3372 Fathers, they are worthy of honour and acceptance as orthodox.

ON THE BAPTISM OF THE APOSTLES.

Some curious people were puzzled and asked, "By whom were the apostles baptized? And if they were not baptized, how could they baptize?" They were also puzzled and asked, "By whom were they ordained? And if they were not ordained, how could they ordain?" They urged our humble self to take the trouble to look into these questions. In the Memoirs of Saint Sophronius we found many other things worth remembering, and among them the very things we were looking for. He says that our Lord and God Jesus Christ baptized only Saint Peter with his own hands. Peter baptized Andrew, Andrew baptized James and John, and John and James baptized all the rest of the apostles. He also says that Peter, together with John the Theologian, baptized our all-immaculate Lady, the Theotokos and Mother of our life. He adds that John the Theologian was a nephew of our Saviour Jesus Christ according to the flesh. Joseph, the betrothed of the Virgin, had four sons by the wife of his ordinary life: James, Simon, Judas and Joses. He also had three daughters: Esther, Tamar, and a third, Salome, who had the same name as her mother. Joseph gave Salome in marriage to Zebedee, and with her Zebedee fathered James and John the evangelist. John had three mothers on earth. The first was Salome, of whom he was born in the body. The second was Thunder, because the Lord spiritually called him a son of thunder. When they were standing by the cross, the Lord said to the Theologian, "Here is your mother," and again to the Virgin, "Woman, here is your son,"

ANGELO MAI'S PREFACE [?] thus: Sophronius, suffering from a cataract in his eyes, is healed by Saints Cyrus and John, and as payment for the cure they ask him to put into writing the miracles they performed day by day. [?] luminary of the Church, of the country [?] Phoenicia [?] Libya [?] Stephen, of the city of Damascus, pious [?]

…he says: "Let no one think that the holy things are antitypes of the body and blood of Christ. Rather, let him believe that the bread and wine that are offered are changed into the body and blood of Christ." [?]
ENCOMIUM OF THE BLESSED SOPHRONIUS, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF ABBA THEODOSIUS IN THE DESERT OF THE HOLY CITY OF CHRIST OUR GOD, ON THE HOLY MARTYRS CYRUS AND JOHN.

1. We came to the martyrs Cyrus and John because of a disease of the eyes and were staying at their church. Seeing the waves of healings there, we wanted to find records that would teach us about the martyrs' contest and tell of some of their earlier miracles. We found nothing of the kind, except two short homilies by the great Cyril, the champion and herald of the truth, and this stirred in us a zeal we could not bear. The pagans wrote falsehoods, said nothing true or free of illusion, and still wrote so many books on behalf of demons.
