Shall we then keep silent like four-footed beasts, like the friends of Job the just, when we see so many great and wonderful works of the truth (and Christ our God is that truth) done through ascetics and through his servants? Shall we do so especially when we hear him crying out plainly,

"Whatever you have said in secret will be heard in the light, and what you have heard whispered in the ear, proclaim on the housetops"? Shall we do so when the blessed apostles say in the Acts to those who ordered them to be silent, "We cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard"? So we too, burning with an even warmer zeal, ran to the tomb of the saints. Falling devoutly on our faces, we prayed with all our soul that, now that our sight was already serving us again, we might write more fully about their contest and compose an account of the miracles they had worked, with their divine grace and power helping us in the labour. On their behalf we resolved to produce the present work, imitating Hannah when she offered the prophet Samuel, and gratefully following the example of Peter's mother-in-law: the one offered her son and the other offered herself for service to God who had saved them. Afterwards we got up and went off by ourselves. When we considered how exalted the martyrs are and looked at the great number of miracles being performed, we grew afraid, like the great Peter when he walked on the waves of the sea. We were drowning in our own thoughts, and we blamed ourselves severely for the rashness that had made us reach for things beyond us without first taking our own measure.

2. Our fear was increased by the divine Moses, or rather by the Lord who spoke with Moses. He demands a single contribution from rich and poor alike. He does not let the rich man give a larger ransom when he wishes to ransom his soul, and he does not allow the poor man to offer anything less. "For everyone," he says, "who passes through to be counted, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the contribution to the Lord. The rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less than the half didrachm, when you give the contribution to the Lord to make atonement for your souls." So we too, being poorer in words than even the very poor, wanted to excuse ourselves from the ransom-contribution that we had promised to God and to the martyrs in our prayers. But another saying kept us from doing so, the one Solomon wrote down as the Preacher: "When you make a vow to God, do not delay to pay it, for he takes no pleasure in fools. So pay whatever you vow. It is better that you do not vow than that you vow and do not pay." David, his father, also says in his songs, "I will pay my vows to the Lord," and he urges everyone to follow his example: "Make vows," he says, "and pay them to the Lord your God." In the same vein the prophet Jonah sang, "All that I have vowed I will pay to you, my Saviour, the Lord." Even before them the law of Moses required that what was pledged in vows be paid: "If

you make a vow to the Lord your God," it says, "you shall not delay to pay it. For the Lord your God will surely require it of you, and you will be guilty of sin. But if you choose not to vow, you will not be guilty of sin. You shall keep what passes your lips, and do as you vowed to the Lord your God, the gift you promised with your mouth."

3. So we were hard pressed by our thoughts. At one moment the first passages made us afraid to write; at another the second passages made us tremble at the thought of not writing. Not knowing what to do, we took refuge with the martyrs and asked their holiness what we should do. They accepted the intention behind our zeal and did not hold our rashness against us. They allowed us to write and promised to supply their own help. And often, while we were writing, they appeared to us,

…he prescribed food, and he ordered a seven-branched lampstand to be made. [?] For this reason Enoch was seventh from Adam, and Moses seventh from Abraham. We learn that the eyes of the Lord that look upon the world are seven. We hear Isaiah speak of the same number of spirits. Solomon counted seven pillars of wisdom, and the apostles, following the law, appointed seven deacons. The perfection of ten is celebrated even by the philosophers outside the Church, who went so far as to regard it as a god, as the Pythagorean tetractys holds. For ten is both the end of the units and is known as the unit of the tens, and it is the base of the numbers that come after it, since it is always compounded with itself. The law of Moses celebrates it more clearly. Noah is shown to be tenth after Adam, and he becomes the second root of the human race, reflecting the decad. Abraham, after his victory, offered tithes to Melchizedek, and so the Hebrews are commanded to bring God tithes of what they own. The law also decreed that ten obols be offered as the ransom of the soul. On the tenth day of the first month the lamb is taken, and on the tenth day of the seventh month the atonement is prescribed. Ten commandments, written by God, shone on the tablets of the covenant. The Lord too handed down the words of the prayer as ten. David sang the Psalms on a ten-stringed psaltery. And Abraham brought God's love for humankind, and the postponement of the sentence against the people of Sodom, down to ten righteous men.

5. The sacred oracles likewise make known the product of these two numbers, seven and ten. Thus Moses and the people found seventy palm trees in the desert, and afterwards he appointed seventy elders. The Lord, too, appointed seventy other disciples after the twelve. To speak in the words of the blessed Daniel, seventy weeks were decreed from the flood of Noah and the burning of Jerusalem until Christ the leader. There were seventy years until Israel was called back from Babylon. Isaiah also says that Tyre will be abandoned by the Lord for seventy years, and that after the same number of years it will be visited again. The Lord himself, the new Adam, came to live our life as the seventy-seventh from the old Adam. And he commanded us to forgive seventy times seven, and to forgive the sins of brothers who repent. It would take more time than we have now to collect the testimonies of Scripture about these numbers, for the whole of Scripture is full of them and clearly proclaims their mystical and perfect character.

6. So we too, of the saints, seventy (which is the same as saying seven tens, or sevens

[?] of the miracles we have written. The first three decades, which come after the martyrs' contest, burial and translation, together with half of the fourth, show the power of what Cyrus and John did for the Alexandrians. The rest of the fourth and the fifth decade proclaim what they did among the Egyptians and Libyans. The sixth and seventh tell of their benefactions to foreigners. For the whole body of the miracle accounts is divided into three: those for the Alexandrians, those for the Egyptians and Libyans, and those for people from abroad who seized hold of healing. We will give the reason for this division when we come to the places themselves. We are well aware that a more relaxed and easy style would have suited sacred narratives of miracles. But we have set that style aside and adopted an intense one, so that its very intensity may also show how fervent and ready the saints are to heal the sick.

THE ENCOMIUM ON SAINTS CYRUS AND JOHN. 7. Let others honor the saints in other ways, celebrating their gifts in many forms and proclaiming their benefactions in many manners. Some do so by raising lofty churches, others by adorning them with many-colored marbles, others by setting mosaics of gold-gleaming tesserae, others by the bright skill of painters, others by offerings of gold and silver, and others by fabrics woven from silk. In short, let everyone compete in honoring the martyrs, as far as each one's means and will allow. Let them strive to outdo one another in this and so show the affection for the saints that is in them. In return they will receive unfading things for perishable ones and endless things for temporary ones, for these godly saints are accustomed to repay their lovers with such gifts. But for us, speech is more precious than earthly materials, since it pours forth not from the bodily tongue alone but also from the spirit, and is itself disregarded because of what is fleeting and flowing [?]. So let us honor the saints with speech. I am convinced that the martyrs delight in it most of all, since they were called witnesses of the Word of God, even though our speech has nothing worthy of their festival and falls far short of their grace. We ask them to grant us the opening of our mouth, and to receive kindly, as their own, the speech we offer them.

8. The encomium is a debt, and to repay it we take out another loan in turn by drawing on their help, so that they themselves may be both the givers and the receivers, and may sanctify us who speak. The encomium truly is a debt, and a paradoxical one. It is a debt that is paid and yet does not free the debtor from what he owes. It is fulfilled and yet always owed again. It is repaid and yet receives an increase. It is always being offered and yet does not diminish the substance of the one who offers it. It is always being supplied and yet multiplies the possessions of those who give it with gratitude. It is always being rendered and yet causes the one who renders it to be blessed. The debt is not an old one that has run up interest for the martyrs, who in any case refuse to take interest. They became guardians of the divine commandments and do not wish to transgress them even after this life. But although they want no interest that would bring guilt, they imitate their own King and welcome the grateful while blaming the ungrateful. For he too, after granting cleansing to the ten lepers, welcomed and praised the one who came back and sang the praises of the favor, though he was a foreigner, and testified that goodwill befits those who have been treated well. The rest he blamed as ungrateful (for they were Jews). Not long ago we fell ill in our eyes, which the Savior called the lamp of the whole body, for whoever is deprived of them truly suffers the loss of light. 9. We heard from the physicians that the illness was leading to blindness. Some of them called the condition an effusion, others a dilation of the pupil, but either way the end was blindness and the loss of the eyes. So we hurried to these saints, Cyrus and John, the benefactors. We hung all our hopes of seeing on the grace given them by God, and pushed human help aside as weak and powerless against the disease. They accepted our faith (for whoever comes must first believe, as the divine Apostle says) and swiftly granted healing of the disease. They also assured us that in future we would suffer none of what the Asclepiads had said we would suffer. Through visions, in riddling and gracious fashion, as with someone dear to them, they banished our Homeric blindness, showing plainly that all things impossible for human beings are possible for God. 10. So let the martyrs be praised by our humble self, and let them become a cause of joy for the hearers. For the assemblies of the faithful leap for joy when they see Cyrus acclaimed, and the multitude of the devout rejoices when it learns of John's encomium. Our opening comes from the Gospels and the words of the Lord, which were once spoken to the apostles, but which suit Cyrus and John the martyrs and may be applied to such as came after the apostles: 'You are the light of the world and the salt

of the earth,' O thrice-blessed ones. You are the light that does not set and the salt that does not lose its savor. You are the light that is not quenched and the salt that is not thrown out, the sleepless light and the salt that is not trampled underfoot, light always gazed upon and salt always eaten, light sweetest to all and salt beloved by all. Without salt, speech is devoid of grace and bread becomes inedible. You are light that bestows the knowledge of God and salt that produces love of God, light that dispels darkness and salt that seasons what has lost its savor, light that illumines what is unlit and salt that gives good flavor to what tastes bad, light that exposes what is wrong and salt that binds together what is slack. O pair of saints, through whom the Divine is marveled at! For truly God is wonderful in his saints. O pair of martyrs, through whom the world is made bright! O pair of the righteous, through whom life is renewed! O pair of holy ones, through whom faith is strengthened! O pair of blessed ones, through whom the devout are magnified! O pair of zealots, through whom error is mown down! O pair of mighty ones, through whom the devil is dashed to the ground! O pair of soldiers, through whom demons are punished! O pair of devout ones, through whom idols are sunk in the sea! Hail, truly, O sacred pair who stand beside God! And hail, O holy pair, who dance with the angels and watch over human beings! It is truly fitting that you hear the Savior praising you and proclaiming aloud: 'You are the light of the world and the salt of the earth.' You are light illumined by the true light and salt seasoned by the true salt itself, purely illumining those who believe and constantly seasoning those who honor you. 11. How can we not marvel at the bond of this indissoluble pair? How can we not glorify the union of this strange yoking? For we see the unmixable mixed, the incompatible brought together, the unblendable blended, things that cannot be intertwined intertwined, enemies at peace, opponents made friends, and things that resist becoming one made one through companionship. Cyrus was a monk, and John was a soldier. One pursued the desert, the other the cities. One was eager for peace with everyone, as the one who said, 'If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people'; the other embraced war against people. One scattered his own goods to the poor; the other seized what was not his for the tyranny. One followed the life of philosophy; the other served in a contentious rank. One had a heavenly citizenship; the other held an earthly station. One stretched out his hands in supplication; the other stretched them out to bow and arrows, spear and sword. One healed people who were suffering; the other wounded the healthy. In short, one was enlisted under the heavenly King ...

while the other bore arms for an earthly king. Whose work, then, was their marvelous union? Who removed the difference and brought them into concord? Who fitted together their true yoking? Is it not clear that it was Christ our God? He does great and extraordinary things, glorious and unsearchable. He broke down the dividing wall of the partition and bound both into one. He joined things below to things above and brought earthly things together with heavenly ones. He led back the straying sheep, joined them to those that had not strayed, and made one flock out of all. He made earth accessible to angels and heaven to human beings [?]

12. Let us too tune our lyre with the psalmist prophet and say, as we behold the divine union of Cyrus and John: truly 'This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.' Through it the foolish are made wise and the wisest become foolish. Through it fishermen are caught, tax collectors are taxed and robbers are robbed. 'This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.' Through it the blind see again and those who see become blind. Through it blasphemers bless and the uneducated teach. Through it the unlettered are admired and those who pride themselves on eloquence are mocked. Through it the illiterate become orators and orators become rustics. 'This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.' Through it the rich become poor and the needy become rich. Through it the mighty grow weak and the weak are girded with strength. 'This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.' Through it the barren woman becomes the mother of many and the mother of many becomes childless. Through it rulers are dragged down from their thrones and the poor and needy are raised up from the dunghill. Through it mountains and hills are brought low and the deep valleys are filled. Through it what is crooked is made level and rough paths are made straight. 'This, then, is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.' Through it the wolf feeds with the lamb, and the leopard, the bull and the calf graze together with the lion and are tended by a little child. Through it the bear, the ox and the lion eat straw, and their young herd peacefully together. Through it infants fearlessly put their hands on the hole of asps and the den of their brood, for the snakes have no power to destroy or harm them. 'This,' then, truly 'is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.' It brought Cyrus and John into concord and settled them in one home. It adorned them with one contest before the end, glorified them with one glory after the end, and honored the victors with one crown. For in the words of the Apostle, they 'finished the race and kept the faith,' [?] of the crowns laid up for such as these.

13. Even before, the blessed ones were not at odds in their ways or opposed in their manner of life, even though Cyrus wore the habit of a monk and John the dress of a soldier, and one put on a sheep's skin and the other a wolf's. For both were holy, both good, both true, both blameless, both righteous, both God-fearing, both full of innocence and of divine law, teaching and commandment, as their end and the gifts given them by God bore witness. Their dress did not divide them as much as their faith joined them. Their profession did not separate them as much as their piety united them. Their occupations did not set them as far apart as their hope granted them fellowship. For those who hold to the same faith will also become alike in their ways. Those who practice one piety always do good deeds. Those who look to the same hope take up the same undertakings. 14. So Christ, God of all and Master and Ruler of the universe, who knows all things before they come into being, who searches hearts and minds and beholds the hidden things of human beings with sleepless eyes, brought the martyrs to one glory and bestowed one veneration on both. For he is an impartial judge and a just balance, and knows how to weigh out justice, granting to each their own reward according to their own labor. So, knowing that Cyrus and John were equal in their virtues, he awarded one tomb to both, in the venerable precinct of the divine Mark. From there, through Cyril, a man of the Gospel, champion and herald of true religion, he moved the martyrs, who were like the evangelists in their ways, to the church of the Evangelists, and made them neighbors of the apostles. For he did not judge it right to separate them from the evangelists or the apostles, since no difference had ever raised a wall to divide them. 15. But these things took place many years later, when Theodosius the Younger was emperor and Cyril the Great was guiding the throne of Alexandria. Earlier, God the Father had taken pity on the human race. It was being corrupted by the deceit of demons, wallowing wretchedly on the ground, walking in darkness of mind and worshiping the creation instead of the Creator. Through the Son he had given a law to help it. But the laws that had been given grew weak through the commandment, or rather through the human inclination toward the passions, and could not save those for whose sake they had been given through angels and decreed by the hand of Moses the mediator. Then again, after the law, he sent forth the Lawgiver, Christ, born of a woman and born under the law. Christ arose by generation from the Father's own nature; through him the Father made all things; he sits eternally with the Father and shares his lordship over the creation, which is not eternal. Christ the Master himself had also completed his dispensation for us and fulfilled the purpose of his saving

incarnation. He had rescued the sheep that was once lost, carried it on his own shoulders and offered it to the Father, rejoicing over it more than over the ninety-nine that had not been lost. He had already renewed for us the ascent into heaven, opened the entrance into paradise and given us resurrection from the tomb. He had already brought about salvation in the midst of the earth, made firm the tossing sea, crushed the heads of the dragons in it and drawn out the many-headed dragon with a hook. He had already unveiled the devil's deceit and his face, penetrated the hidden folds of his breastplate, and given us power to tread on snakes and scorpions and all their might. Christ had also put a halter on the dragon's nose, fastened a ring in his nostrils and pierced his lips [?]. He had taken that apostate and runaway, now become a slave, and handed him over bound, like a sparrow to a child, to the people of Christ still in its infancy. The morning star that rose at dawn had already fallen, been driven from his dwelling in heaven and been ordered to live in the abyss. Finally, the apostles' preaching had already enlightened the inhabited world. The fishermen's net had caught the world alive, and the leatherworker's knife had cut away senseless error. They were proclaiming the venerable Gospel everywhere, and all flesh was seeing the salvation of God. The kingdom of God had already been taken from the Jews and given to the nations, who offer its ripe fruit to God who gave it, and the Master's vineyard had the workers of about the eleventh hour as its keepers. The seed that fell on good soil was growing with a fine growth, God granting the sower a yield of a hundredfold, sixtyfold and thirtyfold. Everyone was selling all they had and receiving in exchange for everything the precious pearl. The late-flying birds were nesting in the branches of the mustard plant that grows from so small a seed. 16. Then once again the crooked dragon, whose head had been crushed by the cross, began to lash his tail, thinking he could frighten the devout with it. Once again the sower by night, who had turned from a morning star into darkness, longed to sow his own weeds under cover of darkness. Once again the birds of the air wanted to devour the seed of the good sower that had fallen by the road. Once again he set to work: he who deceived Eve with a hiss and made Adam an enemy of God; who murdered Abel for being righteous and made Cain his brother's murderer; who made the people of old lovers of the flesh and brought them to perish by water; who made Ham accursed and brought the division of tongues on those in Canaan; who multiplied idols for human beings and separated them

from God who created them; who made Israel ungrateful and Pharaoh hard and untamable, and caused the one to perish in the desert and the other in the sea, in the merciless waves; who made the Jews disobedient to the law and the prophets and subjected them to the abominations of the nations; who put it into the Hebrews to envy Christ and to crucify the one who came to save them; who persuaded them to slander his resurrection and to persecute and murder its heralds. 17. Not content with all this, he later waged war on Cyrus and John, the martyrs who shone out in a time of persecution and were soldiers of Christ. But the wretch was defeated, kicking against the goads and joining battle with the invincible. He drew a flashing sword, but the noble martyrs plunged it into his own heart. He bent a soul-destroying bow, but they swiftly broke it, together with the arms that had strung it, before the arrows could be loosed. He dug a pit, but he dug it for himself and not for the martyrs who opposed him. At last, worn out by these clashes and unable to fight any longer, he handed over his commands to those who honored him at that time. Tortured by their bloodstained hands and unable to bear the violence of the torments, the martyrs were to offer him sacrifices and libations and proclaim him a god along with the other demons. If they refused, they were to suffer the loss of this present life. In doing this, the wretch did not realize that he was procuring for the saints a better life and crowns without end, and for himself death, a greater defeat and a blow full of shame. 18. The godly were arrested by the godless when Diocletian ruled the Roman Empire, Syrianus governed the city of the Alexandrians and Cassius was priest of the pagan madness at Canopus. This was after the [martyrdom] of the divine Peter, who shepherded the devout in Alexandria. Their struggle was, on the one hand, against cruel men who used cruel whips, and on the other against the dragon who spurred those men on [?]. They were not arrested only to face killers (that contest would have been lighter for them and caused them far less anxiety). A choir of holy virgins was held along with them. There were three of them, and their mother, who had brought them up devoutly and chastely. They had purified both soul and body and betrothed both to Christ, the heavenly Bridegroom. Their names, so they say, were these. The firstborn was Theoctiste, in her fifteenth year. The next was called Theodote and had reached her thirteenth year. Eudoxia, born after the other two, was in her eleventh year. Athanasia was the name of the root that had brought forth this virgin, three-branched tree, the field that had nourished these all-pure ears of grain. At Canopus these

…which they formerly inhabited while they still lived on earth and ran the course of virginity; but now they dwell in heaven itself, for they shared the contest of the martyrs who contended for piety.

19. It came about by the providence of Christ the Bridegroom that these weaker women should be steeled by the steadfast resistance of the athletes, and that the brides should enter the heavenly bridal chamber together with those who escorted them. So the Bridegroom's will is fulfilled, and he receives both the escorts and the brides together into the heavenly bridal chambers. Here, I ask you, look at the care of the martyrs, and consider their concern for others at such a moment. The saints were not in anguish for themselves alone; they feared for those women no less than for themselves, in case their own faintheartedness should become the cause of the women's falling into impiety. How many directions do you suppose their minds were pulled in at that time? How many unseen thoughts do you think they were wrestling with then? How many assaults of the envious and malicious [?] demon were they grappling with? The devil perhaps set the present life before them, and painted the God-made beauty of the world as if it were his own: to see the sweet sun rising, to watch the moon adorning the sky with the stars, to breathe gentle breezes, to tread the many-colored earth, to sail the broad sea, to delight in springs and rivers, to exult in the flowers and meadows of the earth, and to gather and enjoy their fruits; to feast on the creatures born in the sea and to eat one's fill of the produce of the rivers; to be fed on birds that course through the air, and to partake of the flesh of edible animals.

20. These things, perhaps, the devil suggested, and often pressed them hard [?] even before the present contests. For the shameless one watches for our departure from life—and perhaps this is what the divine oracle hinted at by the "heel"—and as long as we live here he does not cease his assaults, and though he keeps coming at us he is forever put to shame. But his champions and the servants of his wickedness—Syrianus, accursed of God, and those with him who foully practiced paganism in the service of imperial commands—offered respite from tortures and a soul-killing release from the deaths they had threatened. They promised wealth, swore to bestow ranks, announced that they would enroll them among the city magistrates, and insisted that they would make them known to the Caesar Diocletian, if only they would obey their orders and worship with them—or rather commit impiety with them—before the shapes of shameless wooden idols and demons; or rather, offer veneration to wretched human beings, and call by the name of gods pieces of wood, mute and senseless, good for nothing but feeding a fire. For they are handed over to the fire,
and drag their own carpenters down with them. Such things and the like were what those men said.

21. But the martyrs, always remembering the words of the Savior and always meditating on the sayings of his disciples, beat back the assaults of their adversaries with these. "We, O judge," they said, "refuse your promises and gifts, and those of the one who speaks and gives orders through you, as harmful rather than beneficial. For what will a man gain if he wins the whole world but loses his own soul? Or what will anyone give in exchange for his soul? Or what will possessions profit in the day of wrath? What will anyone give in exchange, or give to God as a ransom for himself, as the price of the redemption of his soul? The senseless and the foolish will perish together, and they will leave their wealth to strangers; for their glory does not go down to Hades with them, but their tomb will become their everlasting home. Heaven, as a created thing, will pass away, and like a garment grown old it will be changed; for since its composition is temporal, its dissolution too will be temporal, whenever God, who stretched it out like a skin, so commands. The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, whenever he who made the one to rule the day and the other to rule the night so decrees. The stars will fall like fig leaves from the vault of the sky, whenever God, who set them for signs and seasons, so wills. The earth and everything in it, which received its formation out of water and through water by the word of God, will come to an end whenever God wills, he who made it not in vain but to be inhabited by human beings. For the day of the Lord will come like a thief, on which the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the elements will be burned and dissolved, and the earth and the works in it will be burned up; but we look for new heavens and a new earth, and for what he has promised. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal. Always reckoning on these things and keeping them in mind, and believing that we hold them as our own inheritance, we strive to be found spotless and blameless before God. That is why we do not fear your tortures, nor dread your threats; for we have been taught [?] not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. And we abhor your promises, because they separate us from God and join us to demons. For Christ, the Master of all, has given us better promises: an inheritance imperishable, undefiled, unstained and unfading, kept in heaven, and what eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and what has not entered the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him. We have no wish to become friends of an earthly king, for we are a chosen race and a royal priesthood, called a holy nation and a people for his own possession. We do not think it worth priding ourselves on the ranks you offer, since we are children of God and

hold rank according to the measure of our faith. We take no satisfaction in being enrolled among your city magistrates, since we are citizens of heaven and believe that our names are written in the book of life. That is why we dare to say: Who shall separate us from the love of Christ—of him who brought us out of darkness into his marvelous light; who for our sake became poor in the flesh, so that we might be enriched with his divinity; who died for us, so that we might escape death and corruption? Shall tribulation, from the love of him who rescued human nature from tribulations? Distress, from the love of him who guides us by the narrow way into his boundless kingdom? Persecution, from the love of him who was persecuted for our sake and conquered the persecutors, and gave us, who are persecuted for his sake, the kingdom of heaven as our reward? Famine, from the love of him who hungered for our salvation, and filled with immortal food us who were starving and could not even get our fill of the pigs' fodder? Danger, from the love of him who snatched us out of dangers? Sword, from the love of him who was pierced [?] for us and saved us from the soul-destroying sword? We are convinced, then, that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, because of the love that surpasses knowledge and the surpassing riches of his kindness toward humankind; and because the sufferings of this present time, and our release from the fleeting things of the present, are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us."

22. When the judges recognized this resolve of the saints, they were amazed at their spirit; but thinking it impossible to change their minds with words unless they also tried them with redoubled punishments, and reckoning that their virtue lay in words and not in courage of deeds, they applied crueler tortures to them, aiming at two things at once. They thought that in this way they would bring the saints to what they themselves wanted, the worship of idols, and that the women who were contending and struggling alongside them would be dragged along with them by the blood of the runners. But, as the saying goes, the crafty hunter will not catch his prey. For since Christ clothed both alike with power from on high, the intricate nets of the judges were torn apart, and the souls of the saints were rescued like a sparrow from the snare. Just as the waves of the open sea dash against the rocks and are broken up, and prove to be nothing more than light foam, so the torturers, attacking Cyrus and John savagely and cruelly and applying every form of torture to them beyond all measure, as though they had never attacked,

remained ineffective, driven back by the saints' firmness in Christ. Or as enemies who bring their siege engines against impregnable towers wear themselves out and do themselves harm, and return without having gained anything from the attempt, so the executioners, inflicting tortures on the martyrs, exhausted themselves with the labor, made those who endured them stronger, and failed to obtain what they desired. Hence the brides of the Savior too, putting on invincible courage and arming themselves against every onslaught of the enemy, and wrestling nobly with their adversaries in the theater of faith, remained unbending and unconquered by those who tortured them, heeding the scourges no more than the scourgers themselves felt them. For the hope of heavenly things, and the strong and unshaken steadfastness of those who suffered before them, made them braver, and the pain of the blows was cut short for them.

23. After contending with the martyrs for a long time, the judges were at last defeated. They ceased from the tortures, set aside the scourges, threw away the scrapers, and became the cause of the martyrs' crowns of victory by inflicting on them death by the sword. It was the sixth day of the Egyptian month Mechir, the thirty-first of the Roman January, when the Christ-loving martyrs, having borne witness for Christ, were beheaded. When the holy martyrs had thus finished their contest, seized their crowns of victory, and won the prizes of the upward and divine calling, the faithful people took them up and, singing a hymn of victory, brought them to the shrine of Mark, who had rooted the faith in them, opened the stadium of contests on its behalf, and was the first to win the unfading crowns. Fittingly they joined the disciples to their teacher, handed over the contestants to the judge of the games, brought the sheep to the shepherd, offered the ears full of grain to the farmer, and presented to the general the invincible phalanx of his soldiers. And he gladly received the saints as his true children, joyfully took them in his arms as faithful imitators, and, leaping for joy, brought them to God, crying out in a ringing voice: "Here am I, and the children whom God has given me." And in the presence of the assembled faithful he laid the relics of the martyrs to rest. They did not bury the lambs and the ewe-lambs together in common, nor hide the brides of Christ and their escorts in the earth at the same time, but laid up each as a treasure in coffins of their own; for since they had been taught to divide tribe from tribe, each by itself, they were eager to keep that precept here too. So, to put it briefly, the contests, races, wrestlings and victories of the saints, and besides these their unfading crowns and their deposition in the church of the divine Mark, were accomplished and came to a glorious end.

24. Let us now tell also of their translation from there to here, and the reason for which the translation took place. Many days after that—for why should we not speak like Moses, and grant the martyrs this favor? They will welcome us speaking like Moses in their praises rather than like Plato—after the overthrow of those tyrants, the destruction of those who had tormented [?] the saints, the demolition of the foul worship of idols, and the collapse of the temples and altars built for them; after the blessed Constantine, the first Christian to hold firm the scepter of the Romans, and the succession of his sons; after Jovian, Valentinian and Gratian had departed to the better life; after Theodosius the Great and his descendants had passed away to their lot above; while Theodosius the Younger was governing the empire, and the divine Cyril was shepherding Christ's rational sheep here and proclaiming the wisdom of piety with a loud-voiced trumpet—a dark Egyptian demon appeared, named Menuthis, inhabiting the village that bears its name. It took on the form of a woman, and by this displayed its own weakness—its weakness, or rather its impotence, before those who are manly in soul. It had not escaped the chain of the abyss by its own strength, but had been let loose for a time by God's permission for our safety, so that, seeing its evil deeds, we might always remember from what miseries Christ our God has freed us. This demon, dark as an Egyptian, womanish in mind and in form alike—after the frivolity of Loxias and the tripod, the unspeakable silence of the oak at Dodona, the endless silence of the Castalian spring, the fall of the Rhodian bull, which no longer bellows [?], and the extinction of practically all the Greek oracles; after the unending burning of Asclepius, and the total and incurable maiming of physicians of his kind—put on a show, by means of apparitions, of prophesying and healing diseases, or rather of lying and causing diseases. For how could he prophesy who is a liar from the beginning, who speaks falsehood from his own nature, and who does not stand in the truth at all? Or how could he—who did not keep the rank he once had at the beginning, but has been cast out like an abhorred corpse, swarming with worms, with rot for his bed; who has fallen every kind of fall and is sick with a great sickness ("for they themselves," to speak in the words of the prophet, "grew weak and fell"), and who is wrapped in an incurable deadness to all good—hold out health to others? Or how could he help any who are sick, when he cannot help himself? For what someone has—whether he received it by nature, or took it from another and kept it undiminished—he might perhaps be able to share with others as well; but what he does not have, how will he be able to give to others?

25. Yet although this is how things stand, this [?] demon led many astray by its deceits, and persuaded them to resort to its altar in the hope of health or

prophecy—not only unbelievers and those wholly devoted to its commands, but even believers who bore the symbols of Christ. For wickedness is terribly powerful at drawing the guileless to itself, and perhaps even someone firmly inclined toward better things, unless he gains God as the guardian of his inclination. Besides, the natives of this city, being very simple and known rather for their artlessness, easily shift from the best to the worse, are readily corrupted by harmful things, and are brought back only with difficulty from what has overcome them, since their many-eyed mind is not keen-sighted. So Paul too, seeing that the Galatians were like this, says: "I am astonished that you are so quickly turning away from him who called you in the grace of Christ"; and after much teaching and most wise exhortation he rightly bore witness to their foolishness. Seeing the Hebrews still in need of milk, with the faculties of their soul untrained for distinguishing good from worse, he justly called them sluggish and infants. And to the Corinthians, who had earlier been of sound mind but were now in danger, he said: "I fear that, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may be corrupted from their simplicity and purity toward Christ." And Wisdom says that an evil mind is easily changed [?], and for that reason promises to give shrewdness to the guileless, and understanding, perception and insight to children and the young.

26. But the divine Cyril, the good shepherd, disciple and follower of Christ the Good Shepherd, was always scorched by the heat of the day and frozen by the frost of the night, putting sleep from his eyes and driving it away, so that with sleepless eyes and wakeful mind he might guard the sheep, that they might not be stolen, slaughtered or destroyed, nor be caught by wild beasts. It was in this way that he had caught Nestorius, the corrupter and beast, robber and wolf at once, driven him from the fold, and chased him from the flock with nothing accomplished, keeping the sheep unharmed. This Cyril, successor to the divine Theophilus in both office and zeal, seeing the deceit of the demon and beholding the harm done to the faithful, became a suppliant of the Savior. He implored him to put a stop to the evil, to abolish the demon's apparitions, and to grant the people a complete knowledge of the truth and a love for the knowledge of himself. And God quickly accepted his servant's prayers, granted the desire of his heart, and fulfilled his requests on behalf of the faithful. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer; he will indeed do the will of those who fear him and will hear their prayer, since he is near to all who call on him in truth. So he shattered the demon's power and healed the people's weakness. For God grants a thousand to one righteous man, and often to a people that supplicates him piously.

So it was that he granted Lot a whole city at his request, out of regard for his person; and so he many times pardoned sinful Israel for Moses' sake. So too God granted to Cyril, a righteous man and his servant like Lot and Moses, a whole city and a whole people.

27. While Cyril slept one night after his supplication, God revealed to him through an angel what he was to do, commanding him to transfer Cyrus, the celebrated martyr, from the church of the divine Mark to the shrine of the Holy Evangelists, which the former bishop Theophilus had built in the very village of Menuthis where the idol had been set up and the demon held sway. The admirable Cyril, having received this oracle through an angel, hurried to Saint Mark's, and on opening the venerable casket of Cyrus he found within it, together with him, the thrice-blessed John as well. Wisely reasoning that the God-spoken command had indicated both of them under the name of one because of their oneness in confession and mind, and that those whom neither way of life, nor place, nor tomb, nor time, nor suffering had separated ought not to be divided after death, he took them both and transferred them to the aforementioned holy shrine of the Evangelists, leaping and exulting, closely imitating the blessed David dancing before the ark of the Lord. And so, like the Psalmist himself, he tuned his spiritual and God-inspired lyre and praised the two martyrs in songs, making public the delight within him and becoming for the pious an image and example of joy in the saints. Thus those who read his songs now both come to know his longing and are changed to share his disposition: at once they rejoice and leap like Cyril, honor Christ with hymns, and crown the [?] with praises.

28. For truly one must marvel at the Savior's almighty power and at the boundless resourcefulness of his providence: how he did not rain brimstone and fire from heaven and strike that accursed demon with a thunderbolt, as he once did Sodom and Gomorrah, which found fault with nature and insulted the Maker as though he had not ordered our affairs well; nor did he decide that the earth should open and swallow the unclean one, as it once swallowed the arrogant company of Dathan and Abiram; nor did he pelt the impious one with a hail of stones, as he once did a nation that stood against Israel; nor did he command the foul one's most abominable statue to fall and be smashed to pieces, as of old he ground Bel and Dagon to dust. Rather, he lulled its audacity to sleep by means of dead bodies lying asleep in a tomb, and put to shame the arrogance of those who boasted in it. He wished, I think, to show the intelligent and sound-minded how great is the power of his martyrs even after death, how great the weakness of the gods of the Greeks, and how utterly the gods who boasted of giving oracles are defeated by the motionless, dead bodies of saints, which cannot even walk.

29. When the saints came here and took up their dwelling with the evangelists, their first act, from the very moment they set foot in this holy shrine, was to put the demon to flight. They drove it from the earth into Tartarus, celebrated a triumph over its flight, and showed the house empty of its occupant. The second task they carried out was the plundering, that is, the despoiling, of the demon's possessions. Its possessions were people, and wretched women who sat by the altar, deceived by empty hopes and mocked by a terrible illusion. These people were dead in soul and body. Following the divine saying, the martyrs first bound the strong man by putting him to flight, and then despoiled him as one would a dead man. Next, in their love for humankind, they also gave these people life. They brought them to the fountain of life and gave them the gift of knowing God, whom they had not known and so had been dead. They bestowed on them the true light, which they had not seen and so had been in darkness. This is how they save and take alive what their enemies had seized, just as their Master and teacher seized the world and took it alive. Third, the martyrs then did something no less than what had gone before. There was the demon's loathsome precinct, where the runaway worked his false illusions, where an altar was always [?] with blood, and where the idol in the form of a woman stood. They buried it in sea sand and, like the patriarch Jacob, hid it beneath the earth, so as to bring forgetfulness on later generations and a beneficial ignorance of its foulness and its soul-destroying structure. Fourth, joined to all this was the destruction of the demon's accursed property, which bore the demon's name and was the foul dwelling of its abominable rites. At the martyrs' nod, sand and sea divided it between them: part of it lies submerged under the sand, and the currents of the sea wash around the rest. Fifth, the martyrs accomplished something that is still wondrously being accomplished and will not be finished before the end of all things. It is known to all who know the martyrs and enjoy their grace, to all who have seen the precinct and kissed their coffin, to which so many prayers are made. The marvel is this: the saints' precinct stands in a way that defies belief and astonishes everyone. It is built on a shore that is neither high nor firm. It stands between sand and waves, takes the onslaughts of both, and calms their war like a mediator. To the east it has the roaring sea, rushing to ravage the sand. To the west it has the ridge of sand, which charges the waves like an enemy and pushes in to turn the wet into dry land. But it does not let the water mingle with the sand, nor the sand mix with the waters at the boundary. It appears to both sides at once and holds out its own loose foundation to them. It rises to a great height and its roof reaches the sky, so sailors long to see it. It is visible many stadia away, and it welcomes those sailing to Alexandria as soon as they come into view from the open sea

and gives them no ordinary delight, announcing that what they long for is near. Those sailing out from the city it escorts for a long way, staying in view, and it supplies them with gifts of safety for the journey. 30. Who could count the wonders the saints work from this place, recount them with a daring tongue, or utter them with a mouth of many words? No human being could, "not even if he had ten tongues and ten mouths" and acquired "a heart of bronze" and an unbreakable voice. Only God could. He gave them such great power, and through him they foretold what would be done through them for his glory. He "counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name." He "measures the water in his hand, the heaven with a span, and all the earth in a handful." By him the drops of rain are numbered, the clods of dew are measured, and the grains of sand are known in advance. Through him they cleanse lepers, make the lame sound of foot, heal the sick, give the blind their sight, cast out demons, and raise the dead, above all those who have suffered death of the soul. They freely give to all people the gifts that were freely given to them. These gifts are immense and countless. They grow every day and every hour and allow no reckoning of their number, so it is impossible to tell them. The earlier ones are always covered by the later ones, and these in turn are hidden by those that follow. They are buried in forgetfulness and overshadowed by silence, and they suffer something like the sea's envy. Here one can see the waves cresting and growing, delighting all who watch them. Then they move on and give way to the next, and at once they are handed over to the current of forgetfulness. They flow into oblivion before they flow into the waters, and they are hidden in silence before the following waves hide them. In the same way the miracles of Saints Cyrus and John spring up one after another and gush out richly. The present ones cover the earlier ones in silence, and in truth they too are covered by the onset of those that follow. 31. But even though there are so many of them and they are of this kind, let us try to tell a very few. They too will add their share to the praises, since truth shines before them. What we are about to tell is truly few, seventy in number. Compared with an immeasurable multitude they are like a few small drops compared with a boundless sea. We do not mean by this to limit the grace of the saints, God forbid, or to make light of their kindnesses to us; may we never be so mad as to depart from what is fitting. Rather, we offer them as proof of our praises and as unshakable confirmation of the saints' excellence. That is why we set them down as part of the praises, as if providing our discourse with a watertight roof, so that the unbridled shots of the unbelievers cannot leak through it. Through them we also stop the mouths of those devoted to idols. For this reason we will neither recall ancient miracles nor

narrate things that happened long ago. We do not want to give up the support that recent time offers us and so let the God-haters dismiss them. Instead let us write what has happened in our own times. Some of these things we have seen ourselves, and some we heard from others who saw them. What is more, most of those who suffered, or rather were healed, are still alive in this life of ours. They see this sun, they go about their present affairs, and they testify to the truth for us, telling these things with their own mouths to the glory of God and the honor of the saints. Some have departed to the Lord and been released from the affairs of this world. They too told their stories to many, and they have left us, as truthful witnesses of what we shall tell, those who saw and heard. 32. Even if we had wanted to throw ourselves into investigating the ancient miracles and to set some of them down in writing, the pagans could not have convicted us of lying, since they themselves are clearly refuted by these recent miracles and by those that happen continually before the saints. The sight of what is continually done, and the account of what has recently happened, would have given unshaken credibility to the ancient miracles as well. They would have fortified the truth for us and shut off from the loathsome idolaters any disbelief in what is told. So let us leave the ancients to extol the ancient miracles, which shone in their own times and delighted and honored those who were present then. Let us tell instead of things that happened recently and rained down in our own times, and with our own let us adorn the eternal ones, which are older in time. For Christ is not divided. He brought about both these and those through the saints, and through them he will again provide us with miracles to come. The divine martyrs who worked those miracles are our own as well, and so are the believers of that time who took pride in the martyrs' miracles. We do this so that the accursed cannot say again that we go through the ancient miracles for lack of new ones. For the unholy and shameless are skilled at overshadowing the truth and putting forward falsehood in its place. Among the foolish they make falsehood pass for truth and the truth in turn pass for a lie [?], even though they are caught lying, above all, by the snowstorms of miracles that keep on happening. No one in the world, I think, is unaware of the holy power of Cyrus and John. The God of all and Savior Jesus Christ gave them this power against every kind of disease without exception, as a boast and safeguard for the faithful, for the building up of the [catholic] Church, and

33. [?] all who live in this earthly region know it, even those who are not there in body, as if they were present and watching. For truly "the sound" of them "has gone out into all the earth," and the "words" about them have reached "the very ends of the world." We shall take it that the Psalmist cries this out not only about the apostles but also about all

who have eagerly pursued the immortal imitation of them. Before this, then, we too were only hearers of their grace, like everyone who lives far from their shrine. Now, however, we have also seen for ourselves the truth of what we heard. As was said before, we came to them because of an eye disease. We received health ourselves, and we watched others harvesting cures. Let the prophet tune his sacred lyre and cry out in songs to the ancient Jerusalem, "As we have heard, so have we seen." But let us say to the martyrs: "What we heard about you with our ears was far less than what we have seen with our eyes. Before, we were bedewed with small drops, rained down by tongues that, like clouds, had risen from the martyrs' sea of cures. But now we have seen this sea for ourselves and swum in its streams, and so with Job we will cry out to you, its springs: 'Before, I had heard of you only by the hearing of the ear, but now my eyes have seen you.'" What we saw with our eyes when we were present, and heard with our ears, we will write down. We will pass it on to those who are far away in body and to those who will come after us, and together with the prophet David we say, "Come and see the works of God, the wonders he has set upon the earth." Let us rouse the faithful people and gather them to hear of the wonders that come from God through Cyrus and John. Come then, come, let us put on the prayers of the saints as our help and take in hand the account of the miracles, making truth our ally in everything and the witness of what we say.

On the author.
Who wrote this? Sophronius.
From where? From Phoenicia.
Which Phoenicia? Phoenicia crowned with Lebanon.
And which city? Damascus.
Are his parents living? No, both have died.
Tell me their two names.
His mother was Myro, and his father was called Plynthas.
Did he have a sweet marriage and a flock of children?
He never had a marriage or children; he was unwed.
[?] Where on earth did he live as a monk, and in whose house?
In the land that received God, in the mountains of Jerusalem,
in the great fold of the great Theodosius.
And for whom did he complete and set down this divine hymn?
For Cyrus and John, the martyrs of godly mind.
Why did he take on so great a labor of the mind? Because they
gave healing to his diseased eyes.

By Seneca the iatrosophist.
To Cyrus, who was granted the highest measures of healing

ACCOUNT OF THE MIRACLES OF THE HOLY CYRUS AND JOHN, THE WISE UNMERCENARY SAINTS, BY SOPHRONIUS THE MONK AND SOPHIST.
[1?]. Concerning Ammonius the octavarius, who had scrofula on his neck.

As I begin the account of the miracles, I think it right to tell first those that belong to the city where the martyrs' marvelous contest took place and where their delightful shrine was built. That way we will not grieve the Alexandrians by placing others ahead of them in their own affairs. Nor will we dishonor the city itself, which is very great, beautiful and lovely, and so deserves to come first. And since the miracles that have the beginning of the account are attested as true by such a city, they will pass their credibility on to those told afterward. So let Ammonius begin our miracles, since he too was one of the leading men of the city, distinguished by his wealth and honored by a good father. His father administered the church of the Alexandrians for no short time and was the father of Eulogius, who guided its throne so excellently. Ammonius himself held the office of the octava (a tax levied at one eighth) [?]. It was collected unjustly but administered piously, and he completed [?] before the end [?]. While Ammonius was still young and his bodily beauty adorned the bands of youths, he got a grievous ailment in his neck. Doctors aptly call it choirades, "swine," because the growths that produce this disease resemble such animals and turn the necks of wretched people into empty pigsties. These growths surrounded the young man's neck and were nourished there as if in a mother's womb. As they grew little by little they stretched his neck and forced it to grow along with them. They put the young man in great trouble, gripping and choking him as the skin was pulled tight.

His father summoned the most eminent doctors, showed them the young man's ailment, begged them to help his son in his danger, and offered fees for the treatment. They held Julian (for that was the father's name) in very high honor and swore that they loved the boy more than themselves. They were also rather pleased by the weight of the fees. So they swore that curing the disease was their duty and promised to provide the cure out of respect and honor for the father and out of love and affection for the boy. They set every resource of their art in motion and even ventured beyond their art, if one may put it that way, but they did no good at all, since the boy's recovery was reserved for the martyrs. His father took him away from the doctors and brought him to Cyrus and John, the true doctors. He drenched their precious coffin with tears and begged them to come to the boy's help and not to overlook his son, caught in so great a storm. They heard the old man and did not slight the tears of his prayer. They healed the young man and splendidly freed him from that terrible necklace. I think I would do wrong if I did not also describe the treatment. They saw that the young man was haughty and puffed up by his wealth to the point of boasting, so they did not relieve the swellings of his bodily neck until they had healed the inflammation of his soul. For they care more about healing souls and freeing them from passion. Seeing that Ammonius was sick in soul and in body, and [?] badly affected in the neck of each, they granted him the following treatment. First they ordered him to sweep the floor in front of their venerable coffin, so that he would learn not to be arrogant. By bowing down toward the ground and the earth he would be taught where he had been taken from, and where God says to Adam, the first-formed man: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until I return you to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go." And the divine David says to God: "You will take away their breath, and they return to their dust." So when they had shrunk the swelling of the young man's soul and made him learn who he was, they applied the remedy to the scrofulous swellings of his bodily neck. This was their all-powerful plaster of wax salve, which they told him to mix with bread and put around his neck. When the saints' command had been carried out, the boy was freed from his ailment, for the swellings could not hold out against the remedy for many days. When it was applied to them [?], they fled from the one pursuing them. Suddenly they burst through the skin of the neck that held them in and fell in front of the saints' tomb. Those who counted them said there were sixty-seven. The men who served in the church at that time hung them up in front of the saints' tomb for many days, displaying the
power of the martyrs and moving everyone to praise that pleases God. And so Ammonius, having received a double cure for a double disease, [?] healthy

Some time later he was again lifted up by his disease of pride and forgot the lesson he had learned before. So he was disciplined again by a bodily illness and taught by the martyrs' punishments to think better. He fell seriously ill in the stomach and was in danger. The Asclepiads, however, called the ailment colic. They compared the different kinds of pain with a disorder of the stomach and saw that they were worse than any stomach complaint. He could not take any food without bringing it straight back up through his mouth, because his bowel could not receive what the stomach sent down to it. Squeezed by gripings and enslaved to sharper pains, the bowel would not let the food stay inside it. It sent the food back up faster than it had come down and threw it out through the mouth, allowing no passage through itself. The doctors all came running, including those who wear the philosopher's cloak and rely on elegant words. They were able to identify the ailment, but they could not manage to provide the cure, though they searched very hard for it and were eager to bestow it, so as to win both the fee, which is fine silver, and the even finer glory of a good reputation. So Ammonius gave up on them all. He had received no benefit from them except learning how powerless they were against the ailment, and that they were very capable in words but incapable of healing in deeds. He went out to Cyrus and John, trusting that they alone, after God, would be his doctors. And so he quickly received healing, a fitting reward for his faith in them. For his stomach the purge was oil and wax salve, which [?] light up their coffin with the gleam of fire. For the vainglory of his soul the martyrs overturned it with a fitting remedy. They came to Ammonius by night and ordered him to take off his soft, flowing garment and put on rougher clothing. This was woven from tow and called a "sack," because its roughness comes very close to sackcloth, and the very poor wear it because it is extremely cheap and mean. They told him to put this on instead of his costly, luxurious garment, and they commanded him to carry drinking water on his shoulders for the sick brothers. They decreed that he must carry not one jar but two, one on each shoulder, and that he would not [?] until he had carried out the command. He fulfilled the saints' command and very meekly drew the water while wearing the garment described. Then he received the health that had been promised for this act. In this way Ammonius escaped this illness too, and he went away praising those who were the physicians of this illness and had chased away the previous one. And we too, having hymned the saints (for after God they, of the things told

…[?] of the things mentioned, they have become physicians), let us go on to other admirable miracles of theirs.

2. On Theodore, who had white films on both eyes.

After Ammonius, Theodore comes forward in our narrative. He too had Alexandria as his city. His wealth was moderate and free of care, which is the finest kind of self-sufficiency. His disease was the loss of his bodily eyes. Theodore suffered in his eyes and did not find the proper care, so that white films formed on both of them and darkened them. With these films, and having learned from the physicians themselves that they were incurable, he made his way to the martyrs' shrine. He clothed himself in a single hope that does not put to shame, an unfeigned faith in them, and the visitation that they grant to those who believe in this way. When he came to the martyrs' venerable precinct, he carried off the fruit of his wholehearted faith in them. He spent only a very short time there, and he reaped a fruit that was not cultivated over many years but nursed by simple faith. Repaying this faith, the saints ordered him to go out to their spring and use its waters to recover his sight. He did what he was told most readily. He was led by the hand to the stream, washed his eyes in it and wiped them on a small kerchief, and he could see. Along with the moisture of the water, he had cast off the white films from his eyes. These had fallen from his eyes by some divine power and lay in the kerchief, and he ran in and showed them to everyone in the church. He offered himself as an example of faith and proclaimed how great is the healing that comes from faith.

3. On Kalos, who broke his foot.

There was a certain Kalos, well named, for his character matched his name, which means "good." Through the zeal of the hater of good, and his fierce opposition to good things, he tripped as he was coming down a ladder, and having tripped he was thrown violently from a height to the ground. In the fall he crushed his foot and was in danger, for he had broken the shank of his foot into countless pieces [?]. The physicians came, but he saw that their visits did nothing for his injury. The bones of his foot had almost given out, lost and discharged piece by piece, and the flesh was being eaten away by outflows of pus. Then he took refuge in the help of Saints Cyrus and John. He blamed himself bitterly for having preferred the physicians to the saints and begged earnestly to be forgiven for it, and along with forgiveness he implored them to grant him healing as well. He obtained it by pleading with unhesitating faith. At their command he was anointed with oil from the lamp, and with it he made up for the bones that had fallen out. This, then, is the story of Kalos, and the record of the miracle done for him.

4. On Isidore, who was sick in the lung.

I will tell of Isidore's illness and its wonderful healing. Isidore was a Maiumite, not from the Maiuma of Gaza but from the Maiuma of Alexandria. This lies on Pharos, which was once an island but is now counted as part of Alexandria, since the island has been joined to the city, although the place has kept its old name of Maiuma. This Isidore was in a very bad way. His lung was grievously wasting him, and the disease promised him death as its only remedy. As the lung rotted, he coughed up a little [?] blood and dissolved phlegm, and he was expecting the death that follows, which always and without fail follows such a condition of the lung. Seeing himself in this state, and learning that no hope of recovery was left for him among men, he turned to the holy martyrs Cyrus and John. His faith in them was the kind that moves mountains into the sea and raises the dead from their tombs, for such is the power the Savior has given them, and he fittingly repaid their love for him. So he came from the city to these all-powerful physicians. The martyrs admired his faith and appeared to him, not in a dream but while he was awake. They did not order him to do this or that. Instead they held out a piece of citron and told him to eat it. He took them for some of the people present in the church, so he gladly accepted what they gave and ate it with pleasure. But while he was still chewing the last of the citron, he felt the urge to vomit. When he vomited, he brought up with the food the worm that was devouring his lung. In casting it out he cast out the disease with it, and at once he recovered his strength.

5. On Menas the philoponos, who had the [?]

Now that we have told about Isidore and the wonderful story concerning him, it is time to bring forward Menas the philoponos, who was in charge of the philoponeion attached to the church of the divine Andrew at Perone. The philoponos fell grievously ill. His illness was a violent fever, which struck him intensely and burningly. It dried up nearly all the moisture of his belly, and the excessive dryness brought on an obstruction. The physicians' disciples at first neglected this blockage of the bowels as less dangerous than the fever. Then they set about to clear it, using a great many enemas and various ointments, giving him laxative remedies by mouth, and providing foods that upset the stomach. But after struggling with all these things they finally gave up. Not only had they not helped him at all with what they administered, but they had done him the greatest harm. For since what was sent into his belly stayed inside and would not pass out, the man was in greater
danger. Little by little he swelled up, and his belly became greatly distended, and he found no [?] from the necessity that constrained and oppressed him.

He endured this danger for twice seven days. When he could bear it no longer, he set out for the martyrs Cyrus and John and placed his life and death in their hands. He did not come on foot, or riding on an animal, or seated in a phoreion. (A phoreion is a chair in which those who nurse the sick usually carry them.) He could not sit, because his insides were so swollen that he had become a strange sight. Instead he lay on a pallet, carried in turns by sixteen men. When he arrived, the martyrs pitied him and visited him with kindly zeal that same night. They gave him a dried fig and told him to eat it, since it could rescue him from the disease, or rather from Hades. He woke up, for what he had seen was a dream, and thought he was holding the dried fig. When he could not find it, he was distressed, as though he had lost his life. Even so, he called his wife, told her about the vision, and asked her to bring him a dried fig. When she heard this, she looked closely at her husband's bedding and noticed a dried fig lying on it. She snatched it up at once and showed it to her husband while he was still speaking and describing the vision. He took the fig and declared that this was the one given to him in his sleep, and at once his former joy returned. He ate the fig that the martyrs had given him for his salvation, and he obtained that salvation. While he was still chewing and eating it, the obstruction came to an end. What had bound his belly was quickly loosed, and he felt an urgent need to go to the latrine. There he voided all the matter that the blockage had stored up inside him, and he returned to the same slenderness he had before the obstruction. Completely healed, he became a grateful herald of the saints' grace. He lifted onto his shoulders the pallet on which he had been carried and ran in good health to Alexandria. In this he followed in deed the example of the sick man who lay at the Sheep Pool, whom Christ healed after thirty-eight years and told to take up his bed. He cried out to everyone of the saints' indescribable power and of the work it had wonderfully done for him.

6. On Geddaios the naulomachos [?], who had [?]

From this spectacle the naulomachos draws us to look at him. His name was Geddaios, and his ailment was the disease of the fistula, which tormented him [in the groin ?] more than words can say [?]. He was constantly scourged by it, and the moisture gathered into it from his whole body poured out of it in streams [?]. Geddaios longed to be freed from this

scourge, so he wore out the physicians' doorsteps in every way he could. He kept running [?] and going often to those who were said to excel most others. But he tried them all and did not regain his health, and he spent everything and was not freed from the fistula. Then he came to the saints' shrine. He had no physician left to turn to for a cure and no money left to pay one, but he considered these to be physicians who need no fees. He was granted the martyrs' kindly visit and heard in a vision the remedy for the fistula. It was a mixture of sesame and honey, ground together with paxamas bread so that they made a single poultice. He was told to apply this both to root out the fistula and to fill in the wound. He shook off sleep, quickly did as he had been told, and the healing came at the same moment as the deed. As soon as the potent remedy was applied, the fistula leapt out at once, as though it recognized the saints' command, and the cavity of the fistula was filled up by the martyrs' [?]

7. On Menas, who had weak, strap-like feet.

We have marveled at the skill of these divine physicians and sung the praises of the power God has granted them. Now let us move on to Menas, whose feet had become limp as straps, and make him the theme of our ode to the saints. Menas used to be swift of foot, like a gazelle in the field, as the inspired saying puts it, imitating that Asahel whom Scripture admires for his speed. He was a very fast runner. But he went through a long illness and was changed from swift-footed to strap-footed. At length he was freed from the long illness, but not from what it had produced. When he had been released from the disease, the physicians, who had fought bravely against the lengthy illness [?] but had given up on the weakness it had left behind, Menas remembered the grace of the saints. With faith as his provision for salvation, carried on other people's feet, he reached their house. There he offered prayers to the martyrs for his healing and was ordered to anoint his feet with oil from the lamp that lights up their coffin at night. Menas did this with confidence. He threw off the helplessness of his feet and regained his old swiftness. Then he sang a thanksgiving ode to the saints and covered the road to Alexandria on his own feet.

8. On Christodore the steward, who was in danger while sailing on the lake [?] and broke out in boils because of the hardships of the voyage.

Why, and for how long, should we leave out Christodore,

who was steward of the saints' shrine? The man deserves to be remembered. This is not only for his virtue, for he greatly loves virtue and learning, or for the zeal and care he shows the saints, or for the martyrs' favor toward him. It is also so that those who read the miracles of Cyrus and John may know in whose time they were recorded. This was done at God's command, with the cooperation of those who have worked and still work the miracles. Eulogius of blessed memory, head of the Church of the great city of Alexandria, appointed Christodore to manage the saints' affairs. Before this, Christodore had been in charge [?] at the church of John the Forerunner. The blessed Theodore, who succeeded Eulogius in the see, ordered him to remain over this flock. John, who is called the Almsgiver above all others, received their office with God's help and now pastures their sheep, and he agreed with them and decreed that Christodore should administer the saints' shrine. Under him the wonders worked by the martyrs are being written down and handed on to those who come after us. This is for the praise of those who worked them and for the sake of Christian pride.

You know Lake Mareia, lovers of Christ. All Alexandrians certainly know it, as do many Egyptians, most Libyans, and all of you who have studied Alexandria eagerly. Christodore was sailing across it, intending to go to the Mareotis and inspect the saints' estates. A storm threw the air into turmoil, for it was the season for storms. It churned up the water of the lake and raised harsh waves. The boat was driven this way and that by the swell. It could not keep a straight course but was tossed like a ball from wave to wave. Christodore was in danger. Weeping pitifully, he thought he was going to die. He expected to breathe his last in the water and become food for fish, even if he escaped the jaws of the crocodiles. But before anything like this could happen to him, he turned to the saints with prayers. He knew clearly that they can rescue from death whomever they wish, and he begged them to save him, since he was in danger for their sake. They heard his prayer and quickly came to his side. No place hinders their help or their patient coming, whether on land, lake or sea, whether near at hand or far away. Wherever anyone calls on them for aid, they at once come and help, save and guard that person. If it is an attack of spiritual enemies, they fight alongside him. They win his war against those enemies, chase them off in disgrace, and show that the one who called on them is victorious. If it is the malicious

spite of men, they easily undo it. If savage beasts attack, they grant safety. If illness brings sharp and unbearable torment, they soothe it and heal like gentle physicians. If the danger is on the waters of lakes or seas, they grant calm and rescue those who honor them. So it was then. They appeared to Christodore when he called. One ordered the winds to be still, and the other rebuked the waters and told them to be quiet. Together they spread calm through the air and steered the boat so that it sailed calmly on the current. In this way they saved their wise servant. They showed clearly how much they help when called on for aid. They also meant this to teach the faithful who did not know it, so that calling on them for help in need and danger, they might find the help they long for and escape the most harmful onslaught of the terrors they face.

So Christodore shook off this pitiless death, finding that the saints' all-powerful help came at the same moment as his prayer. But the rough tossing of the voyage, the unbearable turmoil of the air and the savage battering of the waves threw his constitution badly out of balance. Weakened by this, he fell into an unbearable illness. He broke out in eruptions all over his body, as the matter inside him was stirred up and somehow rushed out to the surface of the body. He was in grave danger, though not as pitiably as before.

We all must certainly die, and there is no one who will not travel this road. "For what man is there who will live," it says, "and not see death?" All have one way into life and the same way out. We pray that we may somehow undergo death peacefully, since death is the sentence passed on all human nature.
