But we pray to be spared a departure from this world in fear and turmoil, and above all an end that comes in the waters. The wonderful David also asked for this in his prayers, crying out, "Let not the storm of water drown me, nor the deep swallow me up, nor the pit close its mouth over me." Habakkuk too can be seen praying for something similar: "Were you angry with the rivers, Lord, or was your wrath against the rivers, or your onrush against the sea?" A peaceful end seems to show us in advance God's favor in the life to come, while a terrible end seems to show the unquenchable anger of the one who has already judged. Yet many good people have died hard deaths in this life, and many wicked people have had a most pleasant end. Why this is so is clear to God, who wisely governs our affairs, but it is wholly beyond our grasp and our knowledge. For no one has known the mind or counsel of the Lord, nor been his counselor about the things he created. He set the ways of his governance of the universe in the sea and his paths in many waters. And so, fittingly, it says, "And your footprints will not be known." Christodore, then, as I said before, was in danger,

tossed about by the flood of eruptions and choked by the matter pouring out of him. Even the best of the Asclepiads hurried to his side, but they could do and say nothing more than that he would certainly die and would not see the sun rise the next day. When he heard this pitiful verdict, he remembered the help the saints had given him only recently, and remembering it, he begged to be visited by them again. Along with the martyrs John and Cyrus, he also called on Theodore, the commander among the martyrs, to visit him. Christodore was devoted to Theodore, and out of great affection he often called on him for protection. Theodore received these appeals as coming from a friend and was moved to the greatest compassion. He came to him in his sleep from a great distance to give the help he longed for. He carried a standard in his right hand, with a cross set on top of it, which made it clear that his arrival would bring relief from pain. "Do you know, Christodore," he said, "why I have come?" When Christodore said he did not know, Theodore said, "I have hurried to those who are here to entreat Cyrus, their leader, on your behalf." When the martyr Theodore had said this, Christodore reports, Cyrus appeared at once, bringing his brother John with him. Together and eagerly they came up to the bed and attended to the man lying on it. They touched his sores with their hands and soothed the fury of the eruptions, as if with natron. When they had gently done this, the three of them withdrew again.

All this happened in his sleep. But in waking life the illness ended as the sun shone out. When it had risen above the earth and brightened the day for the world, the boils that the sun had left on him when it set the evening before looked to everyone like fish scales. For the dried-up boils somehow resembled scales as they peeled off the body and fell to the ground. When they had all fallen from his body and left it free of their threat, the martyrs appeared again. It was the fifth day after the first. They told the man who had escaped death beyond all hope to bathe. They also told him to rub his whole body with well-boiled pissarion, a kind of pulse that everyone calls by this name, since it would at once scour away every blemish and every trace of the eruption of boils. And so it happened. When he went into the bath, the marks of the boils went in with him. But when he came out, no trace of them came out with him. Instead he saw that from then on he was free of the blemishes left by the boils and rid of the swellings that had long been visible from so great an illness. So great is the power of the saints that merely by appearing it wipes out every reminder of disease, and merely by willing it erases every sign of sickness. In this way Christodore escaped his double illness. Now that he has been saved, he serves and honors the martyrs. Having brought his story to a close here, and having joined with him in the hymn to the saints, let us turn to things similarly into the

…let us turn our account to the miracles the martyrs worked on his wife.

9. On Theodora, the wife of the steward, who suffered badly from an eye disease.

Since we have told of Christodorus's illnesses and cures, it is good also to remember Theodora (for that was the name of Christodorus's wife) and the miracles the martyrs worked on her. First, then, let us recall the first miracle concerning her. It deserves to be remembered, and it also shows us how the saints urge and visit even those who are absent. Even those who are sick far away they urge to come to them for healing, and to seek this as their merchandise rather than treasures of gold and silver and the brilliance of precious stones. After this, let us set out what happened. The woman had a disease of the eyes and was enduring the illness while living in the city. There a crowd of reputable physicians also attended her, and all of them together were in danger of being defeated by the affliction, so terrible was the malady and so hostile to all the sons of Asclepius. But the saints appeared and broke up this battle of theirs. To use the poet's phrase, they made the victory swing to the other side. Or rather, they awarded each party its due. They healed the affliction by their aid, and neither the disease nor those who wished to treat it, as though defeated by one another, [?]

Let us also tell how the martyrs judged this rightly, for it shows their most particular condescension toward all. At the time when the woman was sick in her sight and the physicians were at war with the affliction, Christodorus was appointed steward of the shrine of John and Cyrus at the urging of the great Eulogius, as we have said. When his wife Theodora learned of this, she at once quarrelled with her husband and disparaged the ministry. "It lies far from the city," she said, "and if we go we leave our home deserted." She objected to the move in every way, bringing forward every pretext that women have ready to hand, and the one she reckoned the strongest and hardest to overturn of all was the weakness of her eyes. And perhaps she would have persuaded her husband to decline the undertaking. Women are formidable at persuading men to whatever they wish, however worthless it may be, for they have nature as their ally, which grants this power to the female sex as the weaker vessel. But the saints learned of it, and since they were pleased with Christodorus's appointment, they stood by the woman in her sleep and made her ready to hasten with her husband to their venerable shrine. "Why," they said when they came to her, "are you preventing your husband from serving us as he has been appointed to do?" She asked the martyrs of Christ, "Who are you?" Cyrus said, "I am Cyrus, and this is John, who carried off the prize of piety together with me." The woman answered, "It is only because of the disease of my eyes. For once I am there,"

"I shall be left without the physicians' help." When the martyrs heard these words, they at once showed her the holy precinct. They pointed out the multitude of the sick lying in it and told her what each one's disease was. "Well then," they said, "along with all these, can we not cure your eyes too?" With these words they persuaded her, working persuasion by deeds and not by bare words. She went out, and merely by looking at their venerable shrine she at once cast off the disease and never again experienced such pain in her eyes. She did not do this or that by way of treatment; by the mere sight of the martyrs' church she gathered an unfading cure. For the sweetest form of the precinct was able to heal the bitterest affliction and to show the immeasurable power of the saints who dwell in it.

Since we have reported the earlier miracle, I will also tell of the other one the martyrs worked on her, and I will not hide it from my hearers in silence. Our subjects do not deserve silence, as do the worthless apparitions of demons. Those deserve silence and oblivion and Tartarus [?] and the outer darkness, a place hidden from the voice of the trumpet, from the loud-voiced herald and from the house whose heights reach the clouds, on which the heralds will stand and cry out. But the things the martyrs do openly and not in a secret corner, full of healing and not filled with shame, are by their nature worthy to be made known to all and proclaimed plainly throughout the whole earth. So let us speak and not hide, let us leap for joy as we speak, and let us dance as [?] proclaims the deeds of the saints, which are the glory and the boast of all the faithful.

Long afterwards this Theodora was bathing to recover from her eye disease, or rather to strengthen her eyes. The bath was the saints' own, for she was living there at the time. While bathing she had a bad fall. She was thrown backward with a crash [?], having slipped on some slimy matter, perhaps from ointments women had rubbed on that had run off. The fall was dangerous because it happened after her bath, as she was going out of the hot rooms into the cold air and waters. At that time the bodies of bathers are sensitive and slack, because the blood, which slackens and loosens them, is spread through them. While we are in colder air, the body's heat flees inward to the heart and hides there, drawn in by contact with the cold. But when we are in warm air, the heat moves back outward [?] and at once comes out to the surface, freed in some way from the cold that confined and contracted it, and recognizing its kinship with the heat outside. Theodora's body was in just such a condition then when she fell on her back and neck. She was struck very deeply on the elbow; the blow opened a great wound there, and much blood poured out of it. But this blow, so dangerous, and

this wound, so hard to heal, the martyrs healed. They appeared at once and did not allow it to be noticed on her arm and injured elbow even to the third day. You are surely eager to hear also the remedy by which the divine martyrs healed so great an injury in a moment of time. I will tell this too briefly and make it plain to my hearers. When night came on and took the place of the sunlight of that day, the saints stood [?] by the woman as she slept. Perhaps she had been granted sleep amid such pains for this very reason, so that she might receive the saints' swift visit. Standing beside her, the kindly martyrs ordered her to sponge her arm with Mareotic wine and to lay the flesh of a labrax on the wound (the labrax is a sea fish called by that name). They also told her to use the baths as was fitting [?], for they saw that the harm came from demons. In this way they would set up the trophy of healing in the very place where the demons' spite had struck. When the saints' command was carried out, Theodora was healed at once. The demons were put to shame for plotting in vain, while the martyrs were glorified, and Christ God, who works wonders through them.

10. On Maro, the daughter of the steward, who suffered [?] from her teeth and ears.

Let us add Maro to these and join the little daughter to her parents, for she was the offspring of Christodorus and Theodora. Let us not pass over her, even though she has lately passed out of this life of ours. She departed in the prime of youth and left those on earth in the flower of her age. She was of fit age for marriage, but she knew nothing at all of a husband's bed. Let us then join her too to her parents as we narrate the miracles of the saints, and let us not imitate inhuman death, which parted her from those who gave her birth, by leaving her unremembered ourselves. For Maro too gained the martyrs' help while she was still alive, and we will set it out, recalling how it happened. The girl was very young and still sucked the breast that nourishes such an age. She had not yet grown the walls of her teeth, and she gathered the milk (for this is the fruit of the breasts) not with her hands but with her lips and mouth. Then the time came for her when teeth grow in infants. They give the mouth a marble-like grace, make clear the indistinct voice that comes through it, and grind the more solid food. But they usually grow in with some suffering: they cause many pains to children cutting teeth, and they bring on dreadful fevers that cruelly parch the body. Maro, as an infant, was in this situation. As she cut her teeth she endured the pains that come before them. These run ahead like bodyguards, preparing the way

for the teeth. They scourge the gums and, through them, every part of the body, even though they serve only to prepare for what is to come [?]. At one point these pains wounded Maro terribly. They kindled fevers, made her mouth sting, pressed on her ears and filled her head with flux, and they afflicted the girl in this way until the teeth appeared. When the teeth flashed out from the gums and the mouth received its proper grace, the pains ceased. But her ears were filled with the flux that had gathered. At last, unable to contain all that flowed into them, they burst like rocks that are the mothers of waters, and from this came springs of discharge, foul smells and a swarm of worms. This threefold affliction gushed out so violently that no barrier or obstacle could hold back the flowing stream.

When the child's mother saw this and could bear it no longer, she decided to go to Alexandria and bring the child to physicians to be healed and treated by them, for at that time she was living at the saints' shrine. On the night before she had arranged to go into the city, she saw in her sleep a physician's room, empty. But she found a monk sitting in it. The monk who appeared sitting there was Cyrus, for he had become a monk and must always appear in the dress of monks. A small cabinet stood in front of the martyr, so that, he says, the physicians' arrangement might be kept there too [?], so that it looked like a surgery. The saint, seated as though on a throne, said to her, "Why have you come here, woman?" She answered him, "I am looking for a surgery, and I took this little house to be one. But I see none of the things physicians keep for their rounds lying about in it, and your cabinet has nothing of the kind inside either." He answered her precisely: "Search, and whatever you find, put it into the affected ears, and your little daughter will be healed." She went all round the house and saw a small niche with a cup of honey set in it. For the cabinet, I think, was a medicine chest for more serious illnesses. Rising quickly from her pallet, she did what she had been told. She poured a little honey into the baby's ears, and drew out a sac full of worms, four fingers long and correspondingly wide. At once the girl was freed from what had been for her a storehouse of pains, and she was delivered from the insatiable torments it bred. So the martyrs healed Maro with plain honey.

There was another pious and Christ-loving woman who bore the same name, Maria (for they called the girl Maro, a pet form of the name Maria), but she was neither of the same time nor of the same age. She had a similar affliction, but from a different cause. After trying many physicians in vain, she came to their venerable martyr-shrine, and they healed her with wax salve and mulberries [?]. In her sleep they ordered her to combine these by

rubbing them together [?] and to put them into her ears. As for us, let us again sing the martyrs' praises together with the women who were healed, and let us hurry on to other wonders of theirs and set these deeds before those who listen with piety.

11. On Maria, the daughter of the deacon, who suffered no harm when she fell from a height [?].

Let us recall another girl of the same name and the same age, and with her, of course, another miracle. This one is greater than the one before and beyond comparison. The earlier cure an excellent physician might perhaps have performed, though not so quickly and not with such a remedy. But this one no physician could have performed, nor even all mankind gathered together to perform it, unless they could also raise the dead from their tombs [?] … of thread … the spindle [?]. And when [?] happened, as often tends to occur, something necessary perhaps occupied her and forced her to leave the child on the window ledge, and she went off to what she had run to do. But the baby, deprived of her mother's care, was alone and by nature did not yet know good from evil, and she fell from a very high window down to the ground. Her body struck with a thud below, and the mother leaned out to see what had caused the thud. She had completely forgotten that she had left her little daughter sitting on the window ledge. Leaning out, she saw her lying flung on the ground, and at once remembered the fall. With her shrieking and wailing she shook that whole place and the heavenly shrine of the martyrs, for her room adjoined it, and she went in and out of her house through the church. She ran down, drenching her cheeks with many tears, and with her ran all who saw her weeping and heard her crying out from afar. They meant to take up the dead girl and give her burial in a tomb. But they found her safe, unharmed and uninjured, sitting on the ground and playing with some pigs that were there, slapping them with clumsy [?] and graceless blows. They quickly snatched her up and laid her before the tomb of the saints, honouring them as the baby's saviours and singing their praises as the helpers and guardians of all who trust in them in Christ.

I think it is not superfluous to add to the story what was seen in sleep concerning this on that night. The man in question is John the deacon. He is not the child's father, but the one who came from Byzantium to the martyrs because of a disease of the feet. The disease was called a chilling of the knees, and neither the emperor's physician nor any of the others who wished to cure it had been able to. He was healed and delivered from the illness, and in gratitude he promised to serve the saints all his life. Afterwards he was enrolled as a deacon. He came from the lay state, but he lived an earnest and monastic life, and he was ordained by the martyrs' decree and command and by the patriarchal laying-on of hands of John, who now shepherds the church of the Alexandrians. He said that as he slept on the night before the day the miracle we have told of was to happen, he saw the martyrs Cyrus and John, and with them a great white-robed assembly of saints. They said to him, "Come with us and enjoy the festivity that is about to take place." John asked the saints where they were going and to what feast. They said, "John the deacon has invited us to dinner today, and we are all being entertained at his house." When they had said this, the brilliant company of the saints, that is, their whole throng, told him to follow them too. "When all the saints had gone off to the house," he says, "I went up [?], fulfilling the command of those who had bidden me. I dined with them and then withdrew again with them, astonished at the dignity and the robes of the guests." He marvelled at the solemn splendour of the dinner, and when the vision he had seen came to an end, he told everything to John the deacon. He did not know what the story signified, but he called him happy and blessed if he should attain such honour as to entertain so many saints of such rank and welcome them into his home. And the dream remained entirely unintelligible until the miracle took place and interpreted it.

I, together with everyone, marvelled at this too in the saints: following Christ, the teacher and God of all, in everything, they fittingly likened the miracle here too to a dinner. For the Saviour, sitting at the well in Samaria and urged by his disciples to eat, answered them, "I have food to eat that you do not know about." By food he meant the salvation and delightful redemption of those who believe in him. "For my food," he says, "is to do the will of the Father [?] who sent me and to complete his work." And the Father's work and will is nothing other than their salvation. So now too the martyrs John and Cyrus rightly called the girl's salvation food and a dinner. They were foretelling the extraordinary miracle that would happen to her, which fed their good and loving hunger and delighted their pure and wise purpose. As for us, we have finished the story of the girl here, and we send up shouts of praise to the martyrs who saved her.

Now let us write down another of their stories.

12. On Count Julian, who was paralysed in all his limbs through sorcery.

Julian, who is now Thaumasius, "the Wonderful," more truly than before, comes forward for our narrative. He is weighed down with abundant wealth and does not lack the possessions of virtue. He is of distinguished family and known to all as a man of dignity. He had a twofold illness and received a twofold healing for it. He is still alive and tells everyone his story. Yet he wished to be included in this very brief collection of ours, so that he might go on announcing his miracle to those who come after, as though he would always survive. We admire his affection and welcome his devotion to these saints, so let us set about writing his story.

Julian was in the prime of youth, and he had wealth as young as his years, which is the father of licentiousness and the teacher of all wantonness. Youth gave birth to pleasures and put them forward, and wealth nursed and nourished them, and his soul was at war with wealth and bodily youth together. But they overcame it by force, took it captive and led it off as a slave, and compelled it to do what they pleased. It did not dare to resist the harsh commands they laid on it, any more than ancient Israel did when it served long ago in Egypt. One could see it like a weak and powerless charioteer drawn by prancing horses. He cannot check their charge but is carried along against his will and dragged violently by them, and in the end he lets go of the reins and is hurled over the cliff with them. So the young man's soul, tyrannized by wealth and mastered by luxury and the vigour of his body, was swept off to shameful pleasures and bowed like a slave to unnatural passions. In this state, before a lawful marriage Julian joined in lawless unions. Before he had embraces of his own, he was held in another's arms. Before he had acquired a spring of his own, he went to draw water from a spring that had no master. Before the foal of graces, he consorted with a wandering foal. For he fell in love with a woman and became entangled with her for pleasure. Later he was joined in honourable marriage and an undefiled bed. Then, perceiving the harm of the lawless union, he broke off his relations with that woman. She could not bear the separation, and in a foul jealousy she took revenge on the young man by sorcery and contrived his death because he had left her. She failed to kill the youth, but she made him no different from a corpse. With her drug she bound his hands and feet and disabled every limb of his body. Rather, God protected the young man. In his goodness God does not remember the sins of youth. He overlooks the sins of mortals and does not bring on wrath for days [?], but

…who is always long-suffering and waits for our conversion and repentance. So he was a pitiable sight. For his parents it was a calamity; for his young wife and his family it was unexpected grief in place of joy; and for everyone who saw him it was a most piteous spectacle. He was carried on other people's feet and made use of other people's hands. Everything that God has granted human beings to do for themselves, he did and accomplished through others. None of the physicians could rescue him from the affliction. Regimens did not help, nor antidotes, nor repeated ointments, nor every kind of remedy. The affliction was stronger than all of these and would not yield to any human hand. When his parents saw this, they took refuge in God and the martyrs, bidding farewell to medical remedies and choosing divine help instead. The most divine martyrs took pity on the young man and blunted the stings of his pains. They granted him the ability to move his hands and stretch out his feet in part, for a certain matter of doctrine kept them from granting him a complete cure. This young Julian was a disciple of the elder Julian, the Apollinarian of Halicarnassus, and he shared his mind and his belief. Julian the younger carried these doctrines in his soul, and he approached the saints because of the illness of his body, not because of them. The blessed martyrs often came to him by night and urged him to give up such doctrine and to embrace the communion of the catholic Church. Often they also carried the cup filled with the holy body and blood of the Lord and urged him to come forward. They seemed to partake themselves and invited Julian to partake with them. Sometimes they also discussed doctrine with him, explaining the truth proclaimed in the Church, and they swore that this is how the proclamation concerning the saving union of Christ our God truly stands. But they did all this and more and still did not persuade Julian, because he did not want to be persuaded. So they reminded him again of his former pain. They brought back the stings of his pains, perhaps with something added, binding his hands and feet as before and increasing the pains still more. In this they were perhaps showing in deeds the words of the psalm, squeezing "with bit and bridle" the jaws of those who do not draw near to God through faith. That fine young man had brushed aside so many exhortations, so many testimonies and such great visions, and before all these the miracle that had been done for him. Yet he could not brush aside those small scourges. He cried out, shouted, entreated, called and implored, and he sent up supplications, calling on the martyrs. There was no one to redeem him or rescue him, no one to deliver him from his torments or able to help, since what was happening was the anger of the saints. But when by such torments his stubbornness

[?], and they had made the formerly disobedient man obedient, then they appeared smiling and joking with him, and they asked why he was shouting and crying out like this. As though they did not know, he told them of his affliction and urged them to help him in his danger. The divine martyrs again reminded him of the faith he had been shown [?]. They indicated that it was because of this that the pains were troubling him, and that they would never release him from his torments unless he first released himself from the heresy that held him and embraced the communion of the apostolic Church. Julian longed to see this and prayed to learn it. When the martyrs saw that the young man was yielding to them, they told him these things as well, to give him greater assurance. Raising their hands to heaven, they swore the greatest and most fearful oaths that Christ does not hold or count either Gaianites or Theodosians in the measure of the faithful or in the number of the pious. Julian learned these things from the saints under oath and was taught the truth by blows and oaths. He was freed from both the heresy and the illness, receiving health of soul and strength of body through [?]

I think I would harm the narrative if I kept silent about the charming and delightful thing the saints did in connection with Julian's communion. It was this. They saw him withdrawing from his former heresy and embracing the true confession of the Saviour. But he felt shame about receiving the holy mysteries and thought it a disgrace in view of [?]. So they did something wonderful and worthy of delight [?]. They appeared to him in his sleep, as they were accustomed to do, and said: "Look, the Saviour's Nativity is near, when the only-begotten Son of God and the Father became incarnate and became man. The Alexandrians who are sons and nurslings of the catholic Church celebrate this holy and venerable festival in the church of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, which is named after Theonas. Go there yourself and become one of those who piously honour the feast of the Nativity. Be counted among the Church of the faithful: share in the psalmody, listen to the apostolic readings and hear the trumpet of the holy Gospels, since people stay until they have heard these. After the dismissal that follows the Gospel readings, leave as you used to do, taking care to avoid suspicion. Once you have left the precinct, wait in the Dromos. This is a famous place in the city of the Alexandrians. It is laid out like a highway, divided down the middle by two colonnades and adorned with columns and marble. It is crowded with a great throng and laden with all kinds of shops, as in the marketplaces. Walk about there," they said, "and watch for the dismissal of the synaxis. When you see that everyone has gone home, and no one is watching any longer, quietly go into the precinct and partake of the venerable mysteries. Then go home and keep quiet [?]

[?] our [?]. Once this is done, you will escape the reproach of the heresy you were known for as soon as the story is told, and you will put an end to the suspicion of shame. And you will have [?] unceasing praise for your salvation." This was the saints' advice. Julian received the advice as coming from saints, and since it fitted his own purpose, he agreed to carry out their commands. But things did not turn out as he thought, or as he longed and craved, even though he believed this was what the exhortation meant. They turned out as the saints had judged and decreed, and as the Saviour's saying declared: "Let your light so shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven." What the martyrs wanted to proclaim on the housetops, he wanted to hide in secret. So when the holy festival of the Nativity arrived, Julian remembered the saints' command and came, it is said, to the precinct called Theonas. He listened to the Gospel and apostolic readings, and after they had been read he went out to the Dromos. He stayed there for the length of the synaxis. After its dismissal, when the faithful had departed, he came to the church again and slipped in secretly, and, as he thought, received the mysteries. But while he was bending down and stooping, as was fitting, to receive the Lord's body, clerics of the heresy called that of the Gaianites, perhaps about a hundred of them, entered the church to pray. Some of them do this out of custom after the dismissal, to keep up their reverence for the place and give the customary veneration to the Mother of God. When they saw Julian receiving communion, they were astonished at the man's change of side, and they nodded to one another, pointing him out to those who had not seen him. He looked up and swallowed the life-giving food into his inward parts. When he saw them, he immediately blushed with shame and realized that the saints had made a public show of him. He told them everything they asked: all that the martyrs had done to keep hold of him, and how they had made a public show of him when he was ashamed to receive communion. In this very way his union with the catholic Church came about, full of wonder and astonishment, and of the gentleness and grace of the saints. And the strength of his body kept pace with the change of his soul. Now that we have completed the account of him and praised the saints, let us pass on to another of their miracles and tell its story.

13. On Elias the leper.

Who will hear of the marvel the saints worked for Elias the leper and not marvel at those who did it, and testify that they can do a great deal? Elias happened to be a leper and had suffered from this condition for a long time. He was known as a leper not in one limb only; in his whole body he bore the marks

of the disease. These were not the marks that Paul had and boasted of. Those were virtues and heavenly deeds, which formed the image of Christ in Paul. They were like rays of the Sun of righteousness and made those who have them children of light and sons of day. His were the marks that were loathsome and unclean under the Mosaic law. They drove the person who had them outside the camp and the city, shutting him off as loathsome and unclean from the rest of his people. These marks are symbols of sin, and the Word, who is God and became man among men, drove them away from human beings both in spirit and in letter. He also commanded the leper whom he then healed according to the letter to offer the gift according to the law of Moses. Elias bore these marks, and no one could help him at all. Here too Hippocrates and Galen were useless, and so was Democritus, the bastard brother of nature, along with those who swagger about their teachings and offer us their names in place of great remedies. So he came to the martyrs Cyrus and John, wanting to obtain healing for his affliction and believing that he would certainly obtain it. When no small span of time had passed and he had gained nothing, he lost heart, since the saints were holding back the healing for certain purposes of their own. This plainly happened to him because of a diabolical scheme: the devil wanted to prevent his cure and cut him off from the saints' compassion. So he could no longer stay in the precinct. For acedia is a heavy passion. It is very hostile to God-loving souls and can do them great harm, unless they quickly and vigorously quench it as an apparition of the noonday demon. The leper put off doing this. He could no longer bear its burning, so he set out and went away, abandoning the precinct and the martyrs' divine gifts and, as far as it lay with him, the healing of his own illness. But the saints saw that the time of his recovery had been grudged him, and they pitied him and had mercy on him, taking no account of his folly and insult toward them. As he was going away, near the shrine of the holy martyr Metras, at midday, they met him in the guise of monks. Pretending a sympathetic ignorance, they asked him where he was coming from and where he was going. He answered as though speaking to people who truly did not know: he named the saints and told them how many months he had spent there. But the martyrs told him to say also why he had gone there. He said, "You can see the reason. It is obvious and needs no one to point it out." The divine martyrs asked again, "And why did you leave before you were freed from the affliction?" He told them how long he had stayed and explained that he had gained nothing by staying, calling those hideous white patches as his witnesses. In this he did not blame the saints for being unable or unwilling. Instead, with reverence and tears, he said that he himself was unworthy of the gift. The most compassionate

martyrs pitied him all the more and said, "Listen to us now and go back quickly, and you will see [?] the wonders of God and the saints' visitation upon you. When you reach their precinct, you will find about four camels passing by the spring. Carefully take the dung of the fourth, dissolve it in the water of the spring, and anoint your whole body with this ointment. Leave no part at all unanointed, so that no part left unanointed will remain spotted and be held by this disease for good." They said these things to his face and suddenly vanished. He at once concluded that the vision was divine, and that those who had appeared and given these commands were the martyrs themselves [?]. He hurried to their venerable precinct, and by the spring he found the camels he had been told about. He took the dung of the last one, as they had said, soaked it in the streams of their spring, and anointed himself all over. But here too the envious demon was at work on him. For he did not anoint his face with the ointment, it is said, because he loathed the very thing that was cleansing him. So it turned out just as the saints' divinely spoken command had said: his whole body at once became clean of the marks, but his face remained spotted for the rest of his life. It was an open proof of his disobedience, and an unsilenced herald and truly trustworthy witness to the martyrs' power and to their unexpected command. Elias blamed himself greatly for his disobedience, but it did him no good at all, just as Esau did not [?] [find a place for repentance], though he sought his birthright with tears.

14. On Theopemptus the demoniac.

After Elias let Theopemptus come forward before us. He has found a fitting place in the sequence, since he keeps to the order of the initial letters of the two names. I will give a short account of the miracle done for him. It will delight those who listen piously and will proclaim the saints' most fearful trophies over the demons. Theopemptus was terribly possessed by a demon, and there was no one who saw him and did not weep. For people generally tend to be more moved by those held by such a disease, perhaps because it is not an affliction of the body. From the beginning the body tasted the tree of disobedience inside paradise, and so it was naturally subjected to passions. It is in bondage to corruption and to the falls that corruption brings, and even before death to its properties, until the common resurrection of all, when corruption and the things that bring corruption in along with death are completely abolished. But this disease is contrary to the nature of an immortal soul. It is an alteration of a nature made incorruptible by the grace of God its maker, a passion akin to corruption, born of the demons' abuse, even though God himself, displaying the excess of his love for humankind, allowed it to happen for the benefit of those who suffer it. Theopemptus had been in bondage to this disease for eighteen years. He could no longer bear the de-

mon's raging, so he came to the martyrs Cyrus and John, who abolish and drive out such things. With much toil he covered the long distance of the journey, since for lack of money he made it on foot. Only after sunset did he finally reach the shrine. By then he had used up his strength through great exhaustion, and he lay down outside the enclosure of the church. He could not walk even that short distance further, so he put off entering the precinct until the next day, as though it were some great and difficult task. While he slept there all night, the benevolent martyrs stood beside him in a dream, appearing in their own forms and not in strange ones. They called him by name and said, "Brother Theopemptus, look: we have driven out the evil spirit that troubled and afflicted you, in the name of Jesus Christ, who endured the cross for us. Now get up, give thanks to God, and go back to your home." He did not wait for the sun to appear to men. Having laid aside the weariness of the journey together with the demon, he quickly got up from where he had been lying and went into the precinct. He sang his thanks for that very great healing to God and the martyrs, rejoicing and leaping for joy, and proclaiming the greatness of the miracle,

15. On John, who was disfigured by disease.

John too did well to imitate Theopemptus and watched for the present opportunity, since he too keeps the order of the letters quite undisturbed. My pen wants to move on to others, but he will not let himself be passed over untold. So let us write his story too at the right moment, admiring his sharpness and sobriety. John had an inhuman affliction, one that is, one might say, greater and more bitter than all bodily afflictions. Perhaps this is why physicians designate it by the elephant's name. That animal surpasses the other four-footed beasts in strength and in size of body. They also say that it bears a grudge against those who hurt it, and after many cycles of years it repays the one who hurt it bitterly, if it can. In the same way, physicians judged this disease far greater in malignity than the others and called it by the elephant's name. Moses also ordered that the person held by the disease of elephantiasis be kept outside the camp and the city together with the leper. By the leper he banished the many-coloured variety of sin, and by the person with elephantiasis he perhaps drove out the savagery of the passions. The divine teachers of the Church also say that Moses took the greatest care with regard to elephantiasis. He kept men from intercourse with women until the woman's complete purification from her monthly flow, which naturally takes seven days. For this, they say, is how the bodies of those with elephantiasis come to be: the disease is conceived and grows along with them, and its cause lies with their parents and their incontinent and untimely intercourse. And that

even beasts by nature keep such a rule, one of the friends of the righteous Job testified, crying out, "He set a season for the beasts, and they know the order of their mating." With good reason he reproached human beings in this, since they do not know a season for intercourse, which even irrational creatures honour and keep. Some also say that the devil struck Job with this affliction of elephantiasis, as being a terrible and great one. "And the devil went out from the Lord," it says, "and struck Job with a malignant sore from his feet to his head." He hoped that the size of the wound would take the righteous man captive. Yet he achieved nothing of what he hoped, since the righteous man had his foundation set on rock and not on sand. And Job, having conquered his attacker by endurance, won the [?] of victory

This John was gripped by this disease and was gradually being consumed by it. Since he found no sweet healing from the physicians, he came to Cyrus, who puts an end to evils, and to John, Cyrus's fellow martyr. He believed that Christ's healers would cure him at once, if only they wished. When they saw the man who had fled to them for refuge, they admired his faith in them. They entertained him kindly at their shrine for a very short time, gave him health as a worthy reward for his faith in them, and sent him away. I will also write down the remedy by which the martyrs easily cured such an ailment [?]. Otherwise the meddlesome among the physicians might think the saints applied some Hippocratic remedy. Then they would scorn the martyrs' ineffable power, proclaiming Hippocrates and Galen as the cause of the healing and not the martyrs who actually did it. The remedy was glass that had been ground down and turned back into its old form, sand. For the saints ordered him in dreams to apply this remedy to the whole body that had the sacred disease. He eagerly did what he was told, and even more eagerly he put off the disease. That water is by nature fluid, so when it was applied to the body it did not stay put. As soon as it was applied, it ran off onto the ground, even though it had the glass mixed in. In the same way the disease of elephantiasis could not stay when this running water was applied to it. It ran off together with the water, in fear of those who had given the command, and perhaps, because of them, in fear of the glass mixed into the water as well. Now that we have written down this miracle too, to the praise of those who worked it, let us write the account of another miracle, hymning the martyrs together with all who have been healed.

16. On Zacharias, who suffered in the testicles.

Zacharias, the slowest of all, almost escaped our notice. He had not become slow through a disease of the feet. Another disease had robbed him of speed: he was hindered by swellings of the genital organs. The parts that ached and swelled were those by which eunuchs are distinguished from other men. Not only

[?] and because of this he walked with a sluggish gait, and showed himself to us like a bee in winter. Perhaps he was also ashamed of such a disease and wanted to hide his weakness, although we have been commanded to be ashamed of the passions of the soul, not of the body. "Let the ungodly be put to shame," it says, "and brought down to Hades"; and again, "Be ashamed, O Sidon, said the sea," where idolatry is meant by the name of Sidon; and again, "Let all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned back." The Lord too spoke of those who are sent away to everlasting shame. He did not mean those weighed down by bodily sufferings, for he himself bore our weaknesses and our diseases. He meant those who have fallen sick in soul and have become doers of wicked deeds. Some diseases are involuntary: all those that are recognized as belonging to the body and concerning the body. Others are voluntary and are the offspring of our own will: all those that defile the beauty of the soul, which is free and rational. For this reason none of the saints has ever been seen to reproach us for the former—not the law, not a prophet, not a righteous man, not an apostle, not a teacher. They were all subject to these things themselves, since they wore a body just as we do. The Lord himself was subject to them as well, when he became man and was called one who suffers as we do, being of one substance with us through his body and rational soul. But all of them have reproached the passions of the soul, which are chosen and not forced on us. The law punishes them and fixes a penalty that fits the passion. The prophets command us to keep away from them and to take up better things. The righteous urge us to abandon them. The apostles lead us by the hand away from them. The teachers show us how to flee them. And the Lord, who was the first to show us the way of righteousness and the first to find the path of complete withdrawal from material passions, said to all in his love for humankind, "Learn from me." It is for these things that we are called to account, since clearly their existence depends on us. We shall render that account when we are judged. We shall stand before the judgment seat of Christ when the Judge comes from heaven to repay each according to his works, not according to the sufferings of his body. "For we shall all," it says, "stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or bad." So Zacharias is ashamed of a bodily suffering for nothing. So are all who, like him, are ashamed of bodily sufferings. They do not know the true causes of shame and wrongly turn its order upside down. Yet, though he appeared late and with difficulty, he did arrive and reach the sanctuary of the saints. He begged them, and kept begging, to be freed from the weight of his testicles. They came to him at night as he slept and said, "Zacharias, why have you come to us?"

He blushed a little and, out of modesty, hinted at the cause. The martyrs wanted to teach him not to be ashamed of bodily sufferings, so they made him show them the ailment and directed him to his private parts. Full of shame, he did as he was told, for his modesty would not let him resist those who gave the order. They gently stroked those parts with their hands and drove the swelling away. Then they let him go home: "See," they said, "there is nothing wrong with you. Get up and go back home in peace." When he woke from that dream, which put an end to his pains, he found that the swelling of his testicles had flown away with it. He had been set free from pain and from a most grievous burden. He crowned with praises the martyrs who had freed him from these things, and Christ, who through them had given him freedom from the disease, and then he departed.

17. On John Chrysones, whose thighs had rotted.

Let us also remember John. We do not do so because he was of noble birth or one of those who pride themselves on gold, though that is why he was called Chrysones, since both his wealth and his business pushed him toward that name. He would not have been called Chrysones while lacking in gold if he had not received from the saints a possession more brilliant than gold: healing. They grant it freely to all who come to them and turn no one away from their gift, unless someone is utterly loathsome and unworthy of their kindness. Such a person has become unworthy either through unbelief or because his wicked deeds have given him a will that refuses to turn back. As the account goes on, I too shall mention one or two people of this kind who gained no benefit from the saints. Then readers will know the saints' zeal for the faith and their hatred of wicked deeds, and will strive to please them in their life and faith. This John, then, who took pride both in owning gold and in his name, fell into a terrible disease. It could not be described in words, and the sons of the physicians could not easily cure it. The man's thighs were being eaten away, as if by some divine wrath. The skin that covered his thighs rotted and burst open everywhere because the putrefaction was so severe. The flesh it had once covered was stripped entirely of its proper garment, the garment nature had given it. It came away from the bones and fell off, rotting little by little along with the skin that wrapped it, and dripped down onto the ground. He spent a long time in this disease, deceived by the empty talk of the physicians. He got nothing from them but words that dissolved into the air and never touched the wound. In the end the long duration of the disease and his pitiable suffering made him learn at last, from Hippocrates himself, that the disease was incurable. He bade the physicians a long farewell and came to the famous clinic of Cyrus and John. And they,

the martyrs who truly deserve the name of physicians, wished to show the difference between their own power and the weakness of physicians. They appeared to him in a dream and healed him with a humble remedy: they told him to grind salt together with cumin and plaster it on his thighs. As soon as he woke, the sick man did this, and he freed himself from grievous pains and no small misfortunes. He had been thought to be wasting away little by little until he met the death common to all. Now he was bound together again by applications of cumin and salt. He was made strong by the counsel of the martyrs, and by a divine decree he sent away the death he had been expecting. After this, having sung the praises of God and of the living saints, we [?] to another of their miracles.

18. On Paul, whose head was full of worms.

A certain Paul, a poor man, very needy and without gold, comes into our narrative after John Chrysones the rich. He reckons that he might gain something from being near him, just as we see the poor doing in the marketplaces. They come up to those who are flowing with gold and walk behind them, hoping to catch a few drops that may trickle from them out of Christ-loving compassion. Paul now comes forward doing the same, and perhaps he gets what he hoped for, since John did not live far from love of the poor. But Paul comes forward with a suffering, an incurable disease. He too wants to gain health from the martyrs and longs to receive healing from them. There, perhaps, he gathered a remedy for his poverty, but here he certainly receives the cure for his illness. His ailment was as follows, and this is how he obtained his treatment. He had pains in his head beyond words. The pain showed itself in his cries and his sleeplessness, and also in a swelling. But no one could be found to explain the swelling and the symptoms that came with it. Some of the physicians said that blood was the cause, others an excessive build-up of some humor, and each of them [?] a different collection of matter. Nothing they said held to the truth. They were guessing at what seemed right to them, and each overturned the others' advice with his own verdicts. But the saints knew the affliction exactly and understood the cause of the pains, and they healed it in a rather playful way. What had seemed impossible to the physicians they showed to be easy for themselves, a kind of game. Let us tell of the sweet and charming side of this treatment as well. It hints at the power of the saints, and the miracle creates a spiritual delight mixed with bodily pleasure, or rather it does so for those who come to hear of it. Against all hope they made Paul fall asleep. He had almost forgotten what sleep was, since his head was being eaten away unseen and the pains held him without relief. They stood beside him at night as he slept, giving him healing and

showing him how he would be cured. "Before dawn," they said, "get up from your bed and go out to the gate facing the sea, the one that closes off the outer precinct of the church. Strike the first man you meet hard on the cheek. Once you have done this, you will very soon find healing for the ailment that afflicts you." He thought that what he had seen was a fantasy, and he did none of the things the saints had told him. Twice he was ordered in a vision to do this, and he did not do it. When the martyrs spoke a third time, he learned that unless he did it, he would not obtain the healing he longed for. So he got up from his bed before dawn and went to the gate he had been shown. A soldier met him at the gate. He held a staff in his hand, and in his heart he held a temper to match. Paul slapped him hard, landing the blow on his cheek. The soldier did not hesitate. He struck back in the same instant, at once raising his stick and hitting the man who had slapped him on the skull, a far harder blow than the one he had received [?]. When Paul took such a heavy blow to the head, he fell to the ground wounded. Blood and worms gushed out of him, and he cast out all the worms inside him. There were very many of them, and they had been devouring him without mercy. So he was rid of the disease, finding an unexpected release that was given to him by a blow and a wound. The wound itself healed quickly. Indeed, we should not call it a wound at all, but a remedy for a wound, a help against disease, a plaster for suffering, and a cure for affliction. Having gained complete health, he sang a hymn to the martyrs and praised God, as was fitting, who had worked the cure through them. Then he went away, and he became for us too the occasion and reason for a song to Christ and to the martyrs.

19. On Stephanis, who had cancer.

Let the extraordinary healing of Stephanis also be counted among the miracles. Let no one disbelieve this miracle. Weigh the strength of the saints and recognize the grace given to them. They heal every disease and, out of compassion, grant healing to all who come to them in faith. Stephanis, then, the woman whose story we are about to tell, had a terrible and incurable affliction. It was called cancer, the "crab," a name well suited to its nature. Since it resembles a crab, it fittingly took the crab's name as well. This was Stephanis's disease, whose pains are known only to women who have experienced it. Physicians, including the founders of their art, Galen and Hippocrates, the elegant pride of the profession, are not ashamed to proclaim their defeat. They decline to make war on the disease of cancer and crown it with the prize of victory. In this way they show its natural crookedness. No well-prepared drug, no powerful remedy, no all-useful plaster such as the [?] plaster, no antidote such as the one called Philo's, nor any other natural and

unmixed remedy, or one made by combining it with another kind, has been able to calm it to this day. So savage is the disease, so fierce has it become, and [?] all the more does it resist being tamed or driven out. Stephanis learned how tyrannical and savage it was. She learned how powerless the art of medicine was against it, as those who practice that art declared by word and deed. She also learned that her disease yields only to God and to the martyrs and obeys their commands. So she at once deserted to God and to Cyrus and John, the servants of Christ, the God of all. When they saw her, they honored her as her faith in them deserved. Their honor was the gift of a swift healing, freedom and release from the disease that held her in secret. They healed the woman, then, not with invisible remedies, as they usually heal the sick, but by touching the affliction with visible hands. One day, as she stood before the martyrs' tomb of the saints and begged to receive treatment, weeping and groaning and offering her prayers with fervent faith, she suddenly cast off the cancer. With it went all the harm and the weakness it had caused, and it fell to the ground writhing. Many people saw it at once, since it was daytime: those who were present praying and asking for help. Many more saw it afterward, hung up high and proclaiming the power of the saints, when they came to pray to the martyrs. We heard this from them and have written it down. Since we have learned it truly, we proclaim it, glorifying the saints for this. We urge those who are sick and held fast by incurable diseases to come to them for treatment. Now that we have told the story of this miracle, we shall go on to the account of another.

20. On Maria, who had dropsy.

Great indeed is the benefit of telling of miracles. It benefits all who hear alike, strengthening their souls together with their bodies. To souls it grants more abundant faith, and to bodies release from bodily sufferings. To both souls and bodies alike it gives a pure and dearly longed-for gladness and a delight full of spiritual exultation, which no words can describe to those who listen. We have gathered this fruit from the previous miracle. Let us gather it from the present one too, sharing in the joy of those who were healed and in the most devout boasting in the martyrs. There it was Stephanis who became the occasion of gladness; here it will be Maria. She had a disease that was hard to cure, and she received healing beyond all hope. Those trained in medical science call the disease dropsy. But they are unable to help anyone who has fallen into such a condition, in small things or great. They cannot even offer any comfort

from their art, as they do in nearly all other diseases, curing some completely and, in others, soothing the sufferers and somehow easing their symptoms with remedies. Maria suffered from this disease and came into extreme danger. She was enormously swollen, a horrifying sight. After the physicians had given up hope and death seemed certain, she reached the church of the saints at great risk. She was laid on the floor with difficulty and lay there groaning in pain, too weak to speak for groaning. As the disease pressed upon her and crushed her with a swelling beyond description, the martyrs, overflowing with mercy, appeared to her in her sleep. They granted her the life she had no hope of keeping, told her the remedy for the disease, and ordered her to use it quickly. The remedy was a hard-baked rusk. It did not come from far away but was baked in Heraclea, a neighboring village. When she told her dream, those near her brought one. They soaked it in the water of the spring and sprinkled it over her whole body from head to foot, as the saints had commanded. As this salve of rusk and water dried, the mass of moisture smoldering inside her dried up as well. The salve drew all of it up, the way a sponge soaks up liquid [?], and painlessly drew it out into the open. The remedy soaked up not only that excess of fluid but also the death that the disease was bringing. So Maria, who had been in such grievous danger, easily escaped it. She received the power of the martyrs, which proved stronger than the disease and was known to be the cause of her cure. Let us once again praise the martyrs and sing of them as the workers of such great works. Then let us write of another very great work of their grace, worthy of just as much praise.

21. On Martyria, whose bowels were afflicted through sorcery.

Let us hear of Martyria's affliction, and let us not pass over its healing, so that we are not only saddened by the affliction but also rejoice to learn of the cure. Her illness was terrible, beyond words or speech. It was not natural, as most afflictions are. These arise from an excess of humors or are caused by other conditions, which the body has been bound to serve ever since the transgression in paradise. Hers came from sorcery and from the wickedness of certain people who had a godless disposition and a perverse ambition to injure their fellow human beings without mercy. Whether they harmed the woman with poisons, or by the harmful attacks and scourges of demons, we do not know, being only human. But God knows this along with everything else, since he knows all things before they come into being. The woman cried out that her bowels were afflicted,
and wailed that they were being devoured and torn apart; but to those who asked the cause [she could say] nothing else [?].

The leading physicians flocked there, but they did not recognize the disease, could not explain its cause, and did not dare to offer any remedy. They went back having helped no more than if they had never come. When the woman's relatives learned this, they quickly brought her to the martyrs Cyrus and John. They were well aware of the martyrs' divine power, by which they give healing to those who come to them and perform marvelous works. No words can tell these works, and no human mind can clearly grasp them. They benefit and save everyone and rescue people from one danger after another. It is as if the saints had been given to humankind for this very purpose, being a good gift and a perfect present from God, who loves humankind, to human beings. They imitate the love for humankind of the one who gave them, and they hasten to grant favors worthy of the giver rather than make his gift useless. So now too they took pity on Martyria, who was being torn apart, as we said, and wailing with piercing cries. They brought her down into sleep and caused her to see a dream and a vision. They themselves were the ones who gave her the vision and the ones who appeared in it. She saw men whose garments alone flashed like lightning, with gentle and kindly faces. They came to her reverently and said, "Why are you crying out like this and not letting those who are waiting here in sickness get any sleep?" She answered that her bowels were in pain. The martyrs answered her again and said, "Are you the only one of all these people who has unbearable pain [?]?" Having said this, the two of them held the woman's head and opened her mouth. The elder of the two, who was the divine Cyrus, breathed into it three times. When they had done this, she says, they withdrew, and she was released from her sleep and her vision. Her pain eased somewhat, and she hurried to the latrine. There she sat down and passed through her bowels a worm a palm long, which had been secretly devouring her insides and which the martyrs had ordered to come out like excrement. Freed from this affliction, Martyria too received mercy, by the grace and love for humankind of Christ our God and the gifts of the venerable unmercenary saints.

22. On Sarapammon, who had a [?] in his foot.

Why do we delay over the illustrious Sarapammon, if indeed we do not wish to pass him by or leave him behind with the rest of the miracles? Their number no human being knows or can even guess; only God knows it, and the martyrs who heal under God. So let us tell of his illness, and with it the healing that showed love for humankind, which the divine martyrs clearly display to all, of God's love for humankind

[?] imitating [?], and readily taking pity on their own kin. He suffered in one of his two feet, and the affliction [?]. It was not a wound, or a small swelling, or some other ailment that is easy to cure, but what physicians call a scirrhus, a most grievous disease. It had seized his whole leg up to the groin and made it like a wineskin, many times the bulk of the healthy leg that remained. This monstrous illness keeps its sufferer in that state for a time, swinging back and forth as it shrinks and swells again, until the swelling grows past the joint of the groin and destroys the whole person. But while the affliction was still young and only beginning to grow, his father Julian (for that was his name) brought in the most eminent physicians and begged them to give him back his son in good health, promising them fees fit for a gift. They turned Galen over and over, unrolled Hippocrates for themselves, and applied many remedies to the sick boy. But they were boxing at the empty air and toiling to no purpose, and since they could do him no good, they finally stopped. Their stopping laid to rest both their defeat and the unconquerable power of the disease. From there the young man was brought to Cyrus and John. His parents had learned that these saints heal every disease and every infirmity, and are not slaves to the rules of physicians or to guesswork pronouncements. For those who grant healings from above stand above all things and are not bound by empty teachings. We know this from all their signs: they prescribe nothing medical, and even prescribe the very opposite. For what fellowship has light with darkness? Here I might add a fitting remark: the blessed martyrs heal from God, while the physicians on earth heal from men and from the earth. So the saints took up Sarapammon, whom the physicians had given up on, and ordered that the suffering leg be anointed with the oil and wax salve that feed the lamp lighting their holy coffin. They told this to his parents in a dream. As the foot was anointed it grew thinner. Fed with the wax salve, it melted away [?]. Given oil to drink, the oil that gladdens the face of the one who drinks it, it dried up and took back its former shape, which the Creator had given to both feet in equal balance. And this was not the only thing worthy of wonder. The size and growth it had gained over a long time, it shed in a few days. Such is the grace of the saints: they heal long-standing and serious diseases in the shortest time and with the smallest command. So Sarapammon was healed, as he himself and his parents believed and as the will of the martyrs had decreed, and he went away with them in good health, giving voice to his thanks to his benefactors. As for us, as though we ourselves had received this healing, let us praise those who performed it no less than those who received it, and move on to another wonder.

23. On Gennadius, whose head was full of flies. Who would not marvel at Gennadius's affliction and at its extraordinary cure? Both were truly strange, foreign to human ailments and unlike Galen's remedies. Let us listen, then, and marvel, not so much at the disease as at the physicians who cured it. Gennadius had pains in his head, not in the way sufferers usually suffer, but as no one among men has ever been ill. He endured his pains along with a kind of noise and a buzzing motion, something strange to all physicians and to all who heard it described. Others only marveled at the affliction. The physicians used many ointments, various rubbings, bloodlettings, purges and other aids, but they did Gennadius no good at all, so terrible and bizarre was the disease. Whether sorcery gave birth to it or some other natural cause, we do not know, for we were able to learn only the affliction and its cure. With it the sufferer came to the martyrs and obtained a swift release, full of the martyrs' grace and showing the charming condescension of John and Cyrus. It happened in the following way. I will not pass it over in silence or hide it, nor rob my hearers of so good a thing, for that would plainly be the work of sloth or envy. Let envy be far from our humble self and from every Christian and godly-minded person. As for sloth, the pauper who makes his friends paupers too, as Solomon's proverb warns, let it always be driven away from our lowliness, and especially now, when with a soul and will that love the martyrs we write of the kindnesses of Cyrus and John.

Gennadius was asleep, but the divine martyrs were awake. They searched out a cure for the sleeper and considered how to treat him. Then they came to him and used the words the Lord spoke to the man lying at the Sheep Pool: "Do you want to be made well?" they said. He answered them, "Yes." Why would he not, when he was being punished so severely by such a disease? Then the saints said to him again, "If you want to be made well, get up from your bed early in the morning and go out of the sanctuary. You will meet three camels with the man who leads them. Take hold of the last of them and do not let it go on until it relieves itself. Its dung, moistened at once with water and applied to your head, will be the remedy for your illness and will free you from this great evil." With these words the martyrs departed. The sick man got up from his bed as he had been told and went out to carry out the command. Finding three camels, just as he had been told, he grasped the last one by its

halter, and holding on to it he kept the others from going on. The man in charge of them first tried to persuade the sick man with words to let go. When he saw that he would not be persuaded, he raised his camel goad and struck the man's afflicted head, and opened for the flies imprisoned inside it the way out they had longed for. Having found a door for escape and flight, they would no longer put up with being shut in. As soon as this happened they flew up. The enclosure had burst, and they left; the prison had been breached, and they escaped. Driven out, they abandoned that strange nest and left the man free of pain and of the harm they had done him without rest, and they filled the place, streaming out as a novel spectacle for those who saw them. So Gennadius was freed from the flies, and he found his freedom by the hand of the martyrs, not by the camel driver's rod. While the wound was still swarming with flies and crowded by their fearsome flight, the camel we mentioned voided its dung, as if at some irresistible command. Those standing by at once snatched it up, quickly moistened it with water, and plastered it over that fly-bearing wound. They blocked the entrance against the flies, so that they would not turn back and come in again, dwell there like the seven most wicked spirits, and make the last state worse than the first. When the dung was applied to the wound, it made the wound vanish at once, so that it was, one might say, unrecognizable to all who wished to see it [?]. It left only the marks of the exit, as a memorial of the kindness of Cyrus and John and as witnesses of their power as martyrs. Now, as we do at every miracle, let us sing the praises of the saints, with the healed Gennadius as partner and leader in our hymn, and so let us turn our discourse to the telling of another miracle. 24. On Juliana the blind woman, and Juliana the lethargic woman. To a double and outstanding miracle let us join a double miracle, which happened not to one person but to two, who shared one nature and one name. Their nature was female, and their name was that of the martyr Juliana. A pair of women bearing one name but held by two diseases came to the saints. Both were called Juliana, but they did not share the same disease, nor the same worldly rank. One was known for her wealth, while the other had poverty as her housemate. One was terribly ill in the chest and in thrall to a lethargic condition; the other's eyes were shut by a blindness beyond comfort. One called in physicians to heal her; the other, because of her poverty, was deprived even of their consolation and of the visits so longed for by the sick. What they had in common was that their afflictions were incurable. Physicians did visit the wife of Marcellinus (for that was the name of the husband of the rich, lethargic woman), but the poorer one, who had lost

her sight, was visited by none of the sons of Asclepius. Truly, as Solomon says, a man great and boundless in wisdom, whose heart was as broad as the sea: "The rich have many friends, but the poor man is deserted even by the friend he has." Solomon wrote this as things really are. But these two women, the one with no money to call physicians, the other having spent much money without helping herself at all, came to John and Cyrus, the almighty physicians who need no money and do not heal the sick for gold. Now that we have described their illness, I shall tell of their healing (for that is what remains), after their arrival at the sanctuary. Before we see it and come to the saints, we humans are sick and often held fast by terrible afflictions. But when we see it and fall down before the martyrs who dwell there, we at once cast off every disease and every infirmity. So the women we were speaking of came to the sanctuary and sought healing from the church, each according to her own rank. The one, who had not cast off her vain pomp or the God-hated arrogance of the rich, lay on a bed before the tomb. The other lay cast out in front of the gateway, like Lazarus, the poor and needy man who shares the bosom of Abraham. The martyrs appeared to both alike, chastening the pride of the one and comforting the lowliness of soul of the other, and granting healing to each. To the lethargic woman with the arrogant mind they said, "Why have you occupied our shrine?" She answered that she wanted to obtain health and strength. They said, "If you want to receive from us what you have asked for, throw away your couch and lie down on the floor. This will be your remedy for the affliction of both soul and body." To Juliana, the poor working woman, they appeared and said, "Get some crocodile flesh, roast it over burning coals, grind it thoroughly in a mortar into a dry powder, and rub it on your afflicted eyes." These were the commands the saints gave to both when they appeared to them in dreams. The women rose from sleep, quickly carried out what had been commanded, and reaped the healings promised with the commands. For the one, sleeping on the ground was enough for a cure; for the other, the burnt remedy made from the crocodile. As soon as the woman with the chest ailment left her couch and lay down on the ground, she was freed from her affliction. As soon as the blind woman applied the powder to her eyes, she regained her sight. Let us join both women in praising the physicians, and then turn to reporting the remaining miracles. 25. On Elpidia, who had a flow of blood. We have only just found Elpidia, for she was hidden in the crowd of those who had been healed. She had stolen her cure

from the saints, but she was afraid, and for that reason trembling, and she tried to escape notice, much like the woman with the flow of blood in the time of the Savior. She too was clearly afraid that the martyrs she had robbed would notice the healing and expose her to everyone, just as the Lord exposed that woman, who thought she had escaped the notice of both him and everyone else. But Elpidia did not escape the notice of her healers now, any more than that woman escaped the Lord then. The saints saw her hiding in the middle of the crowds and brought her out before everyone against her will, and held her up for all to see. This was not because she had done anything wrong, but because she had won salvation by faith and deserved to hear from them: "Take heart, daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace." Elpidia, this most faithful woman, suffered from a flow of blood, which wasted her terribly and consumed her without mercy. She had no way to stanch the source of her affliction, a spring not of ever-flowing water but of gushing blood, a stream forever wetting her, not with silvery waters but with dripping crimson blood. So she looked like a dead woman among the living, as the blood that gives a ruddy color drained away; yet she could not be counted among the dead, since the breath of life still gave her life and held her together. Wanting to escape this disease, she went after the physicians who promised to drive it away. With the greatest zeal she kept tracking down those who wore the philosopher's cloak most conspicuously, who boasted that they knew everything about their art, and who taught those willing to learn with haughty words, as if with knowledge of deeds. She found them flourishing throughout the city, as she wished, but she did not find them as she wished when it came to healing, for there they were scarce. She tried each of them, and then moved on to another as though she had tried none, and after going through them all one by one, she had not driven out the disease that gripped her. When she had spent all her livelihood and property on physicians and had not managed to escape the affliction or obtain any relief from her pains, though she had certainly obtained destitution, with everything spent on them, she came quietly to Cyrus and John, intending to steal her healing by faith. While she was waiting for a good opportunity for the theft and watching for the hour when she could steal the cure, she was overcome by deep drowsiness and robbed by sleep before she could rob the martyrs. She who wanted to steal the healing was herself stolen away instead, and even after being stolen away she was still planning the theft. But when she saw the saints while she slept, though she had not meant to sleep, she was afraid to commit the theft. She did not dare to break into the treasure, seeing that the saints were guarding each other and that no one could steal from them unless they wished it. They understood the woman's aim, and they welcomed her faith and the piety she had shown,

so they came to her and granted her the gift of strength and the healing of her affliction she had so deeply longed for. They were not robbed through ignorance, as some dared to say of the Savior. Such people set their mouths against heaven, speak wickedness on high, and let their tongues roam the earth, saying most wickedly, "How does God know?" and "Is there knowledge in the Most High?" They will be counted with those who said to him, "Why do you, being a man, make yourself God?", and they will share the portion of the fool. No, the saints grant their healings with loving knowledge, as we learn from all their miracles. Standing over her, as we were saying, they told her to put myrtle in wine and drink it. She did this after waking from her sleep and was at once healed of her scourge. The blood that had been flowing from her without stopping [?] stopped as soon as it sensed the presence of the remedy. As the remedy flowed down through her mouth, the blood was kept from flowing down. It was taught to stand still instead of flowing, and its loose and unstable nature was changed into one that was firm and solid; or rather, it was stanched entirely and ceased altogether to exist and to flow. In this way Elpidia regained her strength, and after offering thanks for it to those who had given it, she was sent away by them to go in peace. As for us, let us pray for peace, sing a double thanksgiving to God and the martyrs for peace and for the miracle, and direct our tongue to the telling of further miracles. 26. On Theodora, who swallowed the frog. While we were tracking down the woman before her, sailing across the sea of those who had been healed and running along the roads that flow like rivers, we found another woman. We heard the frog croaking inside her before we saw it, and we bring her to you along with the frog, loudly proclaiming the wonder the martyrs worked on her. Theodora was the name her parents gave her. While drinking water she swallowed a small frog, which lived in her belly as if in a pond. At first, while it was still small, it did not harm her so cruelly, but by moving around it caused some cramps in proportion to its small size.
