The woman thought she was suffering these from some other cause, not knowing she had swallowed the frog. But when it grew large, feeding in her belly and growing, it increased the pains of the woman who carried this strange and misshapen fetus. She could no longer bear them and rolled about on the ground, with no hour of rest and no time of quiet, so that she was suspected of suffering from a spirit, or thought to have [?] affliction. Even the most respected physicians shared this opinion, since they were entirely at a loss about the disease and could not make any diagnosis of it. So in the end she was brought to the martyrs as one possessed by a demon. And when she came into their

most venerable church, the disease was at once exposed, and the ignorance of the physicians also became plain to all. The martyrs stood by her as she slept and told her to drink water before eating, promising that drinking the water would put the disease to flight. She says that, following that dream which ended her pain, she drank the water as she had been commanded, before any food or meal. When she did so, she was moved to vomit and brought up that bitter frog which she had swallowed without knowing it. Through water she had found ruin, and through water she escaped death. For the kindly saints forged this hook to catch the deadly frog and to bring about the woman's indescribable salvation, using the very thing the man-hating devil had used for Theodora's destruction. Having escaped ruin beyond all hope, she offered words of thanks for her deliverance to the martyrs who had rescued her alive, and left their church. Here too let us sing praises to them, and make this the starting point of another song, joining another wonder to this one. 27. On Theodore, who was ordered by the saints to eat an asp. Theodore, namesake of the woman before him, has fittingly been brought into the narrative after her by the order of the miracles, and set out as an admirable feast for those who delight in the deeds and acts of the saints. This is not only because he shared her name, but because his illness was in part like hers, and the indescribable cure of his affliction bears some resemblance to hers, even though the two differ very greatly, as the account will show as it goes on.

Theodore suffered in his bowels. This was not because a frog had slipped into him and was churning and troubling him with its swimming and producing terrible [?] pains. It was because sorcery in his food, the work of evil men, caused him unbearable pain. For we thrice-wretched people love to take revenge on our own kind, not only with tortures, deadly instruments and swords when someone has done us some injury, or when, gripped by envy that hates our brother, we attack him even though he has done us no wrong, but also to destroy him with poisons. We have lost the natural affection we owe our neighbor, even though, according to Moses the lawgiver, who introduced and taught love for one another, every creature loves its like, and every man his neighbor. We have also completely forgotten the account we must give for everything we do, even though, according to Paul, learned in the law, the worker and herald of every virtue, we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, paying just penalties and receiving what our deeds, good and bad, deserve. And these things, as they have been spoken and are believed, will certainly come to pass, even if we, stricken by a bad conscience, do not want them to. Theodore, terribly punished, his bowels burning from eating the caustic poison,

…he kept treading the halls of the physicians, but as he went, so he came back again, having gained nothing from them. Only one thing did he gain by all his coming and going: knowledge of how helpless they were. When he understood that none of them had any power against the illness, he gave up hope of being delivered and saved by them, and he came to the martyrs Cyrus and John, who truly give help and have the power to save. He lay down in their shrine and waited for them to intervene. They did not delay their visit, for they saw that the disease was unbearable. They stood beside Theodore as he slept, and appearing to him they told him to eat an asp, and by eating it to escape the relentless danger. But he turned over, traced the sign of the cross on his forehead with his hand, and, thinking the vision an evil phantom, did none of the things he had been told. As he went on praying and weeping, the saints appeared to him again in his sleep and gave him the same order. Yet he set aside this command of theirs as well and could not bring himself to do anything they had said. He suspected that the saints' command was the trap of some savage demon eager to destroy and kill him. When the martyrs appeared a third time and still did not persuade him to do what they bade, although the threefold vision had convinced him that the command was theirs, they came a fourth time out of boundless pity and divine compassion and said: "Since you would not do what you were told so many times, rise early in the morning, go out to our spring, and without hesitation eat the food you find there. This will be enough for you to enjoy complete healing." In the morning he went out to their spring as they had ordered, and behind the door he found a cucumber lying there. He took it and ate it with all eagerness and longing. When he came to the end of the cucumber, having found it very sweet to eat, he suddenly saw a piece of an asp left over. He quickly dropped it on the ground and was terribly afraid that he would certainly die. But this was not true, nor anything like the truth. Rather, he was saved by that food; he lived and escaped death, which he would not have escaped had he not eaten a deadly food. For at once, from fear and from disgust, he began to vomit and threw up as much of the asp as he had eaten, bringing up with it the deadly poison he had swallowed before. For the saints do not work cures by opposites, as earthly physicians do, but heal like with like. They are not subject to the rules of physicians and do not treat those who come to them by those rules. Ruling by a heavenly decree, they grant cures that are wondrous and divine. So Theodore, delivered from his disease and having reaped perfect health, went away giving thanks. And we, having brought our account of him to an end here with praise, will now write and narrate another praiseworthy deed.

[?]…of the eyes. Now Nemesion too comes into our midst among those who were healed. Yet he announces Photinus's healing while showing that he himself was not cured. He proclaims the power of the saints while revealing his own folly, and he may even blame that folly for standing in the way of the martyrs' help to him. Let us tell his story as we learned it. The account is not without profit, even if his coming to the martyrs brought him no profit. He too was known as one of the illustrious men in high office. He was adorned not only with rank but also prided himself on his wealth and the splendor that flows around wealth. And he surpassed those who are rich only in money, because he had the learning of Greek letters and a studied eloquence. But he could not bear their arrogance and the conceits that puffed up his mind, and he "stiffened his neck," to speak in the words of Scripture, against the God of all. So far as he could, he robbed God of His providence over all created things and assigned it to the motion of the stars, and the wretch tied our affairs to the configurations that arise one after another from that motion. He made us slaves, we who share in soul and reason, who were created in the image of our Creator and honored with freedom of will and the power to choose for ourselves. He made us slaves to stars that have no soul and no reason and lack all perception and will. Yet the stars were appointed for the opposite purpose: to serve those on earth and the divine commands, and only to mark the divisions of time and the changes of the air, as God, who created them for our sake, ordained. For the writer and teacher of the origin of all things says, in explaining how they were made: "And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth, to divide between the day and the night; and let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years; and let them be for light in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth. And it was so." This was terrible enough, but something much more grievous followed. He thought that the configurations and motions of the stars bring us to birth and hold the Creator of all as their servant. For the star-mad have tried to give the stars such power that they rule not only men and everything on earth (and these men are more senseless even than the stars), but also God, who fashioned the universe and by a mere command brought into being what did not exist. But those who invented and championed this madness will before long meet the penalty for their godlessness, and it will be the sharper and greater the more widely the crowd of their followers extends. For their sins are evident, and they might rightly be said, in the words of the divine Apostle, to "follow after" them, because of the plain destruction of their

followers. They have become for these wretches not only guides in godlessness but also teachers of sinning as they please. They say that God does not preside over affairs and allow no judgment for what is done. Nor do they admit that we ourselves do what happens by our own will. They declare instead that everything happens by the will and motion of the stars, as their configuration compels. By the unquenchable fire and the worm that never dies they will be taught who is their Maker and the Creator of this universe, since here they refused to perceive Him by analogy from the greatness and beauty of His creatures. Nor did they wish to see and understand the One who is invisible to human eyes, yet has been clearly seen and understood through the things He has made since the creation of the world. Instead, "their senseless heart was darkened, and claiming to be wise they became fools, and they served the creature rather than the Creator." Now Nemesion, who is the reason for this account (for I will turn my pen back to him), was counted among the Christians, as he says, but he followed without reason those who bring in fate. Because of this he experienced the punishment prepared for them. Fittingly, he was deprived of the eyes of his body, through which he had wrongly gazed at the things of heaven and pried into the motion of the chorus of the stars, forgetting his baptism and everything he had pledged to Christ there. When he suffered the maiming of his eyes, he at once bore witness to the truth of Scripture, for he was punished through the very things by which he had sinned. But he did not know the cause of his blindness, nor that it was a scourge and a fetter punishing him for his wicked star-gazing and holding him back. So he went about choosing physicians, and he drew the best of them with the promise of handsome fees. But nothing came of all his zeal for them, for he remained no less blind, though he received them in whole troops, one after another. Yet a man who shamelessly taught the doctrine of fate, and held that it compels and foretells everything that happens, should have done none of this. For if he knew precisely, from his science of fate, that he would certainly recover, see the heavens again, and once more behold the motion of the stars, he ought not to have engaged physicians as if it were their task to produce his recovery. He should have waited for fate's decree, which would arrive even without physicians. For to such men the boasts of fate thunder as irrevocable, sure to come to pass whatever anyone wishes. But if fate did not foretell his recovery at all, and even declared outright that it would not come, why did he gather physicians and use them to make war on his nativity? He knew that he would be defeated by it, even if he brought Asclepius himself as his ally. But it is evident that he had received his hope of recovery from the physicians [?] rather than from the stars [?], even if he went astray in calling the physicians, eager perhaps to recover his sight [?] sooner than had been foretold.

He spent a great deal of time and money on them, yet he received no benefit at all from them, and the decree of fate was not fulfilled. So he decided to go to the martyrs Cyrus and John, perhaps thinking that its decree would be accomplished through them. But here too he was shown to be astray, and with him the unspun threads of the Fates went astray as well. When he arrived at the sanctuary, he perhaps begged the saints to grant him seeing eyes and to fulfill the decree of fate, so that he might credit his recovery to fate and be ungrateful to the martyrs who had brought it about. And he would have done so had he obtained his request. But the martyrs did none of the things Nemesion wanted. Wishing to strike the fool and to show the difference between unbelief and faith, they did something like this. A certain Photinus, one of the very humble, who sold fruit in front of the church of the Holy Three Children, had lost the sight of his bodily eyes. At that time he was waiting upon the saints Cyrus and John, longing to recover his sight through their grace. The martyrs appeared to him in his sleep and said: "Go to Nemesion. He has only to lay his hands on your eyes, and at once you will recover and see the light brighter than before." When he learned this from the saints, he was afraid to tell the man openly, considering the loftiness of his rank and weighing the haughtiness of his wealth. But when he saw the saints ordering him to do it twice and three times, he ventured to tell the vision to some of the people around the church. They went to Cyrus the advocate, a wise and Christ-loving man who was then staying in the saints' shrine (and who also reported these things to us), and they told him what had appeared to Photinus. Cyrus went eagerly to the man and made known the saints' command. With many words he persuaded him to carry it out, though Nemesion called himself a sinner and shrank from undertaking such an act. So Nemesion came and stood before the tomb of the saints. He prayed long and with tears, touched the casket of the relics and the probe of the saints, and then laid his hands on the eyes of Photinus, who was present. As soon as Photinus felt the touch of his hands, he at once regained his sight. This moved everyone to praise, but it moved Nemesion to more tears, and he wept to no profit, since he had not changed his mind as well. So Nemesion fittingly heard the prophet Isaiah addressing him rather reproachfully: "Let the astrologers of heaven stand up and save you; let those who gaze at the stars tell you what is about to come upon you." But Photinus heard the Savior crying out to him: "Go in peace; your faith has saved you." Photinus gave thanks to God and to the martyrs and went away rejoicing. Nemesion, perhaps not left wholly untouched by the miracle, decorated part of the wall near the tomb with paintings,

in which he depicted Christ, John the Baptist and Forerunner, and Cyrus the martyr, and himself proclaiming his thanks for this. Now that we have told their story, made known the power and graciousness of the saints, and so praised them once again, let us go on to other most wonderful accounts of them. [Chapter ?]. Concerning Athanasia, who did not believe in the holy martyrs Cyrus and John. We remember saying earlier that we would write two or three stories through which the strictness and severity of the saints would be made known. They are meant to benefit the more careless and to safeguard the more zealous, so that both may learn that the saints know not only how to do good to the best but also how to punish the worse. In this too they imitate Christ their Master. He opened His kingdom to all, but does not simply grant it to all. He grants it to those who obey His preaching and carry out their faith in deeds and keep His commandments. To those who do not, He gives the sleepless worm, eternal Gehenna, and the outer darkness. To those on the right He says, "Come, inherit," but to those on the left He cries, "Depart from me into the eternal fire." And through the prophet Isaiah He spoke to all alike: "If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are not willing and do not listen to me, the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord Almighty has spoken these things." So let no one blame the saints as harsh or suspect them of being cruel and hard. They follow in their Master's footsteps: they do good to the sensible and punish the wicked. And they do this too for our benefit, just as the common Teacher of all does, if those who endure their scourges can come to their senses and show a good repentance. With God's help, what we are about to tell will show that they had mercy on those who repented and destroyed those who did not. For they were not disciples and offspring of inhumanity, so as to refuse those who repent. They were sons and offshoots of love for humankind

…and she declared that they had neither struggled nor suffered for Christ, which is the height of wretchedness. I cannot say whether she disparaged the saints in this way because she was held by some error and bowed to pagan phantoms, or out of simplicity of mind and heart, because no written account has come down to us reporting their contest and martyrdom for Christ, and only the God-inspired trumpet of the divine Cyril proclaims it. Either way, it is impious and ignorant. If she slandered the martyrs for the first reason, it is plainly full of impiety and error. If for the second, which is what we suspect, she deserves punishment and blame. For if we were to have only those martyrs whose written acts we possess, then Christ died in vain, having made only a few people sharers in His sufferings, for those martyrs are very few indeed. And then we too would be in danger, though we are guarded by countless martyrs and have them interceding with Christ for us through the outpouring of their own blood. Let us suppose there were no written acts at all proclaiming the saints' contests and revealing their calling. I will even pass over Cyril's discourse, which is entirely sufficient to give assurance. Even so, the multitude of miracles constantly worked through them should have earned them recognition as martyrs. If they do not perform the works of martyrs and have not received the gifts of miraculous power by which they make the sick well, then let such people not call them martyrs, even though we do not think so (for we are not of that opinion). But if they work even greater wonders than martyrs, for what reason should they not be called martyrs? This is especially so since the Savior said to the Jews who did not believe in Him: "If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe my works." And He gave us an unerring, firm understanding and a discernment that never deceives, so that we might judge the doers by their works. "For by their works," He says, "you will know them; and the tree is known by its fruit." It would be foolish indeed if the blind man who was healed recognized the Lord without having heard these words, and acknowledged the working of God: "For if this man were not from God," he says, "he could do nothing," while we, who hear these words every hour, turned out to be the blind ones, failing to recognize those who heal us and bestow so many benefits upon us. For what is there that martyrs do and accomplish which Cyrus and John are unable to do? Nothing. If there is something, let someone come forward and show it, and we will offer our defense. For we cannot claim anything beyond this, as though these martyrs did certain things that

other martyrs do not do. We revere all the martyrs alike, both those who work miracles and those who do not, and we strive to speak for the saints, not against them. This, then, is what we hold and will hold about the holy martyrs Cyrus and John and about the rest of the army of holy martyrs, and we urge all who shine in the faith to think and believe the same about them. But Athanasia, about whom this account is written, did not revere the martyrs in this way. She turned to terrible slanders, often holding them up to ridicule and always maligning them in conversation. She not only refused to call them martyrs herself but also stopped those who wanted to. Since Athanasia held this view and had formed such an opinion of the holy Cyrus and John, she needed to experience their sharper correction. Otherwise she would go on sinning without end. Instead, by learning the truth clearly, she might escape the death that such madness brings. And so, through the love for humankind of the very martyrs she had slandered, she was corrected. One day, while she was talking about such things with some people in her house and irreverently laughing and mocking the saints, a single flea leaped up from the ground and, as if fighting on the saints' behalf, bit her hard on the ankle. The woman bent down to scratch it [?] and at once remained fixed in that posture. From then on she could not straighten up, nor could she show the upright stance and form that belong to human beings alone. Because she had sinned irrationally against the martyrs, they corrected her with the bent-over posture of irrational beasts. Nor was the torment painless. It brought pain fitting so great a punishment. Scourged by it most violently, she revealed her hidden pains with loud and tearful cries. She did not know their cause (this too she gained from the abundance of her slanders), and, longing to escape the danger, she sent for physicians by the troop. They flocked to her eagerly, exulting in their hopes of fat fees. But they failed with her, because they did not know the cause of the affliction and did not know what to do. When the martyrs had struck her as she deserved, or rather out of love for her, and had made her recognize their might through these punishments, they appeared standing beside her in her sleep and said, in gentler words: "Come to us" (for she was in her own house), "and we will give you health." She answered them: "Who are you, that you are stronger than so many physicians?" They said: "Woman, we are Cyrus and John the martyrs, whom you are always mocking. But if you come to our house with faith, you will soon experience our gift, just as you experienced our scourge." When the martyrs had said this, they departed. She at once threw off sleep and called upon holy Cyrus and John, Cyrus's fellow martyr, whom she had been jeering at only a short time before. And she hurried to go to them, she who a little earlier had been insulting those who went to them.

But when she came to them, she was in no way disappointed in her hope. How could the martyrs deceive her, imitators of the Saviour that they are? Wishing to show the woman their unsurpassable and unattainable power and the overwhelming greatness of the martyrs' gifts, they brought about her recovery even more swiftly than the scourge had come. They held it back until she reached them, and the moment she set foot on that sacred threshold of the shrine, she was at once freed from the scourge that had gripped her. Casting off her stoop there, she walked through the martyrs' shrine upright, moving as nature intended, and offered the saints words of thanks both for the chastisement and for the healing. Having experienced their power in both ways, I mean in healing and in the scourge, she honoured and revered them more than those who had not experienced it. She not only proclaimed them martyrs but said that they held the first place among martyrs. From then on she sought their favour with many tears and served them with many rich offerings, because of her earlier insolence and her later love for them. So Athanasia profited from the chastisement and by repentance made amends for her former madness, coming to think rightly about the saints. As for us, let us always honour and revere them, celebrate them as holy martyrs, and rank them with those who suffered for Christ. Having now praised them as they deserve, let us write another account, through which both their severity and their compassion will likewise be made known. Once known, this benefits all who listen to what is said with real attention.

30. On Gesius the Iatrosophist.

Now Gesius too comes before us. He is not here to reduce the saints' remedies to a system or to boast that they heal the sick by the rules of medicine. He comes sick and in severe pain, longing to share in the divine gift. Having enjoyed it in full measure, he bore witness that the martyrs heal by God's power and declared that the refinements of physicians are nothing compared with the might of the saints. Let us tell, then, of his illness, of the cause of the illness, and of its most charming remedy, even though he is still ashamed of it to this day and does not want it made known to everyone in writing. Gesius was a most learned sophist. He did not expound rhetorical speeches and wear the philosopher's cloak for that reason. Instead he presided over the art of medicine and was known at that time as a meticulous teacher of it to his students. Though he was exalted in learning and reputed a physician among the finest physicians, the thrice-wretched man was not free of pagan superstition. So said those who knew his affairs well, and they made public his unwilling baptism, which he underwent out of fear of an imperial threat. As he came up out of the divine font, he impiously recited that line of Homer: "Ajax [? perished], since he drank the salt water." Although initiated into the most divine mysteries, he kept this [? impiety] hidden within himself and mocked the Chri-

-stians for worshipping Christ most irrationally and serving his inspired laws. He belched out many other abominable things as well, bringing evil words out of the evil treasure of his heart, for truly the mouth speaks and utters out of the abundance of the heart. He also mocked the martyrs Cyrus and John, claiming that they healed people's diseases by medical art and not by some divine and supreme power. Whenever he learned of the remedies they prescribed to the sick, some of which we too have recorded, he insisted that these were the teachings of physicians. This remedy, he said, was Hippocratic: "for he says such and such in such and such a treatise." That one he loudly declared to be a Galenic drug, and he announced that it was found in such and such a work. Another poultice, he explained confidently, was from Democritus, and he named the place where, as he put it, Democritus had mentioned it. Hearing of yet another plaster, he boasted that it came from some other physician still. In short, he maintained that everything the saints prescribed was patchwork stitched together from various physicians. He was forever explaining the diseases in terms of natural science, along with the qualities of the substances prescribed, and claiming that these were prescribed according to medical reasoning and that this was how they brought about the removal of the ailments.

But against this nonsense of his the martyrs offer no other refutation than the deranged Gesius himself, its author and begetter, even though such claims are plainly refuted by the facts themselves. The wretched man fell ill in his back. His shoulders, together with his shoulder blades, and his neck withered as if from some divine impulse and lost all movement. (At the time he spoke of them and described them as dry and bloodless as wood, even though they were part of a living body, and he made his pain match such a punishment.) Not knowing the cause of the affliction, he who healed others struggled to heal himself. He used various ointments and no fewer purgatives than ointments. He changed between diets of many kinds and took warmer foods, thinking that cold and phlegm had settled in those parts and believing that in this way the cause of the illness would be dispersed. He did everything his art prescribed, everything Galen and Hippocrates and the whole swarm of other physicians had taught him. But the affliction did not lessen at all, and he could not give his motionless limbs the movement he longed for. So he sent for the most accomplished physicians, and when they came he described his illness and demanded a remedy for it. Each of them gave his opinion, and at the end Gesius told them that he had already done everything they had suggested. When they heard this they were struck speechless, and at once declared that the only physician for such an affliction was the God of the [? Christians], who can do more than human beings and does what no human being can do. To the saints Cyrus and John [?]…

…[?] the visit, and to receive the healing that comes from it, since they share in divine grace and work their miracles by divine power. Gesius immediately answered them that the saints, too, effected their [? cures] by medical means and displayed nothing divine or wonderful that the ancient physicians had not already described. But they wisely resisted him on this point. They brought forward [? many] of the saints' cures, naming countless remedies and the diseases healed by them, and demanded that the sick man give the reasons for these. Though he wanted to speak, he could find nothing to say, and whenever he did speak they refuted him at once. Since they were contradicting him so well, they asked him to be silent, and in his silence he was persuaded against his will. Persuaded, he went to the martyrs, driven not so much by persuasion as by terrible pains. Even so, once he had come and was begging to be restored to health and importuning the martyrs as best he could, they appeared to him by night as he slept. They revealed the remedy for his affliction, a punishment fitting the sufferer: claiming to be wise, he was shown to be a fool rather than a wise man. "Go," they said, "get a donkey's pack-saddle and wear it, putting it on your shoulders, neck and back, the parts that are suffering. At midday go around our whole shrine, shouting at the top of your voice, 'I am a fool and utterly senseless!' Do this, as we have told you, and you will at once find your body's [? health]." With these words to him the saints departed. But he turned it over in his mind, called the vision a fantasy rather than the command of the Christ-bearing saints, [?] treated the oracle as a phantom, and did none of what he had been told. Yet he prayed to the martyrs again, and learned that he was to do these things with something added. They came to him again as he slept and ordered him to hang a large bell from his neck along with the saddle, and to run around their church shouting, "I am a fool!" But he rejected this instruction too, calling the command an incoherent phantom. He could not reduce the saddle and the bell to a medical system, nor could he determine what their mixture [Anastasius read: "judgement"] might be, or what their natural and essential qualities were. So he pleaded once more and offered supplications to the Lord, asking him rather to heal his illness and not to leave him deluded by phantoms. But the martyrs, truly most divine and loving to humankind, appeared again and again ordered him to do what they had first commanded. They added that he should wear a bridle like the beasts of burden and be led by one of his servants walking ahead, properly decked out with the saddle and the bell and declaring very clearly, "I am a fool!" They were not correcting themselves with the additions of the bridle and the bell. Rather, through them they were making the folly of the [?] Gesius more evident and scourging his stupidity with a sharper and greater shame. Having said this to him, the [? martyrs] withdrew.

When he woke up, he [? could no longer] call the dream [? a phantom] again, since it had been confirmed by appearing three times. He was forced to do it, both to be freed from the disease and so as not to provoke the martyrs to [?] anger against him. So he hoisted the saddle onto his shoulders and back, wore the bell around his neck, and fitted the bridle on his head and in his mouth. Then he followed behind the boy who led him around the shrine and completed the circuits of it (there were ten, according to those who counted), shouting over and over, "I am a fool!" Once he had fulfilled the saints' command, he laid aside the disease of his back along with the saddle, the bridle and the bell, and regained his health, which proved to be a friend of their commands and kept pace with their decrees. Night came on, and as it was giving way to the brightness of dawn, the divine martyrs again stood beside Gesius as he slept and reminded him, rather wittily, of his sin against them. "Since you insist," they said, "that all the remedies we give to the sick are discoveries of physicians long dead and decayed, tell us where your Hippocrates recorded the remedies for your affliction, or where Galen, whom you so admire, prescribed them. Where did Democritus say these things? Or which of the other celebrated physicians mentioned them? If you find them written in those authors, then you will also be telling the truth about the rest. But if you [? cannot] show them saying anything of the sort, know that you are lying about the rest as well." So the saints, having publicly shamed Gesius and plainly exposed him as a slanderer, ended the [? dream].

Even in his sleep he admitted that he had nothing to say against the martyrs, and when he woke he was astounded and amazed at their most wise refutation. Nevertheless, after praising the power of the saints and confessing that they heal the sick by God's power, he left their shrine. It is said that the holy Cosmas and Damian, their fellow physicians and fellow martyrs, did something of this kind, as they did also in the cases of the paralytic and the mute woman, and indeed that of the Hebrew woman who had a cancer hidden inside her. Cyrus and John have done these things too, and many remember them as if they had happened yesterday and proclaim them. But we have passed over those, since they are recorded among the other saints' miracles. The present wonder, however, is not recorded among them, so we have written it down. And let no one be surprised if the saints work the same miracles as one another. Cyrus and John, Cosmas and Damian draw their healings from one spring, Christ our God, and both pairs have and honour one Master, who grants us cures through them and works their many kinds of wonders. Having praised him as God of all things, and the martyrs as his faithful servants, we go on to set out other miracles.

31. On Theodore, who snorted after receiving communion and was immediately blinded.

The young man Theodore, the subject of our present narra-

-tive, becomes the source of great benefit to those who listen to what is said with real attention. He came into the saints' shrine after partaking of the [? immaculate] mysteries of Christ. Moved by something we do not know, perhaps because someone provoked him to anger, he burned with the greatest fury and boiled with the blood seething around his heart. The wretched man insulted the Divine not only with words, blaspheming, thrice-wretched as he was, and [? reviling] it as though it were some fellow servant. He also drew his breath up through his nostrils and produced a noise like fearful thunder, which at once made everyone present shudder, those who saw it and those who heard it with their own ears against their will. Many Christians do this. They think, I suppose, that they are blaspheming, but they are entirely ignorant of what they are actually doing. If they knew it precisely, they would not do it even under countless tortures. Perhaps it is not unprofitable to explain this evil, for some, learning its nature and that it is an invention worthy of pagan impiety, may guard themselves against such madness. The pagans, says Porphyry, when offering their accursed sacrifices to idols, snort most vigorously, producing this sound by a violent drawing in and force of breath, and they make it into a venerable hymn. As a result those who sacrifice feel free to do it without restraint and compete most eagerly to see who can outdo the other in snorting, so that the best may be heard first and be sweetest to the demons. Such is the nature of these noises. They were devised for the service of demons, and they secretly compel those who make them to hymn unclean demons. We therefore urge those who use this practice to learn how harmful and destructive it is and to keep away from it as from a soul-destroying madness. "For what fellowship has light with darkness?" and so on. Theodore made this abominable, idol-loving noise after he had eaten the immaculate communion, and he was at once deprived of his sight and bereft of his eyes, meeting a punishment that came hard on the heels of his blasphemy. When this happened, as we have said, trembling seized everyone present and no ordinary fear spread among them, lest they too fall into similar troubles, since they often committed such sins and, through habit, did not consider the act a sin. Each of those present shed many tears, seeking to appease Christ and the martyrs for himself and asking grace for the sufferer, that God in his pity would receive the wretched man in his repentance and through the saints grant him sight again. So the martyrs appeared in his sleep to the man who had lost his sight and said, "Who made you, wretch, the doer of so foul a deed? Everyone ought to abstain from it throughout their whole life, since it is pagan and dear to the demons. And even if most people do it in ignorance, its performance

ought to be loathed above all when one partakes of Christ's mysteries." [?] until the appointed time was completed. He also had everyone in the church interceding for him, offering litanies on his behalf with tears and fulfilling the command of brotherly love to pray for one another, so that he might be healed. When the prayer of them all had been accepted, Theodore regained his sight and put off his fear of blindness. On the third day Christodorus, who was the steward, was censing the saints' martyr-shrine. As he passed the place where the blind Theodore was sitting, the moment the censer reached him, Theodore suddenly saw the coals and the fragrant smoke rising. He let out a piercing cry glorifying Christ and the martyrs, and once again stirred everyone to fear and joy: joy because he had miraculously regained his sight, and fear because they believed the martyrs were present and punishing every transgression. Everyone gathered to see Theodore, and a loud and great clamour arose. Christodorus was astonished, for he had no idea what had happened. When he learned how great a miracle had been worked, he joined all the others, and Theodore himself, who had been blinded and now saw, in glorifying Christ aloud, and the saints who magnify Christ through their miracles. And we now, as if we had been present then and witnessed the miracle, having offered our hymns to those who worked it, [pass on] to another, weightier wonder.

32. On Agapius the Pagan.

Many knew Agapius the silver dealer. He not only made his living selling silver but also openly practised paganism, [? worshipping idols] and serving the creature rather than the Creator. Convicted of this most abominable impiety, he was arrested and punished in the queen of cities. But beyond all hope he escaped the sword of justice. This was not because he had changed his mind (no one could have persuaded him of that), but by means of a great deal of gold [?]…

…which is utterly godless. Nor was it through the leniency of the laws, for what leniency is there toward those who do not repent? The laws show no leniency when offenders persist in their offences. It was through the greed of those who enforce the laws, for all things obey gold in this way, as Solomon the wise wrote. But even if the wretch bought his life with a gift of money and escaped death at that time, he could not escape the Divine, nor the all-seeing eye of justice. So after his release from prison he fled Byzantium and came to Alexandria, thinking he could escape notice and hide there. The loathsome man, driven by divine wrath, judged from what he thought about his own gods and so did not know that the divine power is everywhere and fills all things. Its being cannot be circumscribed; it holds all things together and is beyond all things. It says so itself through Isaiah to those who think it is confined in a small place: "What house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? Do I not fill heaven and earth?" Compared with it, and the very comparison is a great condescension, all things are as the tipping of a scale and as a drop from a bucket, and are reckoned as spittle from the mouth. This includes heaven and the countless ranks of angels in heaven, the earth and the animals and human beings on the earth, the air and the birds flying through the air, and in short all things visible and invisible. David knew this well and sang: "Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is mighty, I cannot attain to it." Showing its greatness, he goes on to say: "Where shall I go from your Spirit? And where shall I flee from your presence? If I go up to heaven, you are there; if I make my bed in Hades, you are present. If I take up my wings at dawn and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me." So Agapius, though a fugitive who had reached Alexandria, did not escape the right hand of justice. He was seized by it and punished. He was not handed over to the laws as before, for then he would again have escaped punishment with money, since all seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, as the divine Apostle says. Instead he was struck invisibly with a grievous and inescapable blow. The blow was a disease [? spreading] over his whole body, which the followers of Asclepius call paresis. Hoping to escape this illness too, he kept sending for the physicians, for he did not think his affliction was the work of justice but merely a bodily symptom. They came and applied the resources of their art to him. They knew that he would not live or escape this disease, but they deceived the wretched man in the hope of fees. As time went on and the affliction advanced,

so that he even suffered paralysis of the tongue, which the scourge had now loosened, so that it could no longer form words. Yet he did not depart this life; he was simply punished in this terrible way. Some people advised him to go to the martyrs Cyrus and John, since they could free him from his affliction if he came to them with faith and tears. He was afraid that people would judge him a pagan if he refused to go to the saints, for the accursed man pretended to be a Christian and wore the sheep's fleece, though the impious man was known to be truly a wolf. So he accepted the advice and agreed to make the journey. He thought he would escape people's notice in this, and he supposed he would deceive the martyrs, as if they had no divine knowledge of our affairs. He reckoned them like his own gods, who know neither things far away nor the secrets of human beings, nor even what lies at their feet. For "the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but will not speak; they have eyes, but will not see; they have ears, but will not hear; they have hands, but will not feel; they have feet, but will not walk; they will make no sound in their throats." To this it is fitting to add: "May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them." So the wretch deceived himself, not the martyrs, and it was from himself that he hid, not from those who already held this opinion of him. For when he came to the most holy shrine of Cyrus and John, he saw them in the form of Christodorus, who was in charge of the church, going around and offering incense to God. They came up to him and spoke to him rather threateningly: "Why have you come to us, you stranger to all piety, you who are full of every abomination? Have you come here to mock us too? By the Maker and Dweller of heaven and earth, and by the power of his Godhead, here and everywhere, you will not escape us as you supposed. We will scourge you on the back in public, so that you may know more clearly whom you have dared to mock." With these added threats the saints departed. He turned over, still terrified and trembling, and made everything known to those who served him by nods and stammering. When the steward came past at the time of the incense, holding the censer, Agapius still had the fear of the threat in his heart, and he ordered his servant to turn him over. Once he had been turned as he signalled, he seized the feet of Christodorus, who had come up to him, and begged him not to scourge him, for he thought he was the one who had threatened in the dream to scourge him. Christodorus did not understand (he learned everything later from the servant). He was amazed at what was said, but swore that he would not beat him, as the man begged. Not long afterwards it became known among the sick who he was, for he refused to receive the life-giving

mysteries, making a show of it as though for doctrinal reasons. A great uproar arose against him among those in the church. When he learned of this and wished to clear himself of suspicion, he received the holy mysteries of Christ. Immediately after he received them, a savage demon leapt into him, just as Satan entered the traitor Judas after he took the morsel that the Saviour dipped and gave him. He lay on the ground and was convulsed. His eyes rolled, his limbs were cruelly twisted, and he spewed foam from his mouth, pitifully imitating a wave of the sea. Even when he came to himself for a little while, if he ever did, he was quite unable to speak or move his tongue at all. He was twisted by the demon and possessed without ceasing, even when he slept, if he slept at all, because he had approached the mysteries not with faith but with hypocrisy.

The wretch spent three days in this state, convulsed many times by day and night, or rather all day and all night long, suffering everything that people oppressed by hateful demons suffer, so that those who saw him were sure he would die. So his relatives, realizing that the demon would soon kill him, took him up and began carrying him to Alexandria, to his own house, to die there. But after he had left the saints' shrine and travelled only a very short distance, he gave up his spirit in great pain, finding a death worthy of his impiety, for the demon strangled him on the road. He left the church because he was driven out as defiled and profane, and he never saw the city itself, because he was unworthy of it. So Agapius, who had been impious toward God and the martyrs, ended his life. Such indeed is the end of the ungodly, as the saying goes: "His hope will perish [?], and his dwelling will be no more at all." Through him and through those before him we have described how the martyrs deal with those who repent and those who do not turn back, and we have proclaimed it for the benefit of those who come to the shrine. We did this so that people who see only the healings may not think the martyrs too slow to punish, and so harm their own minds by sliding into contempt and carelessness. Now we have offered the saints hymns for the benefit gained from these accounts. Let us write two or three more delightful miracles and make them the end of the wonders recorded about the people of Alexandria, though not the last that have happened. Then these wonders, bounded on both sides by delightful ones, may seem wholly delightful to readers: delightful in the ones that went before, a little astringent in the present ones. The sweet ones heal the souls of hearers, and the more astringent ones purge those souls without their noticing. Skilled followers of Asclepius do the same: they bind the useful and beneficial parts of their drugs in honey, or mix them with it, and so they purge those who need it [?]. Imitating them here, we have attached the present accounts to the sweet ones that came before, and now let us cover them over with other delightful ones,

making the delightful ones the end of our account of the miracles for the Alexandrians, though not the end of the working of miracles. 33. On Cosmiane, who was going to the saints to pray, fell from her animal, and was crushed in body. The present miracle, which the martyrs worked for a woman named Cosmiane, is also a sweet one. Perhaps it comes fittingly after the report of the harsher ones, so that, coming after them like a sponge, it may wipe away the grief we were likely to feel from them. And not only for this reason, but also so that, just as the account of the grievous miracles began with women, so the record of the pleasant ones may again have women as its beginning. For so too the Lord after the resurrection appears first to women and grants them his "Rejoice," since it was to them first, after the transgression in paradise, that he spoke words of grief. He judged it most just that those who first received sorrow should be the first to receive joy, and that there should be no division in the body. So says the divine Apostle, who called the man the head of the woman and declared the woman the body of the man, and who wished that neither woman without man nor man without woman should be the whole body, nor that one part of the body should be first in joy and the other first in grief.

So let the woman come forward. Just as Athanasia came first among the miracles that seem grievous, so may Cosmiane come first among those that bring good cheer. She was healthy in body and had no affliction or illness. While she was staying at home, she longed to go to the martyrs, to venerate their relics and to enjoy the blessing that flows from them. Wishing to fulfil this longing, she mounted a rather unruly donkey and set out for the shrine. The father of envy saw her hurrying to the saints with great longing. He thought he would suffer great loss if she reached the divine church with such zeal and fervour. He wanted her to stumble on the road into his evil snares and turn back home without seeing the holy precinct, without paying fitting reverence, and without receiving the precious gift. For everything that serves God as good, and that benefits and saves God-loving people, grieves and stings him. So when the woman was halfway along the road, he suddenly threw the beast that carried her and made her fall backwards onto the ground. He made her back take the fall, and it struck the ground with great force and was at once completely crushed. For a long time the woman seemed dead, and perhaps he would have sent her to the tomb, had he not found the martyrs reviving her, raising her up when she had all but died, and giving her life again. After a long while she came to herself (for she had died

from the force of the fall, and all her bones had been dislocated). Her companions wanted to turn back to the city so that, as they said, they could take her to the doctors while her injuries were still warm, not after they had cooled and grown numb. For injuries seem readier for healing while they are still warm. They give the doctors less labour, and they cause the sufferers less pain than injuries that cool after the blow and are slow to receive medicine. But she realized that the interruption of her journey to the saints was the work of a demon, and she would not agree to go back before she had fulfilled her longing. So once again they lifted her onto the beast with great difficulty and held her securely in front and behind, because she could not hold herself on the animal at all. At great risk they brought her to the martyrs. When she had prayed and venerated their reliquary, they carried her back to the city, for she did not wish to stay at the church until she recovered. Instead she said this to the saints with great wit: "O martyrs, imitators and servants of Christ, many come to you sick and go home healthy and joyful. But I left the city in good health and came to you to make you guardians of it, and with what danger and illness I go home! Now if I had come from home sick, I would have stayed until I received a complete cure. But I came to you not because of an illness or to stay, but to pray and to venerate. The hater of good wanted to prevent this, but he could not, for he found your pair against him. Now that I have done it as I wished, I am going home again. I will have no other doctors for my illness but you. I urge you to come there, and I will wait for your help, so that, just as you received me healthy from my home, you may heal me when I am there." Having said this to the martyrs Cyrus and John, she left their church and reached the city at great risk, believing without doubt that the saints would surely come and heal her at home. And so it happened. For they are eager to confirm the faith of those who believe in them, doing in deed what those people believe, and making them more faithful through the gift [?]. That very night they came in the form of doctors and asked Cosmiane in her sleep what was wrong with her. She told them of her injury and, as she says, she reproached the saints for giving health to the other sick people while crushing her alone, who had been healthy. The one who appeared in the rank of the superior, with the dignity of a teacher, smiled and ordered his disciple: "Go over," he said, "and quickly free her from her injury." The disciple carried out the order. He came running, struck her on the cheek with a slap, and granted freedom to the sick woman. At the blow

of the slap she turned, thinking that someone had slapped her while she was awake. But when she turned she saw no one: not the doctor who gave the order, she says, nor the disciple who gave the slap. There was no mark of the slap on her cheek, no injuries from the fall, and no unbearable affliction of the back. The pain-relieving arrival of the saints and the saving slap given to her had swiftly made all this vanish and wiped out the pain. So she received her healing in this way. As soon as she became aware of her health, she got up and praised the saints, singing of their grace and the speed of their [?]. We have now completed the account of her and have praised the saints once more. Let us write one more wonder, or a second, and make these the end of the miracles told about the Alexandrians. Then, with God's help and the martyrs' support, let us begin those concerning the Egyptians and Libyans. 34. On Dorothea, whose child Callinicus swallowed a snake's egg on the way to the saints. Another woman has come to us at just the right moment. She too was on the road leading to the martyrs, suffered harm through her small child, and received the clear and swift help of the saints. She wishes to be joined to the woman before her, so that she may proclaim the triumph of those who saved her not only by word of mouth but also in writing. Let us admire her gratitude and fulfil her longing by lending her our tongue and pen, so that by God's command we too may receive the reward of gratitude along with her. The woman was called Dorothea, and she had two boys, Callinicus and Epimachus. Callinicus, the elder, was about twelve years old, and Epimachus was in his ninth year. Their mother was travelling with them to the shrine of the saints to pray and to venerate their revered relics. When they had covered most of the way, they sat down under a tree to rest from the weariness of the journey. They were travelling on foot, because lack of money kept them from riding animals. The author of evil saw them under the tree and at once remembered his ancient plot against us under the tree, by which in Adam and Eve he killed the whole human race with the arrows of envy, and they were made slaves of death. So he showed the boys a snake's egg [?] lying by the trunk of the tree. It was a snake through which he had brought about that destruction of ours too. The egg was neither good for food nor beautiful to look at, though it seemed so to the children, as the fruit did to Eve, because of their immaturity. Their age had not yet trained the senses of the soul to tell good from what is not good. Lacking these, as I said, the boys rushed without examining it to the thing that had appeared, thinking it was the offspring of one of the birds that dance through the air. Callinicus snatched it up and took it, for he got there ahead of Epimachus, the younger. He held it in his hand as if it were something great. Since his brother had missed the prize

and was crying, their mother told Callinicus to give the find to him too, to stop the younger child's tears. But he quickly brought his hand to his mouth and at once swallowed the snake's egg. It was already formed and had inside it a complete likeness of its mother. Having disobeyed his mother's command, he would have reaped death as the fruit of disobedience, if the martyrs Cyrus and John had not made him escape the deadly net. They then finished the rest of the journey and arrived at the shrine. When they reached it, they offered their prayers to God and kissed the saints' tomb. Not long after the veneration, Callinicus began to have pains in his bowels, because the egg had opened in his belly and released that most evil treasure. At first the pains were like colic, but as they gradually grew worse, they lost the marks of colic and became like the convulsions caused by demons. For the most dreadful offspring had just come out of the shell-like membrane that enclosed it. Not finding its mother there, it crawled about in an evil search for her and ran here and there through the boy's bowels, and perhaps it bit them too, since it could not find its nurse there. So at first he wept, and then, as it went on, he increased his weeping with louder cries. When he could no longer bear the torment of the snake, he fell to the ground and rolled about, convulsed and twisting his limbs in every way. In the end he could not even utter a sound, and to those who saw him he seemed about to die at any moment. Dorothea, who had borne him and his brother, as I said, was tormented in her bowels even more than Callinicus, as she watched her son perishing so pitiably. She quickly went to the martyrs and offered her supplications with cries and tears. "Alas, saints!" she said. "How have you received my offering? Alas, with what gifts have you honoured me? Alas, what a welcome you have given me! Other women who have no children take refuge with you and give birth, but I came here escorted by two, and unless you hurry, I will leave here with one. Others come breathing their last and go away laughing at death, but my child, wretched woman that I am, came to you playing and dancing, and he will surely die unless you rescue him. He will not go back alive by the road he came. You have taken the staff of my old age. You have taken the support of my weakness. You have snatched away my hope of rest in my last days. You have the one I expected to support me, after God. If I sinned, martyrs, why do you punish my child? If I sinned, punish me. Why do you bring a mother's sins upon innocent children? Why do you become avengers of the curse of the Law and of the Mosaic condemnation? For it says, 'The sins of the fathers upon the children.' But Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law by becoming a curse for us, and through the prophet he cancelled this condemnation,

saying plainly that this proverb will no longer be spoken: 'The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth were set on edge.' From now on no one will give account to God for another, but each for himself. The soul that sins is the one that will die, and no one else will undergo judgment and punishment for it. It is others who are slaves to the curse of the Law, those who did not receive Christ, the liberator, the Son of God. But we have gained adoption through him. We did not receive a spirit of slavery leading to fear, but a spirit of adoption, by which we cry, 'Abba, Father!' From now on we are free, with the freedom by which Christ has set us free. So either punish me and spare the child, or punish me along with him, so that I may not live to see my child's destruction. But if you will do none of these things, give my son back to me, imitating your compassionate God and Master." She said these things and more to the martyrs and wept all night long. Toward dawn she fell asleep for a little while. She was not overcome by the arrows of despair and weariness; she slept so that she might see the saints' visitation. They stood beside her, as they do for everyone, and told her to carry the child out of the shrine at about the third hour of the day. They commanded her to place him in the middle of the outer open court. No one was to come near him, not even his mother. She was to sit a short distance away and watch the wonder that God would work on him. The martyrs said this, and having said it they flew away. At the appointed hour Dorothea did as she was commanded. She took the boy, carried him out of the shrine, and laid him down in the place they had named. He kept rolling this way and that. Most people expected him to die, but his mother believed he would live. When a short half hour had passed since he was laid there, and a great crowd stood by waiting to see the outcome, suddenly the female serpent that had laid that egg arrived, looking for it, crawling and hissing. She called out just as a woman searching for her lost infant usually does, with wailing and lamentation. She came in openly through the outer door, parted the people standing there, and at her first appearance put them to flight. Then she ran to the sick boy and circled him again and again. Now she whispered at his ear, now she came close to his mouth, and she quietly called back and forth with her offspring, which lay somewhere below and was being nourished in the boy's belly. The young snake sensed that its mother was there and recognized her hissing. It ran upwards and came out through the mouth to her, as though it had been born once and for all and no longer wished to be carried in a womb. Or rather, it knew the saints' command (for it is more pious to say this; the mother also obeyed that command when she came so quickly to look for it), and it could no longer stay in the belly even if it wanted to. When it leapt out of the mouth, as soon as the

…had given birth, and recognized it as the very offspring she had been looking for, her own, she snatched it up in her mouth the moment she saw it and went back to her den, leaping and rejoicing. In the same way the poor woman Dorothea, after the serpent-like offspring had come out, took up her son Callinicus, who was at once restored to health, and with him sang her thanks to the martyrs who had saved them, and made her way back to the city exulting and rejoicing. The crowd that was there, having witnessed the miracle, cried out the words of the Gospels: "Truly we have seen strange things today." At this they praised God and the martyrs as best they could. We too join them in offering fitting praise to Christ our God and to his holy martyrs, and we will go on to fulfil the task we set ourselves.

35. Concerning Theophilus, who was bound hand and foot by sorcery.

Theophilus is truly wonderful, and the story about him is wonderful too. Perhaps that is why he has kept himself for us until last; or rather, it was not he who put himself later, but the wonderful martyrs. We have told it last only among the miracles written about the Alexandrians, so that it might adorn the miracles that came before it and delight the hearers richly and brilliantly, and [?] not be overshadowed by the account of another. We too, then, admiring it for its wisdom, tell his story, setting it as a marvellous crown upon those already written.

The father of misanthropy and teacher of hatred between brothers, who from the beginning led man astray and, as far as lay in him, stripped him bare of divine grace, is not content with his own madness and rage against mankind, nor with all the calamities and misfortunes with which he ceaselessly surrounds people, as the divine Job says. He also often stirs them up against one another, sowing in them the seeds of his own hatred of mankind, and he inflames them to such mutual enmity that they even choose him as an ally of their own wrath, and so do the greatest harm first to themselves (for the death of the soul is born from an agreement with him), and then to the brothers whom we were commanded to love as ourselves. Certain people who wished to harm Theophilus made this one their own, along with their own wicked intent, and in their eagerness to carry it out they drew him in as a helper in their plot. Persuaded by their foul invocations, he did the man no small harm. He bound the hands and feet of his body and tormented him with terrible pains as he wished, though perhaps not as much as he wished and desired (for he would have killed him if he could), but only as much as God had permitted him to afflict him. Theophilus, however, did not know the cause of his illness. He sent for the doctors and begged them to help him with all their might and implored them to save him quickly, since he lay idle and motionless

and was perishing wretchedly from his pains. The doctors, who were just as ignorant as he was of the cause of the harm, did not practise their art, for the art prescribes nothing for those who do not know the disease. Instead they did whatever their own minds and painstaking thought suggested. They administered many antidotes and still more purgatives (for they thought the affliction came from an excess of humours), and tried other things too, with ointments and various diets. When none of this did any good, they stopped. Having barely admitted their ignorance of the illness, and with that ignorance their helplessness, they told him to have himself carried to the saints, who know the illnesses of mortals from God and hold out cures to them from that source. So he came to the shrine of Cyrus and John and begged the martyrs to undo the evil. Not long afterward he was heard and regained his health. For they are compassionate toward those who suffer and grant them swift cures, unless people are wholly unworthy of them, or need longer discipline because of some irrational and hidden faults, which only the Ruler of all knows, and those to whom he might reveal them as worthy.

Since we have described the disease, we will also describe the manner of the cure. It deserves great wonder, and it was for its sake that we spoke of the illness at all. The saints stood beside him in his sleep and commanded him to do the following. "Go out early in the morning to the sea," they said, "and urge the philoponoi to carry you and take you there. When you come upon one of the fishermen casting a net into the sea, agree on this fee with him: that he spread his net in the water on your behalf. Whatever he catches will serve for your healing, for once it is laid bare it will free you from your ills." Having said this in a dream, the martyrs departed. Early in the morning he called the philoponoi (these are those among the sick who are able to help), told them what the saints had commanded, and begged them to pick him up quickly. When they learned of the martyrs' oracle, they quickly picked him up and left the shrine. As they came near the sea they found a fisherman with his nets, hunting the offspring of the waters. They went up to him and set the sick man down on the sand. The sick man addressed the fisherman: "What do you want to be paid for one cast, and one only, if you give me whatever the net catches? Whether it brings something up or draws up nothing, whether it is small or large, more or less, whatever the net catches will be mine as my catch." The fisherman answered, "One keration." So he spread his net and threw it into the sea, expecting to catch a small fish, perhaps, or some other creature of the waters, and the man who had hired the cast evidently expected the same [?]. After a short while he drew in the net and brought up a very small box, which was not what either of them had hoped for. This box did not carry Moses hidden inside, but the evil work of Jannes and Jambres:

not a refined lawgiver, meeker than all men, as Scripture shows, but something lawless, a product of demonic savagery. The fisherman did not know this, and neither did the sick man, and they fought over the box. One said, "I did not sell you a box, but a fish coming up." The sick man claimed he had bought not just a fish, but whatever came up. What bred the quarrel between them was not only that the box suggested something important inside, but also how elaborately it had been secured. It was fastened not only with locks but also with lead seals

After they had quarrelled for a long time and could neither persuade each other nor bring themselves to give way, they went to the steward of the shrine to have him judge the case. When he had heard both their stories, he would not give his verdict until, as he said, "I open the box and see what is inside." So with great effort he opened the box in full view of everyone, and found a terrible and most grievous sight. It was nothing like what the finders, or all the others standing there watching, had expected. It was what the saints, swimming in a sea of love for mankind, had brought up from the depths. It was a figure of a man made of bronze, shaped in the likeness of Theophilus. It had four nails driven into its feet and hands, one nail in each limb. Those present were astonished in many ways at the sight, and did not know what it was they were seeing. And so the quarrel between the two men came to an end, since the find had been revealed to them. They would very nearly have thrown it into the sea and hidden the impious sight in the waves, and Theophilus would have gained nothing from it, had the martyrs not moved the steward to ask what the nails fixed in the statue's four limbs might be. So he ordered one of the bystanders to pull out the nails if he could. The man took the statue, grasped the nail fixed in the right hand, and with great force pulled it violently out. As soon as it was out, Theophilus's right hand was released at once and threw off the weight of pain, and with the pain the immobility. Then everyone who saw it realized the foul sorcery that had been worked against him. Those sorcerers had worked it with foul and most evil demons and had cast it into the depths of the sea, thinking it would never be undone. But they were exposed as weak and mad, for Cyrus clearly refuted them, together with John, Cyrus's fellow martyr. The martyrs plainly showed that nothing in creation is beyond their reach, neither heaven nor earth, nor air, nor fire, nor water, nor sea. They pass through all things to save the pious and faithful. These things are clear to everyone, even if we do not proclaim them.

When those who were with the steward saw and understood the evil deed, and saw Theophilus moving his right hand, they were overjoyed. They praised the martyrs and hurried to draw out the rest of the nails. As they loosened them, the sick man was loosed from his bonds and torments, until they had pulled them all out. And so the sick man was delivered from all the devil's sorcery and scourge. When they removed the nail in the statue's left hand, the sufferer at once stretched out his left hand; and when they drew out the nails fixed in the image's feet, the sick man moved his feet without pain or ache. At this he got up and ran to the coffin holding the saints' relics. There he sang the saints' praises in a loud voice, lifting his hands on high, and those who saw him joined in the hymn. We too, once again praising the martyrs as best we can, and setting this present story as the finishing touch to our miracles written about the Alexandrians, now begin those about the Egyptians and Libyans, praying that Christ our God may supply us with words, and also the martyrs Cyrus and John, who work the miracles through him.

I hear that Alexandria is the metropolis of Egypt and of the Libyans, and I think it is not right to separate the Egyptians and Libyans from it, since it is their head and root, and their base and foundation as well. Alexandria itself does not wish to be apart from them, nor do Libya and Egypt wish to be apart from it. A body does not live when it is separated from its head, branches cut off from the root do not stay fruitful, a statue whose base is taken away will not stand without falling, and a building deprived of its foundation cannot remain standing. So I think it consistent and right that, just as a body joined to its head, a shoot to its root, a statue to its base and a house to its foundation are splendid and secure, so too Libya and Egypt, placed alongside Alexandria in the collections of the miracles of Cyrus and John, should rejoice and delight, shining with its brightness and taking pride in being sharers in the saints' magnificent possession. Let the Egyptians, then, be united with the Alexandrians, and let the Libyans not be cut off from them. Let them be led like children by their parents, reap the same glory from the martyrs, and have one undivided fame.

First, then, among the miracles of the Egyptians and Libyans, let Theodore of Thennesus shine (this is a city in Egypt). At that time he was counted among the laity and among those who cut themselves off from the Catholic Church,

but now, by the grace of God and through the illumination and command of the martyrs, he is reckoned among the Church's children. He has obtained the priestly rank that comes after the deacons, and serves as a subdeacon in the holy house of the saints. This Theodore, so they say, fell from his youth into the disease of the feet which doctors have, rightly I think, called podagra, because of the great savagery of the affliction. The wilder sort of beasts, being untamed by nature, will not submit to those who want to tame them, and will not take the bridle [?]. In the same way this untamed disease, intractable to the sons of physicians, will not bear the bridle of health. It cuts through the very remedies applied to it as if they were cobwebs, and goes its way, taking up its own savagery again.

Theodore had fallen into this disease at an early age, as we said, and the affliction kept advancing and was unbearable. The young of animals, and the shoots of plants and trees, show their excellence and noble breeding right from the start, and the good nature they will have later flashes out from the womb itself and from their first growth for those who know how to see it. In the same way, this disease showed its full magnitude as soon as it appeared. Ugly and ever-growing chalkstones immediately sprouted on his feet and hands, through the violence of the pains and the flux that dripped down constantly over every part [?]. His fingers were reshaped into the shapelessness of stones before they had even reached their full growth, and the soles of his feet came to resemble the bumps of the ground. Perhaps his feet, and his hands with them, would have turned wholly into these things, renouncing their own shape and changing their form entirely, had he not found Cyrus fighting against the disease, together with John the martyr, his companion. At first he had put himself in the hands of doctors. But when he saw the illness getting the better of him and clearly overcoming their art, he fled to the saints before it could overcome him too. He had learned that they alone after God could, if they wished, put the affliction to sleep, holding out a divine bridle that is not made by mortal art.

So he came to their shrine and begged to be healed along with everyone else. The loving martyrs often stood beside him as he slept and commanded him to enter into communion with the Catholic Church. They promised him on oath that if he followed their counsel about the right faith, they would grant him health, provide him with gifts useful for this present life, and count him worthy of the priestly clergy; for he belonged to the heresy of Julian of Halicarnassus. But although he heard all these promises made on oath, he remained just as disobedient and unmoved. Since the martyrs could not persuade him with words, they tested him with the scourges of illness. When not even this persuaded the man, they decided to show him how great his illness was, so that, frightened of what was to come, he might make himself obedient

[?] … to us, as we keep advising you, and you become of the same belief concerning the faith, then we too will heed you [?] and entreat Christ our God and Master on your behalf, and we believe he will certainly grant you healing. For how could we pray to him for you

while you remain [?] … to us?" He heard these and many other things, but did not change his mind at all. When he rejected this exhortation of theirs as well, they no longer urged him as lovers of mankind, but [?] …

to receive Theodore and grant him pardon for his past disobedience. The martyrs, he says, accepted their requests and relented a little from their anger. They ordered those holding him to lead him away, and to release him once he had agreed to enter into communion with the holy Church. As those holding him led him away, they asked whether he knew the reason for so great a threat. He said, "Yes, I know the reason." They asked again, "And what is it?" He declared, "That I am unwilling to come to the Catholic Church and to the mysteries of Christ celebrated in her." "Will you come, then,"

they said, "if we release you from the wrath being prepared against you?" He agreed, and they released him. When he woke from the dream he was still terrified and trembling, and he turned over in his mind what he had seen. To this extent he was persuaded, but his mind was still in doubt and his reasoning was swaying this way and that. While he was considering these things, before he had weighed what was best and firmly decided what to do, he fell asleep again. Again he saw the martyrs, this time in the appearance and dress of Julian the deacon, who at that time had been appointed to serve in the church. They stood beside him and said, "Come, let us go to the tomb of the saints and pray." They said this to test him, to see whether he had changed his mind and become obedient to them after such a vision. And indeed they went to their precious coffin, with Theodore following them. When they came in front of the baptistery, where the life-giving mysteries of Christ are kept, they urged him to go in and partake. "Come in with us," they said, "and partake of the holy mysteries of Christ." He said, "No, I will not go in. I am of another belief, not of the Church's preaching. I am expecting my mother today, and she is bringing me the gifts of communion. But for now," he said to the deacon, "let me go in while the railings of the tomb are open and receive the oil of the lamp." For many who are not in communion do this: they receive the oil burning in the saints' lamp instead of the holy body and blood of Christ, the God and Saviour of us all. They do not know, I think, what they are doing, nor do they understand the harm in it.
