The oil of the saints' lamp has been sanctified, I too say so; but what is that compared with the one who sanctifies the saints themselves? We grant that it has some power against diseases; but what is that compared with Christ, who is the wisdom and power of God, and who distributes gifts of power to the martyrs themselves? I say that it deserves honour because it burns above the reliquary; but what is that compared with the one who is seated upon the cherubim? And what is the oil of the saints' lamp, set beside even the saints themselves, who sanctify the oil of the lamp? For everything that is ranked as a creature, not only on earth but in heaven too, whether Thrones or Principalities or Authorities or Dominions or angelic Powers, and others besides these, or the Cherubim themselves and the Seraphim, the many-eyed and six-winged living creatures, far more precious than the multitude of creatures and therefore bearing God upon them, or any other creation there may be among spiritual beings, known to God who made it but hidden from us humans — all of it counts it a joy and prays to bear the yoke of servitude, and [?]

to be, and to be called, a servant of the Lord's body of Christ our God, and not to be compared with it or to wish to claim equality with it or anything close to it; which not even [?] would accept. For this is the mindset of the author of evil. Through it he too counted equality with God a thing to be grasped and imagined a throne like God's above the clouds of the heavenly vault, and so he who was once the morning star fell; and he enticed our forefathers, who were in paradise, and dragged them down into corruption. We say these things not to correct the errors of the people we have mentioned ("for what have I to do with judging outsiders?" as the Apostle says), but to safeguard our brothers, lest, seeing those people do this so often, they join them in impiety. But let us come to what remains of our story.

The martyrs, then, appearing to the sick man as Julian the deacon, heard that he wanted to receive the oil of the lamp. They stood on the step in front of the railings of the tomb and kept him from going in. They placed themselves in his sight, ran ahead of him as he tried to enter, moved now to the left and now to the right, and blocked the entrance with their own bodies. After many such moves, when they still could not persuade him to go to the baptistery and partake of Christ's mysteries, they let him have the entrance leading to their coffin. Theodore passed through it and entered the vestibule, but before he could reach the railings and receive the oil, they took hold of his cloak from behind and made him turn toward them. Again they urged him to listen to them and to obey them rather than the leaders of his own heresy. When they saw that even so he would not be persuaded, they let him go on to the tomb. But when he turned, he saw that the railings of the tomb were shut. Finding no way left to take any of the lamp's oil, he went away downcast and grieving. The loving martyrs did not slacken at all. They waited in front of the baptistery, and as he came out from the tomb they again exhorted and urged him, teaching him and admonishing him at length. When they saw him so unbending and unwilling to be persuaded, they sent him away with this fearful oath: "By the Son of God the Father, the Lord and God of all, who reigns over the army of martyrs and grants the gift of healings: unless you obey us and come to his Catholic Church alone, and to the mysteries [?] celebrated in her, with a pure and chaste conscience, you will leave this place sick, just as you came here, with no benefit from us." These things were said and done in a dream.

Early in the morning he went out to pray at the saints' tomb, and in front of the tomb he saw a man named Paschasius, who was troubled by an evil spirit. When Paschasius saw Theodore, he glared at him fiercely and, with his teeth [?] …, shouted these words at him in a piercing voice:

roaring, and speaking as if the words came from the saints: "Go quickly and illuminate your soul! For by the power that dwells here, just as you came here gripped by the frenzy of gout, so you will go away without obtaining healing. The holy martyrs command me to tell you this." When he heard this from the demoniac he was seized with fear. He also remembered what he had seen in his dream, since the words and the threat were so alike. So he went at once into the baptistery and partook of the mysteries of Christ, and by partaking of the mysteries he illuminated his soul. But through the working of a demon he fell into a terrible despondency after receiving communion. Grieving, he threw himself down on his own bedding, and his grief soon put him to sleep. Again he sees the martyrs, who had taken the form of Julian the deacon, and they asked him the cause of his despondency. "Because the saints forced me to take communion," he said. They replied: "Does this trouble you or grieve you at all [?]? Rather, you ought to rejoice and exult, considering the benefit to your own soul and expecting the healing of your illness. In any case, this was God's will, and without it the saints [?] do nothing." With these words the martyrs consoled him and departed. He then turned his thoughts to his mother's arrival, and was anxious above all because she was going to bring the consecrated remnants of his own sect. Not long afterwards she arrived, bringing nothing of the kind, though that was the very reason she had made the journey; by the dispensation of the martyrs she had plainly forgotten. When he learned this he was glad at first. Then he told his mother everything the martyrs had done to him, and how they had forced him to run to the Church. In this way, then, he ran to the Church. Now let us show (24) the restoration of his body as well, telling it briefly. A few days later he was asleep again, and he sees the martyrs standing beside him and ordering him to go along with them. He, he says [Damascene: with them], followed more eagerly, for he knew that following the saints was not without profit. They came to a perfect temple [Damascene, wrongly: a Greek temple], fearsome in appearance and exceedingly bright, so tall that it touched the very heavens. When we had gone inside, we saw a very large and wonderful icon. In the middle it had the Master Christ painted in colours. On Christ's left was our Lady the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary, and on his right John the Baptist, Forerunner of the Saviour himself, who announced him in advance by leaping in the womb, since though he spoke from within [Synodicon and Damascene: being within] he was not heard. There were also some of the glorious choir of apostles and prophets [?]

and of the assembly of martyrs. Among these were Cyrus and John the martyrs themselves. They stood before the icon and fell down before the Master, bending their knees [Synodicon: the knees], touching their heads to the ground and interceding for the young man's healing. These were the words of their intercession: "Master, lover of mankind, do you command that we give healing to this man too?" They bowed to the ground many times and poured out words of supplication, but the Master Christ did not consent. So they stopped interceding and came to me, he says, downcast and dejected, as I stood not far from the icon. Coming close, they said [?]: "You see, the Master does not wish healing [?] to be given to you [variant: to give you healing]. But do not despair at all, for he will surely be kind to you as he is to everyone." After a pause of about a short half-hour they went again and pleaded, and again, he says, they came back unsuccessful, downcast [Damascene adds: and dejected] as before, since the Master Christ gave no command, and on returning they told me the same things again [Synodicon: these things]. As they were going the third time, they said [?]: "Take courage, for now we will certainly receive the grace. But you too, since you see us supplicating, come with us and supplicate the Master." Coming before the icon a third time, they used the same gestures and words as before. They pleaded for a long time, and lying on the ground they cried out only, "Do you command it, Master?" Then [one manuscript: and] Christ, moved with compassion as one who is merciful, consented, and from [one manuscript, wrongly: before] the icon he said, "Give it to him." The martyrs rose from the ground and first gave thanks to Christ our God for having heard [variant: obeyed] their prayer. Then, rejoicing and exulting [variant reading noted], they said to me: "See, God has granted the grace. Go, then, to Alexandria and sleep fasting in the great Tetrapylon. Take a little of the oil from the lamp that burns [?] before the icon of the Saviour in a small flask, and come back here again without tasting food. Anoint your feet with it and you will have the gift of healing [?]." After the dream he goes to Alexandria. While he was sleeping in the Tetrapylon, he sees an enormous serpent crawling out from his feet, and after it had come out, turning back towards him again. But the martyrs suddenly appeared and prevented it from going back in. They crushed the serpent's head with a staff and told him to take courage, for the illness would no longer bind his feet or his hands. He rose after his sleep, took the oil from the lamp and came to the shrine of the saints. There, as he had been instructed, he anointed his hands and feet, and at once he put off the disease and recovered his strength. He was also counted worthy, along with the most beautiful [?]

[?] for all of which, giving thanks [?] earnestly to the martyrs. Let us too sing their praises and then pass on to another of their miracles.

37. Concerning John the subdeacon, who had leucomas in both eyes.

Since we have written of Theodore's disease, of his forced and unwilling entry into the Church, and of his thrice-blessed progress [?], come, let us weave John into the story with him. Like him, John [?] became a communicant against his will, and reaped health as the reward for communion, and he too came to be called a brother in priestly rank [?]. This John, the occasion and [?] of the present writing, [?] from the city from which he had set out [?], had leucomas on both pupils. Their light gave way before the advance of the leucomas, since the pupils of the eyes cannot live together with leucomas. "For what fellowship has light with darkness?" as the divine Paul said. Light will not stay in fellowship with darkness, and darkness cannot take in light as a housemate. Since they are opposite in nature in every respect, their workings are opposite too: those who have the one cannot see, and those who have the other are not darkened. John, then, having the causes of darkness, failed to obtain the light. Once darkened, he was cut off from it, and in his darkness he could see nothing at all. Having fallen into this disease of the eyes and been deprived of light, as has been said, he was brought to Cyrus and John the martyrs, guided by the eyes of others. When a year had passed, [he obtained] the help and grace of the saints [?]. The saints' visitation took place in this way. John was asleep on his bed, and in his sleep he saw himself standing before the tomb of the saints and praying for the restoration of his eyes. While he was doing this he seemed to see the saints sitting in front of their own coffin, in the form and dress of elders. They rose from their seats, took John by the hand and led him to the divine altar. Setting him beside it, they gave him holy bread that had become the life-giving body of Christ. After he had partaken of it, they took a cup from the mystical table again and gave him to drink. It was filled with divine milk, perhaps the milk with which, as the apostle Paul wrote, he gave drink to those who are infants in Christ. After this they sent John away, fortifying him with these words: "See, young man, you have learned the way of true life. From now on, then, partake of the mysteries of Christ here." For John shared the beliefs of Theodosius and Severus, and had been appointed to the rank of subdeacon in their confession.

When the man who until then had been blind saw these things in his sleep, he cast off sleep but held firmly to the initiation he had received in it. He took it to be divine, and believed that the recovery of sight in his bodily eyes would be granted if he carried it out. So he rose and immediately partook of the mysteries where he had been told to, putting aside all his former tradition and embracing the Church's preaching, which profits the soul. Having done this as he had been commanded, on the third day he saw the light with his eyes, the light following close on the heels of the illumination of his soul. He became as he had been at birth, and the eyes of his body were as though they had never been diseased. But while he was in this state and seeing most clearly, the destroyer of good things envied him and hastened to rob him of the gift of the saints. [?] Having fallen into this misfortune, John recognized its cause. Recognizing it, he repented; repenting, he obtained forgiveness; obtaining pardon, he amended his ways; having amended them, he recovered his sight again; having recovered it, he serves the martyrs; serving them, he was granted a kindly welcome; and having been granted this, he advanced into the clergy of the Church. At that time, however, having received this loving blow and become blind as at first, he turned back again and gave up entering the city he longed for, knowing the compassion of the saints and that they would receive him when he returned and heal him, having trained him for salvation. Indeed, that night as he slept he saw, or rather, since he could not see, he heard: "Return quickly, and appease these angry martyrs." The voice was that of the steward of the shrine [?], the admirable Christodorus, who made himself known by name. The dream was true in this respect too, for the saints were perhaps bringing this about by divine dispensation: he had left, it says, without the permission of Christodorus. So when John came, Christodorus would neither see him nor let him be counted among the sick in the precinct. Instead he lay in the venerable priests' quarters of the shrine, where all the visitors stay, since they can find no other place because of the crowd of sick people there. John lay there for three days without being given a place as a sick man, as has been explained, for the most gracious power of the martyrs was arranging this. After the three days, as he slept, he sees a deacon standing in the place

of the ambo, carrying the book of the holy Gospels and proclaiming the Gospel in a loud voice. The passage that the figure in the vision was reading from the Gospel according to Matthew was the Saviour's answer to John the Baptist, who had asked through his own disciples, "Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?" "And Jesus answered and said to them: Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind see again, lepers are cleansed, the lame walk, and the deaf hear." John heard these words in his sleep, and at once he rises, putting off his blindness along with his sleep. For his bodily eyes recovered their sight, and he sees the light of the sun just risen, for it was dawn. Just as the night was departing and the air was being whitened by the rays of the sun, John, hearing the saving voice say, "The blind see again," suddenly recovered his sight, his soul having first been illuminated by faith and having gained bright eyes. Yet he did not [?] receive his sight as it had been at first. Instead he carried in his eyes only the salutary reproof of such ingratitude, so that others who saw him might become more careful themselves. Let us too sing the praises of the martyrs for this all-profitable instruction, and then take up another of their instructive miracles.

38. Concerning Stephen, who likewise had leucomas in his eyes.

After this John let Stephen come, and let the [?] follow the man from Cynopolis in this writing, increasing the praise of the saints and adding to their eulogy. He too was ill, having leucomas in his eyes, and belonged to the heresy of [?]. He took great pains over his eyes, lamenting the loss of the sweetest light, and ran about here and there, longing to find what he had lost. Let us hear how the divine and loving martyrs heal him. Let us also admire their zeal for the right faith and praise the power of healing given to them. First, for four months after Stephen came they left him unvisited. By this they softened his stubborn mind and made it gentler and readier to accept what was better. Then, after that period, they visit him and grant him health, a single visit being enough for so great a disease. They appear to him in his sleep in this way. They were standing in the priests' quarters of the shrine, wearing monastic habits, and with nods they beckoned Stephen, who was outside, to come to them. When he had hurried into the priests' courtyard, they offered him a blessing; it was a loaf of pure bread with a cross stamped on it. He received the blessing given to him, but involuntarily let it fall to the ground. Cyrus, who had given it, picked it up and put it back into the young man's hands, but it fell from his palm. And when it fell again, the

Rising from sleep, Stephen hastened to the communion of the catholic Church, and found that the recovery of his sight followed upon its mysteries. Thereupon his servant too became one of the Saviour's sheep in the Church. Barbarian though he was, he reckoned that to fight against God and the saints, against the catholic Church and the orthodox faith, was plain madness. But the one who always envies everything good begrudged their salvation and took away half of the gift. He wanted to take away the whole of it but could not, for he found the martyrs standing as shield-bearers over their gift. After the health of soul and body and the recovery of sight in both eyes, while they were still staying in the precinct, the servant asked Stephen: "See, master, here we have obeyed the commands of the saints and become communicants of the catholic Church. But when, God willing, we reach our homeland, shall we abide by their commands, or go back to our former ways?" He answered him: "While we are here, let us do what seems good to the martyrs. But when we leave this place, let us hold once more to our own doctrines as before, and to the faith that our fathers handed down to us." So far these things were said only in conversation, and no deed of that kind had yet been joined to the words. But Justice heard the words as though they were deeds and pursued the speaker as though he had already acted. For when the sun had set at the close of that day, night came and awarded rest to people on earth, bringing sleep, of course, on its wings and proclaiming clearly that it too had not been fashioned in vain by the Maker of all. In that night the martyrs appear to Stephen as to an ungrateful man and, exacting from him the penalty for his ingratitude, they allowed him to use the baths. He used them as he had been told, and was so badly affected that he lay awake for many nights and days, lamenting the long sleeplessness together with the pains, the kind that is apt to drive sufferers out of their minds. But this [?], as was fitting,

for the ungrateful man, ceased through the loving kindness of the martyrs. But his old blindness took its place again, punishing the slip of his tongue and the impious offspring of his mind. Though he deserved to suffer this, the wretched man was sadly ignorant of the cause of his torment. But the martyrs, imitators of Christ, being exceedingly loving and wishing all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, show him the cause through a vision, so that he might recognize it, and recognizing it repent, and repenting be saved. They appeared in the form and rank of the governor ruling the city of Nikiou and reproached him, it says, for breaking the agreement about communion that he had made with Cyrus and John. They ordered him to keep his covenant with them, and threatened him if he should look towards another transgression [?]. When he understood the cause of the harm, he rose and swore never again to do any such thing in word or deed, and he asked pardon for what had gone before. When the divine martyrs saw that he had firmly committed himself and was striving with all his strength to keep his covenant with them about the faith, they appeared to him again in his sleep, standing at the altar of Christ and offering the bloodless sacrifice. Having offered it, they gave him a share in it. After he had partaken, they showed him the Bride of the Saviour, the Church, flashing in bright garments, with divine adornment and an incomparable beauty that no human voice could describe. She came to the venerable altar and she too took of the mysteries of Christ lying on it and gave them to Stephen. When the saints said, "What has been given is enough for his perfecting," she answered with these words: "I want him to abound in divine gifts and to receive this in addition to what has been given. For I have received him now as he is being illuminated, and from now on he will be called my son." Having said this to the martyrs, she hung from the young man's neck, over his chest, a golden cross shining with clear and precious stones, giving it to him as a guardian of the illumination he had received. For when Stephen came out of the holy place after the dismissal of that sacred rite, an ugly and profane Egyptian tried to strip him once he was outside the church. Though he struggled hard, he could not, but was overcome and fell into a pit that was hard to get out of. Plainly the cross, giver and guardian of victory, was again strengthening the one who venerated it and granting him victory over darkness. Not long after this victory Stephen also put off the darkness of his eyes. He enjoyed health and saw the light as before, using the juice of endive as a remedy, for the martyrs had ordered in visions that its juice be dropped into his eyes. And having sung again, for this too, the praises of the physicians of bodies and souls,

[?] and before them of Christ, who works the healing through them, let us go on to another healing and the account of another miracle.

39. Concerning Peter the paralytic.

In both of the preceding wonders and signs, and in the accounts we gave before them, the mind of the holy martyrs Cyrus and John concerning the faith has been made plain. That they revere the preaching of the catholic Church and embrace its communion is known through the healing of those just mentioned. It is fitting, I think, to make mention of Peter too. He held the same opinion as those before him, and the divine martyrs compelled him to come into the communion of the most holy Church. Even if this is not our aim, we do it for the benefit of those who have fallen away from the Church. As the saying goes, every word is established on the mouth of two or three witnesses; knowing this, they may now learn the truth anew, abandon their own heresies and come to the Church of the Saviour, following the aim of the saints and being taught what is good by them. This is also why we cite people who are still alive and breathing this visible air: if they do not believe us when we speak, they can ask those people and learn the truth from them. The martyrs will be enough for us as advocates to prove the correctness of every point, as they lead the limping to the knowledge of true religion with bit and bridle. But let us return to our subject, and show this once more through their deeds now. Let us begin this account here. Peter came from the estate of Heraclius, which lies fourteen stadia from the church of the saints. He had paralysis, a disease that had arisen from a serious illness, and that seemed set to stay with him until it saw Peter's death and went with him to the grave [?]. But he came to Cyrus and John the martyrs, and through them to the catholic Church and the orthodox faith. So he cast off the disease before death, and the deadly paralysis before the grave. For nothing is stronger than truth, as the wisdom of Zerubbabel shows: the truth that is strengthened by the heavenly preaching and always keeps the Church unconquered, never yielding to the gates of hell. These gates are the Christ-hating heresies, which serve the gullet of Hades and readily send those who fall into it down into its belly. The martyrs, most fervent in faith, stood beside Peter as he slept and spoke with him gently and kindly. "Do you want," they said, "to enjoy health and strength and to escape this worst of all illnesses?" He eagerly welcomed the question. He said "Yes" with his lips and signalled it with a nod of his head, and by moving his hands as best he could he made the gesture of supplication. When the martyrs saw that he was eager for health

…burning. Such a [?] they set before him, [?] the [Israelite?] people, whose parents and forefathers [?]. Peter therefore said that he did not even wish to receive healing, nor to share the faith of the council assembled at Chalcedon. When he said this the holy martyrs threatened him. They told him that he would not be saved in any other way and withdrew, reawakening the pains that they themselves had lulled to sleep. Terribly tormented by these, he again called on the martyrs to help him. They came again and put the same terms to him as before, and he sent them away with nothing done. He did this not merely two, three or four times, but many times. He kept calling them to his aid, and out of great pity for him they kept answering and urging him to do the same things. Each time he sent them away as though they had never come, because he would not yield to them or be persuaded. For the Egyptians are a nation hard to move. Whatever they have once decided to do, whether it is good or falls short of the better, they do not easily change, and they are all like this. But the excess of pain was punishing Peter, and he could no longer bear the sharpness of his torments. So at last, persuaded only with difficulty even then, he yielded to the saints' commands and called on them one last time. He asked them to take pity on him again and come, to drive away his pains [?] and grant him healing, and he declared that he would willingly carry out whatever they might wish or say. The martyrs, compassionate and kindly as they are, came this time too when he called. They instructed him to do the same things, and they swore that if he was persuaded and did it, they would have him as a partner in their faith. He was still hesitating about receiving the mysteries, so they said to him: “It is not enough, Peter, to believe as we believe and to be ranked with us in the matter of faith.” Again he dared to say to them: “What? Do you too, great servants of Christ, believe as the council at Chalcedon did?” They confessed that they thought in agreement with that holy multitude of priests and believed as the council at Chalcedon had believed. They called what that council had defined the right faith and a divinely inspired proclamation. When the holy martyrs had said this and confirmed it with oaths, they saw that the torments had already persuaded Peter, and they appeared to withdraw, though they did not withhold their power. At dawn he carried out the blessed command, and as the reward of his piety

he reaped healing. He went on keeping the faith that the martyrs had given him, and he has kept his reward beyond losing. It is not cut off from the right faith but abides and remains with it and admits no separation from it. Nor does he suffer what happened to those before him. He is not deprived of faith and healing, only to be disciplined and flogged again as an ingrate and then lay claim to better things. Rather, he remains faithful and unshakable and gathers the grapes of health without ceasing. So Peter became a communicant of the Church and a child of light.

Menas, the notary of Christodorus, the steward of the saints, was an Alexandrian of the same heresy. He was openly flogged and then took communion. While he was sleeping near the saints, he saw them going to the venerable sanctuary and the mystical, heavenly table, as if to partake of the holy mysteries. They turned and saw that he was not following, so they came back to him. Holding rods in their hands, they flogged him hard and vigorously and showed him the reason for his torments. “Why,” they said, “when you saw us going to receive communion, did you not run along with us? If you wish to remain in our house, follow our decrees. Where we enjoy the Lord's food, there you too must partake.” And they stretched out their fingers to point to the holy table. Not even after a great many lashes did they persuade him to agree with them. They threatened him severely and let him go, once he had undertaken to do what he was commanded without fail. And he, [from his?] bed [?]…

John was a Libyan who had formerly lived in Mareotis. But when he came to the saints' sanctuary he changed his race, in a way, since this place lies rather closer to Egypt. The cause of his move, so they say, was a savage demon that had made its dwelling in him and was unbearable because of its great savagery. For this reason John was brought in chains to the martyrs, so that they might take pity on him and free him from the demon living in him. And they did this quickly. They cast out the demon at once and granted him lasting [?] from its madness.

Having obtained this deliverance, John enrolled himself as a servant of the saints who had saved him, and so showed goodwill worthy of his healing. For its sake he became an emigrant: he left his homeland and lived at the shrine of the saints. That, then, is the reason for his move. A good while later he fell gravely ill in the kidneys, and the illness was unbearable. Sometimes he fell to the ground and rolled about. Sometimes he rose from the ground and ran up and down the sanctuary. With his deep groans he robbed everyone staying there with him of the welcome rest that quiet naturally brings them. Perhaps he deserved forgiveness, since his pain was so violent. One might perhaps guess at the pain of other ailments, but no one who has not suffered it can describe the pain of the kidneys and its unimaginable agony. Only those who have had the illness know it. John was in the greatest danger, as we have said, and he might perhaps have received a speedier cure if he had waited for the saints with patience…

It is worth telling how he escaped this illness too, for the way it happened is full of grace. A certain quack saw him in severe pain and longing ardently for health, and said to him: “Give me three coins, and I will cure you with an antidote.” John was eager to escape his torment, so he readily handed over the gold. He took the drug and kept it, meaning to swallow it at dawn. That night, as he slept, he saw the martyrs standing beside him. They reproached him for his lack of faith in them and reminded him of the various healings they had performed for him. For they had freed him not only from a demon but also from the incurable disease of gout, and from countless other ailments that would need a separate treatise if anyone wished to write them down one by one. The glorious victors reminded him of all these, and very elegantly charged him with faithlessness, forgetfulness, ingratitude and everything of that kind. Finally they spoke in irony: “What?” they said. “If you had given us the three coins, could we not have given you the healing?” They used exactly the same words that the fine quack had used to him. “But go,” they said, “and whatever you brought to the doctor who gave you the antidote, bring to our treasury

too, and we will rather [?] you the [?]… [?] goodness [?], of which we are no small way short, as has been shown from what came before.

Since the martyrs have judged that we should tell this story too, let us tell it, as they themselves grant us the telling. Not long ago a woman came to the saints' church. Her name was Mary, and she came from Babylon in Egypt. She had a boy of about eight, whom she called Menas, clearly in honor of the martyr. The boy Menas had his tongue hanging out of his mouth, and it differed greatly in form and size from human tongues. It hung a full span outside his lips and covered his whole chin and throat like a thick beard. It had lost its red color and turned purple, with a kind of blackness to it. It was a strange and utterly hideous sight, and it moved everyone who saw it to nausea and pity alike, and to uncontrollable vomiting. It was always dripping saliva like a spring and pouring out spittle without end, so it soaked his clothes and his chest and passed its own blackness on to them, making them share its color. As a result, many people could not even look at the child. If they happened to meet him, they covered the eyes of their bodies and turned their faces away, so that their stomachs would not turn against their will and make them vomit. Many others, who were able to look at him even briefly, saw how monstrous the affliction was. They repeated the words the Savior spoke about the betrayer and cried out over the boy: “It would have been good for that man if he had not been born.” Some added to this the apostles' question about the man born blind: “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be like this?” Yet the child was not blind, nor had he come out of his mother's womb like this. One night as he slept, some accursed demon, deeply sick with hatred of humankind, seized his tongue and dragged it out of its proper home. The utterly vile creature beat it mercilessly and made it bigger with its blows, so that it hung outside and could no longer fit inside. For not only did he appear hideous,

[but also?] [?] of the present life bloomed painful [?]. He was completely cut off from solid food, because his teeth could no longer grind it as they used to, now that his tongue protruded and had grown so large. He could barely take liquid, runny food, which his mother poured into his mouth while holding back the tongue with some device. Such was the boy's illness. I think no human being has ever endured it, or seen anyone else suffer it, even though the wise Ecclesiastes declared that nothing under the sun is new or recent. Many physicians saw it, including the most eminent of them. They were immediately astonished at the affliction, and almost all of them struck their faces and fled. They no longer knew what to do, nor could they find the condition in the writings of the ancient Asclepiads. But Cyrus and John, the martyrs who bring healing from God, did nothing of the sort when they saw this illness. They were not astonished at the sight, they did not decline the case as too difficult, and they did not declare that its remedy had not been written down by God, the physician of all. For they knew well that the Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in all the deeps. They knew that what is impossible with human beings is possible with God, and that he has mercy on all, because, as Job said, he can do all things. And they knew that, as the singer David sang in the Psalms, his compassions are richly poured out on all his works. So they received the sick boy and first showed him kindness. Then they gave his mother courage as she watched for their wonders. They waited a short time, not because they were considering how to treat him, but so that so marvelous a thing would not reach only a very few, easily counted, but would become plainer and better known to more people. This is clear from the manner of the healing. They did not give orders through a vision to do this or that, as they usually do. Instead, when they decreed that the child should be healed, the healing took place openly. At midday the boy was playing with some children his age in front of the saints' tomb. As usually happens in children's games, sometimes he brought others to the ground and sometimes others threw him down. When he fell and his face came near the marble, his tongue touched it. As soon as it touched, it drew back into its original state, as if something were pursuing it and it were fleeing. It returned to its proper size from before the affliction and at once regained its healthy color, casting off that hideous color and shape and its size, heavy with excess flesh. It had been in the habit of sticking out beyond the teeth against its will, but it suddenly forgot that habit and would not stick out even at will. Instead it settled down inside the lips as if in its own bridal chamber

and regained its former order and functioned according to its nature. It made the boy almost unrecognizable to those who had seen him a little earlier. When this miracle happened, the children at play let out a piercing shout, which gathered everyone in the church to see. They were astonished at the wonder that had been done, and they sang hymns to the saints. They loudly raised the cry found in the Gospels about the Savior's deeds, saying, “We have seen marvels today.” With thanksgiving they glorified Christ himself, who had worked the miracle through the saints, and all of them became hopeful of healing for their own sufferings. And we, who have heard of marvels today and have worthily sung the praises of those who worked them, let us become heralds of other marvels.

Miracle 43 [?]. Concerning Eugenius the surveyor, who had dropsy.

Eugenius the surveyor has come to us from the fields. He had measured every field but could not measure his own belly. A watery substance had collected in it and made it swell, until with its huge, enormous swellings it resembled not the easily measured size of a field but the unreachable height of mountains. He makes measured requests, wishing to be measured alongside the saints' miracles. He considers this a great honor, and so he has asked in advance to be found worthy of it. At the same time he shows what education he has, for he has placed himself sixth [?] among the narratives of the Egyptians and Libyans, admiring the perfection of that number and therefore eager to have it as his lot. So, admiring both his eagerness and his learning, let us grant his request. Eugenius was a surveyor, as I said, and an Egyptian by race. Because of the oppressive heat of the air he drank a great deal of water and fell into a very grievous illness. This illness lost much of its own violence, but it turned the small remnant that was left into a very great dropsy. Even with this, Eugenius did not stop drinking water. Little by little he swelled until he could not move and lay down most of the time, like great sea monsters and huge serpents, which are so weighed down by the bulk and size of their bodies that they cannot move forward. Even then he did not stop drinking water. So although all growth begins from motion, as the experts in these matters teach, he grew without moving at all and outwitted both nature itself and their doctrine. I will decline to speak again of the physicians' helplessness in this disease, since it is plain to everyone. It is obvious even if we keep silent. Let us pass it by in silence, then, and tell of the power of John and Cyrus, the true physicians. For just as much as the helplessness of the former deserves silence,

so much is the power of these proclaimed aloud. For Eugenius, after much experience, rejected the former as powerless and chose the latter as powerful on hearsay alone. So he came to the saints' house of healing, which wards off all despondency and every kind of affliction, and learned by experience what he had known by hearsay before his illness. “As we have heard, so also have we seen,” he proclaimed loudly with the Psalmist. For on the very night following the day of his arrival, as he slept in front of the saints' tomb, he saw the martyrs come forward and heard them say to him: “Get up from here, Eugenius, and hurry off home. For see, Christ has healed you through us and cured the disease for which you came to us. So get up, go to the latrines as quickly as you can, and get rid of all the matter that has collected in you.” As they said this, they touched the sick man's belly as if stroking it, but in truth they were bringing about the evacuation with their hands. Eugenius said that after his sleep (one might equally say after his sickness, since the sickness lasted until he slept) he heard what happened next. While the martyrs were doing this, three women behind them cried out: “Why is it, saints, that we have spent all this time sitting here, suffering from our afflictions, and have still not been freed from our illnesses?” (They were among the patients lying there, as the sick man recognized after his dream.) “This man came only yesterday, gripped by so great an affliction, yet today he is granted health and told to go home?” The martyrs turned to them, he says, and answered with all gentleness: “It is not we, women, who are masters of healing, but Christ, our president and ruler. Some come who need a longer discipline, and others who ought to be healed more quickly. We offer our supplications for all alike, and whomever our Master, God and Savior Jesus Christ, commands us to heal, we heal and at once dismiss. So join us in beseeching him to grant what you ask. If he has compassion and deigns only to command, we quickly carry out his divine decrees. Without his consent we can neither keep nor release those who come to us.” This is what the holy martyrs said to the women. Eugenius got up from sleep and from his bed and hurried to the latrines, because his belly was forcing him to hurry to obey the martyrs' command. When he got there, he at once emptied out all the matter in a single instant. Once he had been emptied of it, as we have said, the man who had gone in bulkier in appearance than anyone came out of the latrines leaner than many. Or rather, here too the surveyor sprang out well proportioned. The only things about him beyond measure were the bulk of his belly and the time his healing took: the one for its very great brevity, the other for its

great and unimaginable size. So Eugenius too escaped the deadly fate of his disease and reaped health swiftly. He sang his thanks in tuneful verse to the martyrs and to Christ, who had given him this harvest through them, and left the church leaping for joy. And we, as if we had received the healing ourselves, delighting in the story and having sung hymns to Christ and the saints, let us hurry on to another delightful tale.

Miracle 44 [?]. Concerning Taurinus “Strap-foot.”

Taurinus is here too, coming from nearby. But he has only just reached us, as though he had travelled from far away, because his feet work rather slowly. And not only for that reason, it seems, but also because of the smith's hammering, which kept him from learning sooner that we were celebrating the saints' miracles. Still, he came and explained the reasons for his delay, and asked not to be passed over unrecorded. Since he has offered a defense that deserves no blame, let us make him too one of those who boast of the martyrs' visits. Taurinus was a villager from the estate of Heraclius, which lies near the saints' shrine, only a Sabbath day's journey from it, that is, a distance of fourteen stadia. He practiced the craft of nail-making. The weakness he had in his feet was no ordinary one, but great and beyond what hearsay can convey. His feet had renounced, so to speak, the form of feet and took on the character of dead straps. Because of this they made their owner too be called by their name. People stopped calling him “the nail-maker” after his craft and called him “Strap-foot” after his feet. Perhaps they were right to give him such a name, since his feet not only had the character of straps but were from then on just as useless as straps. And also, he says, because he had given up nail-making on account of his feet, he was named after the disease of his feet. Taurinus had this terrible infirmity, and the physicians gave their final verdict that such a man would never move his feet (this was the verdict their art gave). So he was carried to Cyrus and to John, the fellow martyr of the holy Cyrus. They are experts in divine medicine, not the kind that claims Hippocrates, Galen and Democritus as its fathers, who speak from the earth. The wonderful martyrs received him when he came and granted him the health that those physicians had despaired of. They appeared to him in his sleep, on his bed, as is their custom. They ordered him to take a roasted quail, grind it up and anoint his feet with it, and then they flew off again like a dream. After he woke he carried out the order and was marvelously restored. He cast off all the infirmity of his feet and that withered, utterly hideous likeness of straps, and became sound and fleet-footed, perhaps quick enough on his feet to catch quails. So Taurinus, now rich in health, gave thanks to God and the martyrs and went away. And we, having sung hymns, and of words [?]…
…having asked for abundant means to tell the remaining miracles, let us set about it eagerly. 41 [?]. Concerning Anna the nun who [?] three samamithia.

Before we go on to another country and city or move to a different village, the natural next step is to tell another miracle, perhaps even greater than the one just told. We learned from the saints themselves that it too came about for a certain nun who lived in the same village. Let us tell it, God granting us the words, and let us not separate the inhabitants of the same village from one another at all, even though another reason forced us to set apart from them Peter, whom we presented a little earlier as belonging to that village. A nun lived on this small estate of Heracleion. Her name was Anna, and she lived there with other virgins. She was about twelve years old, or even younger, and a person of that age cannot be left to herself, because of inexperience and immaturity of mind and judgment. For how could such a one wrestle not against blood and flesh but against the principalities and the powers and the world rulers of this age, and the spiritual forces of wickedness, taking up the struggle against them, if deprived of a trainer? Or how could such a one recognize the many kinds of sickness the demon brings, without a teacher who knows them? Or how could such a one guard against the deceit and cunning of the serpent, which not even Eve guarded against when she was separated a little from Adam? For these reasons it is not without danger for a child to live by herself, especially one who is at war with demons and is wholly unable to watch for the serpent's head quietly creeping in, even though she knows of it, or to cover her own heel, at which he lies in wait. So this nun, who was of childish age and had been left for an hour, as happens, without those able to guide her, fell into a strange and terrible danger that the devil had prepared for her. Finding her alone, he drove her toward death in this way. Left by herself, apart from the others, she was playing, as a young girl will, at girls' games, satisfying her wish to play with some reeds. Sometimes she would pick up a reed and put it to her mouth. Then she would take it away from her mouth and throw it on the ground, pick up another, and do the same with it. But while she was swapping reeds, throwing one away from her mouth and taking another and bringing it to her teeth, she came upon a reed that was pregnant with death and held a grievous and deadly treasure. For three creeping creatures called samamithia lived in this reed, making it their den and their bed, and in her innocence she snatched it up and brought it to her mouth. They sensed the movement and, alarmed into flight, leaped out through the end

nearest her mouth and were carried down into the girl's stomach, sliding there against their will. Once brought down into the girl's belly, they could not bear their strange new dwelling and hurried to escape from there too, but they did not know the way out. Running about like this, they churned the bowels of the wretched girl and twisted her entrails, causing her unbearable pains which no one could depict in writing, not even someone with long experience of the affliction. So the girl ceaselessly beat herself and wailed and shed tears, and could not rest at all. For when one of the swallowed creatures was quiet for a little, if it ever was quiet, the other two tormented the girl; or when two of them were sleeping, as often happened, to grant even this, the other did not stop. They dealt out to her a pain that never slept, now one of them, now two, and often all three tearing at her. So, in ceaseless and piercing pain, she was brought to the saints, finding no other physician able to cope with such a calamity. Having come, then, as has been said, and having found the martyrs compassionate, she was quickly freed from that threefold torment. Let us tell how the deliverance came about, for it is full of the grace of her deliverers. The saints came in a dream to another of the sick brothers and said, "Tell this nun who is crying out" (for she cried out continually and did not sleep at all) "to get up early in the morning and go out to one of the taverns before she tastes food or drink, and to bring herself to drink three cannia while fasting" (this is a kind of cup, so called among the Alexandrians), "and she will quickly receive healing through the cannia."

The man who saw the dream reported it to the sick girl after he woke, as the martyrs had instructed him. When she learned of their command, she went out to a tavern early in the morning and immediately drank the three cups, filled with wine unmixed with water, for she had been ordered to drink the three cannia neat. Having gulped them down, as I said, she was quickly moved to vomit. She brought up the wine, and plainly along with it she threw up the three samamithia through her mouth, and was at once released from all the harm and the grievous pain and scourging which that triplet burden she carried within her had brought on her like labor pains. So Anna the nun escaped the death prepared for her by demons, having found help against their plot more powerful than that of physicians. She stirred all who saw the healing to hymns of the saints, joined them in praising the saints, and left the sanctuary. And we who hear it now, believing as those present then did, and having praised the saints worthily, let us make ready our ears and mouths for other hymns and miracles. 45. Concerning Cosiotes the deaf camel driver. From Egypt let us cross over again to Libya,

and, once in the Mareotis, let us track down Cosiotes the deaf man, for he came from the Mareotis. When we have found him, let us add him to those who came before and report his story to our hearers, for what the martyrs did for him is worth recording. Cosiotes had become deaf. He was not born so from the womb; he was suddenly struck deaf while he was tending the camels. He always looked after these animals, both before his deafness and after it came upon him so suddenly. The affliction was very severe: he heard nothing at all, and could not perceive even very loud sounds, such as the shouting of a crowd, the roar of a rising sea, or the rushing of great winds. Everyone who saw him said the deafness was the work of a demon and not a disease or bodily ailment. And perhaps they hit upon the truth, both because the illness came on all at once and because none of the physicians could do him any good. For he went round to many of them and carried out many of their prescriptions, yet he remained in his affliction and could find no change. So he bade the physicians a long farewell and looked after his camels, no longer expecting to be rid of the illness. And perhaps he would have stayed like this until his death, had he not been mocked by his fellow workers for being deaf and suffered much ill treatment. Unable to bear their harsh abuse, he left everything—his home, his camels, his possessions—and without making any arrangement with anyone about anything, filled with zeal and with divine love for the martyrs (who, I think, had breathed such a thought into him), he ran at full speed to their shrine, saying only this to his companions: "As Christ our God lives, I am going to none other than Saints Cyrus and John, and I will make them avengers of the abuse I have suffered." With these words he ran to the martyrs barefoot [?]. Then something extraordinary happened, worthy of the saints' grace and of his own great fervor. As soon as he had passed through the city gate called the Sun Gate, his ears at once began to open and he began to hear human voices. The further he advanced on his journey, the more sound he perceived. And so, receiving the gift step by step as he went along the road, by the time he entered the saints' sanctuary he had recovered his hearing perfectly, leaving behind every trace and sign of that profound deafness. Having gathered his healing on the way, he came to the saints as a healthy man and not as one with an illness. He at once offered his thanksgivings, which were songs honoring those who had saved him, and immediately went back the same way, not even consenting to sit down in the martyrs' shrine. And we too, having completed the story about him and offered thanksgivings to the saints for it, let us tell of another mira-

This man fell very gravely ill in his sight, and since he found no physician able to cure the affliction, he was driven to complete blindness, so that he could not tell whether it was night or day unless someone was there to tell him. His eyes were shut and would not open at all, and he could not separate his eyelids, which were stuck together as if by glue. Yet the tribune, though suffering such an affliction, did not disbelieve in the grace of Cyrus and John, but piously and rightly believed that if he came to them as a suppliant he would surely recover his sight, and this was fulfilled in deed. For one who is made firm in faith, and holds its foundation unshaken, usually also attains perfection in deeds among friends [?], since no one who has believed has been abandoned by God; rather it has been done for him as he believed, and he has received as the wage of his faith the enjoyment of what he longed for. So, when he was in the saints' shrine, having a faith that rivaled that of the man blind from birth, and sleeping there as that man did, he heard from the grace of the saints: "Go, wash in Siloam, and you will see." For being imitators of the Savior, they use his words, eager to show through all their healings the source from which they draw their grace. Having heard the martyrs' command, the sick man reached the holy city of Christ our God, went down to Siloam, washed in its waters, and at once recovered his sight. Coming back from there able to see, and knowing how great a gift his sight was, he hurried back to the saints and lived with them for the rest of his life, until he fell asleep and went to his rest, showing us the goodwill we ought to have toward our benefactors. So the tribune benefited in this way and obtained the faith and the healing described. Another man, a monk of Tabennesi—one of those who boast of the great Pachomius as their ancestral father and teacher of the best life, since he founded their way of life and became for them a ladder bearing them up from earth to heaven—came to the martyrs with the same affliction as the tribune. When he heard the same command from them, "Go," they said, "wash in Siloam and you will see," he answered them wittily:

"That blind man, blessed ones, who heard this present command from the Master of all, was in Jerusalem and had Siloam as his neighbor; and though he was known to be poor, he needed no money to carry out the Savior's saving command. But I was poor even before, and now I am much poorer than I was then, for I spent even what I had before my eye disease on physicians; and I am so far away from Siloam. What money do you tell me to use to carry out your decree?" They smiled very gravely and, delighted with his fine reply, became generous providers of his expenses as well. "Go," they said, "to the place called the apostasis of Fronto" (in other countries, places, and cities they call an apostasis a storehouse), "and there look for Thomas, the agent of Cuminas the Egyptian. When you find him, say: 'Abbacyrus and John the martyrs have sent me to you, and they decree that you give me one gold coin, so that I may have money for expenses, since they have sent me to the holy city.'" Having said this, the saints departed. When he woke, he went to the city, found the storehouse and the man, and told him the saints' command. He at once received the coin (for Thomas readily accepted the martyrs' decree) and set out for the places of Christ. Hurrying to Siloam, he wiped his eyes with its streams, and with the drops of the water he wiped away the mist from his eyes. For the water recognized the command and the martyrs who had sent him, servants of Christ as they are and attendants of the one who before them had sent the blind man there. Therefore it quickly carried out their commands and sent this man away seeing too, along with the tribune, just as it had once sent the blind man back to its own Master. And we, content with what has been said about the two blind men who were healed, and praising the saints now too, let us hasten to proclaim other miracles of theirs. 4[?]. Concerning Patricius, who had [?] in his eyes.

It is fitting to join Patricius of Pelusium to those who came before. For even if his eye disease was different and the manner of his healing was different, the two cases had one and the same outcome: the illnesses ended in blindness, and the treatments in restored sight. So let us tell of his affliction too, and not separate the healing from the affliction. Patricius was from Pelusium, and he was the slave of the man who shepherded the Church there. He fell ill with an eye disease and advanced in it day by day—not reaching forward to what lies ahead and forgetting what lies behind (for then his surplus of sight would have been enviable), but forgetting what lies ahead and reaching toward what lies behind. For that is how a clever physician treated him! Advancing little by little, he came to a certain end, and was called

"much-seeing"—for that is the euphemism they use for the blind—and no longer gave any trouble to the man who had been treating him. For with white spots on both eyes, he received a most wretched freedom, by which he was no longer subject to the sons of Asclepius, but had blindness as his invincible mistress. She had snatched him as a prisoner of war from the physicians, and from then on it was impossible for any human being to defeat her and take the captive from her, but easy for God alone and for those who bestow healings from him. These are the apostles and righteous men and prophets and martyrs who lived blamelessly and served God, and who therefore have him obedient to them in all they wish. Patricius knew that Cyrus and John were two of this blessed and splendid company, and that they were able to ransom him from that bitter mistress and grant him the freedom which the physicians' help had destroyed. So he came to them with faith, knowing clearly that faith can persuade the martyrs. They appeared to him in a dream and revealed the way to health. They told him to go to the bath, anoint his eyes with the [?] of the bath, and so recover his sight. The main ingredient of this, they say, is quicklime first moistened in water; it is extremely caustic and yields very little to fire in its power to burn human bodies. Without hesitating at all over the saints' commands, he went out to the bath after the dream and quickly anointed himself with the substance mentioned. He waited a little after applying it, as people anointed with eye-salves by physicians usually do. Then he opened his eyes again—for he had been sitting with them shut—and suddenly he could see. He brought the white spots down like tears, and beheld this light as it truly is, which he had lost through the physicians' eye-salves. The miracle was extraordinary: though he could now see, he did not know the way out of the bath, since he did not know how he had come in, and so even then he needed someone to lead him, though he himself could see better than his guide [?]. From there he ran to the sanctuary, astonishing those who saw him and rousing them to praise the saints. Now restored, and having praised the martyrs himself, he went off to Pelusium. And we, having crowned them with hymns, let us bring forward the account of another miracle as the occasion for further hymns to them. 48. Concerning Antony the Theban [?]. I can still hear Antony shouting, still sending out great cries, still crying out with all his might—not because of the illness that has fled, but because of the healing he was given. Out of great gratitude he will not allow it to be passed over in silence, but asks that it be ranked with the others we have already written about and be counted as one among their accounts. Commending his outcry, let us quickly grant his request. Antony was a Theban, and a citizen of the city of Antinoe [?].

He had a very grave illness which, to this day, has not become clear to the sons of physicians, nor to anyone else, nor even to the very man who was sick and suffering. It remained unknown to people both after it ceased and while it lasted. The sick man only cried out that his bowels were being terribly gnawed, as if eaten by worms, though he did not know the cause or understand the affliction at all. Even the wiser physicians, who had a reputation for knowledge and saw him very often on their rounds, judged the disease to be one thing and then another. Now they called it this, now that; sometimes they said the cause was this, [?] now that. What pleased them all today, pronounced with a haughty brow, was spat upon tomorrow with still haughtier conceit, and overturned by them again, as they insisted it was something else and not what they had said yesterday. When the sick man had gone through long experience of many such treatments and found no change in his affliction, but was always in the same pains, he concluded that the only remedy for his ills was to go to the martyrs Cyrus and John. "For if these," he said, "do not deliver me from this distress, since they can search out hidden things and are able to know what is unseen by other people, no one else will be able to save me, not having received such grace from God." Fortified with this faith in the saints, he came to them. He lived in their shrine for two years, and suffered no slackening of his faith in the martyrs, though so long a time might well have produced it in him, while he was, as we said, ceaselessly in pain and crying out, and never stopping at all, by night or by the following day. Then he suddenly received his health. He was not told to do anything, as all the sick are who wait in the church on account of their afflictions, nor did he put anything into his stomach or bring anything up through his mouth. He only said that after his healing he saw the saints, saying: "Behold, we have delivered you from your afflictions, and you will no longer suffer what you have endured until now. Get up, then, and go back to your homeland, no longer fearing this illness. When you are there, plant a vine in our name, and we will tend it with you, and together we will provide it with the protection it needs. We will gather its grapes in common, and come to the winepress and tread them together. And you, sharing the wine with us, take your own portion and spend it as you wish; but bring our share here every year to this house of ours, and distribute it among the sick brothers in it." This is what the martyrs said, and they did not only say it, but having said it they did it. For Antony went up into the Thebaid and quickly planted the vine as he had been told, and he found the saints his helpers in all they had promised: planting with him, harvesting with him, pressing the grapes with him, and above all blessing it abundantly, protecting it, and making everything pleasant and easy. In that very year he dug, he pla-

[?]… he harvested the grapes, he trod them [?], and he brought the saints' share down to their venerable shrine and distributed it to those there who were gripped by various diseases and were waiting for their help. He went on doing this for many years, until he recently departed this present life. So Antony fell ill in an unknown way, had an unknown disease, and received an unknown cure. There was also a woman from Lirnai [?], the name of the village in Egypt she came from (her acquaintances called her Anastus [?]). She was suffering from a similar affliction. She knew neither what the disease was nor what caused it, and since she could get neither healing nor any understanding of her ailment from a physician, she came to the martyrs, believing that they are able to find a way out of every difficulty. She differed from Antony not only in her sex, which is obvious, but also in the disease itself. That is why we have both placed the two together, because their afflictions were alike, and also treated each one separately, to show how the illnesses differed. He suspected that his insides were being eaten away, while she felt something like a leaden weight. He was cured in two years, while she escaped the disease in three. He received his cure invisibly, while she visibly passed the cause of her pains. It was a stone the size of a large egg, which amazed everyone who saw it. She also [hung it?] at the saints' tomb, to be seen for many years as a memorial of the miracle and for the praise of those who had worked it. So let us too bring our account of them to a close and praise the saints for what they gave to each of the two, the knowledge, or rather the healing, and for their care of those who take refuge with them. For they care not only for healing diseases but also see to food and shelter. Let us now proclaim in words the gift of another healing. 49. About Piamoth and George, who kept for themselves the offerings brought to the saints. Piamoth the Egyptian experienced both the martyrs' scourge and their gift, and he ought to be ranked with those we set out among the miracles written for the Alexandrians, when we wrote about the saints' severity and [?]. But since his nation kept him from being placed there, he has come at the proper time to show through himself the martyrs' power. He shows that they can punish not only the Alexandrians, their neighbours, when they behave outrageously toward them (for [?] demonstrated this), but also those who live far away, just as they grant healings not only to those nearby but also to those far off. Piamoth was an Atherophagus, an "athera-eater". This nation is clearly harsh and barbarous and differs in no way from wild beasts. They say the name fits them, since they are always eating athera. What they call athera is bread boiled in pots with [?]. George [came from?] [?]

Metelis, near the city of Sais. These men were coming from different places to venerate the martyrs. Two different women, also from different places, gave them different offerings to bring to the saints. One gave Piamoth two thirds of a gold coin, and the other gave George one [?]. The women said they had intended to bring these themselves, but could not offer them in person because some necessity prevented the journey. So they used these men as their servants and told them: "When you go, bring these to the saints on our behalf, for they are a debt and not a gift." The men accepted the women's requests and took what was given along with them. They did not do it out of brotherly love or honour for the martyrs; had they done it out of reverence for the martyrs and love for one another, they would have been blessed. They did it because they were thieves (for it is fitting to say of them too what the divine John says), and they expected the gift to be a little profit of their own. And that is what they made of it, thinking the saints would not know. But truly both wretches struck a bad bargain. For paltry gains and the smallest sums they reaped great torments and suffered no moderate punishments, so that they might become instructors and teachers of all the Egyptians, teaching them to revere the saints as they ought and not to scorn their power. For they took the women's money, went to pray, spent it on the road, and went home again without having delivered any of what they had brought to Cyrus and John the martyrs. The saints knew this, but they were patient and waited for them to repent, imitating Christ the Lord in his love for mankind in this too. But when they saw the men reach home and come back to themselves without coming back to repentance, they punished both as they deserved. They bound Piamoth's feet and hands and scourged his whole body with the pains of paralysis. As for George, they allowed a most wicked demon to invade him, since he had devoured the offering along with Piamoth. The wretches quickly recognized who had afflicted them and openly confessed their faults to everyone in their households. They also asked the women who had given them the offerings not to assail them with curses. Then they came to the saints, contrary to anything they had expected, and begged to be pardoned for the wrongs they had done them, promising to behave themselves from then on. The martyrs punished Piamoth for six months and then released him from his torments. We will also tell how he was released, for it is worth telling. Piamoth was sleeping on his bedding, and in a vision he seemed to see the saints come to him and say, "Do you want to be healed and escape the torment of this disease?" He answered them, "Very much." "If you want to be rid of this scourge," they said, "bring the two

thirds of a gold coin that you took and did not bring, and you will quickly receive healing." He turned to his acquaintances, since he neither had the coins to give nor could he come bringing them, and told them the dream. They gave him the money in question as a loan. The sick man took it and offered it to the martyrs, and he was freed from the blows. He had been taught their extraordinary power, and he swore never again to dare such things. But the martyrs did not yet judge George worthy to be freed from the evil demon. Since they had him with them, being disciplined by means of it, they ordered him to sweep their church twice a day. So, looking down [?] and imitating the very act of taking that he had committed, he would remember his fault and repent of having acted so very wickedly. We too, having come to know the power of these saints through these events, should win their favour by good works. And having praised them again for these things, let us from now on remember their benefactions rather than their threats. 50. About Nonnus, who had a half-withered foot. The preceding wonder taught us no small lesson about the saints' strength. It showed how severe they are and how loving toward mankind, how they discipline offenders with reason and heal again those who turn toward repentance. Even so, it was not fitting for the account of the wonders the martyrs worked for Egyptians and Libyans to end with it. The account began with benefaction and sympathy toward those who suffer, and it should not end with punishment and the pursuit of faults. Just as it began with love for mankind and grace, so it should come to rest at its end in love for mankind, harmoniously, like the line of a circle, which starts its motion from a point and comes back to the same point to find its rest. So let it have a beginning and an end that show love for mankind. In this way the middle too, held within such limits, will surely be judged to show love for mankind [and whatever does not seem so will be thought to seem so to us because of our fleshly mind]. So let us pass over that story, since it seems grievous, and with this one let us bring to a close what we have written for the Egyptians and Libyans. Then, with God and the martyrs, let us begin the miracles done for foreigners. We thought it good to begin with Egyptians and end with Libyans and come to rest among them. That way, one group receives the beginning of the account and the other its end, and they will not quarrel with each other as though the writing belonged to the Libyans rather than the Egyptians, or to the Egyptians rather than the Libyans. Instead they will consider it common to both, as befits a common peace among themselves…

So let Nonnus come forward into our midst. He completes the account in his own person and puts an end to the miracles written for the Egyptians and Libyans, since he was from Libya. He came from Nikiou, the city there, and was one of those known for their wealth. He was also distinguished by a family of note in that region. This Nonnus, who had excelled in many things, also stood out for a terrible bodily affliction. This was his

illness: a weakness of the right foot. It was half-withered, no different from a piece of wood, and deprived of everything a foot does. It could do nothing to benefit the rest of the body and in fact did it the greatest harm. Not only did it fail to carry what its Maker had assigned it to carry, but it simply hung uselessly from the body, imitating, to put it in an image, a withered branch hanging from a tree. Yet perhaps it was even worse than that for the body. The branch perhaps does no harm to the tree that bears it but itself stays as it is [?]. The tree is seen to flourish in its other branches and its trunk. It is adorned with leaves in season, laden with fruit if it is that kind of tree, draws the farmer to come to it, and shares in his blessing, to speak with the blessed Paul, and is harmed in no way by the withered branch. Here, though, the foot was not only deprived of its own function but forced the whole body to share its pain. If only it had been merely useless and had not made the whole body useless too! It had something still worse about it. Since it suffered itself and was gripped by pains, it made every limb of the body suffer with it. For he spoke truly who said that all the members of the body suffer with the member that suffers, just as they naturally share the glory when one is glorified. This, then, was Nonnus's illness. It began [?] and was not obvious to everyone, and a multitude of physicians stood against it, above all those eminent in words, who often grant the sick nothing but words and put none of them into action. The further it advanced, the weaker it saw its opponents become. As much as it displayed its growth, so much did they shrink little by little. At last it reached its full extent and became known for what it was, and it tyrannized the man without fear, since it no longer had any opponent among men. The sick man, seeing its victory and their defeat, ran to the martyrs Cyrus and John as to invincible physicians, able to do everything they wish to do. For God had given them such power that they could prevail against every illness. And so the man, of the

knowledge in which he had put his faith even before experiencing it. And [appearing?] to him, they told him to rub his foot with the oil that gives off the unsleeping light beside their coffin, or with the wax salve that has power against every disease. He did this after the martyrs had appeared to him, and soon the foot was like the other one. On receiving the gift of healing, he entirely forgot the very grievous illness that had come before it. He offered praise to the saints in a loud voice and prayed to have their help always dwelling with him, and he left the shrine rejoicing and leaping. Now that we have reached the end of these miracles told for the Egyptians and Libyans, of which there are fifteen,
let us praise the martyrs who healed them. And calling on them to help us, let us go on again to a divine narration of the miracles worked for the other nations.

BEGINNING OF THE MIRACLES WRITTEN FOR FOREIGNERS. 51. About George the priest, who suffered from a cataract. It is time now to add to this collection of praises a few of the things the martyrs have done for foreigners: Romans, I mean, and Galatians and Cilicians, Asians, Islanders and Phoenicians, Byzantines, Bithynians and Ethiopians, Thracians, Medes and Arabs, Palestinians, Syrians and Elamites, and all the nations under heaven. For I can no longer bear their complaints and their constant pestering. "The saints," they say, "distribute healing to all without partiality and spread the gifts of their goodness equally over all, yet you have placed us last in their praises." They are hinting that we take them to be perhaps more sluggish, more ungrateful, and slower to sing songs of thanks for the benefits they have received. "And yet we would deserve to be put first," they say. "We endure much toil and the labour of long journeys. We scorn the waves of the sea and put up with harsh dangers. We cross countless distances and come from the ends of the earth to the martyrs out of longing for them, and we proclaim everywhere the miracles of Cyrus and John and their ineffable, God-given power." We admire their zeal and marvel at their eagerness for the saints' praises, and we will briefly heal their grief by granting them a defence and clearing ourselves of the charge against us. We have already said that, for the sake of faith, we wrote first the miracles that shone among the people of the country before those done for foreigners, and we have already woven a defence on this point. We also said that we did not place you last as ungrateful, nor them first as more grateful. In these matters, placing one first or writing another second neither harmed the second nor showed that the one who received first place was better. The Lord of the vineyard, when he paid the workers their wages, did not consider those who had worked first more honourable than the last. Nor, when he began paying from the last, did he blame those who had come earlier, except that they were filled with envy, grumbled, and wanted to receive more than had been decreed.

But I am even afraid that the Alexandrians may look askance at us, as if insulted by what you think is an advantage. After all, helmsmen, who are more honoured than the sailors, sit at the very stern of the triremes, charioteers sit behind the horses, and those

who long to be first are bidden by all means to become last. The last become first, and the first in turn become last. And the less honourable members, those that seem unpresentable, receive greater honour. So accept the reason why those miracles were written first and learn that it was necessary. Do not fight over first place, and do not think you have been ranked after them. Otherwise, by dividing into factions and schisms, you would cut up this beloved encomium of the saints and dim the brightness of their praise. Rather, rejoice and rejoice with one another. Make the honours of others your own and give your own as gifts. And, greatest and most blessed of all, rejoice that you have been found worthy to contribute to the praise of such glorious saints. Come, then, let us too [set forth] the miracles that increase their praises [a word is missing here]. And may you not seem to me inferior to the former, outdone by the abundance of their miracles.
