I seem to hear the aged George calling out this from the midst. He is the leader of their company and is eager to lead also in proclaiming the miracles. He has received precedence through his rank, his years and his wonderful age, and he is rightly the leader. Urged on, he will lead the others, since he is still alive and in the body and proclaims to everyone with his own mouth the wonder the saints worked on him. None of those who have come to the shrine of Cyrus and John in these sixty-seven years is unaware of him. They all know, I think, that for so many years [?] he has been serving Christ and the martyrs. He has passed through all the ranks of the clergy and for some time led the church admirably. George was a Cilician, a citizen of no obscure city. He boasted of Tarsus as his mother city and called Paul his advocate, proud of both his fellow citizen and his city, and with good reason. While still a child and living as a boy, this George left his homeland with his parents. The purpose and occasion of the journey was to venerate Saint Menas in Mareotis. They reached Alexandria and paid this veneration to the martyr. But winter prevented their return, and after a short time the boy's father died and the boy was left an orphan. The orphanhood was followed by the loss of his sight, caused by a cataract.

Every physician gave way before the affliction and openly admitted defeat. Then the martyrs Cyrus and John were at once named as the healers of this affliction. George went to them and did not put to shame those who had said so, for he shed the cataract and recovered sweet sight. This, they say, was the remedy that restored his health. The martyrs, craftsmen of [health?], told him to grate cheese from Bithynia, mix it with wax salve, and simply put it on his eyes.

…the martyrs, craftsmen [?], prescribed. When he had carried out the saints' command, all the fluid in his eyes immediately drained down. His pupils remained clean and clear, [freed] from that thick matter, and took in the light unhindered. From then on they worked as they had before the affliction. This, then, is said to be the wonder worked on him. As for the [other?] gifts the saints bestowed on him, it would take long to tell them one by one. They would need a separate work and more time than ought now to be given them, since every story should receive an equal share. But so that we do not leave them unwritten and unremembered for this reason, and seem to wrong the listener, I will mention one or two, and I will cut them as short as I can. They took him in when he was at once a stranger and blind, an orphan, a wanderer and poor, and they quickly healed all of these. The loss of his homeland they healed by making him their own. His blindness they healed by bringing light to his eyes. His orphanhood they healed by becoming his fathers. They adopted the stranger as their own. His poverty in both, soul and body I mean, they turned to wealth, at least in so far as he was willing to be rich in body. They raised him in their sanctuary like Samuel of old and made him a possessor of virtue. Little by little they advanced him through the clergy, in step with his age. And they judged him worthy to manage their affairs once he was able to do it. Twice they rescued him from death and granted him added years of life. There was a plague, and those who fell sick at that time died before the disease could even be diagnosed. George too fell ill, and when the bounds of his life were reached, he departed this present life. He saw angels take him and lead him away, and the martyrs Cyrus and John meet them and plead for the priest to be given to them. The powers said they could not do this, since they duly serve the divine decree. They told the martyrs to wait [?] and make their supplication to God, and to await a second command from him. On receiving this answer, the martyrs turned to supplication. They bent their knees before God and begged that their servant be given to them. As they did so, a voice came down from heaven ordering that the priest be given to the martyrs and fixing for him twenty more years in the flesh. And so this remarkable man escaped death at that time and received five more years of life than Hezekiah did, through the zeal of the martyrs and divine [?]

…by a word. When he had completed the twenty years of life, he died once more and left this present life, following the angels who had taken him. But again he met the martyrs, and again, as before, he was sent back, and was granted a further span of life with no limit set to it. Having died a second time and escaped death a second time, he stands as proof of the saints' boldness before God, and as an image of their power and grace. Let us ask this marvellous elder to intercede with the saints for us, and beg him to make them our patrons too, and then let us go on to the account of another miracle.

52. About Zosimus the chief physician, who had paralysis.

There once came a man from Byzantium named Zosimus, a chief physician by profession and a paralytic by affliction. Where his affliction came from we cannot say, except that he was paralysed and bore the marks of paralysis. He carried it not in one limb but in all of them, and in the whole body that holds them together. Two people were not enough to carry him; he needed more. When he was laid on a bed he could not turn himself at all, but needed someone else to turn him. He could not take hold of food with his own hands and eat it, but another person stood beside him and fed him. So he was shown up as no physician at all, and he exposed the weakness of his art: he promised healing to others but could not help himself, and instead called on the martyrs to help him. So Zosimus too came to the true physicians. He bore witness to the power they have to ward off evil, begged to obtain it, obtained it by begging, and having obtained it enjoyed good health. After he had prayed to the saints for only three days, he was told to go to the bath and wash his body in the hot waters. He obeyed those who gave the command, for they were the most divine martyrs, and went to the bath. Once he was inside the hot rooms, the men carrying him laid him on a bench. Having set Zosimus down, his bearers left the hot rooms by God's providence, giving as their reason for going out that they were fetching what was needed. When they had gone out, Cyrus the martyr stood beside the sick man in the habit of a monk. This was not in a dream, as he appears to most people, but while Zosimus was awake, as it truly happened and is here recorded. Having appeared, he told the sick man to get up and plunge into the hot waters. Zosimus was not alarmed at the sight and did not take in how extraordinary it was at all. The martyr had arranged this so that his mind would not suffer any harm from fear. He answered that he could not do it. But the martyr who had appeared urged him again to do it, to make his way little by little to the steps into the pool, and to go down and bathe. Then he forced himself to do what he was told, for the one speaking breathed strength into him. Rolling along on hands and feet, dragging himself like a snake, he barely reached the steps. When he had managed to go down into the waters, he came up again in a way he had never hoped.

For as he went down, the disease was buried with him, but as he came up it did not come up with him at all. Then the descent into the hot water imitated the pool at the Sheep Gate. It did not receive an angel coming down to bathe and stir the water by his descent; instead it saw Cyrus the martyr and received his kindly command. So, having received Zosimus paralysed, it gave him back strong to the one who had sent him; having received the sick man unable to move, it released him healthy and nimble. As he went down into the waters he saw the saint standing beside him, but when he came up out of the warm and kindly water he could no longer see the physician. Even after his healing Zosimus was not free of sorrow. He rejoiced that he had cast off the disease and gained his health, but he was distressed that he could not see the one who had given it to him. Rejoicing and grieving at once, he ran out of the hot rooms on his own feet, praising God and the martyr who had healed him. With him all who saw it, his own household and strangers alike, raised a single song of praise, extolling Christ's kindness and the martyrs' manifest visitation. They took over the bath as though it were the church; they went in to bathe and to pray, treating it as both church and bath, and reaping a double blessing there.

53. About the boy from Eleutheropolis.

Let this small and very modest bath be followed by the great and spacious sea, the warm and very sweet stream by the salty and very cold one, Constantinople by Eleutheropolis, and Zosimus by Procopius, or rather by Procopius's slave Theodore. Let them too add to the praise of the saints and become part of their encomia. Procopius lived in Eleutheropolis, which is a city of Palestine, and was known as one of its prominent men. He owned a slave named Theodore. Procopius had an affliction that was hard to cure, an overgrowth of flesh in the nose, which none of the physicians had been able to remove. So he took Theodore with him to Alexandria, intending to approach Cyrus and John and receive from them the healing he longed for so much. He did not fail in his approach, but obtained what he wanted, though only after a long time, and once he had obtained it he had relief. The remedy was pepper roasted in a frying pan and put into the nose. While Procopius was waiting patiently on the martyrs, Theodore, being young, went down to the sea quite often and delighted in its waves. He eagerly dived and swam in them. But one day, as he was swimming and playing and wrestling energetically with the waves, a sea dog rushed at him, bit him on the heel, and dragged him out into the deep. Having dragged him some distance, it heaped sand over him [?], thinking its prey was dead and storing it away as a meal ready to hand. But he was not yet dead, even though he had been hidden in the storehouse of Hades, for he found in the waters a helper in Cyrus and John.

For as he was being dragged, Theodore called on the martyr, and as he lay under the sand he kept Cyrus and John in his mind. Since they were close to him, he remembered them and begged them to help him out of the deep and rescue him from the surge that held him down in the depths. Theodore cried out, and the martyrs heard his plea from heaven. They seized the buried man by the hair, told him not to cry out, carried him out of the water and set him on land, showing Theodore, not yet breathing, to be a new Jonah. Soon afterward they granted him breath and brought him to feel the wound the dog had inflicted with its bite. For it had gripped his heel in its teeth and dragged the man by it, and had split his whole sole right up to the toes. The sole was hanging like a leaf from a tree and swinging this way and that, but they joined it back on with a wax salve. In the briefest moment they granted him his foot, his life, and an unexpected escape from the beast. Let us, together with him, for he is still living in this life, and with those who were present then and those who are hearing it now, sing the praises of those who saved him and ask them to come just as swiftly to our aid in dangers. Then let us make another wonder the occasion for further praise.

54. About Isidore, who suffered from epilepsy.

Let Damascus too take pride in the martyrs' gifts, Damascus which received Paul when he could not see, gave hospitality to the persecutor and made him a herald, hid him when men sought to kill him, and helped him escape by night through a window in a basket. And let it count its share in the saints' grace as more splendid than its earlier prosperity. For this metropolis of Coele-Syria once reigned as the leader of the whole East, having Ninus as its king, and the famous Semiramis. Both of them reigned there, surrounded the city with walls, and sent out colonies from it into Asia and into Arabia, the land called Happy. Damascus remained a royal city until Alexander of Macedon killed Darius, took his treasures from it, and brought down its royal power along with him. These things about Damascus we have learned from secular sources, and we have also seen the tombs of many kings in it. From the divinely inspired Scripture, too, we know that it was a royal city, having as its kings the son of Hadad, Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Hazael and Rezin. More than all these, it has enjoyed the gifts of Cyrus and John, and adding them to its boasts about Paul it glories in these exultations. Dionysius was a Damascene, one of the illustrious men in office, sprung from a family that had always been distinguished. Its origin and root was Nicholas the philosopher, the tutor of Herod and teacher of the children of Antony and Cleopatra. From him twelve Nicholases flourished in succession, priding themselves on philosophy; they brought lustre to the family and raised it to great glory and splendour…

Descended from these, the illustrious Dionysius had a son named Isidore, the heir of the family. While Isidore was a youth and made constant use of the bath, an evil demon attacked him. He fell to the ground and lay there, and those who were bringing him up picked him up and carried him out of the hot rooms. They took what he had suffered from the demon's assault to be something else [?]: they judged the affliction to be a fainting fit, such as often happens to many people in baths, and not the work of evil spirits. But then he suffered the same harm even without a bath, and there was no longer any pretext that could hide the affliction. They recognized the boy's affliction and reported that these attacks were the wrongdoing of demons. Then they realized that the first change that had come over him in the bath had been of the same kind. When his parents learned this, they were grieved and distressed beyond measure, for Isidore was their only male child and all the family's hopes rested on him. So they devoted every effort to the boy's treatment and showed him to reputable physicians, thinking that those continual epileptic fits and long bouts of heaviness in the head came from an excess of melancholic humours. He suffered from both, as we have learned, the first more frequently, the second more intensely and for longer. But they heard one verdict from all of them: the disease could not be overcome by human means, because its cause was an evil spirit and not melancholic humour. Then the boy's father Dionysius, seeing how powerless the followers of Hippocrates were, sent him with his mother to Cyrus and John, just as the king of Damascus once sent Naaman the Syrian to Elisha. The martyrs received them when they came and soon sent them away healed. They appeared to the boy's mother as she slept and told her to anoint him herself from his hair to his nails with pig fat. In this they were acting with a wise purpose, eager to heal her soul as well. For it was rumoured that Julia, as she was called, had been harmed in her faith and was leaning toward pagan error, and that this was why she refused to eat pork, on account of the death of Adonis. Whether these reports were true or the rumours false, God knows, and so do the martyrs who gave this command. That she refused pork was plain and beyond dispute, but why she did not eat it none of those closest to her knew. In any case, the boy's illness compelled her to do as she was told. She smeared him with the fat she had been shown, anointing him while he was visibly ill and the signs of his illness were plain…

The demon that troubled and afflicted him did not wait for the anointing to be finished [?], but fled as though it were being whipped by divine power. For Cyrus and John were invisibly whipping it, accustomed as they are to rout demons by divine power. So from that time on, for as long as

Isidore remained in this life, demons could not come near him, and [?] he received the reward of his flight for refuge to the martyrs Cyrus and John. I believe that his mother too benefited from the miracle, if she really had been harmed in her faith, unless she was someone utterly impious and foolish. Here too let us praise God and the martyrs who worked the miracle, and then arm our tongue for another miracle, making the workers of miracles its helpers.

55. About Theodore of Cyprus, who was left crippled in the feet by sorcery.

Cyprus lies near Phoenicia, with the Parthenian Sea between them. Let us sail across it in our minds, put in at the island from Phoenicia, find Theodore of Lapithus, learn his story accurately, and write it down to the praise of those who did these things. Theodore was a physician, well regarded in his art and therefore famous. Through sorcery he became unable to move. Not knowing the cause of his affliction, he set about treating himself, doing what he thought would cure him, the same things he had applied with success to others suffering, not from sorcery, but from sluggish limbs. But when he had tried everything and could not grant himself release from the disease, he recognized the weakness of his art and took refuge with Cyrus and John, who were able to drive the disease away and grant the sick man healing. After he came, the martyrs appeared to him in his sleep, and once they had appeared they drove off the affliction at once. They told him to take a pig's lung, roast it over hot coals, grind it up with wine once roasted, and anoint himself with it. But since it is not the saints' way to give a grace that is incomplete, they did not stop at healing Theodore with these remedies. They also revealed who had bewitched him, dealt with the instruments of the sorcery, and repaid the perpetrator as he deserved. For when they told Theodore to prepare the remedy, they added this to their command: "Send one of your servants to Lapithus and tell him to dig in front of your bedroom, by the doorway. There he will find the evil work of the man who did this, hidden out of sight under the threshold. Once it is brought to light, it will immediately destroy the one who made it." Theodore sent someone to the place named, as he had been told, and found the cause of his illness. As soon as it came to light, the evildoer vanished at once, for death carried him off immediately, and by the martyrs' power Theodore was avenged. The man was a Jew, and he was not free of a reputation for such things. So he reaped the fruit of his own deeds, receiving sheaves to match what he had sown. Let us marvel at the might of the saints, praise them as best we can, and then recount in writing other deeds of theirs of no less force and power.

56. About George of Cyprus, whose feet were weakened by the action of a demon.

While we are still lingering on Cyprus, let us not overlook George because he is poor and in the grip of poverty. The martyrs Cyrus and John did not overlook him either; as lovers of the poor they took him up and judged him worthy of healing, as true friends of the needy. George was a farmer, and he lived in a village close to Nemesus. The village was called Phaua and lay fifty stades from the city and three and a half stades from the sea. This is how George's feet were weakened. He was inspecting his fields and saw what he thought was a hare, and when he spotted it he gave chase. For this is game that country people love, and it spurs them on to catch it whenever it appears. But for all his chasing he did not catch it, for what he saw was not a hare but an evil, man-hating spirit. When he stopped running, he could no longer move his feet, but stayed motionless after the chase. He had not caught a hare, but he had caught a binding of his feet; such are the gifts of that hare. So George was carried on people's shoulders to the martyrs Cyrus and John, and the family who had raised him laid him at their feet. He spent a long time there, until God and the grace of the saints so willed, and then he was healed in this way. As an invalid he was a burden, and he gave no small trouble to those who worked in the church. He went to the latrines quickly but did not come out of them quickly, so that he was often left to sleep there and, out of habit, lingered sitting there. When the martyrs saw George in this state, they were moved to pity and compassion. One day, when he had fallen asleep in the latrines, they appeared to him in a dream and said, "Get up, go out, and sleep in your own bedding." He woke up, saw no one, and went back to sleep. Again the martyrs stood beside him a second time and gave him the same orders. Again he turned over, again saw no one, and went back to sleep a second time. The saints appeared a third time and told him to walk out of the latrines on his own feet, holding out bread for him to eat. He woke for the third time and did not see the martyrs there, but he found the blessed bread they had given him for his healing. He ate it and was strengthened, and remembering the saints' command he got up from the latrines and went out leaping, leaving his disease behind him there and glorifying the power of the saints. He too is still alive and walks about the martyrs' sanctuary, telling of his disease and his healing alike, and moving his hearers to praise God and to sing of the saints who healed him.

57. About Cyriacus of Rhodes, who was possessed by a demon.

It is not out of place to make mention of Cyriacus of Rhodes as well, to count the islander among the islanders and place the Rhodian alongside the Cypriots. For I suppose that islanders delight in one another more than

they delight in those who are not islanders. Cyriacus of Rhodes, then, had an unclean demon, far harsher than most, savage and man-hating, which surrounded him with many mishaps. It would often have robbed him of this life, had not Christ, the guardian of all things and the sleepless keeper of human nature, rebuked it. For it would not let the man be quiet even for a little while. He would not submit to bonds or yield to iron chains or be held in check by the other devices by which such people are usually restrained. He was fearless and reckless, devoid of reason, bereft of all understanding and a stranger to it. At last he was brought to the martyrs Cyrus and John and was freed of the demon. Little by little they restored his reason and granted him to think as a human being. Having brought the man to this state, they drove out the demon with a most pitiful [?] remedy, wishing perhaps to show the weakness of the Evil One. They told him to take veal and ordered him to burn it on hot coals, and they decreed that he should grind it up with wine and anoint his body with it. Cyriacus did this quickly, and the demon was gone at once. The most wicked demon was not afraid of the remedy; it shuddered at the command of Cyrus and John. It did not return to its dwelling again, but went off in flight to an uninhabited place, crying out [?] its own powerlessness and the power of those who had driven it out. Let us rejoice with the man who was cleansed, glorify the saints who cleansed him, and honour Christ who gave them such power, and then let us begin another miracle.

58. About Peter of Ammada [?], who had scrofula on his neck.

Peter of Charax was a man held in honour, priding himself on his family, his wealth and his good sense. He was a man of note in Third Palestine, of which Charagmata [?] is a city, and his good reputation carried beyond the borders of his homeland, so that he was as well known abroad as at home, known to people not so much by sight as by reputation. This Peter, then, this most excellent man, overflowing with wealth and adorned with family and good sense, fell into a grievous disease. For the lot of human nature does not spare even such people, though they think the advantages we have mentioned set them above their fellows. And the disease was this. You have surely heard of scrofula, and having heard of it you certainly know it and are aware that it is an affliction hard to treat, one that will not obey the rules of physicians, and that it chokes its sufferers savagely. Peter had this on his neck, and having it he was in danger of dying, for such is what scrofula produces. In his danger he could find no one to save him. No physician was able to fight the affliction, or, having fought it, to carry off the victory. Many leapt into the arena, but none won the prize; each was beaten and fled, and by his flight crowned the disease the victor.

The disease had the upper hand for a long time, and the physician who wrestled with it gave up, so Peter came close to death. But the martyrs got there first and rescued him from the hands of Hades. When he was in mortal danger, at his last gasp, he learned of the saints Cyrus and John, who alone could overcome the disease. Without delay he sailed from his homeland, bringing with him a pure faith that was able to win over the martyrs. And so the godlike ones could not bear to see him suffer for more than four days. On that very night they [?] appeared and gave him the remedy for his illness. They told him to [?] and to apply a hot plaster to the scrofulous swellings, and to keep it lying close against his neck for about five hours. Then he was to go to the bath, and once inside in the hot air, to pull the plaster off his neck, and after bathing to use it again, until the affliction was completely healed. When he woke (for he had been given these orders in his sleep), he eagerly carried out the command, and even more eagerly he got rid of the affliction. For he did what the saints had told him: he put the remedy around his neck, then went into the bath, and as he pulled the plaster off his neck he pulled the swellings away with it, and with the swellings [?] the danger that came from them. They say that the swellings that fell from his neck were counted at sixty-seven, and that among them [?] was one that was male and female at once, which had begotten this army hostile to mankind. He put the remedy on his neck again for about three days, and the wounds there were healed too. He offered songs of thanksgiving to the martyrs and went home rejoicing and leaping for joy, having promised [?] to build them a church as his saviours. [?] About Stephen of Aphrodisias, who brought a centipede out of his head. Why should we not also bring forward Stephen from Asia and tell his story to those who love the martyrs? These events are enough, once they become known, both to show the might of the saints and to deepen the devotion of those who love the saints. Stephen was from Asia, from the city of Aphrodisias. He lent gold to some people who [?], handing over the money on trust, as the Saviour commands, and taking nothing as security for himself. He thought that those who took the money were honest, and so he supposed he needed none of the things that force the ungrateful to acknowledge a debt. But they despised his simplicity and were eager to treat what had been given them as a windfall. So they repaid good with evil and went after the man with poison, longing to get him out of the way quickly, so that because the murder could not be traced they might escape justice and [?]

not [?] the loan, for this was what they wanted. Perhaps the wretches also reckoned among themselves that if they escaped the notice of men, they would also escape [?] the sleepless eye of the Lord. So Stephen was poisoned, as I said, and the poisoner aimed at his death. He escaped death by God's protection and will, but he did not wholly escape the harm done by the poison. He fell ill with a hemorrhage, and every day he saw his own death before him. Blood flowed from his belly and his mouth, the amount of it astonished everyone, and it made those who saw him cry out that he would certainly die before the bleeding stopped. So Stephen was in danger every hour, expecting death from the flow of blood, and he could find no physician to drive death away. He sailed to Cyrus the martyr and to John, Cyrus's companion, having learned in secret that they alone, after God, could heal the disease and set him free from his present distress. He came to them and offered his prayers, and he was heard and saved from his dangers. For the saints appeared to him in his sleep and told him to eat leeks that had not been near fire or water. He ate them as he had been told, was freed from the flow of blood, and so recovered his full strength. It was night, and he was standing before the saints' tomb, imploring them for this healing, bending his knees and bowing his forehead to the ground. As he was doing this, now rising, now bowing to the ground, the crown of his head opened in the middle, and out of it leapt a centipede, which fell to the ground: a creature that crawls on [?] feet [so the manuscript], something like a small asp. When it fell out and fled as fast as it could, Stephen stood there astonished. He felt the very middle of his head, where he had sensed the centipede come out, but he found no wound in that place and saw no flow of blood; he felt only a certain moistness and softness of the bones. Having obtained his healing in this way, he still makes those who hear of it marvel and stand amazed, and join him in praising the admirable power of the saints. And we, having here again praised the wonder-working martyrs, let us call to mind another of their wonders. [60]. About Theodore of Byzantium, who had [?]

It is not we who bring Theodore of Byzantium into our narrative; again it is the saints who summon him, just as earlier, when he was suffering, they summoned him to be healed. For they take equal care of everyone on earth: they free from their afflictions those who live near them, and they urge those who live far away to come and gather healing from them, like fragrant flower-buds from a bright and unfading meadow. Theodore too was ill,

and the place of his illness was Byzantium. Its cause was an unquenchable burning in his foot. It inflamed the foot and left not even a small part of it unburned, but changed it entirely into something that no longer looked like a foot. Masters of medicine, leading men and the brilliant flower of the art, came running in with assistants and young pupils, eager to quench that fiery disease, but they proved too weak to put it out. When a fire has gained strength, whatever is brought to put it out becomes fuel and flame that cannot be calmed, because everything thrown on it is at once changed into the nature of fire. So it was here: the inflammation they faced was fierce, and everything the physicians applied to stop it only made the disease worse and the burning greater, and the affliction very nearly burned up his whole body, feeding on it like fire. But the martyrs, who love mankind, are present everywhere and know everything. They saw the disease and pitied the man, and wishing to grant him healing, they used dreams to urge John the deacon to tell him to come to them and receive his cure. We mentioned this John earlier, when we were writing up the miracle of the girl who fell. He too came from Byzantium and knew the man. Theodore received John's letter and trusted those who had ordered it written (for the deacon did not know whether Theodore was gripped by such an affliction). At once he boarded a ship and reached the saints' shrine, carrying the letter written at their command as an unfailing pledge of his recovery. When those who had summoned him saw that he had come in obedience to their summons, they healed him and quickly sent him away, granting him the speed of the cure as a reward for his faith in them. The healing took only a short time. The remedy for the disease, which put out that fire, was clay dissolved in water and smeared on: the clay with which the Egyptians who make Cnidian wine seal the mouths of the Cnidian jars. The all-praised martyrs appeared to him in a dream and told him to do this. So Theodore, having been healed just as the letter promised, sang a song of thanksgiving and sailed back to Byzantium. And we, for the sake of this miracle and of the summons that came before it, have praised those who summoned him and worked the miracle; now let us sail on to the story of another miracle. 61. About Philemon of Makrokome, who suffered in his liver and had a fistula. Let us look at Philemon the deacon, learn about his double disease and see his twofold healing. For the man is here, having come to us in great haste from Phoenicia, from Makra Kome, the village built there. He is present, then, in this account, showing us his diseases and the remedies that drove the diseases away,

which he now wants written down and proclaimed everywhere to the praise of the power of Cyrus and John, who put an end to strong and serious diseases with worthless and simple remedies. So let us add these to the preceding accounts as well, admiring him for his devotion to the saints. Philemon was beset by two terrible afflictions that were hard to heal. One was in his liver; it oppressed him constantly and left him looking like death. The second was a fistula that had settled in his neck and made a stream gush out of it. The pains of his liver had their own season and cycle: at certain times they swelled, reached their peak and tormented the man, and at others they eased off, quieted down and left him free of pain. But no time was fixed for the discharges of the fistula, nor did they come and go in cycles; they always poured out pus and troubled the man without ceasing. For this reason he never stopped bothering physicians. Tormented severely by these afflictions, he looked for better physicians, and pursued now these, now those, but he was sent away by both with no benefit. So after he had changed many physicians and found that he could not change his diseases, he came to the martyrs Cyrus and John. With them, through faith, he exchanged his diseases for health, and he never again exchanged them for other physicians. For when the saints receive someone from God but do not wish to free him from his afflictions, not even the whole array of physicians could free him. But let us come to the rest of the story and tell how Philemon was healed, just as we have told of his diseases, for this is the sweet heart of the account. The deacon was asleep on his bed, and the martyrs stood beside him as he slept. One examined his liver, while the other studied the fistula in his neck. One stopped the pains in his liver, and the other dried up the springs of the fistula. When they had finished, they told him as they left to do the following and so obtain complete recovery from both. The one who had stopped the discharges of the fistula ordered him to crush citron leaves and apply them to the affliction. The one who had healed the liver by his touch told him to bring green olives; he directed him to eat some of them and to grind the rest and plaster them over the area of the liver. When the sick man got up after his sleep, he carried out the commands of both saints and reaped the healings of both saints. So the admirable Philemon escaped his diseases and received his cures, and he went away praising those who had given them. And we, praising the martyrs twice over for both cures, let us turn to a promise that is mother and nurse of other hymns. 62. About Rhodope, who had eruptions on her skin. Rhodope stopped my pen as it was running along, hurrying to inscribe other miracles, and kept it from going on to them,

[?] and forced it to write about her first, just as once, when the martyrs passed her by and turned aside to visit other sick people, she dared to make them turn back and visit her along with all the rest. She gained nothing by doing so, though, since death had come before health and cut off the saints' help. So we too, as we write about the saints and describe their kindness and condescension toward everyone, shall imitate them and record her story, and not leave her unremembered. Rhodope was a native of Theoupolis, which presides over the whole East and was named after King Antiochus, and she shone among its foremost citizens in family and wealth. For a long time she lived in Alexandria with her husband John, together with whom she had moved there. He was a teacher of rhetoric [?] and a most faithful disciple of the great Eulogius, the herald of the faith; and he was a fountain of benefit to everyone else, from what he had stored up while he was with the divine Eulogius during his lifetime. While Rhodope, his wife, was living in this city of Alexander, she fell ill with her last illness: carbuncles broke out all over her body. When she got a little better and the carbuncles no longer seemed so fierce, and the physicians thought they were merely lingering in her body, the woman longed to go to the shrine of Cyrus and John, so that by their help and command she might be rid of the carbuncles more quickly. So she came, and while she was sleeping at night she saw the martyrs going around the ranks of the sick, approaching each one in turn, granting healing to each, and directing one to do one thing and another to do another. They began, she says, at the start of the line and healed each in order until they reached her. But when they came to her, they passed her by as if she were not there and left her unvisited, and went on to the one lying after her. They visited this person and prescribed what to do to regain health, and then came to the one after him, and from there to those lying next in turn.

When she saw that the martyrs had passed her by, without looking at her at all or telling her to do anything for her recovery, she spoke to them while they were still near and not far from her: "O servants of Christ the Master, and imitators of his goodness toward us! O protectors of human nature from evil, and physicians of our afflictions given by God! O pursuers of every disease sent by God, and never-failing givers of every healing! It is because of this help you give to all that I too have come in my suffering, not only to see your grace but also to share in it, and with everyone else to enjoy the health that you grant without stint to all who come to

you. Why then have you overlooked me, as if I had sinned against you? Or what command of yours have I [transgressed], that you passed me by without visiting me? Or how have I grieved you in any way, that you have deprived me of your loving gifts? I know of no such offence that I have committed against you. But if I have done any of these things and it lies hidden under the cloak of forgetfulness, tell me, I beg you, and I will correct it at once." When the saints heard these words from Rhodope, they did not scorn her blameless plea. They turned to her and comforted her with words such as these: "We did not pass you by, woman, as one who had offended against us, nor because you had trampled on any of our commands, as you put it. It is because we see that your departure is drawing near: the end of this passing life, the laying aside of your present existence, and the inescapable coming of your falling asleep in Christ. We are not the ones who give or ward off these things; it is Christ, the God and Master and Ruler of all, who holds the helm of life and death. So what should we do for you in this? What medicine of immortality shall we offer you? For what purpose would health be given you, or what use would the treatment be? Who would receive these things from us, or who would enjoy these gifts? For in a very short time you will leave mortal things behind and, falling asleep, will travel the road that everyone travels, the road travelled by apostles and prophets and martyrs, and by Christ himself, the author of life, when he became man, though by rising on the third day he gave us the pledges of the resurrection. So get up and go, and reach your home before the separation of soul from body overtakes you." When they had said this, the saints went away. In the morning she reached the city, and when her husband was surprised at how quickly she had returned, she told him the martyrs' prophecy. Not many days later the disease pressed heavily upon her, and she departed to the Lord, as she had learned from the saints. And we here too, marvelling at those who foretold Rhodope's death, bring her story to a close; let us set out to tell another miracle. 63. About Elpidius, whose face was made to shake by sorcery. Let Elpidius come forward after Rhodope and at once regale the listeners with his story, for it is well able to provide a feast and to nourish the listeners [?] in piety. He had enemies, it seems, who had always lived in wickedness and were workers of lawless deeds, and he fell victim to their sorcery. He did not suffer a spell through food or take poison through drink; instead he was struck without mercy through a demon, a foul and most harmful spirit. His whole face, where he had received the blow, was constantly shaking, and as it shook against his will and violently of itself,

…shook his whole head and neck together. Suffering this, he lay before everyone as a spectacle of pity, moving to compassion those who watched him move. For in part he resembled Cain, through the ceaseless movements of his face: Cain the fratricide, who received perpetual trembling as the wage of his choice. Yet Elpidius was shaken in his countenance worse than Cain, and was worn down beyond measure by the tremors, inasmuch as God punished Cain out of love for mankind, while a demon scourged Elpidius out of hatred for mankind. While Elpidius suffered in this way and was truly pitied by all who saw him, not one of the physicians attempted to help him; indeed, none even dared to look at him at all. For the illness was beyond their art, and the affliction could be cured only by God and by his divine servants, to whom he has granted power to do whatever they wish. Those who were with him heard of the wonders of John and Cyrus, and not only heard of them but knew them clearly, for their country is a neighbor, and they learn the affairs of the Alexandrians no less than the Alexandrians themselves. So they came bringing him, fell down at the saints' tomb, and begged them to help the sick man. The saints had pitied Elpidius even before his arrival, and were not unaware of the demons' plotting. Appearing to him in a dream [?], they prescribed that he do this for the complete healing of the affliction: they ordered water to be brought from the Adyta. The Adyta is a lake five hundred stadia from Alexandria, toward the west and the neighboring lake. They commanded that some of its water be brought, given to the sufferer to drink, and used to wash his face and head. When the saints' prescription had been given, the water came; Elpidius drank, washed his head and [?], and at once the affliction vanished and was gone. The thing was worthy of wonder: unstable water steadied an unstable head and face, and water, ever moving in its flow, made unshaken a neck that was ever shaken. So Elpidius, having found healing in this way and shaken off his disease, departed singing the saints' praises and reached his homeland in good health. Honoring them as they deserve, let us write of another of their feats.

64[?]. On the man with a speech impediment.

It is not right to wrong the mute man, even if he cannot accuse us of wronging him, nor to let him be passed over in silence. For the glorious martyrs did not leave him forever silent either; they made him speak instead of being speechless, and granted him the power to speak well, so that their perfect gift might not fall short of perfection in this. Let us too, then, imitate the saints, and what they once did in deeds, let us now do in words. Let us not make mute again a man who once spoke, by keeping silent about his story. Otherwise he might denounce us to the martyrs and become the accuser of our silence, since he received speech from them and does not want others to be silent or silenced, so that toward those who made him speak he…

[?] …the affliction was curable. [?] Those [?] hearing of the wonders of John and Cyrus, and not only hearing of them but knowing them clearly; for the country is a neighbor [?] …they learn the affairs of the Alexandrians no less than the Alexandrians [?]. They came bringing him, and [?] fell down at the tomb of the saints, begging them [?] to help the sick man. The saints had pitied Elpidius even before [?] his arrival, and were [?] not unaware of the demons' [?]. Appearing in a dream, they healed him, and [?] they prescribed that he do this for the complete healing of the affliction: they ordered water to be brought from the Adyta, which is [?] a lake, the Adyta, [?] five hundred stadia from Alexandria [?], toward the west and the neighboring lake [?]. They commanded that some of its water be brought [?], given to the sufferer [?], and [?] used to wash his face [?] and head. When the saints' [?] prescription had been given, the water came; Elpidius drank, washed his head and face [?], and [the affliction] vanished and was gone [?] …an unstable head and face [?] …the [?] neck that was [ever] shaken. So Elpidius [?] having found healing, and [?] the disease [?], departed singing the saints' praises, and [?] in good health reached [?]; whom we too [?] …let us write [?].

64[?]. On the man with a speech impediment.

[?] It is not right to wrong the mute man, even if he cannot accuse us of wronging him, nor indeed to let [?] …

It is not right to wrong the mute man, even if he cannot accuse us of wronging him, nor to let him be passed over in silence. For the glorious martyrs did not leave him forever silent either; they made him speak instead of being speechless, and granted him the power to speak well, so that their perfect gift might not fall short of perfection in this. Let us too, then, imitate the saints, and what they once did in deeds, let us now do in words. Let us not make mute again a man who once spoke, by keeping silent about his story. Otherwise he might denounce us to the martyrs and become the accuser of our silence, since he received speech from them and does not want others to be silent or silenced, so that toward those who made him able to speak

he might not be judged unfeeling and ungrateful, if he put up with their gifts being kept silent. The mute man was a Phoenician from the city of Tyre, and by this perhaps he refutes the Greeks and their false old wives' tales. For the Greeks tell the myth that Cadmus, coming from there, was the first father of letters and with them brought novelty to an uncultured Greece. From that same city this mute man has now sprung, and he has appeared as a clear refutation of the fiction, which the Greeks kept hidden through ignorance. They did not see that Moses came earlier, and knew nothing at all about the dates of Cadmus. I could set these out as a still greater refutation and make the error plainer to anyone who wishes, but the present purpose does not allow it; it draws me to itself and forces my pen to fulfill it. The mute man was a Tyrian, as I said, and his disease was congenital. It did not befall him at some point from another illness, but was born with him from his very conception. Having this affliction by nature, he never uttered a sweet sound to his parents. He never lisped the name of his mother or babbled the name of his father, things in which parents always delight in their children, even when the lispings and babblings are inarticulate, as the Athenians once delighted in the orators Aeschines and Demosthenes and their eloquent mouthings. When he became a man, his tongue was immovable and did not work together with his other members. Perhaps he would have departed this life in that state, had not certain Christ-loving and humane people, who knew the grace of Cyrus and John and the wonders granted through them to the faithful, felt for him as believers and brought him to the martyrs. When he arrived there, the faith of those who had brought him interceded for him, and his own pitiable state roused the saints to pity, so he obtained a speaking tongue. He did not acquire another tongue, but was freed from the bond on the one he had. It follows that I must certainly tell the remedy by which he escaped the affliction of his tongue. The saints appeared to him as he slept and ordered him to drink water, prescribing this not with words (for he could not hear) but with nods and by pointing to the water. When he woke, he signed for the water to be brought, for he had learned through signs that he should do on rising what he saw while asleep. The water was given to him quickly, and he took it and drank. As soon as he had drunk, he spoke and heard people speaking. He announced the saints' prescription, recounting the dream in clear words and honoring the [?] of those who had appeared to him. Thus the deaf man heard and the mute man uttered speech. He had not tasted the water of Castalia, nor [?], nor drawn from a Caucasian stream that sings the praises of Pythagorean virtue, as the myths of the Greeks declare and the poverty of their writers regarding the truth. Rather, he had the good fortune to fulfill the command of John and Cyrus, who supplied him with what nature had

conceded to them to fashion. Thus the martyrs might be seen to grant healings, and whatever human beings lack for their perfection, from the same source from which they first received their origin in the beginning. Therefore we too, having praised them as far as we are able, and having begged them to give us speech in the opening of our mouth, as they have now given it to this mute man, eagerly press on to the narration of the remaining miracles.

65. On Theodore, the blind and possessed [?] man.

Theodore the Cilician has come to us at the right moment. He too recounts his escape from a double infirmity and wishes to be ranked with the man before him, who escaped the bond of his tongue and his deafness and obtained a double healing for a double illness. Let us receive him kindly, out of goodwill toward the martyrs. Let us grant him our tongue for a little while, lend him our hand, and supply him our pen as he weaves praise for the saints and strives to proclaim their might aloud. Let us begin, then, the story about him, eagerly becoming everything for him: hand, tongue and pen, the writer eager to compose with skill. Theodore was a Cilician from the city of Anazarbus, and he was gripped by two grievous afflictions. One of them was a demon, an especially wicked one, which attacked him rather savagely and was always found ready for anything. For often, as the father of the demoniac said to the Lord in the Gospels, it threw him into fire and into water, wishing to kill and destroy him without mercy. The other was the blindness of his eyes. It did not arise from weakness of nature but was contrived by the working of the demon; it did not come in from bodily disease but took up residence through the savagery of the spirit. So wicked was the demon, and so hateful to mankind in the excess of its rage. Theodore was in this condition. As time went on he hoped for nothing that could save him, and did not expect to escape these afflictions before the release of death. For death is truly rest for a man, as Job, who practiced philosophy in sufferings, declared; it takes away all the hardship of life and the many sufferings and toils of this present existence. Then Cyrus and John were reported to be God-given expellers of demons and true protectors against bodily ailments. Trusting in God and the martyrs, he came to Alexandria and reached the sanctuary of the saints, proclaiming by his deed the unshakable faith he had in them. Christ's servants took him in, freed him from the evils that held him, and made him a worker of a God-loving life. For not long after his arrival they appeared to him, not while he was awake but while he was sleeping on his bedding, and set agreements and commands before him; only then did they judge him worthy of health. The agreements, and the arrangements made through them, required him to lay aside his turbulent life and take up the calm life of a monk. For this is the thrice-longed-for wage they seek from those who are healed: the amendment of their lives. That is why they

receive such people with joy and, once they are healed, send them away at once. This is clear from many other cases, and not least from the present story. For, as I have already said, they came to Theodore and said, "Do you want to be made well, Theodore?" He nodded and said "Yes" with his mouth (how could he not, crushed as he was by such great evil?). The martyrs spoke again: "If you wish to obtain healing and escape the danger of your infirmity, agree with us that once you are saved you will live in the heavenly desert of the divine river Jordan, where Christ the Savior of all was baptized. Settling there, you will show the habit and the ways of a monk, imitating John the Baptist, who made his home there and lived as its citizen. Then God will grant you health through us and redeem you from the punishment of your present dangers." The sufferer quickly agreed and swore to fulfill their command. At once the saints drove out the demon like some rogue slave and runaway, and healed the blindness of his eyes, which the demon had brought in along with itself. They banished the demon by a command and drove off the blindness by applying a wax salve. Theodore, having seen his tormentors flee and reaped health besides, gave thanks as much as he could and was able. He went to the desert, and there he carries out the God-pleasing and venerable command of the saints. As for us, we marvel at the saints and hymn the grace of their divine care [so the manuscript] for mankind. Let us record other wonders of theirs done for us human beings.

66. On Menas the Lycian, who fell ill with dropsy.

Why do we not bring out Menas too, who lies hidden under sand, and make him known to those who do not know him? His story deserves to be written, not to be covered with sand and oblivion. That covering suits the demon of Menuthis, with its rites, altars and precinct. For these, oblivion is beneficial, and for this reason the martyrs brought it about. The sight of them is very harmful to those who see it, and so it is covered with sea sand, which has entirely wiped out its memory and brings benefit to those who no longer see it. Let the Lycian come, then, breaking through the covering of sand, and let him make plain to us the wonder done for him. Let him not wrongly hide under a bed and a bushel what can shine well if it is set on a lampstand. Menas was known to be a Lycian and said that he came from the city of Patara. His affliction was not slight but very great. It was not easily cured but hard and difficult to heal; indeed, it is incurable for today's physicians as far as their art goes, unless God grants them power to fight alongside them. He had fallen into incurable dropsy and had lingered in the illness for a long time. He was in terrible danger, racked by pains in his bowels and suffocated by the swelling of his whole body.

Yet why should I wish to depict the affliction in writing? Its name alone is enough to make it known to everyone. As soon as people hear what it is called, they picture in their minds the magnitude of its pain. While Menas was at the beginning of his illness, he took care to seek treatment. He sent for physicians and was eager to carry out their orders. But when the affliction advanced, and no physician would come when called, knowing that it could not be cured, he longed for death so that he might escape the disease even that way. But since he could not obtain this either, though he longed for it, he was brought to the martyrs Cyrus and John for one of two reasons: either the saints would take pity on him and heal him, or out of compassion they would intercede for his death. And he obtained one of the two, health, I mean, and strength, and escaped the disease that he thought he could not escape without death. Let us also tell how he was healed, for it was elegant and full of the martyrs' grace and power alike. They appeared to the sufferer as he slept and saw exactly what was in his heart: at times, losing heart, he called on death and wished to go down under the earth, while at other times he prayed for health and asked to live if he were made well. So they ordered him to do both, in a way, at once offering him health and giving him to the earth to be buried. "If you wish," they said, "to obtain release from the disease, get up, go out of the precinct, and bury yourself in the nearby sand." When he awoke after this excellent dream, he took burial in sand to be a sign of death rather than of health. Nevertheless, since because of the disease he longed for both death and health, and not unequally, he promptly carried out the prescription. He preferred either one to a painful life: a painless death or a life without disease. So he went out of the precinct and was covered with sand as he had been ordered, and he obtained health and escaped the danger he had expected. For when he was completely buried in the sand, the disease was buried along with him. But when he rose from it after the burial, the illness did not rise with him. He scattered the sand and stood up as if coming forth from the womb, free of affliction. In this way Menas received his health. He raised a hymn of thanksgiving to the martyrs and returned to Lycia rejoicing and leaping for joy. And we, once again praising the saints, shall present another of their wonders.

67. On George, who was possessed and cut his own throat.

Cyprus has brought us another man, George, to tell about, and urges us to join him to the two before. So in the record of the saints' miracles, having supplied a third, Cyprus might make this an occasion for greater pride. We too admire its zeal for honor, its most fitting piety toward the martyrs, and the manifold boast it strives for in these matters, so let us fulfill its requests.

For these requests are welcome to us as well. Let us tell of the power the saints exercised on George's behalf, a power that holds a surpassing wonder and itself portrays their grace. George was a Cypriot, and he had a demon known for its great wickedness. Of many demons it was by far the most wicked, and it strove to do by itself the evils that many commit; the dreadful thing would have counted it a great defeat to seem even slightly gentler than all the others. It was so harsh and hateful to mankind that it treated the man more harshly than other demons treat theirs. It was always falling upon the wretch and crushing him, and for the most part it made him madder than itself. Longing to be rid of it, George came to Alexandria and reached the church of the saints. He settled there, living with the other sick people. But that savage demon was being scourged by the martyrs' hands, and it could no longer bear George's dwelling there, though the martyrs had not ordered it to leave him. So it devised a most wicked scheme, worthy of its own wickedness, contriving for itself an escape from the saints' scourge. It made the bird called the night-raven nest in the roof and sleep and perch up above the place where George's bedding lay. The night-raven sat there, shot its droppings down on him, and ruined all his bedding. When the attendants of the church learned of it, they pitied him for the wrong he was suffering and moved the sick man to another place. But again the bird, as if bound by some compelling agreement, moved along with his bedding. As though it had been put in charge of guarding the bedding and could not leave it, it dropped on it from above again and [?] George along with it with frequent droppings. Once more the doorkeepers took pity on him and moved him to yet another place. The bird did the same and did not fail to follow the move. It did this not of its own accord (that is unthinkable), but because a demon was driving it along. Again and again, or rather many times, those who served in the precinct moved the sick man (they did so ten times), and the bird never stopped following him. At last they stopped, reasoning that its tracking him was the work of a demon. [?] As a result George, finding a knife (evidently by the devil's arrangement), seized it in his misery, brought it to his throat, and inflicted a great wound on himself. First he stabbed his windpipe, then moved the blade this way and that, as though the first blow were not enough to kill him unless the blade, by moving after the wound, made the blow greater. The thrice-wretched man received the wound very deep. He fell to the ground, rolled about and convulsed as slaughtered animals convulse, thinking that he was losing his life, and those present believed he was dying on the spot. When the gatekeepers and those who conduct the service of the saints saw this, they fell into no small fear, a charge against themselves

…and they blamed themselves for not guarding the man, who was driven by an evil demon, against such an attempt. Afraid that they might be in danger themselves, they ran around the neighbouring villages calling for physicians, hoping that someone could stitch up the wound and save the man, who was not yet dead, and with him themselves, since they were in danger along with him. They found only one, at the Heracleion. After many pleas they persuaded him and brought him to the martyrs' shrine. But when he saw that the wound was fatal, he left without attempting anything. He was gripped by great fear and amazed that George, who had dealt himself this [wound], had not yet died, for his breath went out through the wound and came back in through it, and the [?] also made their way out there. The martyrs came by night and gave the steward the treatment in his sleep. It was wine and oil, the treatment by which the Lord saved the man who fell among robbers, pouring wine and oil on his wounds. By the same treatment the imitators of the Saviour rescued George, [?] Christodorus to do this. They also seized a certain doorkeeper named Caloetes and flogged him with a long whip they had made from rope, because he was the one who had brought that petty doctor into their sanctuary. As they flogged him they said: "Do you not know that our house has been established as the infirmary of the whole world? Do you not know that Christ [?] us as physicians for the faithful? Do you not know that we snatched you from the gates of death? Why, then, did you bring into our house another physician, one who himself needs our healing?" When they had given him a thorough beating they let him go, threatening him never to do anything of the kind again. Those who hear this would say that they were right to flog him, if they learned what the saints had done for him. He had been in danger from his lungs and was constantly camped at the gates of Hades, and he could find no hope of recovery from physicians. The martyrs healed him by giving him nothing but [?] to drink. So they flogged him as an ungrateful man who had forgotten this. But they also flogged him because, although he saw so many people being healed and enjoying the all-powerful help of the saints, he tried to bring in another physician, as if they were too weak to save and deliver. In this way George escaped both the madness of the demon and his own murderous attempt. Now that we have praised the saints for this too, let us write about another wonder of their mighty work. 68. Concerning Joannia, who was poisoned out of malice. Beauty has destroyed many, and the bloom of the body has ruined those who fell victim to grievous envy and became casualties of terrible malice. For what is fine and excellent is always envied, and it is destroyed by the eyes of the envious. Those who are beautiful in soul and body suffer this too, unless they have God as the saviour, protector and guardian of their beauty. For if the eyes of the envious can melt solid adamant, which is more precious than the most prized stones and is said to be unbreakable by bronze and iron,

what would a human body not suffer when it lies before the envious for them to work on? When they cannot destroy the object of their envy with the darts of their eyes, they work to destroy it with other instruments. Joannia very nearly suffered this, and would have, had she not found Christ and the martyrs as guardians of her life. Let us set down in writing both the envy and the cure for the harm it caused. The woman came from Hierapolis in Syria. She was beautiful, her parents were nobly born, and she had wealth that added to both. She married into Caesarea in Palestine, and she was sought in marriage not for her family or her money but for her beauty. For in Hierapolis the discussor Theodore, who had been proconsul of Caesarea and was a native of Caesarea, the city once called Strato's Tower, married her for her beauty alone. When she came with him to Caesarea, her husband's sisters envied her out of jealousy, seeing that she was better than they were. In their envy they poisoned Joannia: they put a deadly poison in her cup and handed it to her, and she drank it without knowing. She drank the poison but escaped immediate death, because God ordered her to escape it. Yet with the poison in her stomach she suffered unremitting cramps, as if snakes were eating her intestines. From then on she suffered unbearably and could not find a physician to cure her, though countless physicians came to examine her [?]. She could not eat her usual food or keep down drink. She could not enjoy sleep, or walk upright, or sit as she used to. She spent every hour bent over, clutching her stomach in her arms and groaning with pain. And so, wasting away little by little, she would have died, if some people had not taken pity on her and told her of the powers of Cyrus and John and the wonders they worked. When she heard this and believed what she was told, she went to the city of Alexander, came to the martyrs' church and begged them to restore her health. They imitated God's love for humanity and took pity on her, since she was dying a terrible death. They appeared to her in visions as she slept and offered her the treatment for her ailment. It was lentils: the pulse was to be boiled and eaten, and also applied as a plaster to her suffering stomach in the bath. As soon as she woke from the dream she quickly did what she was told. Her stomach received the lentils inside and out, and at once she vomited up all the poison she had drunk earlier, for her stomach brought it up to the surface. When this happened her pains eased a little. The saints appeared again and granted her complete health. They offered her a pastellos to eat (this is a kind of cake), and they gave her one of the psalms that are sung in their honour, written as if on a slip of paper, and told her to recite it constantly.

She ate the pastellos and was completely restored to health. She sang the hymn, promised the martyrs that she would always sing it, and set off for Palestine and Caesarea. Now that we have praised the champions for this too, let us hurry on to another of their deeds, which deserve all praise. 69. Concerning John the blind man. How long shall we wear out the pen, drive the right hand to write, and rouse the voice to cry out? For the pen is tired, the hand can run no longer, and the voice has weakened with them; it has stopped straining and given up. And yet we learn from the writings of wise Solomon that "A threefold cord will not quickly be broken." These three, though they have one will, are of one mind and have set themselves one aim, to proclaim the miracles of Cyrus and John, have nonetheless been broken. Toil has laid them low, weariness has made them fall, and they have accepted defeat before proclaiming anything worthy of the saints, or even some small part of their marvellous wonders. All they have strength for is to cry out how great their own weakness is. So after forcing themselves to proclaim the present miracle, they will stop at the wonder that follows it, having earnestly begged the saints to grant them pardon and forgiveness for their rash and very great daring.

But for now let us set these things aside, tell John's story as well as we can, and make it known to those who hear. He was a Roman, not from some city subject to the Romans, but from Rome itself, which first ruled over them; that was his homeland and his city. For Rome truly wished to add this too to her own splendour: to adorn herself with the miracles of Cyrus and John as with something more divine, since she knew that these are far more splendid than crowns, sceptres and the purple. Those things have their origin in the earth and dissolve back into the earth. But the gifts of the martyrs come down from heaven above and are born of divine power, and they do not dissolve into the earth. So let us not begrudge Rome her longing: she has the glory of earthly things and reaches out for the glory of heavenly things as well. Let us call John from Rome into our midst and through him fulfil her desire. He was first afflicted with an eye complaint, and because of it he kept pestering physicians. He longed to be rid of the ailment and to recover the health he had before it, as every sick person does. But he could not achieve this, though he changed physicians many times. Always going after the better one, he made the disease worse. By embracing the physician who was most looked up to, he himself gradually lost the power to look. In the end, by going to the illustrious and brilliant, he was rendered utterly dim and lightless. And

perhaps even then he would not have escaped the physicians' hands, if his emptied purse had not revealed the blindness of his eyes. For along with the light of his eyes the gleam of his purse also went out. Since the purse was incurably sick and could take in no more flow, he learned that he too was incurably sick. As long as the purse was plump, he kept hearing from the physicians: "Take heart, and do not grieve or worry at all, for we hope that you will soon see well." But when the purse had been emptied (for it too had drained away along with his eyes), he suffered with it the same loss that he had already suffered in his eyes. "Go away," he was told by them. "Let no mortal deceive you by saying that you will see the sun. Your pupils have dissolved and your eyelids have [?] each other. Make sure that no physician eats up your money, making you hopeful with words alone when he cannot make your eyes sound." Once John had received these verdicts he could no longer trouble the physicians, not only because he had learned that he would never see again, but also because he had no money left with which to pay court to physicians. In this state he looked for one more powerful than physicians, one with a physician's knowledge who needed no money and who would even feed the sick man. He sought this more earnestly and found it, as the saving prophecy says, and when he knocked harder he found the door opened. For he learned that Cyrus and John were not far away, in Alexandria, just such as he wished and longed to find, more powerful than his diseases. When he learned this, or rather when he was convinced of it, since he had already heard of it by report, he quickly went to the saints. He set himself an unshakable rule: he would not enter the venerable sanctuary unless he first saw the light and was rid of the blindness of his eyes. And after no small ordeal he kept his rule, often saying "I have sworn and confirmed it," and crying out with the Psalmist, "What goes out from my lips I will not break." For he sat in front of the church door, lay there, ate there and slept there. In summer he was scorched, in winter frozen. At times he was drenched by heavy rains, at times burned by fierce rays, with the sun over his head scorching him by day and the moon sapping his strength by night. He went on like this for eight years in the open air, without dishonouring his own decision, and without any intention of dishonouring it by [?] leaving that place, even if he were to remain blind until death. So all who knew him judged him worthy of praise for so steadfast a resolve and so firm a decision, and the martyrs judged him worthy of complete healing. They stood beside him at night as he slept, gave him health and granted him sight. With words

SOPHRONIUS, PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM. they commanded it, they touched his eyes, and they did not tell him to use any medicines. How, or in what way, they opened and cleansed his eyes we did not learn. For when he got up from his bed after his sleep, at the very middle of the night, he took some red ochre (a colour like flame) and wrote these words on the wall in front of the gate of the sanctuary, where he had been lying: "I, John, from the city of Rome, who was blind for eight years, recovered my sight here, by waiting patiently through the power of Saints Cyrus and John." When he had inscribed this in the colour, he went into the church seeing, as he had agreed, and offered his prayers to the martyrs. Then, before the sun rose above the earth and brightened those on earth with its rays, he left that place faithfully, having fixed the inscription on the wall as a memorial of his gratitude and a herald of the martyrs' grace. Now that we have told of his recovery of sight and offered the saints a song for it, let us turn the pen upon ourselves and inscribe the healing of our own eyes, making it the last of the miracles we have written. 70. Concerning Sophronius the monk, the author, who suffered from a cataract of the eyes. Great and splendid was the gratitude of the demoniac who, before his healing, lived among the tombs, as the divine word has testified. For when he received health from the Saviour and escaped the demons that drove him mercilessly into frenzy (he had a legion, a most wicked assembly of many demons), he wanted to become a follower of Christ, who had saved him. He could not show his devotion to Christ in this way (for the man who had been possessed begged him that he might be with him, but Jesus did not allow him). Instead he was told to go away and tell his own people of the saving mercy shown to him. So he went away and became a tireless and zealous herald of the Saviour in the Decapolis, considering it a mark of ingratitude to proclaim his benefactor only to his own people and not to all who had known him when he was sick. So let no one pelt us with reproaches if we wish to imitate him, and proclaim Cyrus and John, our benefactors after God, and record their gift in writing. For no one has ever yet found fault with the leper whom Christ cleansed of leprosy. He had been told to say nothing about his healing and only to offer the gift as Moses commanded, yet he proclaimed the Master everywhere and spread the news of his own cleansing, refusing to keep silent as he had been ordered. Out of gratitude we too emulate these men. We will not hide our healing, but will become grateful

heralds of the saints and add our own story to those already told, even though the saints themselves, imitating Christ their teacher, may wish us to tell no one anything. Let us state the name, the city, the homeland and the monastery: where we were born and where, by God's will, we were placed. Then let us tell of the weakness of the eyes and the divine visit of the saints, as we did for those who came before, granting ourselves nothing more, but recording this too so that readers may know it. Why we placed ourselves last we will explain later, after we have written about the ailment and the cure. The writer's name is Sophronius. His city is Damascus, the metropolis. His homeland is Phoenicia, not the coastal Phoenicia but the one named after Mount Lebanon, whose ancient metropolis is Damascus. His monastery is the one that the holy Theodosius founded in the desert of the holy city of Christ our God. Theodosius, by his virtue, led all the monks of Palestine, both those before him and those after him. Sophronius, then, came to Alexandria for a reason that need not be mentioned in writing, and he became sick in both eyes. He had the disease not just for a few days, but suffered from it for many months. Unable to bear the sea of pain (for the ailment he endured was erratic), he showed himself to the best physicians, especially those thought to surpass the rest in learning and bearing. They often dragged the sufferer out into the open air and examined his pupils against the rays of the sun. At first they said that a change of air was the cause of the ailment, since Sophronius had contracted it immediately after his arrival. But as the sickness dragged on, they reinterpreted it as xerophthalmia, caused not by foreign air but by an imbalance in the body's humours. So they prescribed things that reduce the body, as though such remedies would cure those who fall into this sort of disease. But when they could achieve nothing by these means, though necessity made the patient obey them in everything, they took refuge in incurable cataract and dilation of the pupil. Some gave the ailment the one name, others the other, abandoning the imbalances of foreign air and humours [?]. At first they agreed with one another but fought with themselves by changing names. Later, however, they waged war both on themselves and

on one another, agreeing on this alone: that the ailments they named were incurable. When Sophronius learned this, and realized that he would get no help from human beings, he knew clearly that "physicians will not raise them up," as the great Isaiah had prophesied about them. He was always hearing about the gifts of Cyrus and John, and about the miracles they worked in countless diseases. So he went out to them with faith, the same faith with which all who go to them obtain whatever they long for, finding that the saints repay their faith in them with an abundance of good things. They saw that Sophronius was sick and that he believed in them with his whole soul, and so they deemed him worthy of their healing. First they overturned the physicians' whole babbling diagnosis and convinced the sufferer that he would suffer none of the things the physicians had finally pronounced. After that they granted him the health that the physicians could not

So both of them stood beside him as he slept (it was the third day since he had arrived), and in the following way they gave him confidence that he would be free of the afflictions to come. One of them was clothed in the divine habit of a monk and looked like John, the sick man's spiritual father and teacher, who was also staying at the martyrs' shrine and praying for his disciple and son. This was Cyrus the martyr, who had taken on the father's appearance as a monk and put on a monk's robe. John, Cyrus's blessed companion, took the likeness of Peter of Alexandria, the praetorian prefect. Wearing a gleaming cloak, he came up to Cyrus, who had appeared as the sick man's teacher, and asked him: "Do you have a disciple called Homer?" Even those who have only set foot on the threshold of worldly learning know that Homer was blind, because old age had brought a cataract on him. This is what the saints' riddle was meant to point to. He declared on oath that he had a disciple, but that the disciple was not called Homer. He added that the disciple had never touched a single line of Homer, showing by this that he had no share in Homer's darkness. Saint John answered him as one speaking to the father and teacher: "Trusting him, we [came] to visit him [?]. But if he is called Homer, as we heard, let us glorify God who is over all, who has delivered him from such an affliction and such a name."
