Having appeared to him in this way and convinced him with these words that he would never share Homer's blindness, they left the dream

A few days later they came again, dressed as monks, and told him to put into his eyes their own wax salve, dissolved in the oil left over in the lamp above their tomb. He carried out the rite and received part of the healing that follows it. But when they took pity on him and chose to give him full strength, they revealed the cure in a vision, as follows. It was night, and Sophronius was asleep on his bedding. In his sleep he dreamed that John, his teacher, was giving a feast for all the brothers in the sanctuary. There was one table for everyone. It was round and ran the whole length of the portico of the shrine. The portico has this shape too: although eight angles break up the single line of the circle, the figure it makes is not altogether different from a circle. So the table plainly followed the shape of the portico. At its head reclined Theodore the martyr, whom the sufferer also held in very great honour. After him came the divine Cyrus, with his brother John on his right, so that Cyrus sat between the two champions of piety. They did not take other forms or appear in strange shapes, but looked as they really were and as they are painted. After them the rest of the crowd of sick brothers reclined. Sophronius alone waited on them all, while John, his teacher, prepared the food in what seemed to be a neighbouring cell. When the feast had ended and the three saints had risen from the table, Theodore said to Sophronius, "Go and call your teacher, so that holy Cyrus may pay him whatever he owes [?] him." He ran and did as he was told. When John came (for that was the teacher's name), the martyr Theodore said, "Tell him what holy Cyrus owes you, so that he may pay the debt at once." John fell on his face and said that the martyr owed him nothing. The martyr Theodore answered, "You must certainly tell him." Again the Father gave the same answer. He did this many times. Then he saw that the saint would not give way but was forcing him to speak, and he said, "He owes me nothing. But this I beg and pray, and ask the martyr with all my soul: that he come to our humble cell and visit us there often, to bless us when we are well and to heal us when we are gripped by illness." When holy Cyrus heard this, he answered at once, "Truly I will come, truly I will come, truly I will come." With this threefold saying he confirmed [?] his holy visit, and he truly fulfilled it, and still fulfils it by coming continually. For he knew that the words "I have sworn and confirmed it" and "what has gone out from my lips I will not set aside" belong to the saints. While he lived in the flesh he sang them often, and now that he is separated from the flesh and has flown up to heaven he has never stopped putting them into practice. So John the teacher was cured by these words, since he had received a sworn promise about what he asked. But his disciple Sophronius, seeing that the saints were cheerful,

and that for this reason they were lingering at the table, went up to Theodore the martyr after the feast. Lying on the ground, bending his knees and his neck, he asked Theodore to intercede for him with holy Cyrus. The general Theodore accepted his plea and at once interceded with Cyrus, saying, "For the Lord's sake, and for the sake of this servant of yours, be persuaded." Cyrus answered him, "Yes." He told the man lying there to stand up and fenced him round three times with the sign of the cross. He made the seals in the air between them with the index finger of his right hand, from a very short distance, saying "Blessed be the Lord" at each seal. These were signs that healing was approaching, not of the cure itself. For the martyr's finger came near the sufferer's eyes but did not touch them, and "Blessed be the Lord," said by itself, [?] that recovery was close at hand and would follow.

So soon afterwards, not many days later, the martyrs again appeared to Sophronius as he slept and made good their earlier promises. The vision went plainly like this. The one who is now telling these things was asleep, and he saw himself going into a chapel in his own monastery. At the very porch of the door he met Thomas, apostle and martyr, coming out from inside. He recognized the saint by his robe, by his form, and by every distinctive feature of his appearance. He quickly embraced him and begged to be cured, for in Damascus Thomas displays many mighty works and frequent wonders. He had also, in a few days, raised up Sophronius's brother, who had been paralysed by a very long illness and had spent six months in that condition. For this reason the Apostle is greatly honoured by the people of Damascus, who reap his healings and harvest his gifts. Having found him, then, Sophronius begged for help with his eyes, for he had faith in him and boundless longing for him. Perhaps Cyrus the martyr, knowing this longing, had taken on the Apostle's form. Or perhaps it really was Thomas the apostle, in company with Cyrus the martyr and the whole assembly of martyrs, for a crowd of monks followed him, along with other saints flashing in bright garments. The one who was martyr, disciple and apostle all at once stretched out his right hand, touched the eyelids of the left eye, again with his index finger, and sealed him three times with the cross of Christ. "Let me go," he said to the writer. But the writer begged him to seal the right eye as well. The saint said that eye had nothing wrong with it. With these words he hurried off, and once he was freed from the arms of the man holding him, this was the end of the vision.

When he came round after the dream just described, he felt joy and, at the same time, unbearable grief. He felt joy because he had been visited by the saints, and grief because he had let the saint go away without sealing his other eye. While he grieved like this, he quickly fell asleep again. At once he saw John, Cyrus's companion, asking John the rhetor, who has been deservedly honoured with the rank of prefect, about the help the saints had given. Sophronius himself told of the visit. He said he was troubled about his right eye, because it had not received the seal of the saving sign and had not been fully healed. The martyr gave him ample healing. He said, "Your eyes will suffer no further harm, neither the eye that was sealed nor the one left unsealed," because the saint had already said that the eye he feared for was not sick. The martyr said this under oath. Then, to give the sufferer greater assurance, he kissed the unsealed eye three times with his mouth, so Sophronius says. Having done this, and kindly bestowed full strength and grace, he brought the dream to an end. For those who imitate the God of all, the giver of good gifts and perfect bounties, never hand out a grace or a gift that is incomplete. So Sophronius received the saints' gift and put off the mist from his eyes. Then he set about writing down everything that has been told, always remembering the healing and the promise he had made before he recovered. So immediately after his healing he produced this composition and paid his vows without any delay, imitating the saints' zeal for him. He placed himself last among those he wrote about, since he was the least of all and unworthy of a martyr's healing. He asks to share in that healing all his life, for both soul and body, and to be delivered from every more grievous misfortune.

These things, blessed Cyrus and John, Sophronius has written and dedicated to you. These things, servants of Christ the Saviour, who have become saviours to him as well, he has dared to offer to you, having taken courage from you and made you helpers in his offering. These things, divine martyrs, he has been bold to bring you as fruit. He does not offer them to repay your gifts to him, but intends them as a written tribute of praise. They [?] the warmth of his gratitude, but in every way they fall short of your greatness. Receive them kindly, look on them with a benevolent gaze, and pour abundant grace on them, so that you may not be insulted through them if they are left without divine colouring. Accept him as an unprofitable servant who has done what he ought to have done, and receive him as a grateful debtor. And grant him pardon

for these things, since you know how poor his mind is, recognize how slow his tongue is, and observe how modest his speech is. While he lives, always protect him. Always guard him with divine power, always preserve him from the evils of life, and always rescue him from every temptation, present or future, whether he is awake or asleep, on land or at sea, in cities or in deserts. When he has died and left this life, deliver him from gloomy shame, present him to God, make him a beholder of God's glory, and make him a sharer in the good things promised to those who behold it. May you always count all of us worthy to obtain these things in Christ our God, with whom be glory, honour, might, greatness and majesty to the Father and to the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

THE LIFE, CONDUCT AND MARTYRDOM, WITH A PARTIAL ACCOUNT OF THE MIRACLES, OF THE HOLY AND GLORIOUS UNMERCENARIES CYRUS AND JOHN

1. The Word, our divine source, who is truth itself, Christ our God, plainly proclaims in the Gospels: "All things are possible to the one who believes." And Paul, the herald of the apostolic summit, with Christ himself evidently speaking in him, cries out by divine inspiration that hope does not put us to shame. Besides this, [?] the love of the one who loved us and gave himself for us, our Saviour himself I mean, has given us courage, through the conduct and patronage of the martyrs, to attempt things beyond our powers. So we will tell in part, as far as we can, the life of Saints Cyrus and John, which we have long wanted to do. To say "life" is the same as to say "conduct", and we will also tell of their brilliant, more-than-worldly contest for Christ our God. We will also record a few miracles, that is, healings, out of many. We were eyewitnesses and servants of these, and by divine grace we still are, since we have received them for our salvation, we who are worse than the tax collectors. We will record them for the benefit of our readers.

2. The celebrated Cyrus was a citizen of Alexander's very great city. We do not know who his parents were in the flesh. But in his spiritual birth he had God as Father, who gave him new birth through water and the Spirit, and as mother the orthodox Church [?]. He was a physician by profession, and his workshop is well known to everyone even now, for it has become a church of the Holy Three Children, teeming with healings through the grace of those martyrs. I think it reasonable to relate briefly how the workshop came to be the church of the Holy Children, for I am sure it will be of great benefit to readers.

3. Apollinarius, the great [champion?] of the truth . . . [?] . . . earnestly [?] them, since it was to be laid in the church that he himself had built for them with great longing. This venerable man, renowned throughout the world, neglected nothing of this holy command. He reached Babylon, gave the divine letter to the saints, and said to them, "Saints, the archbishop of God, your servant, has sent you

this letter of petition. Receive it and give an answer." When he had said this, the one in the middle sat up, stretched out his hand, drew the letter to himself, lay back down again, and left the man without an answer. For a whole week the abba pleaded but received no answer, so he went back to the one who had sent him without having achieved anything, and told what had happened.

4. Then the archbishop of God, a most beloved man of blameless faith and good conscience, sent this God-pleasing man out again in the same way. "Go again," he said, "and petition the saints on my behalf. If they do not accept your petition even now, at least take the letter and bring it back, so that I may receive it in place of relics, as something they have received and already sanctified." Yielding to the father, the man who obeyed Christ in everything, in action and in contemplation, reached Babylon once more. Again he implored the saints, saying, "Thrice-blessed martyrs, the archbishop of God has sent me to you again with his request. Do not dishonour him, for he has built you such a great and splendid church, moved by his longing for you." When the saints still left him without an answer, he was prompted by some divine impulse to finish the archbishop's business [?] with the letter. He put his hand to the saint's breast, where the saint was holding the letter in his hand, took hold of it, and the blessed man reverently drew it towards himself. The all-holy hand came with it, still holding the letter. He embraced it with reverence and returned to the city with this untouchable and venerable treasure, showing by his carrying out of the all-holy command that hope in God does not put us to shame.

5. When the great archbishop of God received it, he rejoiced and exulted and urged his nephew to prepare for the marriage. He announced to the people the dedication of the church, delighting in divine joy. The next day he came with all the clergy and had [?] that precious and venerable hand of the saint, together with the letter of acceptance it held, laid in place with due reverence. After he had consecrated the church, he ordained his nephew and said to him, "Here is your wife," meaning the Church, "so take care of her as is fitting." When this was done, it led the young man to make great progress towards God, and

he did what he had heard.

6. As we have said, then, and as we stated a little earlier, the saint was a physician. He practised medicine wearing the dress of the world, though his mind was not worldly. He healed not only the bodies of the sick but also their souls, from the diseases that gripped them, and he led them away from those who were strangers to the faith. When he visited the sick, he did not comfort them with the writings of Galen and Hippocrates and others like them, but with the exhortations of the prophets, the apostles and the Gospels,

and so drew them to true health and life. He counted them among the flock of Christ our God and showed them to be heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

7. When the demon who hates the good saw him bringing many people to Christ, he denounced him to the governor of the city through wicked men. They said that a certain Galilean, a physician by profession, had led astray almost all the people of the city and turned them away from the worship of the gods. He had taught them to worship as God Jesus, whom the Jews crucified, and he was wiping out our ancestral religion. The wretched governor was swayed by this, boiled over with bitter anger, and ordered the saint to be arrested at once. When the blessed man learned of this, he went to Arabia, on the coast of Egypt, and settled in a village called Tzote [?]. When he changed his home, he also changed his dress. He shaved his head and put on the monastic habit. Rising above this lowly and perishable life and passing over to the heights, he grew greater from then on in action and contemplation. He no longer cured diseases with various drugs or relied on the help of herbs. By prayer alone and godly teaching he freed souls and bodies from bitter and incurable pains.

8. At that time Diocletian was impiously wielding the sceptre of the Romans and had stirred up persecution against the churches everywhere. John learned of this. He was a venerable man, of the most eminent family in the flesh, not yet known as a citizen [?] of the faith, but distinguished in military rank. He went to Jerusalem, paid God the vow that pleased him, and then came to Egypt, drawn by reports of holy Cyrus. He lived with the blessed man as one who shared his faith, and seeing the healings that were performed, he reached out still further towards virtue.

The persecution was surging ever more violently, and Kasianos [?] was serving as priest of pagan folly at Canopus. Three virgins who lived in that place, betrothed to Christ, were seized by men assigned to this hunt, who brought them with their mother before Syrianus, the governor of the city. When holy Cyrus heard about them, he was gripped by fear, as a lover of Christ. He feared that the girls, being so young, might take fright at the tortures, forswear Christ and deny the faith because of their very tender age. Theoctiste, the eldest, was fifteen. The second, Theodote, was in her thirteenth year, and Eudoxia, the youngest, was in her eleventh year. Their mother, Athanasia, had a holy name, for she truly became an heir of immortality together with her beloved children. So, as we have said, holy Cyrus, fearing for them, slipped into the city with John. They anointed these holy women for the contest and roused them beyond the strength of nature. They persuaded them to face the tortures boldly and not to be afraid, for the sake of the kingdom of Christ their bridegroom, [?] the crowns of purity . . .

9. But the wicked enemy again used his bitter servants to expose the saints. Once they had been explicitly named to the governor,

they darkened his mind. Before the attendants could bring them to his lawless court, [they reported] that two men, a monk and a soldier, were leading astray the virgins who had been brought in. These men would not let the virgins offer the gods the worship they owed, and they were defying Caesar, since the virgins did not obey his commands but said that Jesus is the eternal King. Syrianus, that governor driven by God's wrath, gnashed his teeth at what he heard and ordered the soldiers to bring the two men before the tribunal as well. He said to them, "Wretches, enemies of the blessed gods, worthy of death! Why do you not let the virgins submit to Caesar's decrees? Or rather, you have shown that you yourselves are rebels against the emperor of the Romans, since you belong to the loathsome religion of the Christians. So repent and propitiate the greatest gods, and you will receive no ordinary honours from the emperor." They answered him, "Syrianus, we do not accept dishonourable honours, for the things that are seen are temporary. We do not offer the worship that belongs to God alone to the wooden images of demons. Nor will we deny Christ, who made all things. We have him as our eternal King, and from him we have been promised gifts that are stronger than death, that never see an end, and that are full of crowns and immortal delight."

10. Syrianus groaned at them, gnashed his teeth and said, "You ought to have yielded to the clemency of the law and gained your safety. But since you are in the grip of arrogance, I will use blows to make you yield to the emperor's commands." With these words he had the virgins brought and set before him, and he inflicted every kind of torture on the saints. He struck them with whips and clubs, burned them with fire and soaked them in vinegar and brine. Then he ordered their burnt limbs to be rubbed with rags of haircloth. He had used every kind of torture, as has been said, yet he saw that the martyrs grew stronger, as though they were suffering in someone else's body, and that they contradicted him all the more fiercely. So he filled their feet with boiling pitch. [He saw] that many were being drawn to imitate them and won over to the faith by their steadfast resistance, for in their endurance of such sufferings and in the untroubled cheerfulness of the martyrs, many saw a picture of the imperishable prizes of the life to come. So he ordered the martyrs to be taken away and the virgins to be tortured again, together with their God-loving mother. But like one kicking against the goads, he was defeated by these women too, for the martyrs had anointed them with the courage of martyrdom. At last he pronounced the sentence and ordered the heads of these brides of Christ to be cut off; this was his command for them and for the mother who bore them.

11. Then he tortured the martyrs Cyrus and John again, and like waves dashing against rocks he was broken once more. He could not persuade the saints by flattery, by entreaty or by warnings, by the offer of what he thought were the greatest honours, by whips, by boiling pitch, by hot water, or by

…by fire, nor by the instruments that twist the limbs, he grew weary and passed sentence on them as well, saying: “Cyrus, the leader of the Galileans, and John, who shares his mind, have not yielded to the decrees of the emperors and have refused to worship the greatest gods. We sentence them to capital punishment.” By this sentence they were crowned with the crown of incorruption. It was the thirty-first day of the month of January when the saints, having kept the faith, finished the athlete's course. They were three virgins and brides of Christ, Theoctiste, Theodote and Eudoxia; Athanasia, who bore them and piously raised them; Cyrus, the [?] lover of God; and John the soldier, who shared his faith and his honour. The three holy virgins and their mother were laid to rest on the east side of the church of Saint Mark, where a fitting coffin was built for them. The celebrated Cyrus and John, Cyrus's fellow martyr, were laid in a single tomb in that same house of the Apostle and Evangelist Mark.

12. A good deal of time passed. The tyranny of the Hellenes was overthrown and Christians came to hold the sceptres of Roman rule. Theodosius the Great held the empire and adorned it with works of faith, as the church historians testify in their books and as the facts themselves proclaim to everyone. To prove what has been said, let us also recall one of his virtues. They say that a war was stirred up against him from the western regions. A great many nations rose up by some agreement, nation mingling with nation. They were like torrents that pour together after rains [?] and flow into one another until the mass of water makes a sea, or like locusts and sand, beyond number. This pious Theodosius did not resort to sending embassies to other nations to arrange truces, as the weak tend to do when wars break out. Instead, as was his custom, he ran back to God and called on faith to help him.

13. He learned that in Scetis (a desert towards Egypt that goes by this name) there was a man who was Egyptian by birth but rich in every divine virtue. This man had been counted worthy of divine grace and was a worker of the greatest miracles. Theodosius at once wrote to Theophilus, who was known at that time as the guardian of Christ's flocks in Alexandria, asking him to send this wonderful man to him. Theodosius wanted the man begged to help him in the war with his supplications to God, for he rightly believed and fully hoped that this would surely bring success. The bishop hurried to the man, explained the reason, and urgently pressed him to go up to the emperor. But Senuphius (for that was the blessed man's name) begged the archbishop to excuse him. He said he was a sinner and called himself a useless servant of the Lord. When he could not obtain release, he stood facing east, and the mantle he was wearing

on his shoulders he held, together with his staff, in his hands. Stretching them up to heaven, he cried out to Him: “Lord Jesus Christ, our God, grant to this staff of mine and to this mantle the same power that you have given to me, your sinful servant.” Then he gave them to the archbishop and said to him: “Send these to the emperor, and write to him that he should put the mantle over his head and hold the staff in his hand. Then he should go out to the war and against the enemy's battle line ahead of everyone, even ahead of his own army. For if Christ our God has reckoned me his servant and has heard my prayer, he will also give the victory through these things, by faith in God.”

14. So these things were sent. Theodosius, crowned by God, adorned himself with the mantle as a helmet, the hope of salvation. He took the staff in his right hand and went out to the war ahead of his most faithful army. As soon as the barbarians saw him, they turned to flight and destroyed themselves without receiving a single arrow or blow from the army. And to the end of his life, they say, the pious and God-loving emperor took more pride in this saving helmet than in any diadem. Because of these events they hold a public festival in Alexandria every year, which they call the Eikonion. For they have an icon of him, that is, of the most pious emperor Theodosius, with his head covered by the mantle and the staff held in his right hand. Through its annual festival this icon always proclaims the miracle.

15. By divine grace and with the help of the faithful and pious emperor Theodosius, Theophilus, the president of the Church and the sure shepherd of the flocks in Alexandria, was filled with divine zeal. He pulled down practically all the objects of Hellenic worship and adorned the whole city with houses of prayer. In the place called Canopus he raised a great and extraordinary church to the apostles. This place lies outside the city, twelve miles away. It was very famous, so much so that it was truly venerable even to the children of the Hellenes, because, they say, the assembly of the gods was believed to meet there. The whole road leading there from the city was paved with slabs and lined with crowded suburbs and baths; twenty-four baths are recorded. Many who know about it say that until recently they had been laid waste [?]. They also say that the city's [?] was reckoned to extend as far as Canopus itself, and that markets were laid out all along the way. A village two miles away from it had an idol called Menuthe, in which spirits openly worked. There, in turn, the divine Theophilus built a church to the Evangelists.

16. After Theophilus fell asleep, Cyril the Great took over the helm of the Church. He was a lover of piety and a destroyer of those who corrupted the faith. He took no small pains to put an end to the apparitions of Menuthe and to cut off certain of the simpler Christians who were deserting to that place on the pretext of being healed. After he had prayed to God at length about this, he saw an angel from God announcing that his prayer had been accepted

and commanding him to take the remains of Cyrus, great among the martyrs, from the church of Saint Mark to Menuthe [?], and to lay their relics in the church of the Evangelists. For they also named the village after it, out of reverence for the demon and attachment to her [?]. By the one name the angel meant both martyrs, as will be shown from the writings of the blessed Cyril. Without delay the archbishop, who was most dear to God, carried out what he had been commanded. He made the translation of the martyrs' relics on the twenty-eighth of the month of June and gave short addresses to the Christ-loving people. We shall also append these addresses, both to assure and to benefit those who read them. In God [?], with [?] the only-begotten, together with the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, be glory, majesty and magnificence, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

ANOTHER PASSION OF THE HOLY MARTYRS CYRUS AND JOHN, WITH ITS BEGINNING MISSING

…ascetic discipline, nobly drawn up in battle against the spirits of wickedness. John served as a soldier of an earthly king in one of the regiments, but he strove all the more to please the heavenly King. These saints were arrested at the place called Canopus, for they lived there. They were not arrested alone, however, but together with three ever-virgins and their mother. The first of the virgins was named Theodote and was in her fifteenth year. The second was named Theoctiste and was thirteen. The third was Eudoxia, and she was in her eleventh year. Their mother was called Athanasia. She had nourished the girls on the doctrines of piety more than on milk, and she persuaded them to choose chastity and to be wedded to the immortal Bridegroom, so that they might hold the unquenchable lamps of virginity and await his coming. But while they were sailing the voyage of virginity well, the contest of confession overtook them. Yet Christ's glorious martyrs were not terrified by the onset of the wolves. They found no small comfort in the holy martyrs Cyrus and John, who by their inspired teaching anointed the holy virgins for the contest on behalf of piety. The saints were in fact deeply anxious, and they prepared themselves all the more for the battle against the madness of idols, because they feared that the holy virgins were so young that they might not endure. So the saints said to them: “Remember the words of the Lord, and do not be terrified by what is coming. For he himself

said, ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul,’ and again, ‘The one who endures to the end will be saved.’ Imitate your teacher among women. You have longed for her virginity, so emulate her confession too.” With these and similar words and examples the holy martyrs of Christ, Cyrus and John, armed those blessed virgins, and so they stripped with them for the stadium of the contest against superstition. The soldiers who had arrested them brought them before the tribunal of Syrianus at Alexandria. There they cast aside every other care, as the Lord commanded. They did not prepare their defence before the judge with reasonings of their own, but they answered his questions with wisdom given by the Holy Spirit. He summoned the saints together with the celebrated virgins and urged them to deny Christ, to abandon him and to sacrifice to the demons. But they taught him to recognize the Creator through the visible creation. They urged him to abandon the gods he worshipped, since these were not gods but destroyers of human beings. Then Syrianus tried flattery. He promised to give them gifts and assured them that he would make them friends and intimates of his own emperor. But the holy martyrs called to mind the good things stored up for the righteous, the kingdom of heaven, and the freedom to speak openly before Christ. These they set against the judge's promises and showed how much more glorious and precious they were than his. The judge emptied his whole quiver of venomous words, but he could not wound the martyrs at all, for they were armed with faith and had put on the breastplate of love for Christ. In the end he turned to deeds. He inflicted terrible tortures on the saints and on those blessed women, on their sides and over their whole bodies. The servants of that hostile man grew weary without achieving anything more. The saints did not even deign to answer the judges, but persevered under the torments as if they were at a banquet rather than under torture. Then Syrianus saw that Christ's noble athletes could not be defeated. Against his will he let them raise trophies over him and over his gods, for he ordered the saints and the honoured virgins to be perfected by the sword. The governor's order was carried out. By shedding their own blood the prize-winning martyrs imitated their own Master, Christ. They exchanged their earthly dwellings for the dwellings in heaven and received the crowns of the contest from God, who presides over the games. These things took place on the sixth of the month Mechir by the Egyptian reckoning, which is the thirty-first of January by the Roman reckoning. This was after the martyrdom of the most holy Peter, bishop of Alexandria. He was a true imitator of that Peter who was entrusted with the keys of the kingdom of heaven and on whom the Church was founded. He brought down the hostile Arius, the enemy of the Holy Trinity and a stranger to it, just as the apostle Peter brought down Simon Magus.

The martyrs Cyrus and John and the celebrated virgins were perfected by the sword, and their all-holy bodies lay unburied as food for beasts and birds. Then, by God's providence, the pious part of the people of Alexandria, armed with zeal and divine longing, seized the relics of the saints, whole and unharmed. With a great escort and with great honour they laid them in the venerable church of the holy Apostle and Evangelist Mark. They put the saints Cyrus and John in one coffin, and the holy virgins Theodote, Theoctiste and Eudoxia, together with their mother Athanasia, likewise in one fitting coffin. For the people knew well that those who kept the commands of the Gospel and imitated Mark's contest should share his dwelling. As they did on earth, so in heaven they will surely be counted worthy to stand with him at the right hand. So much for the contest of the saints.

I think it necessary to tell briefly also why the holy relics of Cyrus and John were moved from the house of prayer of the holy Apostle and Evangelist Mark to the church beyond Canopus. That church was originally built in the name of the Evangelists, but it is now called the church of the Holy Martyrs. I tell it as we were able to learn it from the writings of the Fathers. In the place where the oratory of saints Cyrus and John now stands, by the sands, an unclean demon used to appear in the form of a woman. It produced many illusions and pretended to give oracles that had no truth in them. It also prescribed certain drugs with great show, but these were of no help whatever. Instead it dragged people to destruction. Many, then, were caught in the hidden snare of the evil spirit. They thought they were honouring the demon with sacrifices and the smoke of burnt offerings at the altar they had raised in its name. The Egyptians called it Menuthe. In the time of the Christ-loving emperor Theodosius the Younger, Cyril, now among the saints, was truly governing the throne of Mark and had inherited the most fervent zeal for orthodoxy. He heard about the apparitions of the wicked demon at Menuthe (for from then on they named the place after the demon that appeared there). The holy man was grieved and distressed over the souls being lost through this deception, and he turned to litanies and supplications. He besought God to reveal a way by which his own creature might be freed from the deadly demon and its illusions. He prayed for a long time and fell down before God with tears. Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him by night and said: “Since you, as shepherd of the rational sheep, offer supplication, the Creator and God of both you and us gives you this command through me. Go to the burial place of Mark the Evangelist, and you will find a coffin in which the relics of my martyrs Cyrus and John are treasured. Take them up and transfer them to the house built in the name of the Evangelists beyond Canopus. When this is done, the illusion that occurs in that place will be brought to an end.”

Cyril, now among the saints, was overjoyed and gave thanks to God, who always provides for the salvation of his own creature. Neglecting nothing, he carried out what the divine oracle had commanded. He gathered the God-loving clergy together with the most faithful people and explained to them what God had revealed to him. Then he went in a procession of prayer with nearly the whole city to the house of prayer of the holy Apostle and Evangelist Mark. He prayed to God for many hours with all the people. Then he went forward and opened the precious chest of Christ's athletes. He found the relics of saints Cyrus and John whole and shining with the grace of the Holy Spirit. With fear and with spiritual longing he took them up, wrapped them in clean linen cloths with ointments and spices, and placed them on a carriage. So, with the clergy and the people in procession, they went out from the oratory of the Evangelist Mark and came to the church of the Evangelists beyond Canopus. There he celebrated the divine mysteries. Then he laid the relics of the martyrs of Christ our God, more precious than gold and costly stones, in the coffin that had been prepared. Christ's noble soldiers Cyrus and John had scarcely arrived at the place when they began to raise trophies against the most wicked demon that lurked there. While the holy relics were being laid to rest, they healed many who were possessed by demons or held by other illnesses. They even healed the priests of the deadly demon of the error in their souls. These priests at once came to the holy archbishop Cyril and were purified in the bath of grace, holy baptism. The temple itself, or rather the abomination of the deadly demon, vanished along with the statue and the altar in it. Through the working of the holy martyrs, the nearby sand, and indeed the sea as well, laid it waste and made it disappear. The sea flooded over it and the sand buried it, so that the place became completely unknown. In place of the former deception, such grace has blossomed through the coming of the holy martyrs that the sick hasten from the ends of the earth to the oratory of Cyrus and John. All who run there in faith receive healing for their sufferings. “For whatever you ask in your prayers, believing that you will receive it, [?]” said our Lord Jesus Christ to the disciples, and through them to all who believe with sincerity [?] … now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.

[?] OF [?] WHO WAS ONCE A COURTESAN AND THEN LIVED AS AN ASCETIC IN THE DESERT OF THE JORDAN

1. “It is good to hide the secret of a king, but it is glorious to reveal the works of God.” So the angel said to Tobit after his eyes had been wonderfully opened from their blindness [?], and after the dangers he had experienced [?] and been rescued from because of his piety. For not to keep a king's secret is [?], but to keep silent about the wonderful works of God brings danger to the soul. So I too am struck with fear of keeping silent about divine things. I am wary of the danger that threatened the servant who received the talent from his master, buried it in the ground, and hid what had been given him to trade with, leaving it idle. I will by no means keep silent about a sacred account that has come down to me. Let no one disbelieve me as I write what I have heard, and let no one think I am telling marvellous tales at all because he is astonished at how great the matter is. May it never happen that I lie or adulterate an account in which God is spoken of. To have small thoughts, unworthy of the majesty of the incarnate God the Word, and to disbelieve what is said in this way does not seem reasonable to me. But if some who read this writing are astonished at how extraordinary the account is and are unwilling to believe it, may the Lord be merciful to them [?]. For they consider the weakness of human nature, and so they regard as unacceptable the extraordinary things that are told about human beings. Now I will go on to the account itself, which concerns something that happened in our own generation. A holy man, who had learned from childhood to speak and do divine things, related it. Let no one [?] who reads this disbelieve it, thinking it impossible for wonders to happen in our generation. For the grace [?], passing from generation to generation into holy souls, makes friends of God and prophets, as Solomon taught. It is now time to begin that sacred account.

2. There was [?] a man in the monasteries of Palestine [?] who had been brought up [?] in monastic ways and

[?]. This elder's name was Zosimas. Let no one think from the name (10) that I mean the Zosimas who was once accused of heterodoxy in doctrine. They were two different men, and the difference between them is great, even though both bore the same name. This Zosimas, then, was orthodox. He had been a monk from the beginning in one of the monasteries of Palestine [?]. He practised every form (11) of asceticism and became proficient in every kind of self-control (12). He kept every rule handed down by those who had trained them (15) for such a wrestling-school, and he devised many further practices himself, seeking to subject the flesh to the spirit. And he did not miss his aim. The elder was so renowned in spiritual matters that many monks from the nearby monasteries, and sometimes even from distant ones, often came to him to be formed and governed in self-control by his teaching [?]. Though the elder was so devoted to the practical life, he never neglected the study of the divine Scriptures. Whether he was lying down or rising, or holding in his hands the handiwork by which he earned his food (15) — and if you wish to learn what food he took [?] — he had one unceasing work that was never used up: to sing psalms continually and always to meditate on the sacred Scriptures (16). Indeed, some say, the elder was often counted worthy of divine visions, an illumination being granted him from God, as the Lord said [?]. That is, those who have cleansed their own hearts [?] and are always sober, with the eye of their soul awake, see visions of divine illumination, and receive here the pledges of the good that awaits them. 3. Zosimas used to say that he had been given to this monastery straight from his father's (17) arms, and that he had completed the ascetic course in it up to his fifty-third year (18). After this, as he said, he was troubled by certain thoughts [?] (19), as though he were perfect in all things and in no way needed anyone else's teaching. For, as he said, he reasoned thus within himself: "Is there a monk on earth who can pass on to me something new and help me, something I do not know and have not practised as a form of asceticism? Is there a man among those who pursue the philosophic life in the desert who surpasses me in practice or contemplation?" As the elder was reasoning thus, someone stood beside him and said to him: "Zosimas, you have run the ascetic course well, as far as a man can [?]. Yet no one among men possesses perfection. The contest that lies ahead is greater than the one already past, even if you do not know it. So that you too may learn how many other ways to salvation there are, go out from your land and your kindred and from your father's house, like Abraham, revered among the patriarchs, and come to this monastery that lies near the river Jordan." 4. At once the elder obeyed the command and [left] the monastery in which he had been a monk from childhood. He came to the Jordan, holiest of rivers, and was guided by the one who had commanded him to the monastery in which God had bidden him to be [?]. ([?]) Alternatively: "and for every kind of self-control," as in "having trained for such a wrestling-school of theirs." (18) Alternatively: "to complete as far as possible." (19) Likewise: "as if he were perfect in all things in the"

[?]. Then he knocked at the door [of the courtyard] with his hand and met the monk who kept the door. That monk [announced] him to the abbot [?]. The abbot received him, and seeing his habit and his devout bearing, after Zosimas had made the customary prostration to the monks and received a prayer, he asked him (21): "Where are you from, brother, and why have you come to us humble old men?" Zosimas answered: "There is no need for me to say where I come from. I have come, Father, to be helped. For I have heard glorious (25) and praiseworthy things about you, things able to bring a soul close to Christ our God." The abbot said to him: "Brother, God, who alone heals human weakness, will himself teach both you and us his divine will and guide us to do what is fitting. For one man cannot help another unless each attends to himself continually and does what is needful with a sober mind, having God as fellow-worker in what he does [?]. Yet since, as you say, [?] has moved you to see us old men, stay with us, if this is why you have come. And the Good Shepherd, who laid down his life as a ransom [?] for us and calls his own sheep by name, will nourish us all by the grace of the Spirit." When the abbot had said this to Zosimas, Zosimas again made a prostration, asked for a prayer and said "Amen," and he stayed in that monastery. 5. He saw elders who shone in practice and contemplation, [fervent] in spirit and serving the Lord. Their psalmody was unceasing and went on all night. They always had their handiwork in their hands and the psalms on their lips. No idle word was heard among them, and concern for affairs had no place with them. Yearly revenues [and money gathered] and the cares that go with worldly labours were not known among them even by name (25). Their one [first] and only aim [?] was to be as though dead in the body, like men who had died once and for all to the world and to the things in it, and no longer existed. For food they had what is never used up, the divinely inspired words. They nourished the body only with necessities, bread and water, so as to be [?] ablaze with divine love. Seeing these things, as he said, Zosimas was greatly edified. He strained forward to what lay ahead and [quickened] his own course, having found fellow-workers who tilled the divine paradise well. 6. When a good many days had passed, the time drew near at which Christians are taught to keep the holy fast, purifying themselves beforehand to worship the divine Passion and the Resurrection of Christ. The monastery gate was never opened but always kept shut, so that the monks' asceticism was undisturbed. There was no need to open it unless some monk came by on necessary business. The place was deserted, and to most of the neighbouring monks it was not only untrodden but even unknown [?]. A certain rule had been kept in the monastery [from of old], and it was on account of this, I think, that God brought Zosimas to that monastery. What the rule was and how it was kept I shall now tell. On the Sunday from which the first week of the fast usually takes its name, the divine liturgy was celebrated as usual. Each of the monks partook of the immaculate and life-giving mysteries, and they took a little food, as was the custom. After this they all gathered in the oratory, and when they had prayed earnestly and knelt for a good while, (24) Likewise: "these things" [?]. Likewise: "nor were they named among them"; "were known"

the elders embraced one another and the abbot and [set out] [?]. Each went off to a different part, relying on himself alone [?]. 8. They spent all the days of the fast in this way. They returned to the monastery on the Sunday before the Saviour's life-giving Resurrection from the dead, the day on which the Church received the custom of celebrating the eve of the feast with palm branches. Each returned with his own conscience as the tiller [?] of his aim. It knew how he had worked and what seeds of labour he had sown, and no one ever asked another in what way he had carried through the contest set before him. This was the rule of the monastery, and it was kept well. For each of them in the desert strove by himself, with God as the judge of the contest [?], [free] from pleasing men and from practising self-control for show. Things done for the sake of men and performed to please them not only fail to benefit the doer at all, but even become causes of great harm to him. 9. So Zosimas, following the usual custom of the monastery, crossed the Jordan. He took a few small provisions for the body's needs, and the very rag he was clothed in. He kept the rule as he crossed the desert, eating only when nature required it. At night he slept wherever evening overtook him, lying briefly on the ground and taking a little sleep. Then at early dawn he set off walking again, always keeping up his pace without slackening. As he said, he came to desire to go into the [inner] desert [?] and find some father living in it who could help him toward what he longed for. So he pressed on with his journey vigorously, as though hastening to some famous and well-known dwelling. When he had travelled for twenty days and the hour of the sixth [?] came, he paused briefly in his journey, turned toward the east and said his usual prayer. For at the appointed times of the day he was accustomed to break off the strain of the journey and rest a little from his toil, and to stand singing psalms, bend the knee and pray in this way.

10. As he was singing psalms and gazing at the sky with an unwavering eye, he saw on the right of the place where he stood praying the sixth hour what looked like the shadow of a human body. [?] At first he was troubled [?]. He suspected that he was seeing a demonic apparition and began to tremble. But he sealed himself with the sign of the cross [and shook off his fear], for his prayer [?] had by now come to an end. Then he turned his gaze and saw that someone really was walking toward the south. What he saw was naked, with a body blackened as if by the heat of the sun. Its hair was white as wool and short [?], so that it reached no further down than the neck. When Zosimas saw this, he was beside himself with delight, as it were, and overjoyed at the wondrous sight. He began to run toward the place to which the figure was hurrying, and he rejoiced with unspeakable joy. In all those days he had not seen the form of a human being, [or of a living creature, bird or land animal,] or even a shadow (28). He wanted to know who the figure was and what kind of being, hoping that he would become the viewer and witness of great things. 11. When the figure perceived Zosimas coming from afar, it began to flee and run into the inner desert. But Zosimas, as if he had forgotten his old age and taken no account of the toil of the journey, strained every nerve and hastened to overtake what was fleeing from him. He pursued, and it was pursued. Zosimas ran faster and little by little came nearer to the one fleeing. When he had come so near that a voice could now be heard, Zosimas began to cry out with tears and utter words like these: "Why do you flee from me, an old man and a sinner, servant of the true God? Wait for me, whoever you are, by the God for whose sake you have made your home in this desert. Wait for me, weak and unworthy as I am, by the hope you have of reward for this toil of yours,

by God, who never abhors anyone." As Zosimas said these things with tears, they both came running to a place marked with the trace of a torrent-bed. But it seems to me that no torrent ever ran there (29); the place just happened to have that shape. 12. When they reached it, the one fleeing went down and climbed up again on the other side. But Zosimas was exhausted and could run no further. He stood on the other side of the gully, adding tears to tears and groans to groans (30), so that [?]. Then the fleeing body uttered these words: "Abba Zosimas, forgive me for the Lord's sake. I cannot turn and let you see me face to face. I am a woman, and naked, as you see, with the shame of my body uncovered. But if you are truly willing to grant a sinful woman one favour, throw me the cloak you have wrapped around you, so that I may cover my womanly weakness with it, turn to you and receive your prayers." Then trembling and amazement seized Zosimas, as he said, on hearing that she had called him Zosimas by name. Being a keen man and very wise in divine things, he recognised that she would not [?]

have called by name someone she had never seen or heard of unless she clearly shone with the gift of foresight. 13. He quickly did as he was asked, and taking off [?], he threw it to her, turning his back. She took it and covered those parts of the body that most of all ought to be covered. Then she turned to Zosimas and said to him: "Abba Zosimas, why did you decide to see a sinful woman? What do you wish to learn or see from me, that you did not shrink from taking on so great a labour?" But he knelt on the ground and asked to receive a blessing, as is customary, and she too made a prostration. Both lay on the ground, each asking the other for a blessing, and nothing could be heard from either of them but "Bless me." After a very long time the woman said to Zosimas: "Abba Zosimas, it is fitting for you to bless and to pray. You have been honoured with the dignity of the priesthood. For many years you have stood at the holy altar, and you have often served as minister of the divine gifts." This threw Zosimas into greater fear and anguish. The elder trembled, was bathed in sweat and groaned, and his voice failed. He said to her, in broken and laboured breaths: "It is clear, spiritual mother, from your very way of life [?], that you have gone forth to God and have largely died to the world. And the gift given to you is made all the clearer by your calling me by name and calling me a priest, though you have never seen me. But since grace is recognised not by rank but by the dispositions of the soul, bless me for the Lord's sake, and grant a prayer to one who needs your help (32)." 14. Then the woman said: "Blessed is God, who cares for the salvation of men and of souls." When Zosimas had said "Amen," they both rose from their knees, and the woman said to the elder: "Why have you come to me, a sinner, O man? Why did you want to see a woman naked of every virtue? Yet since the grace of the Holy Spirit has led you to render me some service suited to my time, [tell me]: how is the Christian people governed today? How are the emperors? How are the affairs of the Church shepherded?" Zosimas said to her: "Through your holy prayers, mother, Christ has granted lasting peace [?]. But accept the request of an unworthy elder and pray for the whole world and for me, a sinner, so that my journey through this desert may not be fruitless." She answered him: "You, Abba Zosimas, as I said, are the one who ought to pray for me and for all, for this is the very office allotted to you. Yet since we are commanded to obey, I will willingly do what you bid." Having said this, she turned to the east, raised her eyes to heaven, stretched out her hands and began to pray in a whisper. Her voice could not be heard distinctly, so Zosimas could catch none of the words of her prayer. As he said, he stood trembling, looking at the ground and saying nothing at all. But he swore, calling God to witness, that when he raised his eyes from the ground he saw her lifted about a cubit from the earth, hanging in the air and praying thus. When he saw this, he was seized with still greater fear and anguish, and did not dare to utter a word at all. He only said to himself again and again, "Lord, have mercy," lying on the ground. ([?]) In the Royal manuscript there was: "She too asked to receive a prostration [?]"

"I am ashamed, I am ashamed, Abba [?], to tell you the shamefulness of my deeds. Forgive me for the Lord's sake. But since you have seen my body naked, I will lay my deeds bare to you as well, so that you may know with how much shame and disgrace my soul is filled. It was not, as you supposed, out of a wish to boast that I did not want to speak about myself. For what have I to boast of, I who became a chosen vessel of the devil? (34) I know, though, that if I begin to tell about myself, you will flee from me as from a snake, unable to bear hearing with your ears the unworthy things I have done. Yet I will speak and keep nothing silent, having first adjured you not to cease praying for me, so that I may find mercy in the hour of judgement." As the elder wept uncontrollably, the woman began her account of herself, speaking thus: 18. "Brother, my homeland was Egypt. While my parents were still living, when I was [?] years old, I rejected my love for them and went to Alexandria. How I first destroyed my virginity, and how insatiable and unrestrained my craving for intercourse was, I am ashamed even to think of. It is more decent to tell it now briefly, so that you may know my passion and my love of pleasure. For seventeen years and more, forgive me, I lived as a public kindling of licentiousness, and not for the sake of payment [?], I tell you the truth. For I did not take anything even from those who wanted to give. I contrived this so that I might draw more [?] men to me, doing for nothing what gave me pleasure [?]. And do not suppose that I refused payment because I was well off. I lived by begging [?],

and often by spinning flax tow. But I had an insatiable desire and an uncontrollable passion to wallow in the mire. This I counted as living [?]: to practise the outrage against nature continually. 19 [?]. While I was living this way, I saw one summer a great crowd of men, Libyans and Egyptians, running toward the sea. I asked someone who happened to be near me, 'Where are these men running to in such a hurry?' He answered, saying, 'They are all going up to Jerusalem for the Exaltation of the precious Cross, which is usually held in a few days.' I said to him, 'Will they take me with them, if I want to go along?' He said to me, 'If you have the fare and the money for expenses, no one will stop you.' I said to him, 'Brother, I really have neither fare nor expenses. But I will go too and board one of the boats they have hired, and they will feed me even if they do not want to. I have a body; they will take that instead of the fare.' The reason I wanted to go (Abba, forgive me) was to have plenty of lovers ready for my passion. I told you, Abba Zosimas, not to force me to tell you my shame. For the Lord knows I shudder at defiling both you and the air with my

…this. [?] the [?] assigned to bar my entrance. In this way some power suddenly [thrust me back], and once again I was standing in the forecourt. 23. After this had happened to me three or four times, I was worn out at last and no longer had the strength to push or be pushed, for my body had become [exhausted?] from the struggle. At last I thought it over, withdrew, and stood in a corner of the [?] of the church, and only with difficulty [?] did I come to realise the reason I was being prevented from seeing the life-giving wood. For the word of salvation touched the eyes of my heart and showed me that it was the filth of my deeds that barred the entrance to me. I began to weep and lament, to beat my breast, and to bring up groans from the depths of my heart. As I wept, I saw an icon of the all-holy Mother of God standing above the place where I stood. Gazing at it steadily, I said to her: 'Virgin Lady, who gave birth to God the Word according to the flesh, I know, I know that it is neither fitting nor reasonable that I, so filthy and so utterly debauched, should look upon your icon. You are ever-virgin and pure, and you keep body and soul clean and undefiled. For it is right that I, a debauched woman, should be hated and loathed by your purity. Yet I have heard that the God to whom you gave birth became man for this very reason, to call sinners to repentance. So help me, for I am alone and have no one to help me. Command that I too may be allowed to enter the church. Do not deprive me of seeing the wood on which God, your son, was nailed in the flesh, he who gave his own blood as a ransom for me. Command, O Lady, that the door to the divine veneration of the cross be opened to me too. I give you to the one born of you as my surety that I will never again outrage this flesh with shameful [defilement]. As soon as I have seen the wood of your Son's cross, I will renounce the world and everything in the world, and I will leave at once for wherever you yourself, the surety of my salvation, direct and lead me.' 24. When I had said this, I received a kind of assurance from the fervour of my faith and took courage from the compassion of the Mother of God. I left the place where I had stood to make my prayer, came back again, and mingled with those who were going in. No longer did anyone push me back or thrust me away, and no one stopped me from coming near the door through which they were entering the church. [?] Awe and astonishment [came over me], and I was shaken and trembled all over. Then I reached the door that until then had been shut against me, and every power that had hindered me before now opened the way for me to enter. So I entered without effort. So I came to be inside the holy places, and was counted worthy to see the life-giving cross. I saw the mysteries of God, and how ready he is to accept repentance. [?]

So I, the wretched one, threw myself on the ground and kissed that holy floor. Then I ran out, hurrying to her who had stood surety for me. I came to the place where the bond of that surety had been signed, knelt before the ever-virgin Mother of God, and spoke these words: 25. 'You, O Lady who love what is good, have shown your love for humankind [toward me]. You did not loathe the prayer of an unworthy woman. I have seen glory that we debauched people rightly never see. Glory to God, who through you accepts the repentance of sinners! What more could I, a sinner, think or say? Now, Lady, it is time for the terms of the surety you gave to be fulfilled. Now lead me wherever you command. Now be my teacher of salvation instead, and lead me by the hand onto the road that leads to repentance.' As I said this, I heard someone crying out from far away: 'If you cross the Jordan, you will find good rest.' When I heard this voice, I believed it had come for my sake, and I cried out in tears and called to the Mother of God: 'Lady, Lady, do not abandon me!' After crying this out, I left the courtyard of the church and set off quickly. 26. As I was going out, someone who saw me gave me three coins and said, 'Take these, mother.' I took what was given me, bought three loaves with it, and took them as a blessing for the journey. I asked the man selling the loaves, 'Sir, which road leads to the Jordan?' When I had learned which city gate led out in that direction, I went out [?], running, and kept to my journey in tears. Asking the way as I went [?], I walked the rest of the day; it was, I think, the third hour of the day when I saw the cross. At last, as the sun was sinking toward its setting, I reached the church of John the Baptist that lies near the Jordan. First I prayed in the church. Then I went straight down to the Jordan and washed my face and hands in that holy water. I received the immaculate and life-giving mysteries in the church of the Forerunner and ate half of one loaf. Then, [drinking] from the water of the Jordan, I lay down on the ground for the night. The next day I found a small boat there and crossed to the other side, and once more I asked my guide to lead me wherever she pleased. So I came into this desert, and from then until today I have gone far away as a fugitive. Here I live, waiting for my God, who saves from faint-heartedness and storm those who turn to him.' [?] And she said to him: 'Believe me, abba, for seventeen years I wandered in this desert [?]

…wrestling with my irrational desires as with wild beasts. Whenever I tried to eat, I longed for the meat and the fish that Egypt has. I longed to drink the wine I loved so much, for I drank a great deal of wine when I lived in the world. Here I had not even water to taste, so I burned terribly and could not bear the need. An unreasonable desire for lewd songs also came over me, constantly troubling me terribly and urging me to sing the songs of demons that I had learned. But I wept, beat my breast with my hand, and reminded myself of the [vows] I had made when I went out into the desert. In my thoughts I would go before the icon of the Mother of God, my sponsor, and weep before her, begging her to drive away the thoughts that were assailing my wretched soul. When I had wept enough and beaten my breast as hard as I could, I would see a light shining all around me, and calm came to me after the storm. [29.] And the thoughts that drove me back toward fornication, how shall I describe them to you, abba? A fire was kindled inside my wretched heart. It burned me through and through and stirred me to desire for intercourse. Whenever such a thought attacked me, I threw myself on the ground and soaked the earth with my tears. I imagined that she who had stood surety for me was standing before me as my protector, that I had broken my pledge, and that she was imposing punishment for the transgression. So I would not get up from my prostration on the ground, which sometimes lasted a whole night and day, until that sweet light shone around me and drove away the thoughts that were troubling me. From then on I lifted the eye of my mind to my surety constantly and without ceasing, asking for help for one in danger on the sea of the desert. And I had her as my helper and as my partner in repentance. In this way I passed the span of seventeen years, struggling with countless dangers. But from then until today my helper has stood by me in everything and has led me by the hand through it all.' 30. Zosimas said to her, 'Did you not need food or clothing?' She answered him, 'When I had used up those loaves, as I said before, I lived for seventeen years on herbs and whatever else could be found in the desert. The garment I had when I crossed the Jordan tore apart and wore out. I endured great hardship from the cold and again from the heat of summer. I was scorched by the burning heat and frozen stiff and shivering in the frost, so that often I fell to the ground and lay almost without breath or movement. I struggled with many, many misfortunes and with temptations that could not be overcome. But from then until now the power of God has preserved my sinful soul and my humble body in many ways. When I simply consider the evils he has rescued me from, I have food that never runs out: the hope of my salvation. For I am fed and clothed by the word of God, who holds all things together. For "man shall not live by bread alone", and those who have no covering "have clothed themselves with the rock", all who have stripped off the garment of sin.' 31. When Zosimas heard that she quoted passages of Scripture, from Moses, from Job and from the book of Psalms, he said to her, 'My lady, did you study the Psalms or other books?' When she heard this she smiled and said to the elder: 'Believe me, sir, I have not seen another human being since I crossed the Jordan, except your face today, nor any wild beast or [?]

[?] But she took hold of the elder and would not let him make a full prostration. She said to him: 'All these things you have heard, I adjure you by Christ, our Saviour and God, to tell no one until God releases me from the earth. For now go in peace. Next year you will see me again, and I will see you, kept by the grace of God. But for the Lord's sake, do what I now command you. During the holy fast of the coming year, do not cross the Jordan as you monks usually do.' Zosimas was astonished to hear that she even knew the rule of the monastery, and he said nothing but 'Glory to God, who gives great gifts to those who love him.' She said, 'Stay in the monastery, abba, as I said. Even if you want to go out, you will not be able to. On the holy evening of the Mystical Supper, put some of the life-giving body and blood of Christ in a sacred vessel worthy of such mysteries and bring it. Wait for me on the side of the Jordan that borders the inhabited world, so that I may come and receive the life-giving gifts. [?] I received them in the church of the Forerunner before I crossed the Jordan, and since then I have not had this sanctification until now. Now I long for it with a love I cannot resist. So I ask and implore you not to refuse my request. Be sure to bring me these life-giving and divine mysteries at the hour when the Lord made his disciples sharers in the divine Supper. And tell this to abba John, the superior of the monastery where you live: "Look to yourself and to your flock, for things are being done there that need correcting." But I do not want you to tell him this now. Tell him when the Lord allows you.' After she had said this, she told the elder, 'Pray for me,' and ran off [again] into the depths of the desert. Zosimas knelt down and kissed the ground where her footprints had stood, giving glory and thanks to God. Then he went back [rejoicing?] in soul and body, glorifying and blessing Christ our God. He crossed that desert again and reached the monastery on the day when the monks living there usually return. 33. And the [?]…

34. When the monks came back again and the evening of the Mystical Supper arrived, he did what she had told him. He took some of the immaculate body and precious blood of Christ our God in a small cup, and put a few dried figs and dates and a little lentils soaked in water into a small basket. Late in the evening he set out and sat on the bank of the Jordan, waiting for the holy woman to arrive. The holy woman was slow in coming, but Zosimas did not doze off. He kept gazing at the desert, waiting to see what he longed to see. As he sat there, the old man said to himself: 'Could it be that some unworthiness of mine has kept her from coming? Or did she come, not find me, and go back?' As he said this he wept, and as he wept he groaned. He lifted his eyes to heaven and pleaded with God, saying: 'Master, do not deprive me of seeing again what you once allowed me to see. Do not let me go away empty, carrying my sins to reproach me.' After praying this with tears, he [fell into] another thought: 'And if she does come, what will happen? There is no boat. How then will she cross the Jordan and come to me, unworthy as I am? Alas for my unworthiness! Alas for my wretchedness! Who has justly deprived me of such a blessing?' 35. While the old man was thinking this, the holy woman arrived and stood on the far bank of the river, the side she had come from. Zosimas jumped up, rejoicing, exulting and glorifying God. Yet he was still [troubled?] by the thought that she could not cross the Jordan. Then he saw her make the sign of the precious cross over the Jordan (for the night was moonlit, as he said). As soon as she had made the sign, she stepped onto the water and walked on the surface of the waters, coming toward him. [?] When he wanted to prostrate himself, she stopped him, calling out while still walking on the waters: 'What are you doing, abba? You are a priest and you are carrying the divine mysteries!' He obeyed her words. She came up out of the water and said to the elder: 'Bless, father, bless.' He answered her, amazed at the sight: 'Truly God does not lie, for he promised that those who purify themselves would become like God as far as possible. Glory to you, Christ our God, for you did not reject my prayer or withhold your mercy from your servant. Glory to you, Christ our God, for through this servant of yours you have shown me how far I fall short of the measure of perfection.' When he had said this, the woman asked him to recite the holy Creed of the faith and to begin the 'Our Father, who art in heaven'. When this was done and the prayer had come to an end, she gave the elder the kiss of love on the mouth, as was the custom. Then she received the life-giving mysteries, raised her hands to heaven, groaned with tears, and cried out: 'Now, Master, you are letting your servant go in peace, according to your word, for my eyes have seen your salvation.' 36. Then she said to the elder: 'Forgive me, abba, and grant another wish of mine. Go back now to the monastery, guarded by the grace of God. Next year come [?] to the place where I first met you. Be sure to come, for the Lord's sake, and you will see me again as the Lord wills.' He answered her, 'If only it were possible to follow you from here and see your precious face always! But grant an old man one request, and take a little of the food I have brought here.' As he said this, he showed her the basket he had with him. She touched the lentils with her fingertips, picked up three grains and put them in her mouth. She said that the grace of the Spirit was enough to keep the substance of the soul undefiled. When she had said this, she spoke again to the elder: [?]

…greeting him only by its movements and its intent. Zosimas said to the lion: 'Beast, the Great One has instructed that her remains be buried. But I am old and do not have the strength to dig a grave, for I have no digging tool fit for the job, and I cannot go back so far to fetch a suitable tool. [So you] do the work with your claws, so that we may give the holy woman's mortal tent back to the earth.' At once, at his word, it dug with its front paws a pit large enough to bury the body. Once again the old man washed the holy woman's feet with his tears and earnestly begged her to pray now [all the more] for everyone. Then, with the lion standing by, he covered the body with earth. The body was naked, as it had been before, with nothing but that torn cloak which Zosimas had thrown to her and with which Mary, turning her back, had covered parts of her body. Then both went away. The lion withdrew into the inner desert like a lamb, and Zosimas returned, blessing and praising Christ our God. When he got back to the monastery, he told the monks everything. He told them all of it from the beginning, in detail, so that everyone who heard was amazed at the mighty works of God. With fear and longing they [celebrated?] the memory of the blessed woman. And John the superior found some in the monastery who needed correcting, so that even in this the holy woman's words were not idle or useless. Zosimas died in that monastery at nearly a hundred years of age.

[?] The monks went on teaching these things from one generation to the next without writing them down, holding them up as an example of [benefit] for anyone who wanted to hear. But no one has heard of anyone handing this story down in writing until today. What I [received by hearing?] I have now made known in a written narrative. Perhaps others have also written the life of the holy woman, and certainly in a grander style than mine, but nothing of the kind has yet come to my knowledge. All the same, I too have written this narrative as best I could, wishing to add nothing to the truth. May God, who richly rewards those who take refuge in him, grant the reward for the benefit of those who read this narrative to the one who ordered this account to be handed down in writing. May he count him worthy of the portion and rank of this blessed Mary, whom the narrative is about, together with all who from the beginning of time have pleased him through contemplation and action. Let us also give glory to God, the King of all the ages, that he may count us too worthy of mercy on the day of judgement, in Christ Jesus our Lord. To him belong all glory, honour and worship, always, together with the Father who has no beginning and the all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen. [?] is called the Ennaton ('Ninth') of Alexandria, because [?]: 'We took my lord Sophronius and went away to the laura of the Eighteenth [Mile] at Alexandria' (ηὶ). [?] c. 162: 'Twenty miles from Alexandria there is a laura called that of the Calamon [?]' [?] the Cilician, that 'When we were living at the Ennaton of Alexandria' [?] 'we, at Alexandria, at the Ennaton.' Whose [?]: 'At the Ennaton, in the monastery of Tougora, abba Menas, the superior of the monastery, told us about Eulogius of blessed memory [?].' And in the following chapter: 'Abba [?] also told us this' [?] (ιι) 2. His synaxis is held in his venerable church of the Apostles, which is at the Hebdomon. [?] translated: 'On the island of Samos the God-loving Mary, a lover of the poor, mother of the lord [?], told us…'
